questions.stem: Six weeks into a plant automation project, the operations director tells you the point of the work is to cut headcount, the plant manager tells you it is to reduce defects, and the finance sponsor tells you it is to defer a capital purchase. All three signed the charter. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Bring the three of them together to agree a single statement of what success looks like, and record where they had been differing.
options.rationale: The gap is between people, not in a document, so it closes in a room. Capturing the divergence matters as much as the agreement: it is what stops the same three views resurfacing at the first hard trade-off.

options.text: Re-read the charter with all three, then remind them of the objective it already records and ask them to work to it from now on.
options.rationale: The charter clearly did not create a shared understanding, or three signatories would not be describing three different projects. Walking them back through the document and asking for compliance treats the symptom and leaves the disagreement in place.

options.text: Ask the finance sponsor, as the funder, to rule on which of the three objectives takes priority, then brief the other two on the ruling.
options.rationale: It produces a decision quickly and buys none of the alignment. Briefing the other two on a ruling informs them without converting them, and the first time the project has to choose between defects and headcount the argument restarts.

options.text: Build a benefits map showing how all three objectives can be met by the same delivery, then circulate it to all three of them for comment.
options.rationale: Assuming the three are compatible is the thing that has not been tested. Cutting headcount and cutting defects can pull in opposite directions, and a map drawn and circulated before that is checked papers over the conflict and invites three sets of comments instead of one answer.

questions.explanation: A charter that three people read three ways has not done its job. The work is to converge them on one articulation of purpose, in a session where the differences surface and are resolved rather than averaged. Naming the divergence in the record is what makes the alignment durable, because the next trade-off will test exactly the seam that has just been closed.
questions.mindset: Signatures on a charter record that people agreed to a document, not that they agree on what the project is for.

questions.stem: Four sprints in, an agile team is delivering steadily but the product owner notices the team is building whatever sits at the top of the backlog without ever asking why. In the last review, nobody on the team could say who the product is for. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Add the product vision as a standing item at the start of every sprint planning session, so that the team hears it before choosing work.
options.rationale: Reading the vision aloud at a ceremony makes it a ritual rather than a tool. Teams stop hearing a statement repeated on a schedule, however close to the choice of work it is placed, and this one has already failed to land once.

options.text: Run a session where the team meets real users, then have the team draft the product vision themselves.
options.rationale: Contact with the people who use the thing is what makes purpose concrete, and drafting the statement themselves is what makes it theirs. Both are needed: exposure without ownership fades, ownership without exposure invents.

options.text: Ask the product owner to write more detailed acceptance criteria, so that the team understands each item's purpose before starting it.
options.rationale: More detail per story makes the team better at building the right thing item by item, and does nothing about their inability to see the whole or say who it is for. It also pushes them further into order-taking.

options.text: Raise it as an impediment in the retrospective and let the team decide how to fix it.
options.rationale: Reasonable, and it is where the conversation might start, but a team that cannot say who the product is for is poorly placed to design its own cure. This defers the problem to the people who have it.

questions.explanation: Shared purpose is built by exposure and ownership together. Putting the team in front of users replaces an abstraction with faces and problems, and having the team write the vision statement themselves converts that into something they will actually use when they are deciding how to build the next thing. A vision recited by someone else is a slogan; one the team wrote is a decision aid.
questions.mindset: Purpose sticks when a team has met the people it serves and has put the vision into its own words.

questions.stem: A hybrid programme delivers a customer portal through two vendors: one runs iteratively on the front end, the other delivers back-end services to a fixed plan. Each vendor's team is clear on its own goals, but integration testing keeps surfacing features neither side thinks it owns. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Hold a joint session where both vendors work from one statement of what the portal must do for the customer, and map the seams between them against it.
options.rationale: The gaps appear because each vendor optimises against its own scope rather than the outcome. One outcome statement, worked jointly, is what makes the seams visible before integration finds them.

options.text: Have the two vendor leads write a RACI covering every integration point, and review it after each integration test so ownership of every gap is unambiguous.
options.rationale: A responsibility matrix settles who does the work once the work is known. The problem here is that features are being discovered late, so the matrix would be written against a list that keeps changing, and reviewing it after each test only assigns gaps that integration has already found.

options.text: Move the back-end vendor onto the same iterative cadence through a contract variation, so that both teams plan their work together from now on.
options.rationale: Aligning cadence is often useful, but a contract variation is a large contractual and operational change aimed at a problem of shared understanding. Two teams on the same cadence can still work to two different pictures of the goal.

options.text: Add an integration workstream with its own manager and test budget to own everything that falls between the vendors until go-live.
options.rationale: Creating an owner for the gaps, however well resourced, institutionalises them. It also gives both vendors a reason to define their scope more narrowly, because someone else is now catching what they drop.

questions.explanation: Two teams each clear on their own goals and unclear on the shared one will always produce orphaned work at the seam. The fix is a single articulation of the outcome that both are accountable to, built jointly so that each can see where its work meets the other's. Structural answers like a RACI or an integration team are useful afterwards; used first they organise a misunderstanding rather than resolving it.
questions.mindset: Teams that each own a piece need one outcome they all answer to, or the gaps between them belong to nobody.

questions.stem: Match each situation to the conflict-handling approach that fits it best. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: A production outage is live, two engineers disagree on the rollback path, and every minute of debate costs money.
Two team members disagree about a coding standard that neither feels strongly about, and a decision is needed before the sprint ends.
A designer and a developer disagree about an interaction pattern, both have good evidence, and the answer will shape the next six months of the product.

options.text: Direct the decision
options.rationale: Asserting a decision is the right tool when the cost of delay is high and someone has the standing to carry it. It spends goodwill, which is why it is reserved for exactly this kind of moment.

options.text: Find a middle position
options.rationale: When neither party is invested and the decision is reversible, a quick split-the-difference is proportionate. Nobody gets everything, everybody gets on, and the sprint closes.

options.text: Work it through to a solution both own
options.rationale: Two well-evidenced positions on a decision with a long shadow is the case that repays the time collaboration costs. It is the only approach that reliably produces an answer better than either starting position.

options.text: Withdraw from it
options.rationale: Not used. Withdrawing suits a disagreement that is trivial or that will resolve itself, and none of the three above will go away on its own.

options.text: Emphasise where they agree
options.rationale: Not used. Smoothing buys calm and defers the decision, which helps when relationships need protecting more than the issue needs settling. All three situations here need the issue settled.

questions.explanation: The mode follows the stakes and the clock rather than a preference for being collaborative. High urgency with a clear decision-maker points to directing; low stakes and low investment point to a quick compromise; high stakes with two credible positions is the case where collaboration earns back the time it costs. The two unused options both trade resolution for peace, which is why neither fits a situation that has to be decided.
questions.mindset: Choose the conflict mode from the stakes and the clock, not from the style you are most comfortable with.

questions.stem: In a matrix organisation, a functional manager has twice reassigned your lead analyst mid-sprint without telling you, and the analyst is caught between you. You have raised it with the manager once, politely, and it happened again. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor with a record of both reassignments, and ask for the analyst to be formally assigned full time to the project.
options.rationale: This is the premature-escalation error. The record makes the case better evidenced, but going over the manager's head after one polite conversation spends a relationship you still need, and it asks for a resourcing change when the unresolved problem is an agreement about notice.

options.text: Meet the functional manager, set out the delivery impact of the two reassignments, and agree in writing how competing demands will be handled in future.
options.rationale: A second attempt with evidence and a concrete ask is the proportionate next step. Writing the agreement down is what distinguishes it from the first conversation, which was polite and produced nothing.

options.text: Agree with the analyst that she will tell you as soon as she is approached for other work, so that you can adjust the sprint plan before the reassignment takes effect.
options.rationale: This is the make-the-analyst-the-messenger error. It improves your visibility and leaves the analyst carrying the conflict between two managers. Making the person with the least authority responsible for policing the arrangement is the least fair available option.

options.text: Re-plan the remaining work so the analyst is off the critical path, then confirm the revised plan with the team so that a further reassignment cannot stall delivery.
options.rationale: This is the design-around-it error. It is sometimes pragmatic, but here it accepts that a lead analyst can be pulled at will without notice and quietly reduces what the project can attempt, while the agreement with the functional manager is never tried.

questions.explanation: Conflict is worked at the lowest level that can resolve it, and escalation is what happens after a genuine attempt has failed, not after a polite one. The second conversation differs from the first by bringing evidence of impact and asking for something specific and recorded. If that fails too, the escalation is then well founded and the record of the attempt is what makes it land.
questions.mindset: Make the second attempt different from the first, with evidence and a recorded ask, before going over anyone's head.

questions.stem: Two technical leads on your programme have been arguing for a month about whether to build a shared service or let each stream build its own. Both have written papers. The team has started routing around them, making local decisions to avoid asking. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask both leads to present to an architecture board, and have the board decide.
options.rationale: The decision has a legitimate owner outside the two of them, and a month of stalemate is evidence they will not converge. Sending it to the body that owns architectural standards resolves it without either lead losing to the other.

options.text: Choose the shared service, since duplication across streams is the more expensive failure mode.
options.rationale: The project manager taking a technical decision away from two technical leads settles this argument and teaches the team that persistence in disagreement gets the decision taken elsewhere. It is also a judgement you are less qualified to make.

options.text: Run a facilitated session and keep both leads in the room until they reach an agreed position.
options.rationale: Collaboration is the right instinct and it has already had a month. Repeating it without changing anything about the process usually produces a third paper rather than a decision.

options.text: Timebox a spike to build both, and let the evidence decide.
options.rationale: Evidence is attractive here, but building both costs real capacity, and the disagreement is about long-term coupling rather than something a short spike would demonstrate. It also delays the decision the team is already routing around.

questions.explanation: The signal that matters is the team routing around the disagreement: the cost has moved from the two leads to everyone else, so the priority is now a decision rather than a consensus. When the parties have genuinely tried and stalled, escalation to the body that legitimately owns the decision is the resolution, not a failure of it. What the project manager owns is recognising the stalemate and routing it, not adjudicating the architecture.
questions.mindset: When the people disagreeing have genuinely stalled, route the decision to its legitimate owner rather than taking it yourself.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence with the leadership response that fits. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: A newly formed team is willing but has never used the technology and keeps stalling on basic decisions. The leader should mostly
A long-standing team knows the domain better than the leader does and is frustrated by being checked on. The leader should mostly

options.text: give clear direction and close guidance
options.rationale: Competence is low and commitment is high, so what the team lacks is know-how rather than motivation. Direction here is support, not control, and it is withdrawn as capability grows.

options.text: delegate and stay available
options.rationale: High competence with the willingness dented by over-supervision calls for handing over the decisions and being reachable. Continued checking on a capable team is the thing causing the frustration.

options.text: explain the reasoning behind each decision
options.rationale: Not used. Coaching fits a team gaining skill but wobbling in confidence, where the value is in the reasoning rather than the instruction. Neither sentence describes that.

options.text: encourage and share the decision-making
options.rationale: Not used. A supporting style suits a capable team whose confidence is low, where the leader's job is mostly reassurance. The second team is capable and confident, and merely wants to be left to it.

questions.explanation: Situational leadership varies the style by what the team currently has rather than by what the leader prefers. Low skill with high willingness takes direction; high skill with dented willingness takes delegation and availability. The two unused styles sit between those poles, and picking one of them by default is the common error: a leader who coaches everybody is under-serving the new team and irritating the experienced one.
questions.mindset: Match the style to what the team currently lacks, not to the style you are most comfortable using.

questions.stem: During a daily standup, a developer mentions for the third day running that they are still waiting on a test environment from another department. Two of the sprint's six stories depend on it and the sprint ends in five working days. The team has stopped mentioning it. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Take the blocker away from the team and pursue the other department's manager yourself until it is cleared.
options.rationale: Clearing impediments that sit outside the team's reach is the core of the role. Three days of repetition and a team that has stopped raising it are both signs that it will not clear on its own.

options.text: Ask the developer to work on something else from the sprint backlog until the environment arrives.
options.rationale: It keeps the person busy and leaves the blocker untouched. Work that is started to fill a gap tends to end the sprint half done, and the environment is still missing tomorrow.

options.text: Add the environment as a risk to the register and review it at the next risk meeting.
options.rationale: This is no longer a risk. It has happened and is costing the team days, so recording it as something that might occur is the wrong instrument and the wrong tempo.

options.text: Ask the developer to escalate directly to the other department's manager.
options.rationale: Asking a team member to negotiate across a department boundary puts them in a position they usually have no standing in, and it is the part of the job the project manager is best placed to do.

questions.explanation: An impediment raised three times and then dropped has been absorbed by the team as normal, which is exactly when it costs the most. Removing obstacles that live outside the team's authority is the project manager's work, and doing it visibly is also what teaches the team that raising a blocker is worth the breath. The register and the backlog are both ways of recording the problem rather than solving it.
questions.mindset: The impediment a team has stopped mentioning is the one that most needs the leader's attention.

questions.stem: You take over a project mid-execution. Within a week you notice that meeting attendance is optional in practice, decisions get reopened, and nobody can tell you who signs off a deliverable. The previous project manager left no team charter. What should you do first?

options.text: Issue a set of ground rules covering attendance, decision-making and sign-off, effective immediately, and explain the reason for each one.
options.rationale: Rules arriving from a new manager in week one get complied with and not owned, and explaining the reasons does not change who wrote them. The team also has context you do not yet have about why the current habits formed.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to clarify the governance and decision rights for the project, then brief the team on them and record them in the management plan.
options.rationale: Sign-off authority may need confirming from above, but attendance and reopened decisions are team norms rather than governance. Routing all three upward and writing the answer into the plan makes the team a spectator in its own working agreement.

options.text: Work with the team to agree how they will operate, and write down what they agree, including who decides what.
options.rationale: A team charter written with the team is the artifact that fixes exactly these three symptoms, and involving them is what makes it stick. It is also fast: this is a session, not a phase.

options.text: Observe for another two sprints before intervening, so that you understand the causes.
options.rationale: Some patience is wise on arrival, but decisions being reopened is actively costing the project now, and a new manager has a short window in which changing how the team works is expected.

questions.explanation: Undefined norms are what produce optional attendance and reopened decisions, and the remedy is an explicit working agreement rather than a directive. Building it with the team converts a set of imposed rules into commitments they made, which is the difference between a charter that is followed and one that is filed. A new project manager also has a natural licence to run that session, and it closes quickly.
questions.mindset: Norms a team has agreed for itself are kept; norms handed to it are merely obeyed.

questions.stem: Your sprint reviews are attended by the product owner and nobody else. Three business units will use the product at launch, and their managers have all declined the invitation more than once, saying they will review it when it is finished. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Find out from each manager what would make attending worth their time, and change the review to match.
options.rationale: Repeated declines are information rather than rudeness. The invitation is not paying for the hour it asks for, and the only people who can say what would are the ones declining.

options.text: Take working software to each business unit in their own setting, on their own schedule.
options.rationale: If the stakeholders will not come to the demonstration, the demonstration goes to them. Feedback from real users before launch is the thing being protected, and the ceremony is only one way of getting it.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to make attendance at sprint reviews mandatory for the three managers.
options.rationale: Mandated attendance fills seats and rarely produces engagement. It also converts a relationship you need at launch into an obligation someone imposed on them.

options.text: Record the reviews and send the video, so the managers can watch when convenient.
options.rationale: A recording is a broadcast. It removes the one thing a review is for, which is the conversation that happens when the people who will use the thing react to it in front of the team.

options.text: Note in the risk register that late business feedback may cause rework, and continue as you are.
options.rationale: Recording a risk you have the means to reduce is a way of documenting a decision not to act. The exposure is real, but the register is not the response.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder engagement is tailored to the stakeholder rather than run as a standing invitation everyone is expected to accept. Two moves follow: find out what would make the session valuable to them, and if the format is the obstacle, take the product to where they are. Compulsion and recordings both preserve the ceremony at the cost of the thing the ceremony exists to produce.
questions.mindset: Tailor engagement to what each stakeholder will actually value, rather than repeating an invitation they have already declined.

questions.stem: You have identified twenty-eight stakeholders on a regulatory reporting project with a filing deadline in nine months, spread across finance, compliance, IT and two external audit firms. Your sponsor asks why you are spending time classifying them rather than starting the requirements workshops. What is the best explanation of the value of the analysis?

options.text: It produces the stakeholder register, which is a required project artifact that the project office checks at each stage review.
options.rationale: Answering that an artifact is required, or that the project office will look for it, is the weakest defence available, and it invites the reply that the artifact can be written afterwards. It also does not say what the analysis is for.

options.text: It shows which stakeholders have the power and interest to affect the outcome, so engagement effort goes where it changes something.
options.rationale: Classification exists to allocate a finite amount of attention. Knowing who can stop the project and who merely wants to be told is what makes the difference between an engagement plan and a mailing list.

options.text: It identifies who must formally approve the requirements before the filing deadline, which prevents rework later.
options.rationale: Approval authority is one output and a narrow one. Plenty of stakeholders who approve nothing can still sink a regulatory project, and the analysis is what surfaces them; avoiding rework from late approvers is a by-product, not the purpose.

options.text: It ensures all twenty-eight are invited to the requirements workshops, so that no requirement held by a less visible stakeholder is missed.
options.rationale: Inviting everyone to everything is the outcome analysis is meant to prevent. Twenty-eight people in a requirements workshop produces a worse result than the right six, and less visible stakeholders are better reached through tailored engagement than through a crowded room.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder analysis is a rationing tool. Attention is the scarce resource on any project, and classifying by influence and interest is how it gets pointed at the people whose position will actually move the outcome. The register and the approval list fall out of that work, but treating either as the purpose leads to a document that is complete and an engagement plan that is undifferentiated.
questions.mindset: Spend stakeholder attention where it will change the outcome, because there is never enough of it for everyone.

questions.stem: A senior operations manager with no formal authority over your project has begun criticising it in forums you are not invited to. Your delivery depends on her team's cooperation in three months. She has declined two meeting requests. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the sponsor to speak to her peer group first and correct the criticism before you request another meeting.
options.rationale: Countering criticism through hierarchy answers the noise and hardens the position, and a meeting requested after her peers have been briefed against her reads as a summons. It also tells her that the way to be engaged with is to be complained about upward.

options.text: Document the resistance in the risk register and build a contingency plan that avoids depending on her team.
options.rationale: Sensible to think about, but the dependency is real in three months and engineering around a senior operations function is rarely available. It also concedes the relationship.

options.text: Send her the project documentation and a summary of the benefits first, so that any misunderstanding is corrected.
options.rationale: This assumes the objection is an information gap. Someone criticising in private forums usually has a substantive concern about impact on her operation, which more documentation will not touch, and a benefits pack sent to a critic reads as a sales approach rather than an enquiry.

options.text: Find out through people she trusts what her objection actually is, then address that before asking to meet again.
options.rationale: Two declined meetings mean a third invitation will not land either. Understanding the substance first is what turns the next approach into something worth her time rather than a repeat.

questions.explanation: Resistance from someone with informal influence is handled by understanding it, not by out-communicating it. Declined meetings mean the direct route is closed for now, so the work goes through the network she does trust to find out what the actual objection is. Escalating or broadcasting benefits both treat her as an obstacle to be overcome, which is what turns a concern into an opposition.
questions.mindset: Understand what a resistant stakeholder actually objects to before trying to change their mind.

questions.stem: Your sponsor has told the board the new system will go live in March. Your schedule, which the sponsor approved, shows a June go-live with a March pilot. You discover the discrepancy when a board member congratulates you on the March launch. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Correct the board member politely on the spot, since an inaccurate expectation at board level grows each time it is repeated.
options.rationale: Correcting the sponsor's message publicly and without warning damages the relationship you need to fix it, however politely it is done. The board member is not the person who created the gap, and you do not yet know whether March was an error or a commitment the sponsor made deliberately.

options.text: Go to the sponsor, establish whether March was a misstatement or a commitment made on your behalf, and agree who corrects it.
options.rationale: The gap could be an error, a deliberate stretch, or the pilot being described as the launch. Which it is changes the response entirely, and the sponsor is the only source for that.

options.text: Model a March go-live, identifying what would have to be descoped or added in resource to make it, before raising the discrepancy with the sponsor.
options.rationale: It moves quickly to a solution for a problem you have not yet diagnosed. If March was misspoken, or the pilot was being described as the launch, the re-planning is a serious amount of work aimed at nothing, and arriving with it signals that you already accept March as the target.

options.text: Send the board a written schedule summary showing the pilot and go-live dates clearly, copying the sponsor in.
options.rationale: Copying the sponsor does not stop this being a correction that goes around them: it is a public contradiction with a document attached. It also assumes the board's problem is that they were not shown the dates, when the sponsor may have reasons for March you have not yet heard.

questions.explanation: A mismatch between what a sponsor has said and what the plan holds is diagnosed before it is corrected, because the three plausible causes need three different responses. The conversation is with the sponsor, promptly and privately, and it ends with agreement about who corrects the record. Fixing it around them, in public or on paper, costs the working relationship that any correction will need.
questions.mindset: Find out why a sponsor's statement differs from the plan before deciding how, and by whom, it is corrected.

questions.stem: A sponsor new to iterative delivery has asked for a fixed scope, fixed date and fixed budget commitment for a twelve-month product build, and is frustrated that the team will only commit to the next quarter in detail. What is the most constructive response?

options.text: Establish what the sponsor actually needs the commitment for, then offer the strongest commitment that fits it — a fixed date and budget, with scope prioritised and reviewed each quarter.
options.rationale: The request is usually a proxy for a real need such as a board sign-off or a marketing window. Meeting that need with what can honestly be fixed is more useful than either refusing or pretending.

options.text: Explain, before the next planning session, why fixing scope, date and budget together is not possible in an agile delivery, and that scope must therefore be the variable the team manages.
options.rationale: It is true and it lands as a lecture about method to someone asking about risk, and holding it before planning only moves the lecture earlier. It also offers nothing in place of the certainty they were looking for, because it never asks what that certainty is needed for.

options.text: Produce the twelve-month plan they asked for, committing the first quarter in detail and marking the later quarters as indicative until each is planned at its quarterly review.
options.rationale: A plan labelled indicative is read as a plan, whatever the label says about the later quarters. It buys short-term peace and sets up a much worse conversation in month seven, when the indicative dates are quoted back as commitments.

options.text: Invite the sponsor to the next three sprint reviews so they can see the delivery rate for themselves, and offer a firmer long-range forecast once that velocity data exists.
options.rationale: Valuable over time and far too slow for a commitment being asked for now: a forecast promised after three sprints leaves the sponsor with nothing to take to whoever is asking them. It also answers a question about predictability with an invitation to watch, without asking what the commitment is for.

questions.explanation: A demand for total certainty is nearly always a proxy for a specific obligation the sponsor has to someone else. Finding out what that is turns an argument about method into a solvable problem, and usually two of the three variables can genuinely be fixed. Offering the strongest honest commitment beats both a refusal on principle and a plan whose later half everyone privately knows is fiction.
questions.mindset: Ask what a demand for certainty is protecting before deciding what can honestly be promised.

questions.stem: Halfway through a customer-facing implementation, the client's business has been reorganised and their new operations lead wants a different reporting model from the one specified. The contract fixes the specification. The relationship matters more to your organisation than this project's margin. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Deliver the specified reporting model, since the contract fixes it, and offer the new model to the operations lead as a separately priced follow-on engagement once this one closes.
options.rationale: Contractually clean and commercially short-sighted. Pricing the new model as a follow-on still means handing over something the client has already said does not fit their new organisation, which produces a delivery nobody uses while the relationship waits for a second contract.

options.text: Assess what the change would cost in schedule and effort, put the options and their consequences to both sponsors, and let them decide.
options.rationale: The decision is commercial and belongs to the people who own the relationship and the margin. The project manager's job is to make it an informed decision rather than to make it.

options.text: Absorb the change within the current scope and re-plan the remaining work around it, since preserving the relationship is the stated priority and the margin is secondary.
options.rationale: Quietly absorbing scope teaches the client that changes are free and hides a real cost from your own organisation, however tidily the remaining work is re-planned. Prioritising the relationship over margin is a decision someone accountable should make explicitly, not one the project manager makes by giving work away.

options.text: Raise a change request for the new reporting model, with its cost and schedule impact, and proceed once the client signs it.
options.rationale: Right instrument, incomplete answer. A costed change request the client signs still skips the decision that actually matters here, because your own leadership never gets to weigh the relationship against the margin before the work is committed.

questions.explanation: Shifting customer expectations are neither refused nor absorbed. They are quantified and put to the people who own the trade-off, with the commercial and relationship consequences stated. What makes this case sharper than a routine change is that the priority stated is relationship over margin, and a priority like that is exercised by sponsors making an explicit choice, not by a project manager giving work away.
questions.mindset: Put a shifting customer need to the people who own the trade-off, rather than refusing it or quietly giving it away.

questions.stem: At a sprint review for an expenses tool, the customer representative says the new receipt-matching feature works exactly as specified but is not what her finance team needs in practice. The product owner points out that the acceptance criteria were signed off. Planning for the next sprint is tomorrow morning. What should happen next?

options.text: Treat the feature as accepted, since it met the agreed criteria, and log the new need as a separate request for the product owner to pick up at a later refinement session.
options.rationale: Technically correct and it wastes what just happened. The review has produced exactly the information iterative delivery exists to surface, and filing it for a later session loses the moment when the person who can explain the need is in the room.

options.text: Explore what the customer needs in practice, and let the product owner decide where that sits in the backlog against everything else.
options.rationale: The gap between specified and useful is the normal output of a review, not a failure of sign-off. Understanding it and letting the product owner prioritise is the mechanism working as designed.

options.text: Rework the feature in the next sprint, since delivering something the customer cannot use is not done, and have the representative review the reworked version before it is accepted.
options.rationale: Jumping straight to rework skips the prioritisation, however carefully the rework is reviewed. The new need may be worth less than what else is in the backlog, and that judgement is the product owner's to make before the next sprint is committed.

options.text: Review with the team why the acceptance criteria missed the real need, and tighten the criteria process for the next feature.
options.rationale: Worth a retrospective conversation, and it is a process improvement rather than a response to the customer standing in front of you. It also assumes better criteria would have caught something only use of the working feature revealed, and leaves the need she has just described unexplored.

questions.explanation: Signed-off criteria being met while the need is unmet is the ordinary result of specifying ahead of use, and iterative reviews exist to find it early. The response is to understand the real need and hand it to the product owner to weigh against everything else competing for the next sprint. Both closing it out as accepted and committing to immediate rework skip the prioritisation that makes the feedback useful.
questions.mindset: Treat a gap between what was specified and what is useful as information to prioritise, not a failure to assign.

questions.stem: Your organisation runs a lessons-learned workshop at the end of every project and files the output in a shared drive. Reviewing three years of these, you find the same five problems recurring on project after project. What is the most useful change to make?

options.text: Build the recurring lessons into planning: checklists, estimating assumptions and risk templates that new projects start from.
options.rationale: A lesson only transfers when it changes what the next project does by default. Embedding them in the artifacts people actually use at planning is what closes the loop.

options.text: Redesign the workshop with a trained facilitator and root-cause prompts, so each lesson is captured precisely and with its underlying cause.
options.rationale: This is the improve-capture error. The lessons are already being captured well enough to be recognised three years later, so a better-run workshop polishes the part of the process that is working and leaves untouched the point where the lessons stop travelling.

options.text: Move lesson capture from the end of the project to the end of each phase, so it happens while memory is fresh and the detail is still intact.
options.rationale: This is the capture-timing error. It is a genuine improvement to capture quality, and it still leaves the lessons in the same drive being read by nobody at the moment a new project is being planned.

options.text: Require project managers to review the lessons repository during planning and record in the plan which of the lessons they have applied.
options.rationale: This is the mandate-the-reading error. Required review produces a recorded entry and a skim, and it leaves the burden of finding the relevant lesson in three years of files on each new project manager rather than on the organisation that owns the recurring pattern.

questions.explanation: Knowledge transfer fails at the point of reuse far more often than at the point of capture, and a repository nobody consults at the right moment is a filing system rather than an asset. Recurring lessons are converted into defaults: the checklist, the estimating assumption, the standing risk. That way the next project inherits the learning without anyone having to remember to go and look for it.
questions.mindset: A lesson has transferred only when the next project inherits it by default, without anyone having to go and look for it.

questions.stem: Your hybrid programme is rebuilding a regional courier's parcel-sorting software: hardware changes follow a fixed plan and the software is built in two-week sprints. The lead developer returns next Monday from six months' parental leave. Before she left, the plan named her lead for the routing phase, which starts on her first day back. While she was away a colleague covered the role, and the team changed its message format and dropped one of her design choices after a failed load test. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep the colleague who covered for her as routing lead for her first two weeks back, with her working alongside on the code and taking over once she has seen the changes in use.
options.rationale: Six months is long enough for an expert's knowledge to be partly out of date without her knowing which parts. Working beside the person who made the changes surfaces them in context, including why her design was dropped, before she holds the authority to reverse it.

options.text: Send her the decision log and the sprint review notes from the past six months before Monday, so she can read up on the changes and lead as planned from her first day.
options.rationale: This is the read-it-up error. The log records what changed, not which of her assumptions it overturned, and she would be leading from her first day on knowledge she has only read, including the design choice the load test ruled out.

options.text: Let her take the lead as planned on her first day, since she designed the original routing approach, and keep the covering colleague on hand to answer her questions.
options.rationale: This is the trust-the-expert error. Her original knowledge is exactly what is now partly out of date, and relying on her questions assumes she knows which parts have expired, which is the one thing a returner cannot yet see.

options.text: Hold a half-day briefing on her first morning in which the colleague and the team walk her through every change made in her absence, then hand her the lead.
options.rationale: This is the one-off-briefing error. A morning of explanation gives familiarity with the changes rather than working knowledge of them, and the reasons behind a failed load test land far better in the code than on a slide, so she still leads on a partial picture.

questions.explanation: A returning team member is a knowledge-transfer case in reverse: what they knew was right when they left, and some of it has quietly stopped being right. The risk is less ignorance than confident action on stale knowledge, so the transfer needs a short period of working alongside whoever holds the current picture before authority passes back. Reading the record, a single briefing or relying on the returner's questions all assume she can already tell which parts of her knowledge have expired.
questions.mindset: Treat a returning expert's knowledge as partly expired until the changes have been seen in use.

questions.stem: Your weekly project report goes to forty-one people. You learn that the steering group reads only the first paragraph, the delivery teams do not read it at all, and two regulators' representatives on the list need detail nobody else wants. Which two changes should the project manager make?

options.text: Segment the communication: a short decision-focused summary for the steering group, and a separate detailed pack for the regulatory readers.
options.rationale: Different audiences need different content at different depths, and one document that serves all of them serves none well. Segmenting is the standard fix and it is cheap.

options.text: Find out what the delivery teams actually need to know and deliver it in the channel they already use.
options.rationale: A group that reads nothing is telling you the channel is wrong, not that they need no information. Meeting them where they already look is what converts a broadcast into communication.

options.text: Reduce the distribution list to the people who demonstrably read the report, and offer everyone removed a monthly summary on request.
options.rationale: It tidies the list and drops people who need information but are not being served by this format. An on-request summary leaves the delivery teams, who have already shown they will not go looking, to ask for something they do not know exists; the regulators would survive the cut, the delivery teams would be quietly cut off.

options.text: Put the full report on a shared site and send everyone a link each week, so each reader takes what they need when they need it.
options.rationale: Pull communication shifts the effort of finding the relevant part onto every reader. A weekly link is still one undifferentiated document, and the steering group that reads one paragraph will read no paragraphs behind a link.

options.text: Add a decision-focused summary paragraph at the top of the existing report, so the steering group's needs are met first and the detail stays available below it.
options.rationale: A partial improvement that leaves the same document trying to serve three audiences. It helps the group already being served best, leaves the regulators digging through the same report for their detail, and does nothing for the delivery teams who do not open it.

questions.explanation: Communication is planned by audience and need rather than by document. Three audiences with three different requirements point to segmented content pitched at the depth each one needs, and to using the channels people already have open rather than the one that is convenient to produce. Trimming the list or bolting a summary onto the front both preserve the single-artifact habit that caused the problem.
questions.mindset: Plan communication around each audience's need and habits, not around the document that is easiest to produce.

questions.stem: You have just confirmed that a critical supplier will miss a milestone, which will delay your project by around a month. Your sponsor is presenting to the board in two days and has not been told. Analysis of options will take a week. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Tell the sponsor now, with what is known and what is not about the delay, and say when the options will be ready.
options.rationale: A sponsor going into a board meeting needs to know what they do not know. Reporting a confirmed fact with the analysis still open is honest and gives them two days rather than none.

options.text: Complete the options analysis first, so the sponsor receives the problem and the solutions together.
options.rationale: A good general principle applied at the wrong moment. Waiting a week means the sponsor stands in front of the board with information you already had and they did not.

options.text: Tell the sponsor after the board meeting, so the presentation is not disrupted by an unresolved issue.
options.rationale: Protecting a sponsor from information before they speak on the record is how a delay becomes a credibility problem. It also makes the eventual conversation about why you waited.

options.text: Send a written note to the sponsor and the board together, so everyone has the same information.
options.rationale: Informing the board at the same moment as the sponsor removes their ability to decide how to handle it. Bad news travels up one step first.

questions.explanation: Bringing options rather than problems is sound practice that stops applying the moment someone is about to speak publicly on the basis of information you know to be wrong. What goes to the sponsor immediately is the confirmed fact, the honest boundary of what is not yet known, and a date for the analysis. It goes to them alone, and to the board through them.
questions.mindset: Someone about to speak on the record needs what you know now; the analysis can follow.

questions.stem: You are planning a programme that replaces a core banking ledger and, on top of it, builds a customer-facing mobile app. The ledger work has fixed regulatory requirements and a hard compliance date. The app requirements are still forming. Which two planning decisions are best supported?

options.text: Plan the ledger replacement predictively against the compliance date, and run the app iteratively.
options.rationale: Delivery approach follows the nature of the work rather than an organisational preference. Fixed requirements with a hard date suit a plan-driven approach; forming requirements suit iteration.

options.text: Define the integration points between the two and manage them as a single set of dependencies across both approaches.
options.rationale: Two approaches under one programme fail at the seam. Making the integration points explicit and managing them once is what keeps the hybrid a design rather than an accident.

options.text: Run both workstreams to the same cadence so that progress can be compared on a single programme report for the board.
options.rationale: Reporting convenience is a poor reason to impose a cadence. Forcing a regulatory ledger replacement into sprints so that the board sees one report usually produces sprint-shaped waterfall with extra ceremonies.

options.text: Hold a single integrated baseline covering scope, schedule and cost for both workstreams from the outset.
options.rationale: You cannot baseline scope that is still forming without inventing it. A programme-level baseline over the app's undefined scope would be fiction that everyone then manages against.

options.text: Apply the stricter regulatory governance and change control to both workstreams, so that auditors and the board see one consistent control framework.
options.rationale: Consistency is not free. Regulatory-grade change control on a mobile app kills the responsiveness that made iteration the right choice for it, and one framework for auditors is bought at the cost of the app's ability to learn.

questions.explanation: Tailoring means each part of the work gets the approach its own characteristics call for, and the programme's job is to hold the seam between them. Fixed requirements against a hard date are plan-driven work; forming requirements are iterative work; and the dependencies where the two meet need managing explicitly. Imposing one cadence, one baseline or one governance standard across both trades the benefit of tailoring for the comfort of uniformity.
questions.mindset: Give each part of the work the approach its own uncertainty calls for, and manage the seam between the parts as deliberately as the parts themselves.

questions.stem: A project will install identical point-of-sale hardware in 340 retail sites over eighteen months. The technical solution is proven and unchanged from a pilot last year. The sponsor has asked whether the project should be run in an agile way, since the organisation is adopting agile. What should the project manager advise?

options.text: Adopt agile, because organisational consistency in delivery method reduces overhead, simplifies reporting and improves resourcing flexibility.
options.rationale: Consistency, simpler reporting and resourcing flexibility are real benefits and secondary ones. Choosing an approach for the organisation's convenience rather than the work's characteristics is the error the question is testing.

options.text: Run it as a hybrid, with the first fifty sites delivered iteratively and the remainder planned predictively once the approach settles.
options.rationale: It sounds balanced and there is nothing to discover: the pilot already established the solution. Iterating over a proven installation for fifty sites adds ceremony without reducing uncertainty.

options.text: Adopt agile for the schedule and predictive for the budget, so the rollout plan can flex site by site while total costs stay controlled against an approved cost baseline.
options.rationale: Approach is not something you can apply to the schedule and not the scope. This describes a governance arrangement rather than a delivery approach, and a flexing schedule against a fixed cost baseline would immediately conflict.

options.text: Run it predictively, because the solution is known and repeated, while borrowing practices such as retrospectives that suit repetitive rollout work.
options.rationale: Known scope repeated 340 times is the textbook case for a plan-driven approach. Adopting the specific agile practices that help a rollout learn between sites is tailoring rather than method-shopping.

questions.explanation: Delivery approach follows uncertainty. Where the solution is proven and the work is repetition at scale, a plan-driven approach is not a legacy choice but the correct one, and the value to be captured is in logistics and learning curve rather than in discovery. Tailoring still applies: retrospectives between waves of sites are worth borrowing precisely because a rollout has 340 chances to get better at itself.
questions.mindset: Let the uncertainty in the work choose the delivery approach, not the direction the organisation happens to be travelling in.

questions.stem: Your organisation's methodology requires eleven planning documents before execution starts. Your project is a six-week integration with three people and one clear deliverable, and you estimate that producing all eleven would take about nine person-days, most of the first fortnight's capacity. The PMO's assurance manager insists all eleven are produced. What is the best course of action?

options.text: Produce all eleven documents before execution starts, since compliance with the organisational methodology is not the project's decision to make.
options.rationale: Compliance without judgement can consume most of a six-week project's first fortnight. Methodologies almost always contain a tailoring provision, and not looking for it is a choice too.

options.text: Propose a tailored set to the PMO, showing which documents address real risk on this project and which do not, and agree the reduction formally.
options.rationale: Tailoring is negotiated with the owner of the standard and recorded, not taken unilaterally. Arguing from the risk each document addresses is what makes it a professional case rather than a request to skip paperwork.

options.text: Produce shortened versions of all eleven before execution starts, so that the methodology is satisfied at proportionate cost.
options.rationale: Eleven thin documents satisfy the letter and produce nothing anyone will use. It also avoids the conversation about proportionality with the owner of the standard, which is the conversation the organisation needs to have.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor to obtain an exemption from the methodology for this project, then inform the PMO of the decision so that its records stay consistent.
options.rationale: Going over the PMO to get an exemption, and only then telling it, wins this project and damages the relationship for the next ten. The PMO owns the standard and is more likely to have a tailoring route already available.

questions.explanation: Tailoring is the deliberate, agreed adjustment of a standard to the size and risk of the work, and it is done with the body that owns the standard. The argument is made document by document on the basis of what risk each one actually reduces here. Blanket compliance, blanket thinning and going around the PMO all avoid that conversation, and it is the conversation that produces a defensible answer.
questions.mindset: Scale the process to the risk of the work, and agree the scaling with whoever owns the standard.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence with the term that fits. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: The shared standard that every backlog item must meet before the team calls it finished is the
The set of conditions specific to one backlog item that the product owner will check when deciding whether to accept it is its

options.text: definition of done
options.rationale: The definition of done applies to every item equally and covers the quality bar: tested, reviewed, documented, deployable. It is the team's standard, and it does not change item by item.

options.text: acceptance criteria
options.rationale: Acceptance criteria are written per item and describe what that particular piece of functionality must do. They vary with every story; the definition of done does not.

options.text: definition of ready
options.rationale: Not used. A definition of ready describes when an item is well enough understood to be pulled into a sprint, which is about the start of work rather than the end of it.

options.text: minimum viable product
options.rationale: Not used. A minimum viable product is the smallest release that produces learning or value in the market, which is a scoping decision about a release rather than a completion standard.

questions.explanation: The two are constantly confused and the distinction is simple: the definition of done is one standard for all items and covers quality, while acceptance criteria are written per item and cover behaviour. An item can meet every acceptance criterion and still not be done if it has not been tested to the team's standard. The two unused terms both concern the boundaries of work rather than its completion.
questions.mindset: Keep the team's single quality bar and each item's own conditions of acceptance apart, because meeting one proves nothing about the other.

questions.stem: A business analyst on your team has been accepting small refinements directly from users during requirements validation sessions, on the grounds that each is a clarification rather than a change. The build estimate has grown by 18 percent since baseline. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Assess what has accumulated, take it through change control as one package, and agree with the team where clarification ends and change begins.
options.rationale: The accumulated growth has to be surfaced and decided on, and the boundary has to be defined or the same thing happens again. Doing only one of the two leaves the project exposed.

options.text: Stop the practice immediately, confirm with the analyst that every future refinement goes through change control, and brief the users on the new route.
options.rationale: Half the answer. Confirming the new route with the analyst and briefing the users closes the leak, but it leaves 18 percent of unbaselined work sitting in the estimate with nobody having decided to fund it.

options.text: Confirm whether contingency covers the 18 percent growth, absorb it there if it does, and then tighten the process going forward.
options.rationale: Checking contingency first makes this feel controlled, but using a reserve held for risk to absorb unapproved scope growth spends it on a decision nobody made. It also removes the sponsor's chance to say the refinements are not worth 18 percent.

options.text: Re-baseline the scope and schedule to reflect the current understanding of requirements, once the analyst confirms which were clarifications.
options.rationale: Sorting clarifications from changes with the analyst is useful, but re-baselining is what happens after an approved change, not instead of one. Doing it here makes the growth official without anyone with authority having decided to fund it.

questions.explanation: Uncontrolled scope growth needs two responses, and answers that offer one of them are the trap. What has already accumulated is quantified and put through change control so that someone with authority decides whether to fund it. Separately, the line between clarification and change is defined with the team, because it was the absence of that line rather than anyone's bad faith that produced the drift.
questions.mindset: Scope growth that nobody decided to fund is still a change, whatever it was called when it came in.

questions.stem: Your team consistently spends the first two days of each two-week sprint working out what the top items actually mean, and often discovers dependencies that stall them. Sprint goals are met about half the time. What is the most effective change?

options.text: Extend sprint planning to a full day so the team can analyse each top item and its dependencies before committing to the sprint goal.
options.rationale: A longer planning session in the same sprint moves the same discovery a few hours earlier. A dependency found during it still cannot be resolved before the work starts, so the team commits to stalled items with better notes.

options.text: Introduce regular backlog refinement during the sprint, so upcoming items are understood and dependencies surfaced before they are committed to.
options.rationale: Refinement ahead of planning is the standard remedy: it moves discovery to a point where there is still time to act on what is found, rather than into the sprint that has to absorb it.

options.text: Move to four-week sprints so there is room inside each sprint to absorb the analysis, chase any dependencies that are found and still meet the sprint goal.
options.rationale: Longer sprints hide the problem by giving it more space to happen in. Feedback slows, and a team that discovers dependencies late now discovers them late with four weeks committed instead of two, so the goal is no safer.

options.text: Have the product owner write fuller specifications for each top item, including its known dependencies, before it is allowed to enter sprint planning.
options.rationale: Detail written by one person is not the same as understanding held by the team, and the product owner cannot list the technical dependencies the team keeps finding. It also recreates a handover where a conversation is needed.

questions.explanation: Two days of every ten spent working out what the work means is discovery happening inside the commitment rather than before it. Continuous refinement moves that conversation earlier, where a discovered dependency can still be resolved or the item can be swapped out. Lengthening planning or the sprint gives the same late discovery more room; more written detail substitutes documentation for shared understanding.
questions.mindset: Move discovery to before the commitment, rather than giving late discovery more room inside it.

questions.stem: A Kanban team currently has 24 work items in progress and finishes an average of 6 items per week. Work down the average cycle time, then the average cycle time the team would see if it capped work in progress at 12 items and throughput stayed the same.

blanks.label: Average cycle time now, in weeks
blanks.rationale: Cycle time equals work in progress divided by throughput: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 weeks. Every item currently takes four weeks on average to cross the board.

blanks.label: Average cycle time at a WIP cap of 12, in weeks
blanks.rationale: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 weeks. Halving the work in progress halves the cycle time, which is the whole argument for a WIP limit: nothing about the team changed except how much it started.

questions.explanation: Little's Law relates work in progress, throughput and cycle time, so cycle time is simply work in progress divided by throughput. The practical consequence is the one the second figure shows: with throughput unchanged, starting less finishes things sooner. A team that wants shorter lead times has two levers, and limiting what is in flight is nearly always the cheaper of the two.
questions.mindset: When work waits too long, look first at how much has been started, not at how fast the team works.

questions.stem: Your product backlog has 240 items. The product owner prioritises by asking each stakeholder to rank their own requests, then interleaving the lists. Delivery is steady but no stakeholder feels well served, and low-value work keeps reaching the team. What should be recommended?

options.text: Allocate each stakeholder a fixed share of team capacity, proportional to their budget contribution, and let each one order the work within their own share.
options.rationale: It makes the current arrangement explicit and fairer to negotiate over, and it still optimises for share rather than for value, since each stakeholder orders only their own slice. Low-value work continues to arrive, now with a quota behind it.

options.text: Prioritise against a consistent measure of value and cost across the whole backlog, rather than merging separate stakeholder rankings.
options.rationale: Interleaved lists guarantee that each stakeholder's least valuable item outranks another's most valuable. A single comparable measure is the only thing that lets the backlog be ordered as one queue.

options.text: Reduce the backlog by removing anything not touched in six months, then ask the product owner to rerun the stakeholder rankings on the shorter list.
options.rationale: A backlog of 240 items is worth pruning, but that is hygiene, not prioritisation. Rerunning the same per-stakeholder rankings on a shorter list leaves the method that lets low-value work through exactly as it was.

options.text: Have the steering group, with the product owner, review the merged list each quarter and approve the top twenty items before they are released to the team.
options.rationale: It moves the same unstructured judgement to a more senior group at a slower cadence, even with the product owner in the room. Without a shared measure the steering group is approving interleaved lists too, just less often, and the extra gate slows delivery without improving the order.

questions.explanation: Merging separately ranked lists produces an order that no measure of value would ever produce, which is why everyone is unhappy at once. The fix is a single yardstick applied across the whole backlog, so items from different stakeholders can be compared on the same terms. Capacity allocation and senior approval both preserve the underlying problem, which is that nothing is being compared.
questions.mindset: Work can only be ordered by value if every candidate is measured with the same yardstick.

questions.stem: Your schedule shows a specialist welder required at 180 percent of availability across weeks 9 to 14. The client contract fixes the completion date, and the welding activities have three weeks of total float in that path. Which technique should the project manager apply first?

options.text: Resource levelling, shifting start dates until the welder's demand fits availability, and accepting that the path may lengthen if it has to.
options.rationale: This is the reach-for-levelling error. Levelling will certainly remove the over-allocation, and it is allowed to change the critical path and usually the end date. It is the right tool once float has been exhausted, which is not the case here.

options.text: Fast-tracking the affected activities, overlapping them with their predecessors so the welder's work is spread across a longer window.
options.rationale: This is the wrong-toolbox error. Fast-tracking overlaps activities that were sequential, which tends to increase concurrent demand for the same welder rather than reduce it. It is a schedule compression tool, not a resource one.

options.text: Crashing the welding activities by bringing in a second certified welder for weeks 9 to 14, since the constraint is a shortage of that skill.
options.rationale: This is the spend-before-using-float error. A second certified welder costs money and may not be available at all. It is a legitimate option, but not the first one while three weeks of float on that path remain unused.

options.text: Resource smoothing, adjusting the welding activities within their available float so the welder's peak comes down without moving the completion date.
options.rationale: Smoothing works inside existing float and leaves the finish date alone. With three weeks of float available on that path, it is the technique to try before accepting a schedule extension.

questions.explanation: Smoothing and levelling are distinguished by what they are allowed to move. Smoothing works only within existing float and so preserves the completion date; levelling relaxes that constraint and may extend the schedule. Where float exists, smoothing is tried first because it costs nothing and risks nothing. Fast-tracking and crashing are compression techniques aimed at duration, and neither addresses an over-allocation directly.
questions.mindset: Use the float you already have before spending money or moving the finish date to resolve a resource clash.

questions.stem: Four of your six developers are also assigned to two other projects, at nominally 40 percent each. Velocity is erratic, sprint goals are missed, and the developers report spending significant time re-orienting. The resource manager says the allocation is correct on paper. What is the strongest case to make?

options.text: That splitting people across three projects imposes a switching cost the percentages do not capture, and that dedicating fewer people fully would deliver more.
options.rationale: The case is about the arithmetic being wrong rather than the allocation being unfair. Context switching is real, unbudgeted and invisible on a resource sheet, and naming that is what changes the conversation.

options.text: That the allocation percentages should be revised upward, so this project holds a larger share of each developer's week and the resource sheet reflects the true effort needed.
options.rationale: This is the argue-the-number error. It contests the percentage rather than the structure: a larger share of a person still split across two other projects carries the same switching cost, so the sheet improves and the velocity does not.

options.text: That the erratic velocity makes forecasting impossible, so the project cannot commit to release dates until its resourcing is stable and the sponsor should be told so.
options.rationale: This is the complain-about-the-symptom error. It is true, and it presents as a complaint that puts the project's credibility on the line rather than the resourcing model's, while offering the resource manager nothing to act on.

options.text: That the other two projects should be asked to reduce their claims on the four shared developers, with the portfolio board deciding whose need comes first.
options.rationale: This is the zero-sum error. It asks for a contest between three projects to be won by whoever argues hardest at the board, and it does not challenge the assumption that a person divides cleanly between them.

questions.explanation: A resource sheet that adds to 100 percent implies people divide without loss, and they do not: every switch costs re-orientation that appears nowhere in the allocation. The argument to make is that the model is understating cost, with the erratic velocity as evidence, and that fewer fully dedicated people would deliver more than more partly assigned ones. Arguing about percentages or about who gets whom accepts the flawed model and merely competes inside it.
questions.mindset: People do not divide without loss, so question any resource plan that assumes they do.

questions.stem: You are buying a bespoke control system for a paper mill. The functional requirements are firm and signed off, but the integration with your existing plant is poorly understood: your controls engineer puts it anywhere between 200 and 700 days of effort. Your organisation wants cost certainty. Which two approaches best fit?

options.text: Place the firm functional scope under a fixed-price arrangement, and the integration work under a cost-reimbursable or time-and-materials arrangement with a ceiling.
options.rationale: Contract type follows scope certainty, and this scope has two halves with different certainty. Splitting them prices the known work firmly and caps exposure on the unknown.

options.text: Run a paid discovery phase on the integration first, then contract the integration work firmly once its scope is understood.
options.rationale: Buying the information before buying the work is what converts an unpriceable scope into a priceable one. It costs a phase and removes the risk premium a supplier would otherwise load into a fixed price.

options.text: Place the whole scope under a firm fixed price, transferring the integration uncertainty to the supplier, and require bidders to state their assumptions.
options.rationale: Transferring uncertainty a supplier cannot size gets it priced with a heavy contingency, or accepted and then fought over in claims. Stated assumptions do not change that: every assumption the plant breaks becomes a claim, so the buyer gets cost certainty on paper and cost surprise in practice.

options.text: Use a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract for the whole scope, since the integration effort is unknown, with monthly reporting of spend.
options.rationale: It handles the unknown half and gives away the certainty available on the firm half. Monthly reporting makes overspend visible without limiting it, and the buyer still carries cost risk on requirements that were perfectly well defined.

options.text: Use a fixed-price incentive-fee contract across the whole scope with a wide share ratio to motivate efficient integration.
options.rationale: Incentive arrangements need a credible target cost to share against, and with an integration estimate spanning 200 to 700 days that is precisely what cannot be set. Applying it to the whole scope does not help: the mechanism still has nothing to anchor to.

questions.explanation: One contract type across a scope with two different levels of certainty forces the wrong risk allocation onto one half of it. Either split the arrangement so each half is priced on terms that match what is known, or buy the knowledge first through a discovery phase and then contract firmly. Transferring uncertainty nobody can size does not remove it; it converts it into a risk premium or a dispute.
questions.mindset: Price each part of a scope on the terms its certainty supports, and buy knowledge before buying work nobody can yet describe.

questions.stem: A supplier has missed two consecutive delivery milestones. Their account manager assures you the third will be met. Your contract contains a termination-for-convenience clause and liquidated damages. Replacing the supplier would cost four months. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Meet the supplier's delivery lead to establish the root cause of the misses, and agree a recovery plan with verifiable interim checkpoints.
options.rationale: Two misses and a verbal assurance are not enough to decide anything on. Finding the cause and putting in checkpoints that can be verified is what turns the next assurance into evidence.

options.text: Issue a formal notice invoking liquidated damages for both misses, to establish that the misses have consequences.
options.rationale: It protects the contractual position and makes the working relationship adversarial at the moment you most need the supplier to perform. Applying damages to both misses assumes the problem is effort, and does nothing to establish whether they can deliver.

options.text: Begin a parallel procurement now, so that a replacement supplier can be engaged without losing four months if needed.
options.rationale: A reasonable contingency once you know how bad this is. Started now, before the cause is known, it costs real money and, if it becomes known, guarantees the deterioration you are trying to avoid.

options.text: Escalate to the supplier's executive sponsor for a written commitment, since the account manager's assurance has failed twice.
options.rationale: Escalation is a lever worth holding rather than pulling second. Used before you know the cause, it is likely to produce a more senior assurance of the same kind, now in writing but no better founded.

questions.explanation: Two missed milestones establish that something is wrong and not what. Contract remedies, parallel procurement and escalation are all available and each spends something you may need, so none of them is the first move. The first move is to find the cause and replace an assurance with checkpoints that can be verified before the milestone rather than after it, which is what makes the next decision an informed one.
questions.mindset: Find out why a supplier is failing before spending any of the remedies the contract gives you.

questions.stem: The estimate for a county records office's archive digitisation project has been rolled up from four work packages: scanning £410,000, metadata cataloguing £265,000, storage platform £180,000 and public portal £95,000. Risk analysis has sized a contingency reserve of £85,000 for the identified risks, and the sponsor will hold a management reserve set at 5 per cent of the cost baseline. The finance lead plans to load the total approved budget into the earned value system as the budget at completion. Work out the figures below.

blanks.label: Cost baseline (£)
blanks.rationale: The work packages total 410,000 + 265,000 + 180,000 + 95,000 = £950,000, and the contingency reserve for identified risks sits inside the baseline: 950,000 + 85,000 = £1,035,000.

blanks.label: Total project budget to be approved, including management reserve (£)
blanks.rationale: Management reserve is 5 per cent of the cost baseline, 0.05 × 1,035,000 = £51,750, and it sits on top of the baseline: 1,035,000 + 51,750 = £1,086,750. This is the funding the organisation must make available, not the figure performance is measured against.

blanks.label: Which figure belongs in the earned value system as the budget at completion: the cost baseline or the total budget
blanks.rationale: Earned value is measured against the cost baseline, £1,035,000. Loading £1,086,750 would put £51,750 that is allocated to no work into planned value, earned value and every forecast built on them, for money the project manager cannot spend without the sponsor releasing it.

questions.explanation: Budgets are built in layers: work package estimates roll up to control accounts, contingency for identified risks is added to form the cost baseline, and management reserve for unforeseen work sits above that to give the total budget. Performance is measured against the cost baseline because that is the money allocated to planned work and known risks; management reserve only enters the baseline when the sponsor releases it through change control. The funding requirement and the measurement baseline are therefore two different numbers, and confusing them misstates both.
questions.mindset: Know which layer of the budget a figure belongs to before you measure anything against it.

questions.stem: A risk you identified and quantified during planning has occurred, and responding to it will cost 60,000. Your contingency reserve holds 145,000, with three further identified risks still open on the register, and your management reserve, held by the sponsor, holds 300,000. What should the project manager do?
