options.text: Request 60,000 from the management reserve, preserving contingency for risks that have not yet occurred.
options.rationale: Management reserve is for the unknown-unknowns and sits outside the cost baseline. Using it for a risk that was identified and funded skips the mechanism built for the purpose.

options.text: Draw the 60,000 from the contingency reserve and report the drawdown in the next status report.
options.rationale: Contingency exists for exactly this: identified risks that have been analysed and provided for. Drawing it is a project-level decision, and reporting it keeps the drawdown visible.

options.text: Raise a change request to increase the cost baseline by 60,000, since the cost was not in the original estimate.
options.rationale: The cost was in the estimate: contingency is part of the cost baseline precisely so that identified risks do not require a change request when they materialise.

options.text: Draw from contingency and immediately request a top-up from management reserve to restore the balance.
options.rationale: Automatically restoring contingency treats it as an entitlement rather than a provision. Whether the remaining 85,000 is still adequate is a question for the risk analysis, not a reflex.

questions.explanation: The two reserves answer to different owners and different kinds of uncertainty. Contingency sits inside the cost baseline, covers risks that were identified and quantified, and the project manager draws on it. Management reserve sits outside the baseline for genuine unknowns and needs the sponsor. A materialised known risk is the textbook contingency draw, and no change request is required because the money was already in the baseline.
questions.mindset: Spend a reserve on what it was sized for, at the level that owns it, and show that you have.

questions.stem: Finance asks for a cost forecast for an agile product team funded quarterly. The team is stable at eight people, the run rate is predictable, and the backlog is not fixed. Finance wants to know what the total cost will be to complete the product. How should the project manager respond?

options.text: Explain to finance that the team's cost is predictable and its completion is not, and offer a rolling forecast of cost per quarter alongside the value expected to be delivered in each.
options.rationale: With a stable team the run rate is the reliable half of the answer, and the honest framing is cost per period against expected value rather than a total to an undefined end.

options.text: Estimate the remaining backlog in story points, divide by the team's stable velocity, and multiply the sprints needed by the cost per sprint to give finance a total to complete.
options.rationale: It produces a total, and every step of it rests on a backlog that is deliberately not fixed. Using a stable velocity makes the arithmetic look rigorous while forecasting to an end point nobody has defined, which dresses an assumption up as arithmetic.

options.text: Ask the product owner to freeze the current backlog for costing purposes, so that a total cost to complete can be calculated and then tracked against actuals each quarter.
options.rationale: Freezing the backlog to satisfy a reporting format gives away the main benefit of funding a product team, which is the ability to change what gets built as you learn. Tracking against the frozen total then turns every sensible reprioritisation into an apparent variance.

options.text: Provide a range for the total cost based on optimistic and pessimistic assumptions about how the backlog will grow, with a confidence level attached to each end of the range.
options.rationale: Better than a point estimate, and still forecasting to completion for something that has no defined end. Attaching confidence levels to assumptions about backlog growth adds precision to the wrong question: a range around an undefined scope is a wide range around nothing.

questions.explanation: A stable team funded by period has a highly predictable cost and an undefined end, so the honest forecast reports cost per quarter next to the value expected from it. Finance can then decide each quarter whether to keep funding, which is the actual decision. Calculating a total to complete requires fixing a backlog that is deliberately not fixed, and doing so trades the benefit of the funding model for the comfort of a single number.
questions.mindset: Forecast what the funding model makes predictable, and do not invent an end point it deliberately leaves open.

questions.stem: Match each activity to the cost-of-quality category it belongs to. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Training installers on the new torque procedure before the first unit is assembled.
Inspecting a sample of finished units against the specification before shipping.
Reworking units found defective on the production line before they leave the factory.
Recalling units from customers after a fault appears in the field.

options.text: Prevention cost
options.rationale: Prevention is money spent to stop defects being created at all: training, process design, tooling. It is the cheapest category per defect avoided and the first to be cut under pressure.

options.text: Appraisal cost
options.rationale: Appraisal is the cost of finding out whether quality has been achieved — inspection, testing, audit. It detects defects rather than preventing them.

options.text: Internal failure cost
options.rationale: Internal failure is the cost of defects caught before the customer sees them: scrap and rework. Expensive, and far cheaper than the same defect escaping.

options.text: External failure cost
options.rationale: External failure is what a defect costs once it has reached the customer: recalls, warranty, liability, reputation. It is the most expensive category by a wide margin.

options.text: Opportunity cost
options.rationale: Not used. Opportunity cost is the value of the alternative not chosen. It is a real economic concept and it is not one of the four cost-of-quality categories.

questions.explanation: Cost of quality splits into conformance work, which is prevention and appraisal, and non-conformance work, which is internal and external failure. The cost per defect rises sharply left to right, which is the argument for spending on prevention: a defect stopped in training costs a fraction of the same defect found in inspection, and a tiny fraction of one recalled from a customer.
questions.mindset: Spend where defects are prevented, because every later category pays more for the same defect.

questions.stem: Over six sprints, your team's velocity has fallen steadily while the number of defects found in each sprint has risen. The team says shortcuts taken to hit earlier sprint commitments are now slowing everything down. The product owner wants the next release on time. What should the project manager advocate?

options.text: Making the trade-off explicit to the product owner: the falling velocity is the price of the shortcuts, and some capacity now buys the delivery rate back.
options.rationale: This is a prioritisation decision the product owner owns, and they can only make it if the connection between the shortcuts and the falling velocity is put in front of them in those terms.

options.text: Adding a dedicated defect-fixing sprint after the release, so the current commitment is protected and the repairs are handled in one planned block.
options.rationale: Deferring the repair keeps the release date and lets the decay continue for another release cycle. Batching the repairs into one later sprint feels orderly, but the velocity trend says the cost of waiting is rising, not flat.

options.text: Allocating a fixed 20 percent of each sprint to technical debt as a standing policy, agreed with the product owner, so repair work stops competing with features.
options.rationale: A sensible steady-state practice and an arbitrary answer to a specific problem. The right number depends on what is actually causing the decay, which nobody has yet quantified, so agreeing it with the product owner asks her to accept a figure no one can justify.

options.text: Tightening the definition of done with the team so that new shortcuts cannot be taken in future sprints, and reviewing it at each retrospective to keep it honest.
options.rationale: Necessary to stop the bleeding and it does nothing about six sprints of accumulated debt that is already slowing the team. Reviewing the standard at retrospectives keeps it honest and still prevents only the next problem, not this one.

questions.explanation: Technical debt is an economic trade-off, and the project manager's job is to make sure the person prioritising can see it as one. Falling velocity alongside rising defects is quantified evidence that shortcuts have a price, and putting that in front of the product owner turns an engineering complaint into a decision about the release. Standing policies and tighter standards both belong in the answer, but neither is the move that gets this release decided honestly.
questions.mindset: Present technical debt as a cost the person prioritising can weigh, not as an engineering grievance.

questions.stem: In the schedule model, activity D has an early start of day 12 and a late start of day 19. All other activities are unchanged. Work out the total float on activity D, and then how many days late the project would finish if activity D started on day 12 but took 9 days longer than planned.

blanks.label: Total float on activity D, in days
blanks.rationale: Total float is late start minus early start: 19 − 12 = 7 days. Activity D can absorb seven days of delay before the project completion date is affected.

blanks.label: Days the project finishes late
blanks.rationale: The first seven days of the overrun are absorbed by float; the remaining 9 − 7 = 2 days push the completion date out. Activity D also becomes critical at that point.

questions.explanation: Total float is the difference between the late and early dates and measures how much an activity can move before the project finish moves with it. The second figure is the consequence that matters in practice: overrun is only felt at the project level once float is exhausted, and an activity that consumes all of its float has joined the critical path, so any further slip transmits day for day.
questions.mindset: An overrun reaches the finish date only once the float in front of it is spent, so measure the float before judging the slip.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the sequence this project follows to produce a schedule baseline. Select the step at which durations and dependencies are first combined into a model that reveals the earliest date the project can finish.

graphic.title: Schedule development, five steps left to right
graphic.caption: Select a step. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between steps, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Define activities
regions.rationale: Defining activities decomposes the work packages into things that can be scheduled. It produces the list, and nothing in it says how long anything takes or what order it goes in.

regions.label: Sequence activities
regions.rationale: Sequencing establishes the dependencies between activities. It is half of what the model needs, and without durations it still cannot produce a date.

regions.label: Estimate durations
regions.rationale: Duration estimating produces the other half of the input. On its own it gives you how long each activity takes but not how they combine.

regions.label: Develop schedule
regions.rationale: This is where sequence and durations are run through the model together, producing the critical path, the float on every other path, and the earliest completion date.

regions.label: Control schedule
regions.rationale: Controlling compares actual progress against the baseline and manages variance. It consumes the model that step 4 produced rather than creating it.

questions.explanation: The first three steps each produce an input and none of them can produce a date. Developing the schedule is where the network is analysed: the earliest finish falls out of it, and so does the critical path and the float available on everything else. Control is what happens afterwards, against the baseline that this step made possible.
questions.mindset: A finish date comes out of the network model, not out of any one of the inputs that feed it.

questions.stem: Your team has failed to complete everything it committed to in four of the last five sprints, each time by about 20 percent. The team is working hard and the product owner is losing confidence in the forecasts. What should the project manager suggest?

options.text: Commit to roughly what the team has actually completed in recent sprints, rather than to what it hopes to complete.
options.rationale: Consistent 20 percent overcommitment is a forecasting error, not an effort problem. Planning against demonstrated throughput restores the one thing that has been lost, which is the reliability of the forecast.

options.text: Extend the sprint length so the outstanding 20 percent has room to finish inside the sprint, keeping the team's commitment level where it is.
options.rationale: This is the stretch-the-container error. A longer sprint planned at the same overcommitment rate finishes 80 percent of a bigger number, because the ratio between commitment and capacity is the problem and the length is not.

options.text: Carry the incomplete items into the following sprint automatically, at the top of its backlog, so nothing is lost and the product owner sees them finished.
options.rationale: This is the formalise-the-symptom error. Carry-over is already happening in effect and is what makes each sprint start behind; making it automatic hides the overcommitment from the product owner rather than correcting it.

options.text: Investigate in the next retrospective why the team keeps missing its commitments, and address the underlying impediments it identifies.
options.rationale: This is the look-for-a-blocker error. It is a good habit, but it assumes the shortfall has a cause outside the plan, and a stable 20 percent gap across five sprints looks much more like consistent optimism than a recurring impediment.

questions.explanation: A steady, repeated shortfall of the same size is evidence about the estimate rather than about the team. Committing to demonstrated throughput rather than to hope makes the next forecast reliable, and reliability is what the product owner has actually lost. Longer sprints and formal carry-over both preserve the overcommitment; investigating impediments is a good habit that does not fit a gap this consistent.
questions.mindset: Plan against what the team has shown it can deliver, because a forecast nobody can rely on is worth little however hard the team works.

questions.stem: Your organisation measures its nine agile teams on velocity and publishes a quarterly league table comparing them. Velocity across all teams has risen 40 percent in two quarters while release frequency and defect rates are unchanged. Before presenting the table to the executive committee, the head of delivery asks for your reading of it. Which two conclusions are best supported?

options.text: The rise most likely reflects estimate inflation rather than a genuine increase in delivered output.
options.rationale: Velocity is measured in a unit each team defines for itself. When the number rises and nothing observable about delivery changes, the unit has almost certainly moved.

options.text: Comparing velocity between teams is invalid, because story points are calibrated within a team and are not a common unit.
options.rationale: Points are a relative measure local to one team's shared reference. A league table across teams compares numbers that were never denominated in the same thing.

options.text: The teams have become more efficient, and the gain has not yet worked through to release frequency or defect rates.
options.rationale: This is the trust-the-headline error. A genuine gain is possible in principle and unlikely across all nine teams at once with no movement in any outcome measure, and it requires believing the one metric under pressure over all the ones that are not.

options.text: Defect rates should be added to the league table alongside velocity, so that no team can raise its speed at the expense of quality without it showing.
options.rationale: This is the add-a-column error. A second metric on a table that is already distorting behaviour gives teams two numbers to manage instead of one, and leaves the invalid cross-team comparison in place. The problem is the comparison, not the number of columns.

options.text: Velocity should be replaced with hours worked, which uses the same unit for every team and cannot be inflated by re-estimating.
options.rationale: This is the swap-for-an-input error. Hours are comparable across teams, but they measure effort put in rather than value delivered, so replacing a gameable output measure with an input measure is a step backwards.

questions.explanation: Velocity is a planning aid for one team, expressed in a unit that team invented, and it becomes a target the moment it is published for comparison. A rise with no movement in release frequency or quality is the signature of estimate inflation. The deeper error is the league table itself: points are not a common currency, so the comparison was measuring nothing even before it started distorting behaviour.
questions.mindset: Check a metric against the outcomes it is meant to predict before believing it has moved.

questions.stem: Your status report has shown the project as amber for eight consecutive weeks, with the same commentary each week. The steering group has stopped asking about it. What does this most likely indicate, and what should the project manager do?

options.text: The status is accurate and stable; continue reporting it as amber each week, with updated commentary on activity, until the underlying issue resolves.
options.rationale: This is the report-it-faithfully error. A status that has not moved in eight weeks is not stable, it is stuck, and refreshing the activity commentary still reports effort rather than asking for anything. Reporting it the same way is what trained the steering group to stop reading it.

options.text: The report has stopped conveying information; state what specifically is unresolved, what it will cost, and what decision is needed.
options.rationale: Eight identical ambers means the report has become wallpaper. Replacing the colour with a specific unresolved item, its cost and the decision required is what makes it actionable again.

options.text: The status should be escalated to red so the steering group re-engages, and returned to amber once it has been discussed.
options.rationale: This is the change-the-colour error. Moving the rating to be noticed rather than because the situation changed destroys the signal: it works once, and it makes every future rating suspect, including the return to amber.

options.text: The reporting cadence is too frequent for a slow-moving issue; move to monthly reporting so that each report carries enough change to be worth reading.
options.rationale: This is the change-the-cadence error. Less frequent reporting of the same uninformative content produces the same problem more slowly. The issue is what the report says, not how often it says it.

questions.explanation: A status that repeats unchanged for two months has stopped being a report and become a habit, which is why the audience has disengaged. The remedy is specificity: name the thing that is not resolving, quantify what it is costing, and state the decision needed and from whom. Escalating the colour for attention and slowing the cadence both leave the content untouched, and the content is the whole problem.
questions.mindset: A report earns attention by asking for something specific, not by repeating a colour.

questions.stem: Your programme has three predictive workstreams reporting earned value and two agile teams reporting burn-up and cycle time. All five feed a single go-live for a new freight booking service in September. The board, which meets quarterly to decide whether to release the next funding tranche, asks for a single view of programme progress. What should the project manager produce?

options.text: Convert the agile teams' completed story points into earned value against their release plans, so all five workstreams report in the one measure the board already uses.
options.rationale: This is the force-one-metric error. Earned value needs a fixed scope to earn against, and the agile teams' backlogs are deliberately kept open, so the conversion produces a comparable-looking number that is not measuring what it claims.

options.text: Report the predictive workstreams' earned value to the board, since the agile teams are funded separately and already report to their own product governance.
options.rationale: This is the report-what-fits error. Whatever the funding route, the board is deciding on a programme whose go-live depends on all five workstreams, and a partial view will be noticed at exactly the wrong moment.

options.text: Present all five sets of metrics side by side in one report, with a glossary for each measure, and let the board draw its own conclusions.
options.rationale: This is the hand-over-the-synthesis error. A glossary explains the measures and one report collects them without integrating them, so the work of turning five different measures into a view of the programme moves onto the board. That work is the project manager's, and doing it is most of the value of the report.

options.text: Report each workstream in its native measures, and roll up to the board on outcomes and milestones that are common to all five.
options.rationale: The common language across mixed delivery is the outcome, not the metric. Each workstream keeps the measure that works for it, and the board sees the thing it actually needs to decide against.

questions.explanation: Mixed delivery approaches do not roll up through a common metric, because the metrics measure different things about differently-shaped work. They roll up through outcomes and milestones, which every workstream can be assessed against regardless of how it is run. Forcing one measure across all five produces false comparability; presenting five raw sets pushes the synthesis onto the audience least equipped to do it.
questions.mindset: Roll mixed delivery up through the outcomes it shares, not through a metric only part of it can produce.

questions.stem: Your project has delivered a warehouse management system that has been live for three weeks and is working. The sponsor wants the project closed this month so the budget can be released. Which two things must be completed before closure, rather than after it?

options.text: Formal acceptance of the deliverables by the parties named in the acceptance criteria.
options.rationale: Closure without recorded acceptance leaves the question of whether the project delivered what it agreed permanently open, and there is no one left to answer it afterwards.

options.text: Transfer of the system, its documentation and its support arrangements to the operational owner.
options.rationale: Handover is the point of the project. A system running with nobody formally responsible for it after the team disperses is the classic closure failure, and it surfaces at the first incident.

options.text: Confirmation that the projected efficiency benefits have been realised in the first months of live operation.
options.rationale: Benefits from a warehouse system take months to appear and are measured by the operational owner, so three weeks of live use cannot show them. Holding a project open until they land confuses delivery with benefits realisation.

options.text: Completion of the twelve-month defect warranty period agreed with the supplier.
options.rationale: The warranty is a contractual arrangement that outlives the project. What closure requires is that responsibility for administering it has been transferred, not that it has expired.

options.text: Resolution of every item on the outstanding defect list raised during the three weeks of live use.
options.rationale: Minor defects found in early live use are routinely handed over as a known list with an owner and a plan. Requiring an empty list before closure keeps projects open indefinitely for trivia.

questions.explanation: Closure is about finishing the project cleanly rather than about waiting for everything downstream of it to conclude. Two things must land before the team disperses: formal acceptance, which records that what was agreed was delivered, and transfer to an operational owner who will hold the system afterwards. Benefits, warranties and residual defects all continue past closure, and each is handled by transferring ownership rather than by delaying it.
questions.mindset: Close when what was agreed has been accepted and handed to an owner, not when everything downstream of it has finished.

questions.stem: An agile team has delivered the features that account for the bulk of the expected value. The remaining backlog is 90 items of low individual value, and funding runs for another two quarters. The product owner asks what to do. What should the project manager advise?

options.text: Continue delivering the backlog in strict priority order until the funding is exhausted, checking with the product owner at each sprint review that the ordering still holds.
options.rationale: It uses the money and stops asking whether the money should be used. Re-checking the order each sprint refines which item comes next but never asks whether any of them is worth the run rate, which is the exact behaviour value-driven delivery is meant to prevent.

options.text: Assess whether the remaining items justify the run rate, and take a recommendation to the sponsor about closing early or redirecting the team.
options.rationale: Continuing is now a funding decision rather than a delivery one, and it belongs to whoever owns the money. Bringing them the comparison is what lets them make it.

options.text: Close the project now, since the bulk of the value has been delivered, and archive the remaining backlog so that any item can be revived later as a new request if it proves to matter.
options.rationale: It reaches the same conclusion without doing the analysis and without the sponsor, who owns the funding being given up. Archiving for later revival does not repair that: some of those 90 items may matter more than their individual size suggests, and nobody has checked which.

options.text: Reduce the team size so the remaining backlog is delivered at lower cost over the two quarters, releasing the least-needed roles first.
options.rationale: A smaller team on low-value work still spends money on low-value work. Choosing which roles go first settles how to shrink rather than whether to continue, and it breaks up a team that could be redeployed whole to something worth more.

questions.explanation: Once the value curve has flattened, the question changes from what to build next to whether to keep building at all. That is a decision about capital, so it goes to the sponsor with an honest comparison of what the remaining backlog is worth against what the team costs and what else it could do. Grinding through the queue, closing unilaterally and shrinking the team all avoid putting the real choice to the person who owns it.
questions.mindset: When the remaining work is no longer obviously worth its cost, whether to continue is the funder's decision, so put that choice in front of them.

questions.stem: Match each decision to the level that owns it under a conventional governance structure. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Moving 15,000 between two work packages, with no change to total cost, scope or completion date.
Approving a change request that would take the project 6 percent above its approved cost tolerance.
Releasing funds held outside the cost baseline to deal with an event nobody had identified.

options.text: The project manager, recorded in the log
options.rationale: Reallocation inside an approved envelope with no effect on cost, scope or date sits within normal delegated authority. It is recorded rather than approved, so the trail exists without the overhead.

options.text: The change control board
options.rationale: A change that breaches an approved tolerance is exactly what a change control board exists for: it evaluates the impact against the baselines and decides on behalf of the organisation.

options.text: The sponsor, from management reserve
options.rationale: Management reserve sits outside the cost baseline for unknown-unknowns and is released by the sponsor. Its use is a governance act, not a project one, and it changes the funding rather than the baseline.

options.text: The project team by consensus
options.rationale: Not used. Teams properly decide how to do the work, and none of the three above is a question about method. Consensus is the wrong instrument for decisions about money and authority.

questions.explanation: Governance works by defining who may decide what, with thresholds that route a decision upward only when it breaches one. Reallocation inside an envelope is delegated and merely logged; a breach of tolerance goes to the change control board; and money held outside the baseline is released by the sponsor. The unused option is a reminder that team consensus governs how work is done, not what is authorised.
questions.mindset: Know which level owns each class of decision, and send a decision upward only when it crosses a threshold that says it must go there.

questions.stem: Your project's approved schedule tolerance is two weeks. Your current forecast shows a slip of nine days, and your mitigation plan would recover about six of them but will not be confirmed for a fortnight. What should the project manager do now?

options.text: Escalate immediately, since a nine-day slip with uncertain mitigation could breach the two-week tolerance.
options.rationale: Escalating inside tolerance every time a breach is conceivable makes the tolerance meaningless and trains the governance body to filter you out.

options.text: Report the forecast slip and the mitigation plan now, noting that the tolerance is not yet breached.
options.rationale: Nine days is inside tolerance, so no escalation is required, and governance is better served by visibility than by silence. Reporting early with a plan is what preserves credibility if the mitigation fails.

options.text: Wait two weeks for the mitigation result, then report the confirmed position.
options.rationale: Withholding a known forecast for a fortnight leaves the steering group making decisions on stale information, and the eventual report arrives with no time left to respond.

options.text: Re-baseline the schedule to absorb the nine days, since it is within the agreed tolerance.
options.rationale: Tolerance is room to vary against the baseline, not permission to move the baseline. Re-baselining inside tolerance quietly consumes the buffer and hides the variance from everyone above.

questions.explanation: Tolerance defines when escalation becomes mandatory, and it says nothing about when reporting becomes useful. A forecast inside tolerance with mitigation still uncertain is reported as exactly that, which keeps the steering group current without triggering machinery that is not needed. Escalating early empties the threshold of meaning, waiting hides a known position, and re-baselining spends the tolerance without anyone deciding to.
questions.mindset: Tolerance tells you when escalation becomes mandatory, not whether a known forecast should be shared.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence with the term that fits. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: The activity that establishes which laws, standards and internal policies the project must satisfy is best described as
The activity that produces the records an auditor will later use to confirm those requirements were met is best described as

options.text: compliance requirement identification
options.rationale: Identification establishes the applicable obligations and their source. It happens early, because a requirement discovered late is usually a requirement that has already been breached.

options.text: compliance evidence collection
options.rationale: Evidence collection produces the artifacts that demonstrate conformance: test records, sign-offs, calibration certificates. Compliance you cannot evidence is indistinguishable from non-compliance during an audit.

options.text: gap analysis
options.rationale: Not used. A gap analysis compares the current state against a required state, which is a technique used inside compliance work rather than either of the two activities described.

options.text: quality assurance
options.rationale: Not used. Quality assurance checks that the processes being followed are capable of producing the required result, which overlaps compliance work without being the same thing.

questions.explanation: Compliance splits into knowing what applies and being able to prove you met it, and projects routinely do the first and neglect the second. Evidence has to be produced as the work happens: reconstructing it months later for an audit is expensive when it is possible and impossible when it is not. The two unused terms are techniques that support compliance rather than the activities themselves.
questions.mindset: Knowing what you must comply with is half the job; being able to prove you met it is the other half.

questions.stem: Two months from go-live, a regulator publishes a rule change that will make one module of your product non-compliant from a date four months after your launch. Your sponsor wants to launch as planned and fix it afterwards. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Comply with the sponsor's decision and log the rule change in the risk register for monitoring after launch, since launch timing is a business decision within their authority.
options.rationale: Launch timing is theirs; whether they are deciding with full information is the project manager's responsibility. Logging the change records the risk without informing the decision it bears on, and deferring silently to a decision made on partial analysis is not the same as respecting authority.

options.text: Establish exactly what the rule requires, what compliance would cost before and after launch, and put both options to the sponsor with the risk of each.
options.rationale: The sponsor's position may well be right: four months is real headroom. It becomes a sound decision only once the cost of retrofitting versus building it now, and the exposure in between, are quantified.

options.text: Delay the launch until the module has been made compliant and re-baseline the go-live date, since launching a product towards known non-compliance is not defensible.
options.rationale: The product is compliant at launch and for four months afterwards, so this treats a future obligation as a present breach. Re-baselining the date on the project manager's own call also overrides a decision that belongs to the sponsor.

options.text: Escalate the rule change to the compliance function with the regulator's notice attached, so that the launch decision is made by the specialists outside the project.
options.rationale: Compliance should certainly be consulted on what the rule requires, but handing them the notice and the decision skips the cost-and-exposure analysis the choice depends on, and removes the sponsor from a call that is properly theirs.

questions.explanation: A regulatory change with a future effective date is a cost and risk question rather than an immediate breach, and the sponsor is entitled to decide it. What the project manager owes them is the analysis that makes the decision sound: what the rule actually requires, what compliance costs now against later, and what exposure the gap creates. Silent compliance, unilateral delay and handing the decision away all skip that.
questions.mindset: Turn a compliance deadline into costed options for the person who owns the decision.

questions.stem: On a warehouse fit-out, the change control board has approved a request from the client's operations director to add a second loading dock. The change adds two weeks and 40,000 to the project, and the board minuted that it is funded from the sponsor's contingency. Work on the dock has not yet started. What must the project manager ensure happens next?

options.text: The team is briefed on the new scope, the dock work packages are assigned to owners, and execution begins immediately so that no time is lost against the extra two weeks.
options.rationale: Necessary and not sufficient. Assigning and starting the work against an unchanged baseline means every subsequent variance report compares actuals to a plan that no longer describes the project.

options.text: The sponsor confirms in writing that the additional 40,000 is available from contingency before the cost and schedule baselines are changed.
options.rationale: The funding source was part of the board's decision and is already minuted. Re-testing it afterwards second-guesses an approval that has been made and delays the baseline update that is the actual next step.

options.text: The affected baselines and subsidiary plans are updated, and the change is recorded in the change log with its decision.
options.rationale: An approved change that does not reach the baselines produces permanent phantom variance. Updating the plans and logging the decision is what makes the approval real in the system of record.

options.text: The stakeholders affected by the two-week delay are informed today of the revised dates for the milestones they depend on.
options.rationale: It must happen and it comes after the schedule has been re-planned. Telling them today, before the baseline is updated, risks circulating figures that then change.

questions.explanation: The step most often missed is the one after approval. A change is not implemented when the board says yes; it is implemented when the baselines, the subsidiary plans and the change log all reflect it, so that performance is thereafter measured against the plan the project is actually running to. Briefing the team and telling stakeholders both follow from an updated plan rather than preceding it.
questions.mindset: An approval only takes effect once the baselines and records the project is measured against have moved to reflect it.

questions.stem: A finance director on the steering committee of an agile customer-portal rebuild asks why the project needs change control at all, since the product owner reorders the backlog every sprint and nobody raises a change request to do it. The rebuild has a fixed budget of £1.2 million and a launch date committed to the board. How should the project manager answer?

options.text: That reordering within the agreed scope, budget and date is the product owner's to make freely, while anything that moves those boundaries still needs the same authority it would in any project.
options.rationale: It draws the line in the right place. Agile makes change cheap inside the envelope precisely so that the envelope itself can stay governed, and the two are not in tension.

options.text: That agile delivery replaces change control with continuous reprioritisation, which is faster and equally rigorous because stakeholders inspect the increment and agree any adjustments together at every sprint review.
options.rationale: Reprioritisation inside an agreed envelope is not a substitute for control over the envelope itself, and sprint-review agreement covers content rather than budget or date. This answer concedes that nothing governs the boundary, which is not true of a well-run agile project.

options.text: That change control applies to the product increment at each release, so the board reviews the accumulated changes once a release is ready, rather than individual backlog items.
options.rationale: It attaches control to a delivery event rather than to the thing being controlled. A release that stays within scope, budget and date needs no approval, and one that does not needs it before the work is done, not when the release is ready.

options.text: That the product owner holds delegated change authority, so change control has already happened when they reprioritise, provided the sprint goal is set with the team first.
options.rationale: Close, and it overstates the delegation. Product owners are usually delegated authority over content and order, not over the funding envelope or the committed date, and involving the team in the sprint goal does not extend that authority.

questions.explanation: The distinction is between changing what is built and changing what was agreed. Reordering the backlog inside a fixed budget, date and scope boundary is the product owner exercising ordinary authority and needs no ceremony. Moving the boundary itself is a change to the organisation's commitment and needs the same approval anywhere. Agile lowers the cost of the first kind, which is what makes governing the second kind affordable.
questions.mindset: Agile makes change cheap inside the agreed envelope, and the envelope itself still answers to whoever set it.

questions.stem: The board below shows how many items are sitting in each stage of the team's workflow this morning. Select the stage where work is accumulating and the flow constraint sits.

graphic.title: Workflow board, five stages left to right with item counts
graphic.caption: Select a stage. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between stages, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Ready 6
regions.rationale: A queue of ready work is a supply of things not yet started. It says the team has work available, which is a different condition from work being stuck.

regions.label: Build 4
regions.rationale: Four items in build for a team of this size is ordinary work in progress. Nothing here suggests items are arriving faster than they leave.

regions.label: Review 14
regions.rationale: Fourteen items waiting against three or four everywhere else is the accumulation that marks the constraint: work arrives here faster than it can be cleared, and everything downstream is starved.

regions.label: Test 3
regions.rationale: A thin test column downstream of a large queue is a symptom rather than the cause. Test is starved because review is not releasing work to it.

regions.label: Done 41
regions.rationale: Completed items accumulate by design; the column only ever grows. A large done count says the team delivers, not that anything is blocked.

questions.explanation: The constraint is the stage where work arrives faster than it departs, and it shows up as a queue in front of it and starvation behind it. Review has both. The useful responses follow from that reading: limit what is started upstream, or add capability to clear reviews, rather than pushing harder on build, which would only make the queue longer.
questions.mindset: Find the constraint where work piles up, not where people look busiest.

questions.stem: Your team maintains an impediment log. Reviewing it, you find eleven open items, of which nine have been open for more than three weeks and are all owned by people outside the team. Items the team owns itself are usually cleared within two days. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: The team is raising too many impediments, and the threshold for logging one should be raised so the log stays short enough to review properly in each standup.
options.rationale: Nine genuine blockers outside the team's control is not over-reporting. Raising the threshold would give a shorter, tidier log and leave the same work blocked, now invisibly.

options.text: Impediments outside the team's control are not being escalated with enough force, and the project manager should be pursuing them directly.
options.rationale: A log is a record, not a mechanism. Items owned externally and open for weeks are the ones that need someone with reach across the organisation chasing them, which is the project manager's job.

options.text: The log is being used correctly, and the ageing items simply reflect organisational realities beyond the project that the team should record as known constraints.
options.rationale: Accepting three-week blockers as the way of things, and filing them as known constraints, is how a team learns that raising an impediment achieves nothing. Some will be immovable; nine of eleven will not be.

options.text: The team should re-plan its next sprint to avoid the areas where these impediments occur, pulling forward backlog items with no outside dependencies.
options.rationale: Re-planning the next sprint around blockers by pulling forward unaffected backlog items helps occasionally and shrinks what the project can attempt. It also leaves the same obstacles in place for whoever hits them next.

questions.explanation: An impediment log measures how well obstacles are being cleared, and ageing items owned outside the team are the specific signal that escalation is not working. Those are the ones the project manager exists to pursue, because they need standing the team does not have. Raising the logging threshold, accepting the ageing as normal, and planning around the blockers all reduce the visible problem without touching the actual one.
questions.mindset: A log records obstacles; someone with reach still has to go and clear the old ones.

questions.stem: A project carries two quantified risks: a threat with a 30 percent probability and a 250,000 impact, and an opportunity with a 40 percent probability and a 100,000 benefit. Using the convention that threats are negative and opportunities positive, work out the expected monetary value of the threat and then the net expected monetary value of the pair.

blanks.label: Expected monetary value of the threat, in dollars
blanks.rationale: EMV is probability multiplied by impact: 0.30 × 250,000 = 75,000, carried as −75,000 because a threat reduces value.

blanks.label: Net expected monetary value of both risks, in dollars
blanks.rationale: The opportunity contributes 0.40 × 100,000 = +40,000. Netting the two gives −75,000 + 40,000 = −35,000, so the pair is a net threat.

questions.explanation: Expected monetary value weights an outcome by its likelihood, and summing across risks with a consistent sign convention gives the net exposure a contingency provision has to cover. What the single figure hides is shape: a net of −35,000 could come from many small risks or, as here, from one large threat partly offset by an opportunity that may not arrive. The number sizes the reserve; the distribution behind it decides the response.
questions.mindset: Treat an expected value as a sizing figure for a set of risks, and look at what lies behind it before choosing a response.

questions.stem: An agile programme building a benefits-claims portal releases to production every two weeks, depends on two external suppliers and is awaiting a data-protection impact assessment. It has no risk register. The delivery manager argues that iterative delivery manages risk inherently, through short feedback loops and frequent releases. Which two responses are best supported?

options.text: Short iterations genuinely reduce delivery risk by shortening the time between a wrong assumption and the evidence of it.
options.rationale: This part of the argument is sound and worth conceding. Frequent working software is a real risk control, and treating it as one is what makes the rest of the conversation credible.

options.text: Risks that sit outside the iteration — regulatory, supplier, security, funding — are not surfaced by delivery cadence and still need explicit management.
options.rationale: Iteration exposes risks in what is being built. A supplier failing or a regulation changing will not appear in a sprint review no matter how frequent it is.

options.text: A risk register is required by the organisation's methodology, so the programme must produce one regardless of the delivery manager's view.
options.rationale: An appeal to process compliance loses the argument even when it wins it. Overriding the delivery manager's view gives him no reason to use the register once it exists, and it never addresses which risks iteration misses.

options.text: The absence of a register means risk is not being managed at all, so a full risk identification workshop is needed before anything else.
options.rationale: Overstated. Fortnightly releases are a genuine control over delivery risk, so plenty is being managed; the gap is in the categories iteration does not reach. A workshop built on the premise that nothing is managed re-covers ground the team already handles well.

options.text: Risk should be managed by adding a risk item to the backlog whenever one is identified, for the product owner to prioritise each sprint.
options.rationale: Backlog items are work to be done and many risks call for monitoring rather than action. Forcing every risk into the backlog for sprint prioritisation either inflates it or loses the ones with no current task, such as a pending assessment outcome.

questions.explanation: The delivery manager is half right, and the productive answer concedes that half. Iteration is a genuine control over the risk that the wrong thing is being built, because it shortens the feedback loop. It does nothing about risks whose source is outside the delivery: suppliers, regulators, security, funding. Those need identifying, owning and monitoring explicitly, whatever the cadence of the work.
questions.mindset: Credit what a delivery approach genuinely controls, then look deliberately for the risks it cannot see.

questions.stem: You have transferred a threat of data loss to a specialist backup provider under contract. In review, a team member points out that the provider could itself fail, and that some exposure remains even when they perform. How should these two be recorded?

options.text: Provider failure is a secondary risk arising from the transfer response; the exposure that remains after the response works is residual risk. Both are recorded and owned.
options.rationale: The distinction is exactly this: a secondary risk is created by the response itself, and residual risk is what the response does not remove. Both need an owner or they vanish from view.

options.text: Both are residual risks, since both remain after the transfer response has been applied; record them as one entry under the original data-loss threat.
options.rationale: It collapses two different things into one entry. Provider failure did not exist before the transfer; it was introduced by it, and responses that create new exposure need tracking as their own category with their own response.

options.text: Both are secondary risks, since both arise as a consequence of the decision to transfer; record each as a new entry owned by the manager of the provider contract.
options.rationale: Residual exposure is not a consequence of transferring. It is the part of the original threat the response never covered, and it would have existed under most other responses too, so handing it to the contract manager misplaces it.

options.text: Neither needs recording, since the threat has been transferred and the provider now owns it; the contract's service levels are then monitored in supplier reviews.
options.rationale: Transfer moves impact and usually delivery, and it does not move accountability for the outcome. Watching service levels in supplier reviews tracks the provider, not the exposure: a provider failing is still your data loss, and the contract is the recourse rather than the protection.

questions.explanation: Every risk response leaves something behind and often creates something new. What is left over is residual risk; what the response itself introduces is secondary risk. Transfer is the response where the distinction bites hardest, because it feels final and is not: the counterparty becomes a new source of exposure, and accountability for the outcome stays where it started.
questions.mindset: A risk response changes the exposure rather than ending it, so record both what it leaves behind and what it creates.

questions.stem: You are the scrum master for a team building a bus operator's ticketing app. Over the last fourteen sprints, customer-reported defects per sprint have ranged from two to nine, averaging five, and the team's way of working has not changed in that period. Last sprint produced nine. The product owner wants a mandatory manual exploratory test session before every release from next sprint, which the team estimates will cost about 10% of its capacity. What should you do?

options.text: Run a root-cause analysis with the team on last sprint's nine defects before deciding anything, so that any new step targets what actually went wrong in that particular sprint.
options.rationale: This is the hunt-for-a-special-cause error. Nine sits inside the range an unchanged process has produced for fourteen sprints, so an analysis of that one sprint will find the ordinary causes present in every sprint and present them as the reason it was bad.

options.text: Agree to trial the exploratory test session for two sprints, then compare the defect counts against last sprint's nine to decide whether it is worth keeping.
options.rationale: This is the rigged-trial error. Measured against a sprint at the top of the normal range, the next two are likely to look better whatever is done, so the trial would appear to confirm the new step even if it contributed nothing.

options.text: Support the product owner's decision and add the session from next sprint, since balancing quality against capacity is hers to set and the team can review its effect at the next retrospective.
options.rationale: This is the defer-on-authority error. The product owner does own that balance, but she is exercising it on a misreading of the data, and supplying the history before a 10% capacity commitment is made is the scrum master's job rather than an intrusion on hers.

options.text: Show the product owner the fourteen-sprint history, which puts nine inside the range the current process has already produced, and ask whether the average of five is the real problem.
options.rationale: The proposal treats one sprint as a signal when the history says it is noise. Putting the range in front of the product owner turns a reaction into a choice: if five defects a sprint is too many, that is worth improving, and it calls for a change to the process aimed at the average rather than a step bolted on in response to one result.

questions.explanation: Every process produces a range of results, and a result inside that range is not evidence that anything has changed. Reacting to one high point by adding a step, or hunting for what went wrong that week, is tampering: it adds cost and usually makes the process more variable without moving its average. The disciplined response is to ask whether the normal level is acceptable, and if it is not, to improve the system that produces it, then judge the change against the whole history rather than the worst recent point.
questions.mindset: Before changing a process because of one bad result, check whether that process has produced results like it before.

questions.stem: A new expenses system technically launched on time and works correctly. Six weeks later, 70 percent of claims are still being submitted on the old spreadsheet, which finance continues to accept. Which two actions are most likely to shift adoption?

options.text: Work with finance to stop accepting the old spreadsheet from an announced date.
options.rationale: As long as the old route works, the new one is optional, and optional change does not happen. Closing the alternative is usually the single highest-leverage move available.

options.text: Find out from the people still using the spreadsheet what the new system makes harder, and fix what is real.
options.rationale: Seventy percent is too many for the explanation to be habit alone. Something in the new flow is worse for them, and closing the old route without fixing it converts resistance into resentment.

options.text: Issue a communication from the sponsor reminding everyone that the new system is now mandatory for all claims.
options.rationale: A reminder that something is mandatory for all claims while the alternative is still accepted teaches people that the mandate is rhetorical. Announcements do not substitute for closing the old route and fixing the new one.

options.text: Run additional training sessions on the new system for all claimants, with a short guide to what has changed.
options.rationale: Training and a guide answer a capability problem, and nothing here suggests people cannot use the system. Teaching a workforce that is choosing not to adopt, while the spreadsheet is still accepted, is expensive and beside the point.

options.text: Report the adoption figure as a project risk and hand it to the operational owner at closure.
options.rationale: A delivered system nobody uses has not delivered its benefit. Recording that as a risk and handing it on is closure of the project rather than completion of the change.

questions.explanation: Technical delivery and organisational change are different achievements, and a working system with 70 percent non-adoption has only the first. Two things move it together: remove the alternative, and find out what the new flow makes worse before you do. Doing only the first produces workarounds and ill will; doing only the second leaves the change optional. Communication and training address a willingness and capability problem that the evidence does not support.
questions.mindset: A change stays optional while the old way still works, and resented if the new way is worse, so both have to be dealt with.

questions.stem: Eight months into a two-year project building an invoicing tool for small accountancy firms, a competitor releases a product that does most of what yours will do, free. The business case assumes 4,000 paying subscribers by the end of year two. Your project is on schedule and on budget. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Raise it with the sponsor as a threat to the business case, with an assessment of how the competitor's release affects the expected benefits.
options.rationale: The business case is what justifies the spend and it has just been challenged by something outside the project. Surfacing that with an assessment is the project manager's obligation, and the decision is the sponsor's.

options.text: Continue as planned and report the release in the next monthly status report, since the project is performing well against its baselines and market response is not the project's remit.
options.rationale: Performing well against a baseline says nothing about whether the work is still worth doing, and a line in a routine status report is not the same as putting a challenged business case to the person who owns it. A project that delivers perfectly into a changed market has succeeded at the wrong thing.

options.text: Work with the product lead to propose additional features that differentiate your product from the competitor's offering, and submit them through change control.
options.rationale: It jumps to a response before anyone has decided whether to keep going; routing the features through change control makes the process proper but still answers the wrong question first. Adding scope to a project whose justification is in question is the most expensive available way to find out.

options.text: Commission market analysis to establish how much of your expected market the competitor will take, so the sponsor has the full picture.
options.rationale: The analysis may well be needed, and commissioning it is the sponsor's call rather than a reason to hold the news back until a complete picture exists. It also spends weeks before the sponsor knows anything.

questions.explanation: Monitoring the external environment for things that undermine the business case is part of the role, and a competitor giving away most of your value proposition is exactly that. On schedule and on budget is not a defence, because both are measures of execution rather than of worth. It goes to the sponsor with an assessment of the effect on benefits, and what happens next — continue, pivot, or stop — is theirs to decide.
questions.mindset: Being on schedule and on budget says nothing about whether the work is still worth doing.

questions.stem: Your hardware rollout depends on a component manufactured in a single country that has just introduced export licensing for that category of goods. Licences are being granted, but with a six to ten week lead time that did not previously exist. Your rollout starts in nine weeks. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Establish what the licensing actually applies to and what alternatives exist, then take the sponsor a re-plan with the options and their costs.
options.rationale: The exposure is real and its shape is unknown: scope of the rule, availability of alternatives, whether a phased start works. Establishing that first is what makes the re-plan a decision rather than a reaction.

options.text: Place the licence applications immediately for the full rollout quantity so that the lead time starts running, then re-plan around the confirmed dates with the sponsor.
options.rationale: Starting the clock on licences is attractive, but doing it for the full quantity commits you before you know whether a second source or a phased approach is better. It also fixes the plan to the slowest input.

options.text: Notify affected stakeholders that the rollout will be delayed by six to ten weeks, and revise the schedule baseline accordingly through change control.
options.rationale: It announces a delay to the affected stakeholders, and formalises it in the baseline, before establishing whether one is necessary. A phased start, existing stock or an alternative source may absorb some or all of it.

options.text: Raise it in the risk register with a high impact rating, assign the procurement lead as owner, and monitor the licensing situation weekly until lead times settle.
options.rationale: This is no longer a risk. The rule exists and the lead time is known, so giving it an owner and monitoring it as something that might happen is the wrong instrument for an issue that already has.

questions.explanation: An external change that has already happened is an issue rather than a risk, and it is worked by establishing its actual boundaries before responding. What the rule covers, what alternatives exist and whether the rollout can be phased are all knowable in days and all change the answer. The re-plan then goes to the sponsor as options with costs, because the trade-off between delay, cost and a different source is theirs.
questions.mindset: When an external change has already landed, find its real edges before choosing a response to it.

questions.stem: You take over a stalled warehouse relocation eleven months in. The original sponsor has left, the objectives in the charter refer to a distribution contract the company lost last quarter, and the team is still building to them because nobody told them otherwise. The new sponsor is available and engaged. The team is a week from delivering a racking layout sized for volumes that no longer exist. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Let the racking layout complete as planned, then raise the change through the change control process once there is a deliverable to compare against.
options.rationale: This is the process-completeness error: finishing known-wrong work because a procedure has a slot for it later. Change control governs decisions about scope, not permission to keep building against a purpose everyone can already see is void.

options.text: Stop the racking work and take the discrepancy to the new sponsor with a recommendation on what the project should now be for.
options.rationale: The team is a week from spending real money against a purpose that expired. Halting that specific piece and bringing the sponsor a recommendation rather than a problem is what makes the conversation short and the decision informed.

options.text: Update the charter to reflect current volumes and circulate the revised version to the team and the new sponsor.
options.rationale: This is the document-first error. Rewriting the charter yourself asserts a new purpose that the sponsor has not agreed, and a charter is the record of an alignment rather than the means of creating one.

options.text: Run a workshop with the team to re-derive the objectives from what the business needs today.
options.rationale: This is the consultation-misdirected error: the team can describe the work but cannot authorise a change of purpose. A workshop produces a well-argued position that still has to go to the sponsor, at the cost of the week you do not have.

questions.explanation: When the stated purpose of a project has been overtaken by events, the priority is to stop the spend that is running against it and get the decision to whoever now owns it. Speed matters more than completeness here, because every day of delay converts into work that will be thrown away. Bringing a recommendation rather than an open question is what keeps the escalation to one conversation instead of three.
questions.mindset: Work to the outcome the organisation needs now, not the one the paperwork was written for.

questions.stem: A product team pivots from serving small independent retailers to serving two large grocery chains. The product owner announces the change at a sprint review with a slide. Three sprints later the team is still refining stories written for the old audience, and in refinement two developers argue about a feature neither chain has asked for. Nobody has objected to the pivot. What is the most useful thing for the project manager to do?

options.text: Ask the product owner to repeat the pivot rationale at the next review, with more detail on the commercial case and time set aside for the team's questions.
options.rationale: This is the repeat-the-broadcast error. The first announcement did not fail because it was too short or allowed no questions; it failed because a slide cannot be used as a decision aid during refinement, and a longer presentation will not be either.

options.text: Raise the stale stories in the retrospective and ask the team to agree an action to keep the backlog current, with an owner and a date to review it against the pivot.
options.rationale: This is the wrong-forum error. Retrospectives improve how the team works, and an owned action on backlog hygiene, even one checked against the pivot, still treats this as a process lapse when it is a gap in what the team knows about the product.

options.text: Have the two chains' account managers brief the team directly on what those customers need, with time for developers to ask about the disputed feature.
options.rationale: This is the right-move-wrong-order error. A briefing, even an interactive one, lands on top of a backlog still full of items for the old audience, so the team hears the new direction and then goes back to a queue that contradicts it.

options.text: Work with the product owner to rewrite the backlog against the two chains, then have the team walk the revised items and mark what no longer applies.
options.rationale: The pivot has to reach the artefact the team actually touches. Having the team walk the revised backlog is what surfaces the leftovers and converts an announcement into something they can apply on their own next week.

questions.explanation: Direction that lives only in an announcement does not change behaviour, because the thing a team works from is its queue. The reliable route is to change the artefact and then have the team handle it, since that is what exposes the items written under the old assumption. Silence after a pivot is usually a sign that people have nothing to disagree with yet, not that they have understood.
questions.mindset: A change of direction is not communicated until the team can use it to make decisions without you.

questions.stem: Two department heads both need the same test rig in the final fortnight before your go-live. Each has emailed you separately arguing their case, each has copied your sponsor, and the tone has sharpened over three exchanges. Your project needs the rig for two of those fourteen days. Neither head has spoken to the other. The sponsor has not replied to either email. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Convene the two heads, establish what each actually needs the rig for and by when, and work the schedule from the constraints rather than the claims.
options.rationale: Positions harden in email and soften in a room. Separating the underlying need from the stated demand is what usually reveals that the two requirements are not in as direct a collision as three rounds of correspondence made them look.

options.text: Reply to both, copying the sponsor, setting out the two days your project needs and proposing a schedule that splits the remaining twelve evenly between the two departments.
options.rationale: This is the solve-it-in-writing error. A fourth email into a thread that has sharpened three times adds a third position to a dispute that already has two, and an even split commits you publicly to a schedule before you know what either head actually needs.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to arbitrate between the two heads, since both have already escalated by copying the sponsor in and the sponsor holds authority over both departments.
options.rationale: This is the premature-escalation error. Copying the sponsor is not the same as having tried to resolve it: neither head has spoken to the other, so the disagreement has not been attempted at the level that can resolve it, and an arbitrated split leaves both managing the outcome rather than owning it.

options.text: Book the rig for your two days immediately so that your go-live is protected, then leave the two departments to settle the remaining twelve days between themselves.
options.rationale: This is the secure-your-own-interest error. Protecting your go-live first makes you a third claimant in a dispute you will need both heads' goodwill to survive, particularly during a fortnight when either could quietly deprioritise your testing.

questions.explanation: A dispute conducted in writing between parties who have not spoken tends to escalate, because each exchange is a position statement rather than an exploration. Bringing the parties together and working from underlying need rather than stated demand is what makes room visible. Escalation stays available and becomes better founded once a genuine attempt at the working level has been made and recorded.
questions.mindset: Get the people who disagree into the same conversation before you carry either position forward.

questions.stem: On a hybrid programme building a warehouse management system, an agile software squad works alongside a stage-gated rollout of handheld scanners. This week the squad made three decisions that you, as delivery lead, would not have made. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: The squad chose a single-page layout for the picking screen over the step-by-step layout you prefer. Warehouse staff will try it in next sprint's usability session, and either layout can be rebuilt within a sprint. You should
The squad has planned the scanner integration for sprint 9, unaware that the scanner vendor told you yesterday its firmware will ship four weeks late. You should

To speed up testing, the squad has agreed to load real customer delivery addresses into a test environment that agency contractors can reach, which the client's data-processing terms forbid. You should

options.text: let the decision stand and ask what the usability session showed
options.rationale: The choice is cheap to reverse and will shortly be tested against the people who use the screen. Overruling it now buys a preference at the price of the squad's ownership, when the evidence that settles it is one sprint away.

options.text: give the squad the vendor's news and let it re-plan the integration
options.rationale: The decision went wrong for want of information that only you held, not for want of judgement. Supplying the information fixes the cause and leaves the plan with the people who will deliver it.

options.text: stop the decision now and explain the contractual term it breaches
options.rationale: The squad cannot agree away an obligation the client's terms impose, so this decision was never inside its authority. Stopping it at once limits the exposure, and explaining the term is what stops it reading as an arbitrary override.

options.text: refer the decision to the programme sponsor for a ruling
options.rationale: Not used. None of the three needs the sponsor: two are the squad's own decisions, and the third breaches a term clearly enough that the delivery lead can and should stop it without waiting for a ruling.

options.text: re-plan the affected work yourself and tell the squad the new sequence
options.rationale: Not used. It is tempting for the scanner integration because you hold the vendor's news, but what the squad lacked was the information, not the ability to plan. Re-planning for it takes over a decision it is well placed to make.

questions.explanation: Every time a leader overrides a team's decision, correctness is bought with ownership, so an override is worth making only where the cost of the error is higher than the cost to the team's ownership. A reversible choice that will soon be tested against evidence is cheaper to let run than to reverse. A decision made on missing information is mended by supplying the information, not by taking the decision away. A decision that breaches an obligation the team has no power to waive was never inside its authority, and stopping it promptly protects the team rather than overruling it.
questions.mindset: Before overruling a team, weigh what the error would cost against the ownership the override will cost.

questions.stem: In daily standups you have started assigning the day's work item by item, because two sprints ago the team left an urgent defect unclaimed for a day. Velocity has held steady. In the last retrospective a senior developer said, carefully, that standup now feels like a status meeting, and three others nodded. Nobody has asked you to stop. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Continue for now, since velocity has held, and revisit the practice once the team formally asks for it to change or the numbers start to slip.
options.rationale: This is the metric-as-permission error. Velocity measures throughput, not ownership, and waiting for a formal request or a falling number ignores that a team nodding along in a retrospective has already asked in the only register available to it.

options.text: Stop assigning work, explain why you started, and agree with the team how urgent items will get picked up.
options.rationale: The practice was a response to a real failure, so naming that failure is what stops the withdrawal reading as a reversal on a whim. Agreeing the mechanism for urgent work addresses the original problem without keeping the cure that caused this one.

options.text: Keep assigning only the urgent items until the team shows it can pick them up reliably, and let it self-organise around everything else.
options.rationale: This is the split-the-difference error. It reserves exactly the decisions that carry the most learning, sets a test the team cannot pass while you are still taking those decisions, and leaves standup feeling like a meeting where the important calls are made by someone else.

options.text: Ask the team in the next retrospective whether they would like you to stop assigning work, and agree a trial period before changing anything.
options.rationale: This is the false-consultation error. The team has already signalled its view, and asking it to formally request that its manager relinquish control, then wait out a trial, puts the cost of speaking up on the people with the least power to bear it.

questions.explanation: A control introduced to fix a specific failure tends to outlive the failure, because nothing forces a review of it while the numbers look fine. The correction is to withdraw the control, state plainly why it existed, and replace it with an agreement the team owns. Hedged withdrawals keep the highest-value decisions in the manager's hands, which is precisely where the team stops learning.
questions.mindset: Ownership grows where the team is allowed to carry the consequences of its own decisions.

questions.stem: A regulatory reporting project has a general counsel who holds an effective veto at the sign-off gate but has attended none of the six monthly steering meetings and answers emails in about a fortnight. Your gate is eleven weeks away. Her deputy attends everything, is well informed, and has told you twice that he cannot commit on her behalf. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Ask the general counsel what form and frequency of contact would let her form a view before the gate, and rebuild the engagement around her answer.
options.rationale: Six months of non-attendance is evidence the current mechanism does not fit her, and she is the only person who can say what would. Redesigning around the answer is what converts a stakeholder who is absent into one who is merely differently engaged.

options.text: Work through the deputy to surface legal concerns early, while being explicit with him that the decision itself still needs the general counsel.
options.rationale: The deputy is informed and cannot commit, so he is a route to the issues rather than to the decision. Naming that distinction openly stops the arrangement drifting into an assumption that his comfort equals her approval.

options.text: Treat the deputy's attendance and informed participation as the department's representation, and proceed to the gate on that basis with his comments recorded in the minutes.
options.rationale: This is the proxy-as-principal error. He has told you twice that he cannot commit, so relying on him, minuted or not, substitutes the person who is available for the person who holds the veto, and it fails at the gate rather than before it.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to require the general counsel's attendance at the remaining steering meetings, where the other approvers form their views.
options.rationale: This is the compel-attendance error. It fills a seat with someone who has demonstrated for six months that this forum is not how she engages, and it spends sponsor authority on a stakeholder you will need to work with well beyond this gate. Sharing a room with the other approvers does not make it the right room for her.

options.text: Record the risk of late legal objection in the register, with a mitigation of circulating gate documents to the general counsel early.
options.rationale: This is the register-as-action error. Circulating documents to someone with a fortnight's email latency is the mechanism that has already failed, so sending them earlier restates the problem in the column marked solution.
