questions.explanation: A stakeholder with high authority and low observable engagement is not disengaged so much as engaged on terms the project has not discovered. The work is to find those terms from the stakeholder directly, and to use the available deputy for what a deputy can actually do, which is early sight of the issues rather than the decision itself. Substituting the accessible person for the accountable one is the failure this pattern most reliably produces.
questions.mindset: Engagement is designed around the stakeholder you have, not the one the plan assumed.

questions.stem: A finance transformation has three stakeholder groups whose expectations have drifted apart during a long planning phase. The project manager is choosing how to close each gap, and the right move differs in each case. Match each situation to the approach that fits it best. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: Two directors want incompatible things from the same module, both are certain they were promised it, and the contemporaneous notes are ambiguous.
A user group expects a reporting capability that was descoped in month two, and the descoping was recorded but never communicated to them.
A regional head expects a March cutover; the plan has always said June, and he has been told June four times and repeats March each month.

options.text: Bring both parties to a joint session and negotiate one agreed position
options.rationale: Two irreconcilable expectations with no authoritative record cannot be settled by producing evidence, because the evidence is ambiguous. What is left is a negotiation between the two holders, conducted together so neither hears the outcome secondhand.

options.text: Communicate the decision that was already taken, with its rationale and consequences
options.rationale: Here the gap is purely informational: a decision was properly made and never travelled. The group needs the decision, why it was taken and what it means for them, not a renegotiation of a settled question.

options.text: Investigate why the message is not landing before repeating it again
options.rationale: Four accurate communications that produced no change mean the barrier is not the information. Something, whether an incentive, a commitment made elsewhere or a misunderstanding of what cutover means, is holding the expectation in place.

options.text: Refer the disagreement upward for a ruling
options.rationale: Not used. Escalation suits a genuine deadlock between parties who have tried and failed to agree, and none of these three has yet had a serious attempt at the working level.

options.text: Point to the approved baseline and hold the line
options.rationale: Not used. Citing the baseline settles what the project is committed to and does nothing about why someone believes otherwise, which is the live problem in all three situations.

questions.explanation: Expectation gaps have different causes and the technique has to match the cause. Genuinely competing expectations with no clear record need negotiation between the holders; a properly taken decision that never reached the affected group needs communication rather than reopening; and an expectation that survives repeated accurate correction signals a barrier that has to be found before any further message will land. Reaching for the baseline or for escalation treats all three as the same problem.
questions.mindset: Diagnose why expectations diverged before choosing the technique for closing the gap.

questions.stem: Your product owner, wanting to close a deal, told a prospective customer that a bulk import feature would ship in the next release. The team has not sized it, it is not in the sprint, and two developers think it is a fortnight of work. The customer has repeated the commitment in writing. The product owner tells you privately that she may have got ahead of herself. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Agree with the product owner to pull the bulk import into the current sprint, displacing lower-value items, so that the commitment is met.
options.rationale: This is the honour-it-regardless error. Agreeing it with the product owner does not change what it does: it rewards a commitment made outside the team's planning, rests on a fortnight figure nobody has sized, and silently transfers the cost to whichever stakeholders were expecting the displaced items.

options.text: Have the team size the feature, then work with the product owner on what can honestly be committed and get the corrected position to the customer quickly.
options.rationale: The estimate is the missing input and two developers' impression is not one. Correcting the customer early costs a difficult conversation now instead of a broken commitment later, when the customer has planned around it.

options.text: Ask the product owner to contact the customer herself this week and withdraw the date, since she made the commitment.
options.rationale: This is the ownership-as-abdication error. She did make it, and leaving her to unwind it alone forfeits the sizing information the team holds; withdrawing the date with nothing reliable to put in its place risks a second inaccurate position replacing the first.

options.text: Add the feature to the top of the backlog, and update the customer once the next refinement session has sized it and established whether the date is achievable.
options.rationale: This is the defer-the-bad-news error. It leaves a written commitment standing until the next refinement session comes round, and every day of that delay makes the correction more expensive for the customer, who is already planning around the date, to absorb.

questions.explanation: A commitment made without the team's input is a defect in the expectation rather than in the plan, and the repair is to establish the real position and communicate it before the customer builds on it. Meeting the promise anyway teaches that commitments made outside planning will be absorbed, and delegating the retraction to whoever made the error discards the information that would make the second message reliable.
questions.mindset: An expectation that cannot be met is cheapest to correct on the day it is created.

questions.stem: A shared platform is being rolled out to two divisions. The retail division has been told it will get a phased rollout with a pilot; the wholesale division has been told the same platform arrives in a single cutover. Both understandings came from your own steering pack, which used different wording in two sections. Build has assumed a single cutover throughout. Discovery is three weeks from complete. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Confirm the single cutover to retail in writing, since build has assumed it throughout and reworking for a phased pilot now would be expensive.
options.rationale: This is the cheapest-for-the-project error. Explaining the cost does not change that it resolves the contradiction by overruling one division without discussion, and retail may have made staffing or trading decisions on the phased understanding that a cutover would strand.

options.text: Correct the steering pack wording in the next issue, flagging the change on its cover, so that future reporting is unambiguous.
options.rationale: This is the fix-the-artefact error. A flagged revision prevents recurrence and still leaves both divisions holding the two understandings they already have, since neither will read a revised section as a retraction of what they were told or as a prompt to revisit plans built on it.

options.text: Meet each division separately to find out what they now expect and have planned around, then design a rollout that accommodates both.
options.rationale: This is the separate-conversations error. Learning what each has planned around is useful, but handling it division by division risks producing a third position, and it treats a contradiction the project introduced as though it were a genuine difference in requirements.

options.text: Take the contradiction to both divisions together, acknowledge it originated in your reporting, and establish one rollout approach both can plan against.
options.rationale: A joint correction stops each division hearing a different second version, and owning the source is what makes the correction credible. Establishing one approach they can plan against is the actual deliverable, not the apology.

questions.explanation: Where a project's own communication has created two incompatible expectations, the correction belongs in one conversation with both parties, because sequential correction produces a fresh set of divergent understandings. Owning the source plainly is what earns the room to settle it, and the purpose of the session is a single approach both can plan against rather than a determination of who was right.
questions.mindset: When you created the divergence, correct it yourself before it costs either party a decision.

questions.stem: Halfway through a twelve-month customer portal build, your client's own market has shifted and their competitors have launched self-service returns. Your contract, requirements and baseline contain no returns capability and the client has raised nothing formally. In an informal call their operations lead mentioned returns three times. Your delivery is on schedule and within budget. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Continue to the baseline until the client raises a formal change, since the contract is being met and an informal remark is not an instruction to vary the scope.
options.rationale: This is the contract-compliance error. Waiting for a formal change while the customer's need moves produces a project that succeeds against its measures and lands something the client can no longer use, and the formal request may arrive only when the schedule can no longer absorb it.

options.text: Add a returns capability to the design now, before the build moves past the order screens, so the portal is not obsolete at launch and the change costs as little as possible.
options.rationale: This is the anticipate-and-build error. Acting early does reduce the cost of a change, but it commits budget and schedule to a requirement the client has not confirmed, and unrequested scope delivered against a fixed contract is difficult to be paid for and harder to defend.

options.text: Raise the shift with the client, establish whether returns has become a real requirement, and set out the options and their cost while there is still time to act.
options.rationale: Three unprompted mentions is a signal worth testing, and testing it costs a conversation. Presenting options with costs keeps the decision with the client rather than converting an observation into unrequested scope.

options.text: Record the market change in the risk register with an owner and a trigger, and review it at each monthly risk meeting until the client raises it formally.
options.rationale: This is the passive-monitoring error. A well-kept register entry still records an exposure the project could reduce today and waits for the client to act, by which point the remaining schedule may be too short to absorb the change.

questions.explanation: Customer expectations move with the customer's own environment, and a project that tracks only formal requests will discover the movement at acceptance. Informal signals are worth surfacing deliberately rather than acting on unilaterally: raising the question preserves the client's authority over scope while there is still schedule to spend, whereas building ahead of confirmation and waiting for a formal request both remove that choice in opposite directions.
questions.mindset: Track what the customer now needs, not only what the customer formally asked for.

questions.stem: An internal operations team is the customer for a scheduling tool. For four consecutive sprints they have accepted the demo, then raised defects in the following week that turn out to be behaviours the team never agreed to build. Their manager is frustrated, your team is demoralised, and the rework is now about a fifth of each sprint. Acceptance criteria exist and are written by your business analyst. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Require the operations manager to review and sign the business analyst's acceptance criteria before development starts on each item, so that her team is accountable for what is built.
options.rationale: This is the signature-as-understanding error. A signature on someone else's document creates accountability for a misunderstanding rather than preventing it, and the same behaviours will surface in the same place the following week, now with a signed record attached.

options.text: Extend the demo into a longer hands-on session with two or three operations staff, so they can exercise the software on real scheduling cases before accepting it.
options.rationale: This is the too-late-to-help error. Real cases and real users catch the mismatch a few days earlier, but still at the end of the build rather than the start, so the item has already been built to the wrong understanding and the rework is deferred rather than avoided.

options.text: Have the operations team write or co-write the acceptance criteria before each item is built, with the business analyst facilitating, and confirm them together at refinement.
options.rationale: Criteria written by an analyst capture what the analyst understood, which is why the mismatch appears only once operations use the thing. Co-writing moves the disagreement to before the build, where it costs a conversation rather than a fifth of a sprint.

options.text: Track the post-acceptance defects separately as new requirements, agree their priority with the operations manager, and schedule them into later sprints.
options.rationale: This is the reclassify-the-symptom error. Renaming the rework and agreeing its priority makes the reporting tidier and leaves the cause untouched, while the operations team continues to experience the tool as not doing what they expected.

questions.explanation: Repeated acceptance followed by immediate defect reports usually means the acceptance criteria describe someone's interpretation of the need rather than the need. The durable fix is to move the customer upstream into defining what good looks like before the work starts, since that is the only point at which the misunderstanding is cheap. Tightening the ceremony at the end, or formalising sign-off on the same flawed document, both leave the misunderstanding in place.
questions.mindset: Acceptance is only meaningful when the customer helped define what they were accepting.

questions.stem: The only engineer who understands your legacy billing interface has resigned and works four more weeks. Her documentation is thin, and the interface has failed twice in two years, each time resolved by her within hours. Two other engineers are capable but have never touched it. Your project depends on that interface through to a cutover in seven months. What should the project manager do with her remaining time?

options.text: Have her write comprehensive documentation of the interface as her main task for the four weeks, including a diagnostic guide to both past failures.
options.rationale: This is the documentation-only error. A document written under time pressure captures what she can articulate, not what she does under pressure, and even a diagnostic guide records her conclusions about two failures rather than the judgement that reached them, which does not survive being written down.

options.text: Pair the two engineers with her on real interface work, including a rehearsed failure, and have them write the documentation from what they learn.
options.rationale: Working the interface alongside her is what transfers the diagnostic judgement the failures needed. Having the receivers write the document tests what actually landed, because they can only describe what they now understand.

options.text: Negotiate a retainer so she remains available on call through the cutover in seven months, with a guaranteed response time if the interface fails.
options.rationale: This is the retain-the-dependency error. A guaranteed response time buys insurance and removes the pressure to transfer anything, so in seven months the organisation is in the same position with less time and no remaining leverage.

options.text: Record a series of walkthrough videos in which she explains the interface architecture and talks through how she diagnosed the two previous failures.
options.rationale: This is the capture-without-practice error. Video preserves her explanation of each diagnosis more faithfully than a document and still produces engineers who have watched someone else diagnose a fault rather than engineers who have diagnosed one.

questions.explanation: Tacit knowledge, the kind that resolves an outage in hours, moves through joint work rather than through artefacts. The strongest available transfer puts the receiving people on the real system with the departing expert present, rehearses the failure mode that matters, and uses documentation written by the receivers as the test of what was absorbed. Artefact-first approaches capture the explicable residue and leave the judgement behind.
questions.mindset: Knowledge transfers through shared work, not through documents handed over at the door.

questions.stem: A vendor has run your data platform for three years under a contract ending in five months, and will be replaced by an internal team. The contract requires a handover pack at termination. The vendor is cooperative but its staff are being reassigned as work tails off, and the two people with the deepest platform knowledge leave the account in six weeks. Your internal team is hired but not yet started. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Hold the vendor to the contractual handover pack, ask for a first draft early, and have the internal team review it against the platform in detail when they start.
options.rationale: This is the contract-timing error. An early draft improves the document, but the review still waits for the internal team, and by then the two people who could have explained the platform have left the account, so the gaps it finds have no one left to fill them.

options.text: Ask the vendor's account director to keep the two specialists on the account until the contract ends, offering to fund their extra months from the transition budget if that is what it takes.
options.rationale: This is the plan-that-is-not-yours error. Offering to pay makes the request more attractive and it still depends on a resourcing decision inside the vendor, and on two people's own careers; if it is declined at week five, the window has been spent without a fallback.

options.text: Bring the internal team's start date forward if possible and, whether or not that succeeds, secure structured transfer from the two departing specialists within the six weeks.
options.rationale: The binding constraint is six weeks, not five months, and it is set by people rather than by the contract. Acting on the specialists' window is what protects the knowledge even in the case where the internal start cannot be moved.

options.text: Commission the vendor to have the two specialists produce enhanced runbooks and architecture documentation before they leave the account in six weeks.
options.rationale: This is the artefact-substitution error. It does act inside the six weeks, but it uses them to generate a description of the platform rather than to build capability, and there is still no one on your side able to interrogate what was written.

questions.explanation: In a transition the real deadline is the date the knowledge leaves the building, which is often well inside the contractual end. Planning has to be built around that window and around receivers who can absorb what is transferred. Contractual handover artefacts and vendor retention requests are both worth having, but neither should be the primary plan, because one arrives too late and the other is not yours to decide.
questions.mindset: Sequence knowledge transfer around when the knowledge leaves, not when the contract ends.

questions.stem: Your sponsor has twice made decisions in steering that contradict information sent in the weekly status report, most recently approving an extra workstream in a week the report flagged a resourcing shortfall. The report runs to nine pages with a one-page summary at the front. The sponsor is engaged in the meetings themselves and asks good questions. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Ask the sponsor directly what she needs from the report, when she reads it, and what would have changed the resourcing decision.
options.rationale: The gap between an engaged sponsor and a contradicted report is a design problem in the reporting, and she is the only source for what would work. Anchoring on the specific decision keeps the conversation concrete rather than a general request for feedback.

options.text: Raise material items that need a decision at the start of the steering meeting itself, rather than relying on the written report to carry them.
options.rationale: Decisions taken in the room should be informed in the room. Putting the decision-relevant items in front of her at the point of decision closes the gap regardless of when or whether the written report is read.

options.text: Expand the executive summary so the resourcing position is unmissable on the first page, with a red flag beside every item that needs a steering decision.
options.rationale: This is the louder-not-different error. A one-page summary already exists and did not carry the point, so more emphasis and flags in the same channel repeat an approach with two failures behind it, without asking why the sponsor is not acting on what she is sent.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to confirm in writing that she has read each weekly report before steering, so that decisions are taken on the reported position.
options.rationale: This is the compliance-over-communication error. A written confirmation creates an audit trail that shifts blame onto the sponsor for the next contradicted decision, and it does nothing to make the information usable at the moment she decides.

options.text: Circulate the report two days earlier in the week, so the sponsor has more time to absorb it and to raise questions before the meeting.
options.rationale: This is the timing-assumption error. It presumes the cause is insufficient reading time rather than format, relevance or channel, and nothing in the sponsor's behaviour, engaged and asking good questions in the room, points to time as the constraint.

questions.explanation: When a decision-maker acts against information you have supplied, the reporting has failed even though it was accurate. The two moves that reliably help are finding out from the recipient what would actually inform her and putting decision-critical items into the forum where decisions are made. Amplifying, formalising or rescheduling the same artefact all assume the format was right and only the delivery was wrong.
questions.mindset: Reporting has done its job only when the decision-maker can act on it.

questions.stem: Your team works across three time zones with a two-hour overlap. Decisions taken during the overlap are not reaching the engineers who are offline, and twice this month work has been built against a decision that had been reversed. The team already runs a daily standup in the overlap and keeps a chat channel that scrolls fast. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Record decisions and their reasoning in a single durable place the whole team reads at the start of its own day, and reference it from the chat channel.
options.rationale: The failure is that decisions live in a fast-scrolling stream and a meeting half the team cannot attend. A durable record read at each person's start of day matches the artefact to how a distributed team actually consumes information.

options.text: Move the daily standup to a time all three zones can attend, rotating the early and late slots between zones each month so decisions are heard by everyone.
options.rationale: This is the synchronise-everything error. With a two-hour overlap there is no time that suits everyone, and rotating the slots only shares out a recurring out-of-hours meeting. It also leaves the real problem, which is persistence: a decision heard once is still lost when it is reversed later.

options.text: Have the overlap group post a summary of each decision and the reasoning behind it to the chat channel immediately after standup, marked clearly as a decision.
options.rationale: This is the same-channel error. Adding the reasoning and a label improves the post, but the channel is already the place decisions are getting lost, so a summary posted into a fast stream is scrolled past by the people who most need it, and a later reversal is just as easy to miss.

options.text: Assign a liaison in each zone to brief their colleagues on decisions taken during the overlap at the start of their day, and to carry questions back to the group.
options.rationale: This is the human-relay error. It introduces three retellings of every decision, adds a dependency on three individuals' availability, and makes the reasoning behind a decision the first thing to be lost; carrying questions back adds a further day of round trip.

questions.explanation: Distributed teams need information that persists and can be consumed asynchronously, because the constraint is that most of the team is asleep when most decisions are made. A single durable record covering the decision and the reasoning behind it, read at the start of each person's day, is what makes reversals visible. Extending synchronous ceremonies or relying on fast channels and human relays all assume everyone is available at the same time.
questions.mindset: In a distributed team, a decision does not exist until it is written somewhere durable.

questions.stem: A data migration you ran over the weekend has corrupted a subset of customer records. Your technical lead is confident it affects under one per cent but cannot confirm the number for six hours. Meanwhile the head of customer service has already emailed her team saying the issue is fixed, a regional director is asking for numbers, and a journalist has contacted the press office. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Wait for the six-hour analysis so that everything communicated is confirmed and accurate, and tell the regional director when the figures will arrive.
options.rationale: This is the accuracy-before-anything error. Giving the regional director a time does not change the fact that six hours of silence leaves the customer service all-clear being acted on and the journalist's enquiry filling the space with a version nobody in the project controls.

options.text: Issue a single position to all parties stating what is known, what is not yet known, that the earlier all-clear was premature, and when the next update will come.
options.rationale: One position from one source stops the divergence, and correcting the premature all-clear is urgent because it is currently being acted on. A committed next update time is what buys the six hours without inviting people to keep asking.

options.text: Brief the regional director and the press office now with the current under-one-per-cent estimate, and correct customer service once the numbers are confirmed in six hours.
options.rationale: This is the tiered-disclosure error. Briefing the senior and external audiences first leaves the operational team acting on a known-false all-clear for six more hours, and the inconsistency surfaces the moment those audiences compare notes.

options.text: Ask the head of customer service to retract her email straight away, and hold all other communication until the analysis completes and the numbers can be stated.
options.rationale: This is the partial-correction error. Retracting without supplying what is currently known creates alarm with no anchor, and holding everything else leaves the regional director and the journalist unanswered for six hours while speculation runs.

questions.explanation: Incident communication is judged on consistency and timeliness rather than completeness. A single statement covering what is known, what remains unknown, what previously said was wrong, and when the next update will arrive gives every audience the same footing and prevents the vacuum being filled elsewhere. Waiting for certainty, briefing audiences in tiers, or retracting without replacing all leave some group acting on a version of events the project knows to be wrong.
questions.mindset: In a live incident, say what is known, what is not, and when you will next speak.

questions.stem: Three weeks into planning a hospital systems replacement, your scope lead, schedule lead and procurement lead have each produced a credible plan. The schedule assumes a supplier chosen by March, procurement's plan reaches award in May, and scope includes a module procurement has been told is out. Each lead is confident their own plan is sound. The sponsor wants a baseline in a fortnight. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Run a joint session where the three plans are laid against each other and every assumption one makes about another is tested.
options.rationale: The conflicts sit at the seams, which is exactly where individual planning cannot see them. Testing each cross-plan assumption in one room is what turns three internally consistent documents into one that holds together.

options.text: Establish which of the conflicting positions the project will actually adopt, and have each lead reflect that single decision in their own plan.
options.rationale: Surfacing the conflicts is only half the work; someone has to decide the March or May question and the module question. Pushing the decision back into all three plans is what stops the reconciliation living only in a meeting note.

options.text: Baseline the three plans as they stand so that the sponsor's fortnight is met, and manage the differences through variance reporting once execution starts.
options.rationale: This is the baseline-the-contradiction error. Meeting the fortnight on paper produces a baseline containing a known two-month impossibility, which measures execution against a target no one can hit, and every subsequent variance report describes a planning defect as delivery underperformance.

options.text: Ask each lead to review the other two plans in writing and submit comments, then consolidate the comments into a single revised plan for the sponsor.
options.rationale: This is the serial-review error. Written comment exchange between three parties who each believe their own plan is sound tends to produce three defences rather than a resolution, and consolidating those defences consumes most of the fortnight without anyone deciding anything.

options.text: Extend the planning period by a month so that each lead has time to refine their own plan in more depth before the baseline is set.
options.rationale: This is the more-of-the-same error. A further month of individual planning deepens three separate plans, and the defect is that they were produced without contact rather than that they were produced too quickly.

questions.explanation: Component plans produced in parallel are individually reasonable and collectively contradictory, because each carries assumptions about the others that were never checked. Integration is the act of surfacing those assumptions together and then deciding, so that one position propagates back into every plan. Baselining the contradiction converts a planning problem into a permanent reporting problem, and asking for more time or written comment leaves the plans as separate as they started.
questions.mindset: One coherent plan beats three good plans that were never reconciled.

questions.stem: You are planning a payments platform replacement. The core ledger must satisfy a regulator whose requirements are published, detailed and unlikely to change; the customer-facing app has no settled requirements and a business sponsor who expects to learn from usage. Your organisation's method mandates a single delivery approach per project. The programme board is asking which approach you will use. What should the project manager propose?

options.text: Use a predictive approach throughout, since the regulated ledger carries the greater consequence of failure, the method mandates consistency, and the board will expect a single plan.
options.rationale: This is the highest-risk-component-wins error. Consequence and the board's expectation of one plan do not make the app's requirements knowable: it fixes requirements that do not yet exist, so the plan's detail is invented and the sponsor's intention to learn from usage is designed out.

options.text: Use an iterative approach throughout, delivering the ledger in increments against the published regulatory requirements, so that the app's evolving needs can be accommodated as well.
options.rationale: This is the uniform-agility error. Accommodating the app does not require iterating the ledger: iterating toward requirements that are already published, detailed and stable spends discovery effort on questions that have documented answers and complicates the evidence trail the regulator expects.

options.text: Follow the mandated single approach and manage the app's uncertainty through a larger contingency reserve held at programme level.
options.rationale: This is the buy-your-way-out error. Reserve absorbs cost variance, wherever it is held, and does nothing about not knowing what to build, so the money is available and the app is still specified from assumptions nobody has tested.

options.text: Propose a predictive approach for the ledger and an iterative one for the app, with defined integration points, and take the tailoring to the board for approval.
options.rationale: The two components differ in exactly the dimension that should drive the choice, which is requirement stability. Taking the tailoring to the board openly is what distinguishes a reasoned deviation from quietly ignoring the organisational method.

questions.explanation: Delivery approach follows the characteristics of the work, principally how stable the requirements are and how much value there is in early feedback. Where components differ sharply on that dimension, a single approach necessarily misfits one of them. Where an organisational method constrains the choice, the professional route is a reasoned tailoring proposal put to whoever owns the method, not a silent deviation and not a compliant plan you already know will not work.
questions.mindset: Fit the delivery approach to the nature of the work, and justify any tailoring openly.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the sequence your project follows to establish and hold its scope. A stakeholder has just asked for an addition, and you need to know which step produces the reference that determines whether the request is a change or was always included. Select that step.

graphic.title: Scope definition and control, five steps left to right
graphic.caption: Select a step. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between steps, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Collect requirements
regions.rationale: Collecting requirements gathers what stakeholders say they need. It produces raw input that has not yet been bounded, so it cannot settle whether a given request sits inside the project.

regions.label: Define scope
regions.rationale: Defining scope narrows the collected requirements into what this project will and will not do. It is the necessary input to the next step but is not yet the agreed reference against which requests are judged.

regions.label: Baseline scope
regions.rationale: Baselining fixes the agreed statement of scope as the approved reference. Once it exists, any request can be tested against it and classified as already included or as a change requiring approval.

regions.label: Validate deliverables
regions.rationale: Validation is where the customer formally accepts completed deliverables. It happens after work is done and consumes the baseline rather than establishing it.

regions.label: Control scope
regions.rationale: Controlling scope is the ongoing activity of comparing requests and work against the reference. It is where the test is applied, but the reference it applies was created at the earlier step.

questions.explanation: The distinction between a change and an inclusion only exists once there is an approved reference to test against, and that reference is created when scope is baselined rather than when it is drafted or when control activity begins. Projects that attempt to control scope without a baseline end up arguing about what was always intended, because there is no agreed point of comparison and every party remembers the original discussion differently.
questions.mindset: You cannot control scope against a definition that was never agreed.

questions.stem: A developer on your fixed-price contract has added a configurable dashboard to a reporting module. It took her four days, it was not requested, and she is proud of it. The client's analyst has seen it and is enthusiastic. The module passed its review without the dashboard mentioned, and there are eleven weeks left with no float on that workstream. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Remove the dashboard and return the module to its reviewed scope before the client comes to rely on it, then remind the team that any addition must be requested and approved first.
options.rationale: This is the strict-revert error. It is defensible on scope discipline, but the client's analyst has already seen and wants the feature, so removing it without asking the client turns an approval conversation into one about withdrawal.

options.text: Retain the dashboard at no charge as goodwill, since the four days are already spent and the client's analyst is pleased, and record it in the module's delivery documentation.
options.rationale: This is the free-gift error. The build cost is sunk but the testing, documentation and ongoing support are not, and an unpriced feature accepted informally, even if it is recorded, sets the expectation that further additions arrive the same way.

options.text: Log the dashboard in the lessons learned register, and let the client's acceptance at the end of the contract decide whether it stays in the module.
options.rationale: This is the defer-to-acceptance error. Recording the lesson is reasonable, but it leaves an unapproved feature inside a fixed-price deliverable until the latest possible moment, when the leverage to price it or remove it is at its lowest.

options.text: Raise the addition with the client as a change, establish whether they want it, and make the schedule and support consequences explicit before it is retained.
options.rationale: The dashboard is now real and the client has seen it, so quietly removing it is no longer a neutral act. Routing it through change control puts the decision with the client while making the eleven-week and support cost visible rather than absorbed.

questions.explanation: Work added without a request is a change regardless of whether anyone is pleased with it, and the cost of it is rarely limited to the days already spent. Once a client has seen the addition, both silent removal and silent retention are decisions taken on the client's behalf. The controlled route makes the addition visible, prices its full consequence including support, and leaves the decision where it belongs.
questions.mindset: Unrequested additions are scope decisions, and scope decisions are not the delivery team's to take.

questions.stem: Your backlog is ordered by a scoring model the product owner built eighteen months ago. Two features near the top serve a customer segment the company exited in January. The product owner defends the order because the scores are objective and consistently applied. Three stakeholders have separately asked why the team is building for a segment that no longer exists. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Move the two features down the backlog, since the segment they serve was exited in January, and record the reason for the change in the backlog history.
options.rationale: This is the fix-the-instance error. It corrects two visible symptoms and leaves a model that will keep generating the same class of error, and recording the reason does not alter that it overrides the product owner on an ordering that is properly hers.

options.text: Ask the product owner to rescore the backlog against the current strategy, starting with the inputs the model uses rather than the scores it produces.
options.rationale: A consistently applied model producing obviously wrong output has stale inputs, not stale arithmetic. Going after the inputs fixes every item at once and preserves the discipline the product owner is rightly protecting.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor, since three stakeholders have now raised concerns about work that no longer serves the strategy, and ask for the order to be reviewed.
options.rationale: This is the escalate-before-asking error. The product owner has not yet been shown that her inputs are stale, and asking the sponsor to review an order she owns skips her and damages the working relationship the backlog depends on.

options.text: Bring the two features to the next sprint review and let stakeholder feedback there determine whether they should still be built.
options.rationale: This is the demo-as-decision error. It spends a sprint building the features so they can be shown at the sprint review, in order to ask whether they should exist, which is the most expensive available way to answer a question that could be settled in a conversation.

questions.explanation: A prioritisation model is a way of applying current judgement consistently, so when the organisation's strategy moves the model has to be re-fed rather than defended or bypassed. Correcting individual items treats the output while the mechanism continues to produce the same error, and escalating past the person who owns the ordering skips the step most likely to work. The objectivity of a model is only as current as what was put into it.
questions.mindset: Prioritisation models serve current value; they do not outrank it.

questions.stem: Your programme was funded to save two million a year by automating claims handling. Nine months in, a competitor's acquisition has halved the claim volume your company expects to process. The automation works. Delivered as planned it would now save roughly six hundred thousand a year against three million of remaining spend. Your delivery metrics are all green and the team is performing well. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Present the revised benefit case to the sponsor and governance board with options including reduced scope and termination, and let them decide.
options.rationale: The investment decision belongs to the people who made it, and they cannot revisit it without being told the numbers have moved. Bringing options rather than a single recommendation respects that this is a funding judgement rather than a delivery one.

options.text: Continue to plan, since the programme is performing well against its baseline, the automation delivers what was specified and the board approved the full scope.
options.rationale: This is the on-track-therefore-fine error. Green delivery metrics measure whether the work is being done as agreed and say nothing about whether it is still worth three million to finish, and the board's approval was given against a benefit that has since halved.

options.text: Reduce scope to the components that still pay back at the lower volume, and inform the board of the revised plan, with the new figures, at the next reporting cycle.
options.rationale: This is the decide-then-report error. Rescoping may well be the right answer, but choosing it unilaterally takes an investment decision that belongs to the board and presents it as a delivery adjustment, however fully the figures are reported afterwards.

options.text: Recalculate the benefit case and re-forecast, then continue while monitoring claim volumes monthly in case they recover.
options.rationale: This is the monitor-and-hope error. It correctly identifies that the numbers have changed and then declines to act on them, spending real money against a recovery nobody has forecast, however closely the volumes are watched.

questions.explanation: Value is not fixed at approval, and a project delivering exactly what was agreed can stop being worth its remaining cost through no fault of its own. The project manager's obligation is to notice the shift and put it in front of whoever owns the investment, framed as options with numbers attached. Continuing on the strength of good delivery metrics, or rescoping without sanction, both substitute delivery judgement for an investment decision.
questions.mindset: Keep asking whether the work is still worth doing, not only whether it is being done well.

questions.stem: Your team can start only one of two features next. Finance estimates that delaying the express checkout feature costs the business about £48,000 a month, and the team sizes it at 8 points. Delaying the saved-baskets feature costs about £27,000 a month, and the team sizes it at 3 points. Both are technically independent and either could start immediately. Work out the delay cost per point for each, then state which should be started first.

blanks.label: Express checkout, delay cost per point (£ per month)
blanks.rationale: 48,000 ÷ 8 = £6,000 per point per month. This is what each unit of the team's effort on express checkout buys back in avoided delay cost.

blanks.label: Saved baskets, delay cost per point (£ per month)
blanks.rationale: 27,000 ÷ 3 = £9,000 per point per month. The smaller prize on the smaller job returns more per unit of effort than the larger prize on the larger job.

blanks.label: Which feature should be started first
blanks.rationale: Saved baskets returns £9,000 per point against express checkout's £6,000, so starting it first releases more value per unit of capacity and finishes sooner, after which express checkout begins.

questions.explanation: When capacity is the constraint, sequencing by absolute value systematically favours large items and leaves cheaper, faster value sitting in the queue. Dividing the cost of delay by the size of the job puts every candidate on the same footing and tends to promote small high-value work. The larger headline figure is the trap here: express checkout is worth more in total and is worth less per unit of the scarce thing, which is the team's time.
questions.mindset: Sequence by the value released per unit of effort, not by the size of the prize.

questions.stem: You are building the resource plan for a two-year infrastructure refresh and different parts of the work give you very different kinds of evidence to estimate from. Complete each sentence with the estimating basis that fits the situation described. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: Cabling twelve floors of an office the company refitted last year, to the same specification. The estimate should mostly be based on
A migration nobody in the organisation has attempted, where two engineers give confident but very different figures. The estimate should mostly be based on
Installing 400 identical access points, where a reliable per-unit installation time is already known. The estimate should mostly be based on

options.text: the recorded effort from the comparable job
options.rationale: A near-identical piece of work completed recently by the same organisation is the strongest evidence available. Building up from first principles here would discard real data in favour of an assumption.

options.text: an optimistic, likely and pessimistic range from both engineers
options.rationale: Wide disagreement between credible experts is information about uncertainty, and a range captures it where a single agreed number would conceal it. It also gives the reserve conversation something to work from.

options.text: the known unit rate multiplied by the quantity
options.rationale: A reliable per-unit figure and a large repeated quantity is the situation where scaling the rate is both accurate and cheap. The repetition is what makes the unit rate trustworthy at this volume.

options.text: a full decomposition of every task and its effort
options.rationale: Not used. Detailed decomposition earns its cost where work is novel and divisible into understood parts, and each situation here already offers a faster basis of comparable data, expert range or unit rate.

options.text: the supplier's quoted figure taken as given
options.rationale: Not used. A quotation is a commercial position rather than an estimate, and adopting one without an independent basis leaves you unable to tell whether it is padded or optimistic.

questions.explanation: The estimating basis follows the evidence available rather than a house preference for one technique. Recent comparable work supports estimating by analogy; a known unit rate across a large repeated quantity supports scaling that rate; and genuine expert disagreement on novel work is best expressed as a range, because forcing consensus hides the uncertainty that the reserve is meant to cover. Decomposition and supplier figures both have their place, but neither is the strongest basis when better evidence is already to hand.
questions.mindset: Estimate from the best evidence the situation actually offers.

questions.stem: A manager has asked you to raise your team's utilisation from about seventy per cent to ninety-five, arguing that the difference is waste. Your team's throughput has been stable for six months and its cycle time is predictable. Two of the engineers use part of that slack to handle production support, which arrives unpredictably. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree to the ninety-five per cent target as a two-month trial, then track cycle time and support response weekly and revert if delivery starts to deteriorate.
options.rationale: This is the comply-and-measure error. Queueing effects appear as a growing backlog of part-finished work rather than an immediate signal, so over a two-month trial the deterioration is well established by the time the weekly metric moves.

options.text: Propose moving production support to a separate team first, so that the two engineers' time can then be fully allocated to project work at the higher target.
options.rationale: This is the relocate-the-variability error. It may be worth doing on its own merits, and it does not answer the manager's point, since unpredictable arrivals still need slack wherever they land, including in the new support team.

options.text: Explain to the manager that utilisation above about eighty per cent lengthens cycle time sharply in any queueing system, and decline the target on that basis.
options.rationale: This is the correct-but-unevidenced error. The principle holds, and refusing a manager's request with a general argument about queueing invites the reply that your team is the exception, which only local data can answer.

options.text: Show the manager what the slack is currently absorbing and what raising utilisation would do to cycle time and support response, then agree a target from that.
options.rationale: The manager is treating unbooked time as waste because nobody has shown him what it does. Making the support load and the queueing effect visible converts an assertion about idleness into a decision about which outcome the organisation wants.

questions.explanation: In any system with variable arrival of work, pushing utilisation toward full capacity lengthens queues sharply and makes delivery less predictable. The persuasive move is local evidence rather than the general principle: showing what the slack is currently absorbing and what the trade would cost in cycle time turns the conversation into a choice between predictability and apparent efficiency, which is the choice actually on the table.
questions.mindset: Slack is what lets a system absorb variation; removing it buys utilisation and sells predictability.

questions.stem: You are letting three packages on a rail depot project, and the right contract form differs across them because what is known and who is best placed to carry the risk differ. Match each package to the contract arrangement that fits it best. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: Supply and install 60 identical charging points to a published specification, with a well-understood market and several capable bidders.
Ground remediation where the extent of contamination will not be known until excavation begins, and no bidder will price the unknown.
A specialist signalling upgrade where the scope is clear but delivery six weeks early is worth a great deal to the operator.

options.text: Fixed price for the whole package
options.rationale: A published specification, a competitive market and no meaningful unknowns is the case where a supplier can price with confidence. The buyer gets cost certainty and the supplier carries an efficiency risk it can actually manage.

options.text: Reimbursement of actual cost plus an agreed fee
options.rationale: Where the extent of the work is genuinely unknown, a fixed price would either be refused or loaded with contingency the buyer pays for regardless. Reimbursing actual cost keeps the buyer's exposure tied to what is actually found.

options.text: Fixed price with an incentive for early completion
options.rationale: Clear scope allows a firm price, and an early-completion incentive puts money behind the outcome the operator values. The supplier is the party able to influence the date, so that is where the reward should sit.

options.text: Time and materials with no ceiling
options.rationale: Not used. Open-ended time and materials suits small or urgent work where defining the scope costs more than the work itself, and all three packages here are substantial and definable.

options.text: A call-off framework with rates fixed for four years
options.rationale: Not used. A framework is for repeated purchasing of similar items over time, whereas these are three one-off packages on a single project.

questions.explanation: Contract form is a risk allocation decision. Where scope is clear and the market is competitive, fixed price transfers cost risk to the party that can manage it. Where the extent of work is genuinely unknowable in advance, insisting on a fixed price simply buys someone else's contingency. Where scope is clear and timing carries value, an incentive aligns the supplier's interest with the outcome the buyer actually wants.
questions.mindset: The contract form should place risk with the party best able to control it.

questions.stem: A county library service is replacing its self-service kiosks. Phase one, 14 branches, has been installed and accepted without defects. The contract includes a priced option for phase two, 26 branches at £10,000 each, exercisable by written notice before 30 November; after that the supplier may re-price, and it has mentioned that component costs have risen about 15 per cent. Phase two is in the approved baseline and budget, and the charter lets you commit spend within budget up to £300,000. The head of finance suggests waiting for the portfolio review on 12 December. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the supplier to hold the option open until after 12 December, so that the portfolio review can confirm the spend before any commitment to phase two is made in writing.
options.rationale: This is the defer-to-the-calendar error. The supplier has just said its costs have risen, so an extension depends on goodwill it has every reason to withhold, and it waits for a forum to confirm spend that is already approved and within your authority.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor for an out-of-cycle approval of the £260,000 before 30 November, so that the commitment carries senior sign-off as well as your delegated authority.
options.rationale: This is the borrow-someone-else's-authority error. It meets the deadline if the sponsor responds in time, but it pushes upward a decision the charter has already delegated, spends sponsor attention on a routine commitment and teaches the governance structure that its delegations are not relied on.

options.text: Give the supplier written notice exercising the option before 30 November under your delegated authority, and brief the head of finance on why it could not wait for the review.
options.rationale: The spend is budgeted, baselined and inside the £300,000 you may commit, so the decision is yours and the option deadline sets its timing. Briefing finance keeps the use of that authority transparent without handing the decision to a review that meets after the price has gone.

options.text: Let the option lapse and run a short competitive tender for phase two, so that the re-priced offer can be tested against the wider market before the project commits a further £260,000.
options.rationale: This is the test-the-market error. The option price was won competitively before costs rose, so any new tender faces the same higher market, adds months, and risks losing a supplier whose phase one is accepted. A fixed price below today's market is an asset that expires, not a figure to be re-tested.

questions.explanation: A priced option holds a price the buyer secured while it had competitive leverage, and it is worth most exactly when the market has since moved against the buyer. Its deadline is a hard limit, so the timing of the decision is set by the contract rather than by the governance calendar. Where exercising it falls within approved budget and delegated authority, the decision belongs to the project manager; using that authority openly, with the people who might have expected a say kept informed, is what makes it accountable rather than unilateral.
questions.mindset: Use the authority you have been given when a deadline will not wait for a forum that meets too late.

questions.stem: You are the client-side project manager for a school's sports hall extension. The contractor is valued monthly for work done, and each valuation is paid at the end of the following month, less 5 per cent retention held until practical completion in October. Valuations were £60,000 in January, £110,000 in February and £200,000 in March, and the programme forecasts £180,000 for April, £150,000 for May and £90,000 for June. Finance's draft cash requirement for April to June is the £420,000 of work forecast in those months. Work out the figures below.

blanks.label: Cash payable to the contractor from April to June (£)
blanks.rationale: April pays March's valuation, May pays April's and June pays May's, each at 95 per cent: 0.95 × (200,000 + 180,000 + 150,000) = 0.95 × 530,000 = £503,500. June's own work is not paid until July.

blanks.label: Amount by which finance's draft understates the quarter's cash requirement (£)
blanks.rationale: 503,500 − 420,000 = £83,500. The draft counts work done in the quarter, but the large March valuation falls due in April while June's smaller one slips into the next quarter.

blanks.label: Retention held by the client at the end of June, owed to the contractor later (£)
blanks.rationale: Retention has been deducted from every valuation paid so far, January to May: 0.05 × (60,000 + 110,000 + 200,000 + 180,000 + 150,000) = 0.05 × 700,000 = £35,000. It is a liability that must appear in the cash forecast for the month it is released.

questions.explanation: Cost is incurred when work is done, but cash leaves when the contract says it is paid, so a cash forecast is built from the payment terms rather than from the work programme. A payment lag shifts each month's outflow into the next period, and retention lowers each payment now in exchange for a lump sum later. When the work profile is uneven, the lag can move a large sum across a quarter boundary, so a cash requirement taken straight from the programme can be wrong in either direction even while the total cost is right.
questions.mindset: Ask when the money actually leaves, because work done and cash paid run on different clocks.

questions.stem: Defects found after release have tripled over four sprints. Your testers are working longer hours and finding more, but the escape rate keeps climbing. The team has no automated regression suite, code review is optional and often skipped when a sprint is tight, and the definition of done does not mention testing. Velocity has risen across the same four sprints. Which two actions should the project manager prioritise?

options.text: Work with the team to add testing and code review to the definition of done, so an item is not complete until both have happened.
options.rationale: Optional review skipped under pressure is not a discipline, and rising velocity across the same period suggests done currently means written rather than working. Putting both into the definition of done makes the quality work part of the item's cost.

options.text: Invest team capacity in automated regression coverage, starting with the areas where escaped defects cluster.
options.rationale: Escapes rising while manual testing intensifies is the signature of regression the team cannot re-check by hand each sprint. Targeting the clusters first is what makes the investment pay back inside a few sprints rather than eventually.

options.text: Add two more testers so that more defects are caught before release, and have them concentrate on the areas where escapes cluster.
options.rationale: This is the more-inspection error. It scales the activity that is already failing to keep up, and aiming the extra testers at the clusters makes the inspection better targeted without changing how many defects are created. It also confirms to the team that quality is the test function's responsibility rather than part of building the thing.

options.text: Introduce a quality gate requiring your sign-off before any release goes out, backed by a checklist of the test evidence each release must show.
options.rationale: This is the gatekeeper error. It places one person at the end of a pipeline producing defects upstream, and a checklist of evidence makes the gate more rigorous while it still slows release without improving what arrives at the gate.

options.text: Report the escape trend to the steering committee and request additional budget for a quality improvement initiative.
options.rationale: This is the escalate-for-funding error. The two effective actions cost the team's own capacity and a working agreement rather than budget, so the request buys delay while the escape rate continues to climb.

questions.explanation: A rising escape rate alongside intensifying test effort means defects are being created faster than inspection can remove them, so the leverage is upstream. Building the quality activity into the team's definition of done changes when the work happens, and automating regression addresses the specific failure that manual testing cannot repeat at sprint cadence. Adding inspectors, adding gates or seeking funding all scale the response at the end of the pipeline.
questions.mindset: Quality is built in during the work, not inspected in at the end.

questions.stem: Your finance business partner has flagged that the project is spending £180,000 on inspection, testing and audit activities, and asks whether this can be cut to protect a strained budget. The product is a medical device component. Field failure would trigger recall costs the business case estimates at several million, and the regulator requires evidence of the testing regime. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Decline the reduction on the grounds that the regulator requires the testing regime, and set out for the finance partner which regulatory clause each activity satisfies.
options.rationale: This is the compliance-shield error. Listing the clauses makes the refusal look thorough, but the regulatory requirement covers some of the spend and probably not all of it, and it still declines to examine whether any of the £180,000 is genuinely duplicated or poorly targeted.

options.text: Set out for the finance partner what the £180,000 buys against the recall and regulatory exposure it reduces, and identify any activity that is genuinely duplicated and could be cut.
options.rationale: The request deserves an answer in the terms it was asked, which are financial. Separating the exposure argument from any genuine duplication is what distinguishes a defensible spend from an unexamined one.

options.text: Reduce inspection activity by the amount requested and increase the contingency reserve to cover the additional failure risk, recording the change in the risk register.
options.rationale: This is the reserve-for-recall error. Contingency covers estimating variance within the project, not a multi-million recall borne by the wider business, and recording it in the register documents the exposure without changing who would bear it. It does nothing about the regulator's evidence requirement.

options.text: Propose moving the inspection cost into the operations budget so it no longer sits against the project, since inspection continues into production after release.
options.rationale: This is the move-the-cost error. The point that inspection continues into production is plausible for part of the spend, and the transfer still relieves the project's budget position without changing what the organisation spends, presenting an accounting move as a saving.

questions.explanation: Money spent preventing and detecting defects is judged against the cost of the failures it avoids, and in regulated or safety-critical work that comparison is usually decisive. The professional response to a challenge on the spend is to make the trade-off explicit in financial terms rather than to defend the budget on principle, and to use the challenge as an occasion to find any duplication that genuinely exists. Reclassifying the cost or reserving against the exposure changes neither the risk nor the total spend.
questions.mindset: Weigh what prevention and appraisal cost against what failure would cost.

questions.stem: Your satellite ground station build has four independent paths — civil works, antenna procurement, power supply and control software — that all converge on a single integration test. Each path lead has given an estimate they are 80 per cent confident of meeting, and the deterministic schedule shows integration starting on 2 March. The planner has told the sponsor the date is therefore '80 per cent safe', and the sponsor intends to give it to the licensing authority this week. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Tell the sponsor before the date goes out that four paths at 80 per cent give about a 41 per cent chance together, and run a schedule risk analysis to set the authority's date at the confidence needed.
options.rationale: Independent paths that must all finish before a merge multiply their probabilities: 0.8 to the fourth power is about 0.41. Correcting the premise before a regulator relies on it, and replacing the guess with an analysed confidence level, gives the sponsor a date that means what it says.

options.text: Let the sponsor issue 2 March, since each path lead owns and stands behind their estimate, and track all four paths weekly so that any slip is reported to the licensing authority early.
options.rationale: This is the accept-the-premise error. Weekly tracking reports a miss sooner but does nothing to the odds of it, and the date being issued rests on a confidence figure that does not hold for four paths that must all arrive together.

options.text: Ask each path lead to re-estimate at 95 per cent confidence so that the deterministic date carries the assurance the planner described, then issue the later date that results to the authority.
options.rationale: This is the pad-every-path error. It still treats each path's confidence as the date's confidence, so any improvement is accidental, and it hides contingency inside four estimates where nobody can see or manage it and where work tends to expand to fill it.

options.text: Add a two-week buffer after integration testing, sized from experience on the last ground station build, and confirm the later date with the sponsor before it goes to the authority.
options.rationale: This is the size-by-feel error. A visible buffer is the right instinct, but one sized by analogy has no stated confidence attached, so the sponsor still cannot say how likely the new date is, and it may be too small for four converging paths or larger than needed.

questions.explanation: A deterministic schedule calculates one date by assuming every estimate is met, and where several uncertain paths converge on one successor that date is more optimistic than any single path suggests, because the successor waits for the latest arrival. The confidence of meeting a merge point is roughly the product of the paths' individual confidences, so it falls quickly as paths are added. Before a date is committed externally, its confidence should be established by analysis rather than inferred from the estimates, and any contingency should be sized to the confidence the commitment needs and held where it can be seen.
questions.mindset: Where paths converge, the chance of meeting the date is the chance that every one of them arrives, which is lower than any of them alone.

questions.stem: A site handover has two independent chains of work that must both finish before commissioning. Chain one runs survey, four days, then fit-out, six days. Chain two runs permits, seven days, then connections, five days. Commissioning takes three days and cannot start until both chains are complete. All activities start as early as possible. Work out the shortest possible project duration, then the total float on the survey activity.

blanks.label: Shortest project duration, in days
blanks.rationale: Chain one takes 4 + 6 = 10 days and chain two takes 7 + 5 = 12 days. Commissioning waits for the later of the two, so the duration is 12 + 3 = 15 days.

blanks.label: Total float on the survey activity, in days
blanks.rationale: Chain one finishes in 10 days against the 12 that chain two needs, so everything on chain one can slip 2 days without delaying commissioning. Survey therefore carries 2 days of total float, shared with fit-out.

questions.explanation: Where parallel chains converge, the longest of them determines when the successor can start, and every shorter chain carries float equal to the difference. That float is a property of the path rather than of any single activity on it, so it is consumed once by whichever activity slips first. Compressing an activity that sits on a chain with float buys nothing at all, which is why identifying the driving path comes before any decision about where to spend effort.
questions.mindset: Float belongs to the path, and the path with none of it sets the date.

questions.stem: Your programme reports monthly using a status pack assembled by hand from six workstream spreadsheets. Assembly takes three days, the figures are between two and five weeks old by the time the board sees them, and last month two workstreams reported the same milestone under different names. The board has asked for weekly reporting. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Agree one definition and one identifier for milestones across all six workstreams before changing the reporting cadence.
options.rationale: Duplicated milestones under different names mean the workstreams are not describing the same reality, and moving to weekly would produce that inconsistency four times as often. Common definitions are the precondition for any increase in frequency.

options.text: Have workstreams maintain their status in a single shared source that the report is generated from, rather than submitting spreadsheets.
options.rationale: Three days of manual assembly is what makes the data stale, and weekly reporting would spend most of each week assembling. Generating the report from one live source removes the delay and the transcription errors together.

options.text: Move to weekly reporting immediately, since the board has asked for it, and improve the underlying process afterwards.
options.rationale: This is the comply-first error. Weekly assembly of a three-day pack from inconsistent sources is not sustainable, and it puts the reconciliation errors in front of the board more often rather than less.

options.text: Reduce the pack to a summary so that weekly assembly is achievable within the current process.
options.rationale: This is the shrink-the-symptom error. A shorter pack is quicker to assemble and is built from the same stale, inconsistent inputs, so the board gets less information with the same defects.

options.text: Ask the board what decisions it needs weekly reporting to support before making any change.
options.rationale: This is the clarify-before-fixing error. The question is fair in general, and here it delays two fixes worth making regardless of the answer, since stale data and duplicate milestone names are defects at any cadence.

questions.explanation: A request for more frequent reporting is a test of the reporting mechanism rather than of the team's willingness. Where the pack is assembled by hand from inconsistent sources, increasing frequency multiplies both the effort and the error rate. Establishing common definitions and generating the report from a single current source addresses the constraint, after which cadence becomes a choice rather than a burden.
questions.mindset: Report from one current source rather than reconciling six stale ones.

questions.stem: Your sprint burndown has been flat for eight days and then dropped almost vertically on the last day of the sprint, for three sprints running. Every sprint has completed its committed scope. A stakeholder has begun citing the flat period as evidence the team is not working. The team says the pattern reflects how the work naturally integrates. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Explain to the stakeholder that burndown shape varies with how work integrates, and that committed scope was delivered every sprint.
options.rationale: This is the defend-the-metric error. It is accurate, and it leaves in place a chart that will produce the same alarm next sprint, having spent your credibility asking the stakeholder to disregard what they can see.

options.text: Replace the burndown with a cumulative flow diagram, which shows work moving between stages rather than remaining effort, and walk the stakeholder through reading it.
options.rationale: This is the swap-the-chart error. A different visualisation of the same large late-integrating items shows a similar plateau, and coaching the stakeholder to read it changes the display while the underlying invisibility of progress stays.

options.text: Work with the team to break items down so progress is visible during the sprint, and explain the current pattern to the stakeholder in the meantime.
options.rationale: A chart that only moves on the final day genuinely cannot distinguish a team integrating late from a team in trouble. Smaller items make progress observable, and the interim explanation stops the stakeholder acting on a reading nobody has corrected.

options.text: Stop publishing the burndown to stakeholders and report completed scope at each sprint review instead, where the stakeholder can see the delivered work demonstrated.
options.rationale: This is the remove-the-transparency error. It answers the stakeholder's objection by withholding the in-sprint view, which is a poor trade for a relationship that depends on being able to see how delivery is going between reviews.

questions.explanation: When a progress measure repeatedly gives a misleading impression, the useful response is to change what the measure can see rather than to argue with the people reading it. Breaking work into smaller pieces makes progress genuinely observable during the period, which serves the team as well as the audience. Defending the chart, substituting a different chart or withdrawing it all leave the underlying problem, which is that nothing verifiable happens until the last day.
questions.mindset: A metric that misleads its audience needs fixing, not defending.

questions.stem: Your system has passed acceptance testing and gone live. The operations team that will run it has raised no objection but has not confirmed it is ready to take over, and two of the four runbooks are still in draft. Your team's contracts end in nine days and your sponsor is keen to announce completion at Thursday's board. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Close the project on the basis of successful acceptance testing, and pass the outstanding runbooks to operations as a residual action with a named owner and a due date.
options.rationale: This is the acceptance-equals-closure error. Passing the test proves the system meets its specification, not that anyone can operate it. A named owner and a date make the residual action look tidy, but it lands on a team that has just lost access to the people who wrote it.

options.text: Extend two team members' contracts by a month so they can complete the two draft runbooks and support operations through its first weeks after the announcement.
options.rationale: This is the extend-the-tail error. It spends budget finishing two draft runbooks that the remaining nine days can absorb, and it lets the board be told the project is complete while its handover is not. Extra support weeks treat the readiness gap as a staffing shortfall rather than something operations has to confirm.

options.text: Use the nine days to finish the runbooks and secure explicit operational readiness confirmation, and tell the sponsor what is outstanding before Thursday.
options.rationale: Nine days is enough for both, and the sponsor is about to make a public statement on an incomplete picture. Explicit confirmation matters because silence from operations is not agreement that they can run it.

options.text: Ask operations to confirm readiness now, and treat no response by Thursday as acceptance so that the sponsor can announce completion at the board as planned.
options.rationale: This is the deemed-acceptance error. Converting silence into agreement transfers responsibility without transferring capability, the sponsor then announces on the strength of that silence, and the first incident will find the runbooks that were never finished.

questions.explanation: Closure has two distinct conditions: the deliverable meets its specification, and the organisation that inherits it can run it. Acceptance testing establishes only the first. Where time remains, it is spent completing the handover and obtaining explicit confirmation rather than converting silence into consent, and the sponsor is told the true position before making a public statement rather than after.
questions.mindset: Closure is complete when the receiving organisation can actually run the thing.

questions.stem: Your programme has been cancelled after fourteen months because the parent company was acquired and the acquirer already owns an equivalent platform.
