The team is being redeployed within three weeks and morale is low. Two components you built are genuinely reusable, and a great deal was learned about integrating with the legacy estate. Your sponsor has asked you simply to stand the team down. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Stand the team down as instructed, since the programme is cancelled and further effort cannot deliver its objectives, and record the cancellation decision in the project file.
options.rationale: This is the literal-instruction error. It reads a stand-down instruction as covering the closure obligations too. Recording the cancellation documents that the programme ended but not what it leaves behind, and it discards reusable assets and hard-won integration knowledge that the wider organisation has already paid for.

options.text: Run a full closure within the three weeks, capturing lessons, documenting and transferring the reusable components, and settling contracts and records.
options.rationale: Cancellation changes why the project ends, not what closure is for, and three weeks with the team still in place is the only window in which any of it can be captured. The reusable components have real value that disappears the moment people redeploy.

options.text: Focus the three weeks on a thorough lessons learned exercise, since knowledge is the only remaining value from a cancelled programme.
options.rationale: This is the lessons-only error. A thorough exercise correctly secures one salvageable asset and overlooks the two working components, along with the contract and record settlement that will otherwise become somebody else's untidy problem.

options.text: Propose to the sponsor that the two reusable components be completed before the team disperses, so that they can be offered to the acquirer's platform team.
options.rationale: This is the rescue-the-work error. Completing components on a cancelled programme continues spending against an objective the acquirer no longer wants, and nobody knows whether its platform team would take them. The task is to make what exists transferable, not to finish it.

questions.explanation: Termination for reasons outside the project's control still triggers the full closure obligation: capture what was learned, transfer whatever has value elsewhere, and settle contracts and records properly. The window is defined by how long the team remains, so the work is scheduled against that rather than against how much there is to do. Standing down without closure discards paid-for value, and narrowing closure to lessons alone leaves both the assets and the administrative tail behind.
questions.mindset: A cancelled project still owes the organisation everything it can salvage.

questions.stem: Your project has a steering committee that meets monthly, a technical design authority that meets fortnightly, and a sponsor available weekly. In three months, four decisions have been taken twice by different bodies and two have been taken by nobody, sitting unresolved for six weeks each. Everyone attends willingly and no one is obstructing. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Define which body owns which class of decision, with the value and risk thresholds that route a decision to each, and have that agreed by all three.
options.rationale: Decisions taken twice and decisions taken by nobody are the two symptoms of undefined boundaries, and both disappear once each class has one owner. Agreeing it across all three bodies is what stops the definition becoming your view of their authority.

options.text: Establish a route and a timescale for decisions that fall outside the defined classes, so nothing can sit unowned.
options.rationale: Any classification will meet cases it did not anticipate, which is how the two six-week stalls happened. A default route with a deadline is what converts an unclassifiable decision into a slow one rather than a permanent one.

options.text: Take the two unresolved decisions to the sponsor, who is available weekly and can act fastest, and ask her to rule on both before the steering committee next meets.
options.rationale: This is the fastest-route error. It clears the two current items ahead of the committee and establishes that anything difficult ends up with the sponsor, which hollows out the two bodies that were created to handle exactly these decisions and leaves the next orphaned decision with nowhere defined to go.

options.text: Align the meeting cycles so that all three bodies meet in the same week, with the design authority sitting first, and decisions can be passed between them in sequence.
options.rationale: This is the calendar-as-cure error. Cadence is not what caused a decision to be taken twice, and putting the three bodies in a fixed order adds coordination cost without telling any of them which decisions are theirs, so two of them can still take the same one in consecutive days.

options.text: Circulate the minutes of all three bodies to every member after each meeting, so that each body can check what the others have already decided before it takes up an item.
options.rationale: This is the transparency-instead-of-authority error. Shared minutes might let someone spot a duplicate before it happens, but they leave two bodies each believing the decision is theirs to take, and do nothing for the decisions that sat for six weeks because no body thought they were its own.

questions.explanation: Duplicated and orphaned decisions are the standard signature of a governance structure whose boundaries were never drawn, rather than of bad faith or poor attendance. The fix is to allocate classes of decision to bodies using explicit thresholds, agreed by those bodies, and to provide a default route with a deadline for whatever the classification misses. Routing round the structure, synchronising diaries or sharing minutes all leave the underlying ambiguity intact.
questions.mindset: Governance works when everyone knows which body decides what, and by when.

questions.stem: Your hybrid programme's governance requires board approval for any scope change above £25,000. The product teams make small scope decisions continuously, and in the last quarter forty-one changes were individually below the threshold but totalled £310,000, none of which the board saw. The board believes it has visibility of scope. Your programme is meeting its objectives. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Continue under the current delegation, since each of the forty-one changes fell within the authority the teams hold and the programme is meeting all of its stated objectives.
options.rationale: This is the letter-of-the-rule error. Every change did comply, but technical compliance with a threshold does not cure the board's mistaken belief that it can see scope movement, and good performance against objectives does not make a governance blind spot acceptable.

options.text: Lower the programme's internal approval threshold so that changes of this kind come to you before they are made, and keep a running total.
options.rationale: This is the private-fix error. It restores control to the programme rather than to the board, keeps the running total inside the programme, leaves the board's mistaken belief about its own visibility undisturbed, and slows the teams for what is a problem of reporting rather than of decision quality.

options.text: Add a quarterly summary of sub-threshold scope changes, with their cumulative total, to the standard board pack, starting with the papers for the board's next scheduled meeting.
options.rationale: This is the quiet-remediation error. It is sensible as an ongoing control and inadequate as the first move, because it lets £310,000 of unseen change surface as a routine table in the pack rather than as the governance gap the board needs to be told about directly.

options.text: Bring the aggregate position to the board, explain how the threshold is being met while the cumulative effect is invisible, and propose a control that catches it.
options.rationale: Every individual change complied and the board's belief about its own visibility is nevertheless false, which only the board can decide how to correct. Bringing a proposed control alongside the disclosure keeps it a governance improvement rather than a confession.

questions.explanation: Thresholds govern individual transactions and are routinely satisfied by a stream of decisions whose combined effect would never have been approved. Where that is happening, the governing body is operating on a false picture of its own oversight and is entitled to be told plainly, together with a proposal for the control that would catch the aggregate in future. Tightening internal limits or quietly adding a report addresses the mechanism while leaving the misapprehension in place.
questions.mindset: Report the aggregate when the individual figures are the only thing being governed.

questions.stem: An external audit of your programme is six weeks away and three compliance obligations are in different states of readiness. Each needs a different response from you now. Match each situation to the action that fits it best. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: A control is being operated correctly by the team every week, but nothing is recorded to show that it was.
A regulation that applied when the programme started was amended four months ago and nobody has assessed the effect.
A control has not been operated at all for two months because the person responsible left and was not replaced.

options.text: Establish a record that captures the control operating from now on
options.rationale: The control itself is sound, so the gap is purely evidential. Starting a record now allows the auditor to see the control working, and the historical gap is disclosed rather than reconstructed after the fact.

options.text: Assess the amendment against the programme and act on what it changes
options.rationale: Nobody yet knows whether the amendment affects the programme, so the required action is the assessment. Anything else, including reassurance to the auditor, would be asserting a conclusion that has not been reached.

options.text: Reinstate the control, then disclose the gap and its exposure
options.rationale: A control that has not operated for two months is a live exposure, so restoring it comes first. Disclosing the gap is not optional, since concealing a known lapse is a more serious finding than the lapse itself.

options.text: Note it for the post-audit improvement plan
options.rationale: Not used. Deferring suits genuinely minor enhancements, and each of these three is either an unevidenced control, an unassessed legal change or an active gap.

options.text: Ask the auditor to place it outside the audit scope
options.rationale: Not used. Audit scope is the auditor's to set, and requesting the exclusion of an area you know to be weak is the request most likely to draw attention to it.

questions.explanation: Compliance issues resolve differently according to whether the failure is in the control, in the evidence, or in the assessment of what applies. A control operating without a record needs evidence started and the gap disclosed; an unassessed legal change needs the assessment before anything can be said about it; and a control that has lapsed needs reinstating and reporting. What none of them tolerates is deferral or an attempt to steer the audit away, since a concealed known gap is treated far more seriously than a disclosed one.
questions.mindset: Compliance is demonstrated with evidence, not asserted with intention.

questions.stem: A team member proposes copying live customer records into the test environment so testing can use realistic data. The test environment sits outside the controls that protect the production database, and the records include names, addresses and payment details. She points out that the project is two weeks behind and that generating synthetic data would take four days. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Decline the copy, and have the four days for synthetic data planned in and the schedule impact reported.
options.rationale: Moving personal data into an environment without the protecting controls is a legal exposure that the schedule position does not license. Reporting the four days rather than absorbing them keeps the cost of the correct route visible to whoever owns the date.

options.text: Allow the copy for a strictly limited period, with the data deleted immediately after the test cycle completes.
options.rationale: This is the time-boxed-breach error. The exposure exists from the moment the records land outside the controls, and a deletion commitment made under schedule pressure is the kind that slips.

options.text: Allow the copy with payment details removed, since the remaining fields are lower risk.
options.rationale: This is the partial-anonymisation error. Names and addresses are themselves personal data, so stripping the payment fields reduces the severity of the exposure without changing the fact of it.

options.text: Escalate to the data protection officer and pause testing until a ruling is received.
options.rationale: This is the referral-as-delay error. Consulting the data protection officer is sound practice in a genuinely uncertain case, and pausing testing here treats a clear answer as an open question while the project falls further behind.

questions.explanation: Legal and regulatory obligations sit outside the trade space a project manager works in, so being behind schedule does not open an option that was closed before. The right handling is to take the compliant route, plan its cost in, and make that cost visible in reporting rather than absorbing it silently. Partial and time-limited versions of a breach are still breaches, and referring an unambiguous question upward mainly buys delay.
questions.mindset: Schedule pressure is never a reason to step outside a legal obligation.

questions.stem: The diagram shows your project's change control sequence. A developer has begun building a requested change as soon as the impact assessment was returned, reasoning that the assessment showed the change was small. Select the step that should have been completed before any build work started.

graphic.title: Change control, five steps left to right
graphic.caption: Select a step. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between steps, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Request logged
regions.rationale: Logging captures the request so that it cannot be lost and can be tracked. It records that someone has asked for something, which confers no authority to build it.

regions.label: Impact assessed
regions.rationale: Assessment establishes what the change would cost in time, money and risk. This is the step the developer relied on, and it produces the information for a decision rather than the decision itself.

regions.label: Decision by change authority
regions.rationale: This is where the change is approved, rejected or deferred by whoever holds that authority. Only an approved change may be built, and a small assessed impact does not pre-empt the decision.

regions.label: Baselines updated
regions.rationale: Updating the baselines records an approved change in the scope, schedule and cost references. It follows the decision and cannot precede it, since there would be nothing approved to record.

regions.label: Change implemented
regions.rationale: Implementation is the build itself, which is what the developer started early. It is the last step precisely because everything before it establishes whether it should happen at all.

questions.explanation: The purpose of assessing a change is to inform a decision, not to substitute for one, and the size of an assessed impact has no bearing on who is entitled to authorise it. Work started between assessment and decision commits the project to an outcome the change authority has not chosen, and if the change is rejected the effort is wasted and the baselines no longer describe what exists.
questions.mindset: An assessed change is not an approved change.

questions.stem: Your team works from a prioritised backlog under a contract that pays for a fixed number of sprints. The client's product owner reorders the backlog freely, which the contract permits. This sprint she has added an item that requires a third-party integration not contemplated anywhere in the agreement, and has placed it at the top. She sees this as ordinary reprioritisation. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Accept the item, since the contract gives the product owner authority over backlog order and the sprint count is unchanged, and confirm the integration's effort with the team at sprint planning.
options.rationale: This is the authority-overreach error. It reads a right to order agreed work as a right to introduce anything, and confirming the effort at planning sizes the work without asking who may authorise it; an unpriced third-party integration will consume far more than one item's worth of the fixed sprints.

options.text: Accept the item this sprint so the team is not left idle, then raise the contractual position with the client's commercial lead if similar requests recur.
options.rationale: This is the precedent-setting error. Accepting once establishes that out-of-scope items enter through reprioritisation, and deferring the commercial conversation makes the objection much harder to sustain the second time.

options.text: Decline the item and ask the product owner to select something from the existing backlog before the sprint starts.
options.rationale: This is the flat-refusal error. Acting before the sprint starts is right, but it protects the contract by treating a possibly valuable requirement as inadmissible, when the available route is to price it and let the client decide whether to fund it.

options.text: Explain that this item falls outside what was contracted, set out what it would require, and route it as a change before it enters the sprint.
options.rationale: The product owner's reordering right is genuine and does not extend to work outside the agreement, and a third-party integration brings cost and risk the contract never priced. Raising it before the sprint starts is what keeps the conversation about scope rather than about an overrun.

questions.explanation: Adaptive delivery under a contract distinguishes between reordering work that was agreed and introducing work that was not. The first is the flexibility the arrangement was designed to give; the second changes what is being bought. The productive response is neither to absorb it nor to refuse it, but to make the requirement visible with its cost and route it through change so the client can decide whether to fund it.
questions.mindset: Reordering agreed work is not the same as introducing work nobody agreed.

questions.stem: Your team's board shows six items in progress and four of them blocked, three waiting on the same external security review that takes about two weeks. The team continues to start new items rather than sit idle, and work in progress has risen every sprint for two months. In standup, blockers are mentioned and then the team moves on. What two actions should the project manager prioritise?

options.text: Take the security review bottleneck up directly with that team and its management, and pursue a faster or parallel route for the three waiting items.
options.rationale: One external dependency is blocking three items, so it is the single highest-value thing to attack. Removing impediments the team cannot reach itself is precisely the work the project manager is placed to do.

options.text: Agree a work in progress limit with the team so that blocked work must be cleared before new work is started.
options.rationale: Starting new items whenever something blocks is what has driven work in progress up for two months. A limit forces the team to converge on unblocking, which is the behaviour that actually shortens delivery.

options.text: Ask the team to raise blockers more prominently in standup and track each one on a visible blocker wall, so that they are not passed over the next morning.
options.rationale: This is the visibility-only error. The blockers are already being mentioned and the problem is that nothing happens next, so a louder mention or a blocker wall changes the volume rather than the response.

options.text: Reduce the sprint commitment to reflect the capacity lost to blocked work, and tell the product owner the forecast now assumes the two-week security wait.
options.rationale: This is the plan-around-it error. Telling the product owner makes the forecast honest, and it accepts the two-week security wait as permanent when it is the specific constraint most worth attacking.

options.text: Escalate the security review delay to your sponsor for resolution, setting out the three blocked items and the two-week wait so the sponsor can intervene.
options.rationale: This is the escalate-first error. However well the case is set out, nobody has yet approached the security team directly, so escalation arrives before the working-level attempt that would either solve it or justify escalating.

questions.explanation: Rising work in progress alongside persistent blockers means the team is responding to impediments by starting more work, which lengthens everything without finishing anything. The two effective moves are to attack the specific constraint at its source and to limit starting so that clearing blockages becomes the team's default response. Making blockers more visible, planning around them or escalating before trying all leave the constraint operating.
questions.mindset: Clearing the blockage matters more than keeping everyone busy.

questions.stem: A dependency owner in another division has missed two agreed dates for an interface your programme needs in five weeks. She has been responsive and apologetic each time, explaining that her own priorities keep being reset above her. You have a good relationship with her and do not want to damage it. Your programme has no float left on that path. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Escalate to your sponsor and ask him to raise the missed dates with her division's leadership, so the interface gets the senior attention it now needs.
options.rationale: This is the escalate-over-them error. Seeking senior attention routes a solvable priority conflict through two layers as a performance complaint, and she will hear about it as having been reported rather than supported.

options.text: Continue working with her and agree a third date, with twice-weekly check-ins to catch slippage earlier and a written note of each commitment.
options.rationale: This is the repeat-with-monitoring error. Two dates have failed for a reason neither of you controls, so a third arrangement, however closely tracked and documented, changes only how quickly you will learn it has failed again.

options.text: Agree with her jointly to escalate the priority conflict to whoever is resetting her work, framing it as a decision they need to take.
options.rationale: The constraint sits above her and she cannot resolve it, so escalating with her rather than about her puts the decision where it can be made. Framing it as a priority call protects the relationship you will still need in five weeks.

options.text: Re-sequence your programme to remove the dependency from the critical path, so her division's delays no longer set your end date.
options.rationale: This is the design-around-it error. Worth examining as a fallback and, with no float and five weeks left, unlikely to be available at reasonable cost; it protects your end date while leaving the underlying priority conflict to recur on the next interface.

questions.explanation: When a cooperative counterpart repeatedly misses commitments because of pressures above them, the obstacle is a priority conflict rather than a performance problem. Escalating jointly puts the trade-off in front of whoever is making it, preserves the working relationship, and produces a decision rather than an apology. Going over the person's head, agreeing another date on the same basis, or redesigning around them each leave the conflict unresolved for the next time.
questions.mindset: Escalate the constraint, not the person.

questions.stem: You are sizing contingency for three independent uncertainties on a bridge refurbishment. A ground condition risk has a 30 per cent chance of costing £200,000. A supplier failure risk has a 55 per cent chance of costing £40,000. An opportunity to reuse existing steelwork has a 40 per cent chance of saving £75,000. Work out the expected cost of the ground condition risk, then the net expected exposure across all three.

blanks.label: Expected cost of the ground condition risk (£)
blanks.rationale: 0.30 × 200,000 = £60,000. This is the probability-weighted cost, not a prediction that £60,000 will be spent, since the actual outcome is either £200,000 or nothing.

blanks.label: Net expected exposure across all three, in £, entered as a positive cost
blanks.rationale: Costs are 60,000 and 0.55 × 40,000 = 22,000, giving 82,000. The opportunity contributes 0.40 × 75,000 = 30,000 against it, leaving a net expected exposure of £52,000.

questions.explanation: Expected value weights each outcome by its likelihood, which lets a mixed set of threats and opportunities be combined into one figure for sizing contingency. It describes the set rather than any individual event, so it is only meaningful across a portfolio of uncertainties and never predicts what will happen on any one of them. Opportunities belong in the same calculation as threats, since ignoring them systematically overstates the reserve required.
questions.mindset: Size contingency from expected value across the whole set, not from the worst single case.

questions.stem: Your team's retrospectives are well attended and people speak openly. Reviewing the last eight, you find forty-three actions recorded, six completed, and the same three themes recurring throughout: unclear requirements, slow environment provisioning and interruptions from support. The team says retrospectives are useful. Nothing has measurably changed in four months. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Limit each retrospective to one or two improvement actions, with an owner and a date, and treat them as work that takes capacity.
options.rationale: Forty-three actions against six completions means improvement is being recorded rather than resourced. Restricting the number and giving each one capacity is what converts an intention into something that competes fairly with delivery work.

options.text: Take the two themes the team cannot fix itself, environment provisioning and support interruptions, and pursue them outside the team.
options.rationale: Themes recurring for four months usually persist because their causes sit beyond the team's authority. Carrying those outward is work the project manager can do that the team cannot, which is why they keep reappearing on the team's own list.

options.text: Change the retrospective format, rotating facilitators and techniques each session, to surface different issues and prevent the same three themes recurring every time.
options.rationale: This is the blame-the-format error. The retrospective is doing its job by identifying real recurring problems accurately, and new facilitators and techniques would produce different conversation about problems that would still not be fixed.

options.text: Review the outstanding thirty-seven actions with the team, close any that are obsolete, and reassign owners to the rest so they can be progressed.
options.rationale: This is the clear-the-backlog error. Pruning and reassigning tidies a list that grew because there was no capacity to work it, and it still leaves more open actions than the team has room for, so the remaining items stall for the same reason as before.

options.text: Reduce retrospective frequency from fortnightly to monthly, since they are generating more actions than the team can absorb and the backlog needs time to clear.
options.rationale: This is the reduce-the-reflection error. It lowers the rate at which problems are identified rather than raising the rate at which they are fixed, and waiting for the backlog to clear assumes capacity will appear that nothing has created. The team also values the sessions.

questions.explanation: Retrospectives that generate actions faster than the team can complete them stop producing change, and the recurrence of the same themes is the diagnostic. Two things restore it: constraining improvement work to a volume that fits alongside delivery, and recognising that some recurring causes sit outside the team's authority and must be pursued elsewhere. Changing the format, redistributing a stale backlog or meeting less often all treat the ceremony rather than the capacity.
questions.mindset: Improvement is measured by what changed, not by what was discussed.

questions.stem: At closure you have a substantial lessons learned report. Your organisation has a lessons repository, and searching it you find eleven earlier reports describing the same integration testing problem your project hit, one of them from a project that finished four months before yours started. Nobody consulted the repository during your planning, including you. What should the project manager do?

options.text: File your report as required, since capturing the lesson is the project's obligation and applying it is each future project's responsibility.
options.rationale: This is the discharge-the-duty error. It adds a twelfth report to a repository with a demonstrated retrieval failure, which is the action least likely to change anything for the thirteenth project.

options.text: File your report and raise with the process owner that a repository nobody consults is not preventing recurrence, with the eleven reports as evidence.
options.rationale: The eleven prior reports are the finding: the capture step works and the retrieval step does not. Taking it to whoever owns the process with concrete evidence is what makes it a fixable organisational problem rather than a personal oversight.

options.text: Circulate your report directly to the project managers currently in planning, and offer each of them a short walkthrough of the integration testing problem so they benefit from it immediately.
options.rationale: This is the personal-broadcast error. Walkthroughs help a handful of colleagues who happen to be in flight now and depend entirely on your continued presence and goodwill, while the retrieval failure that let eleven reports go unread stays in place for everyone after them.

options.text: Propose that consulting the repository be made a mandatory step in project planning, with a sign-off at the planning gate showing that a search was carried out.
options.rationale: This is the remedy-before-diagnosis error. The proposal is plausible as an eventual outcome and premature now, since nobody has yet established why eleven reports went unread, and a gate sign-off for searching a repository that may be unsearchable adds a step and a signature without a result.

questions.explanation: Continuous improvement fails at retrieval far more often than at capture, and eleven reports describing a problem that recurred is direct evidence of exactly that. The valuable act at closure is to surface the systemic failure to the person who owns the process, with the evidence attached, rather than to add another document, to distribute it personally, or to propose a specific remedy before the cause of the retrieval failure is understood.
questions.mindset: A lesson only counts once it changes what the next project does.

questions.stem: A new scheduling system is being rolled out to four depots, and each depot is resisting for a different reason. The programme manager wants the response at each site to address the actual cause rather than applying one adoption plan everywhere. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: Depot staff believe the system will be used to monitor individual productivity, and management has said nothing on the point. The response should be to
Depot staff are willing but the new process takes longer until it is familiar, and their targets have not been adjusted. The response should be to
Depot supervisors quietly prefer the old system because it gave them discretion the new one removes, and that discretion was never sanctioned. The response should be to

options.text: state plainly how the data will and will not be used
options.rationale: An unanswered question about surveillance will be answered by the workforce's own assumption, and the assumption is always the worse one. An explicit statement removes the vacuum that the fear is filling.

options.text: adjust the targets to reflect the learning period
options.rationale: These staff are not resisting the change, they are resisting being measured as though it had not happened. Adjusting targets removes the penalty for adopting and costs nothing in commitment.

options.text: bring the loss of informal discretion into the open and decide it deliberately
options.rationale: An unsanctioned practice removed by a system change needs to be named before it can be settled, since some of that discretion may have been genuinely useful and some of it may be exactly what the new system is meant to stop.

options.text: run further training sessions on the new system
options.rationale: Not used. More training addresses a capability gap, and none of these three sites is failing to adopt because the staff cannot operate the software.

options.text: require use of the new system and withdraw the old one
options.rationale: Not used. Enforcement produces compliance without addressing any of the three causes, and where the concern is surveillance or unadjusted targets it confirms the workforce's reading of the change.

questions.explanation: Resistance to an organisational change is usually a rational response to a real cost, and the response has to match the cost rather than the fact of resistance. Unspoken fears about how data will be used need explicit answers; a learning curve that collides with unchanged targets needs the targets adjusted; and the loss of informal discretion needs to be surfaced and decided rather than left to erode adoption quietly. Training and enforcement are the reflexes that address neither.
questions.mindset: Resistance is information about what the change costs the people absorbing it.

questions.stem: Six months into an agile transformation, teams run every ceremony correctly and their boards are immaculate. Yet requirements still arrive as fully specified documents, dates are still fixed before estimation, and the annual budget cycle still allocates by project. Team members privately describe the change as theatre. Your executive sponsor points to the ceremony adoption metrics as evidence of success. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Focus on deepening team practice and coaching the team leads, since well-executed ceremonies will gradually change how the organisation works around them.
options.rationale: This is the bottom-up-osmosis error. Teams already execute correctly and the surrounding structures are unchanged after six months, so more depth and coaching at team level push against constraints the teams and their leads have no authority over.

options.text: Report the gap between ceremony adoption and delivery outcomes in the transformation dashboard each month, so that the sponsor sees it widening and reaches the conclusion himself.
options.rationale: This is the wait-for-the-data error. The evidence is already sufficient, and presenting a widening gap on a monthly dashboard leaves the sponsor to draw a conclusion he has shown no sign of drawing unaided while the structures stay as they are.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor's peers in finance and business planning, since they own the budget and requirements practices that block the change and could alter them without waiting for him.
options.rationale: This is the bypass-the-sponsor error. Those functions do own the practices, but approaching them without your own sponsor forfeits the person best placed to carry the argument at that level, and invites them to defend their practices against a delivery lead rather than an executive.

options.text: Show the sponsor the specific organisational practices that contradict the change, with the evidence of their effect, and set out what leadership would need to decide.
options.rationale: The constraint is fixed dates, upfront specification and annual project funding, none of which a team can change. Naming them as decisions for leadership is the only route, since the sponsor currently believes adoption metrics are measuring the outcome.

questions.explanation: Adopting the visible practices of a way of working, inside structures that still assume the previous one, produces the appearance of change without its effect. The teams cannot resolve that, because fixed dates, upfront specification and annual project funding are decided elsewhere. The productive move is to make the specific contradictions and their effects legible to the sponsor as decisions requiring leadership action, rather than deepening practice, waiting for metrics to make the case, or going round the one person able to carry it.
questions.mindset: Practices adopted inside a structure that contradicts them will not survive it.

questions.stem: A regulator has published a consultation proposing rules that, if adopted as drafted, would require a reporting capability your product does not have. The consultation closes in three months and any rules would take effect eighteen months after that. You are nine months from launch. Building the capability speculatively would cost about eight per cent of your remaining budget. Nothing is certain. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Build the reporting capability now, since regulatory requirements are rarely relaxed and retrofitting after launch would cost more.
options.rationale: This is the assume-the-worst error. It commits eight per cent of remaining budget to rules that are still in consultation and may change materially or not be adopted in this form at all.

options.text: Record the consultation in the risk register with an owner and a trigger, and reassess the design once the final rules are published and the requirement is known.
options.rationale: This is the wait-for-certainty error. An owner and a trigger make the watching tidier but do not change its timing: by publication you will be past launch and past the architectural decisions that determine whether the capability can be added cheaply, so the reassessment happens with the options already gone.

options.text: Assess what the proposal would require, identify the design decisions that would be expensive to reverse later, and take the options to the sponsor with costs.
options.rationale: The live question is not whether to build the capability but which imminent design choices would foreclose it cheaply or expensively. Separating those from the full build gives the sponsor a decision with real optionality rather than a bet on the consultation.

options.text: Work with your industry association to submit a response to the consultation before it closes, setting out the implementation burden and cost for products like yours.
options.rationale: This is the influence-instead-of-plan error. The response is worth submitting on its own merits and is not a substitute for a plan, since the regulator may not adopt your position however well it is argued and the project still needs to decide what to do about the design decisions falling due now.

questions.explanation: External developments that are probable but not certain are handled by protecting optionality rather than by committing or by waiting. The analysis that matters is which decisions in the immediate window would be expensive to reverse, because those are the only ones where uncertainty has a present cost. That framing turns an unanswerable question about what the regulator will do into a tractable one about what it is worth paying now to keep a door open.
questions.mindset: Watch the external environment early enough that you still have choices.

questions.stem: Your sponsor leaves the organisation nine months into an eighteen-month logistics programme. The replacement arrives from a different division, reads the business case, and tells you in your first meeting that she does not think the stated benefit is the one the company actually needs. The team has heard a rumour that the programme is being reconsidered and delivery has slowed. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Reassure the team that the programme has an approved business case, explain that sponsor changes often bring questions, and continue to the current plan.
options.rationale: This is the false-reassurance error. The person who funds the work has just said she doubts its purpose, so an assurance built on the old approval, with her doubt framed as routine sponsor-change noise, will be contradicted within weeks and will cost you the team's trust when it is.

options.text: Ask the outgoing sponsor to brief the incoming one on the original rationale and the options rejected at approval, before she forms a view.
options.rationale: This is the defend-the-history error. It treats the new sponsor's judgement as a misunderstanding to be corrected rather than a position that may be right, and the outgoing sponsor, however thorough the briefing, is the one person with an interest in the answer.

options.text: Pause delivery, explaining why to the team, until the new sponsor has reviewed the business case and confirmed the programme's objectives in writing.
options.rationale: This is the over-correction error. A pause converts uncertainty into a visible stoppage, however well explained, costs the team momentum it will not recover, and is disproportionate when most of the scope is likely to survive whatever the review concludes.

options.text: Work with the new sponsor to establish what she believes the programme is for, test that against the current scope, and take the difference to the steering group.
options.rationale: The purpose is genuinely in question and the new sponsor has the standing to change it. Surfacing the difference formally is what converts a private doubt into a decision the programme can be replanned against.

questions.explanation: A change of sponsor is a change of the person who owns the answer to what the project is for, and a new holder of that role is entitled to reach a different answer. The work is to make the difference explicit and route it to the body that can decide, rather than defending the original framing or freezing until someone else resolves it. Delivery continues while that runs, because most of the scope is usually unaffected and stopping is expensive to reverse.
questions.mindset: When purpose is questioned at the top, the team feels it before anyone tells them.

questions.stem: A reorganisation splits your programme's delivery teams across three new departments. Nothing about the scope changes, but within a month the teams are prioritising differently: one optimises for its department's cost target, another for its own service metrics. Your programme's outcome is no longer anyone's departmental objective. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Establish with the three department heads what the programme's outcome is worth to each of them, and get it written into their own objectives.
options.rationale: Teams follow the objectives their management chain is measured on. Until the programme outcome appears there, restating it to the teams asks them to work against their own appraisal.

options.text: Restate the programme outcome in terms of the metrics each department now owns, and show where they pull together and where they conflict.
options.rationale: Translation is what makes a shared purpose survive a structural change. Naming the genuine conflicts matters as much as the alignment, because the unacknowledged ones are what quietly decide the trade-offs.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to have the three teams formally reassigned back into a single reporting line for the programme's duration, with the department heads consulted.
options.rationale: This is the undo-the-reorganisation error. Consulting the department heads does not change what is being asked: that the organisation reverse a decision it has just taken for reasons that have nothing to do with your programme, which is very unlikely to be granted.

options.text: Introduce a weekly programme-level prioritisation meeting where you set the order of work for all three teams and publish it to their department heads.
options.rationale: This is the authority-you-do-not-have error. Setting and publishing priorities for teams whose managers are measured on something else creates a standing conflict that the teams, not you, will have to absorb every week.

options.text: Escalate the divergence as a programme risk with the sponsor as owner, and monitor whether delivery dates start to slip before acting further.
options.rationale: This is the watch-and-wait error. The divergence has already happened and is already changing behaviour, so treating it as a future possibility to be owned and monitored records the problem at exactly the point where acting on it is still cheap.

questions.explanation: Reorganisations do not change a project's scope and routinely change what its people are rewarded for, which is the stronger force. Purpose is re-established by translating the outcome into the vocabulary of the new structure and by getting it into the objectives the new managers are held to. Approaches that rely on reversing the structure or on issuing priorities across it both assume authority the project does not have.
questions.mindset: Structure quietly rewrites priorities, and the project's purpose has to be restated in the new structure's language.

questions.stem: Two developers on your team have started leaving blunt comments on each other's pull requests. Nothing is abusive, but the tone has hardened over a fortnight and other team members have begun routing their reviews around both of them to avoid getting drawn in. Neither developer has raised it with you. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Raise review tone at the next retrospective without naming anyone, and ask the team to agree how review comments should be worded.
options.rationale: This is the address-the-room error. A general remark that everyone can decode names both of them without giving either a chance to respond, and asking the whole team to agree wording makes the rest of the team an audience to a disagreement they are already avoiding.

options.text: Speak to each developer separately, then bring them together to agree how they will handle review disagreements.
options.rationale: Two private conversations establish what is actually going on before either has to defend a position in front of the other. The joint conversation is what produces a working agreement rather than two people each promising you separately to be nicer.

options.text: Introduce a written code review standard on tone and response times, and confirm it with the team at the next sprint planning.
options.rationale: This is the policy-for-a-people-problem error. A standard, however carefully confirmed with the team, tells two people who already know how to be civil that they must be, and it imposes process on the whole team to manage a disagreement between two of its members.

options.text: Wait for one of them to raise it, since neither has asked for help and adults generally resolve these things between themselves.
options.rationale: This is the it-will-settle error. The evidence points the other way: rather than resolving it between themselves, the two have let the tone escalate over two weeks, and the rest of the team has already started changing its behaviour to work around it.

questions.explanation: The signal to act is not the severity of any single exchange but the trend and the spread. Once colleagues are altering how they work to avoid a disagreement, it has stopped being private and has begun costing the team. Individual conversations first, because each person will say things one to one that they will not say in front of the other, then a joint one to convert that into an agreement they both own.
questions.mindset: Deal with friction while it is still about the work rather than about the people.

questions.stem: Your client's project manager insists that a data migration capability is within the fixed-price scope; you read the specification as excluding it. Both readings are defensible from the wording. Four weeks of correspondence have produced no movement, the work sits on the critical path, and your delivery team has stopped work on the surrounding module because it does not know which way to build. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Build the capability under protest so that the critical path keeps moving, record the cost as the work proceeds, and pursue it as a claim once the migration is complete.
options.rationale: This is the deliver-now-argue-later error. Keeping the critical path moving is the right aim, but performing the work without any agreed reservation substantially weakens the argument that it was never owed, and a claim raised after the fact is the hardest kind to win.

options.text: Hold the surrounding module until the client accepts your reading, explaining in writing that resuming work before the scope question is settled would concede the point.
options.rationale: This is the leverage error. It converts a contractual disagreement into a schedule failure that both parties will be blamed for, and the client is likely to read a deliberate stoppage, however carefully explained in writing, as bad faith.

options.text: Ask the client to raise a change request for the migration capability, so that the work can be formally authorised, priced and scheduled through the change procedure.
options.rationale: This is the assume-you-are-right error. A change request presumes the work is outside scope, which is the very thing in dispute, so routing it through the change procedure is likely to read as a negotiating move rather than a resolution and will stall on the same disagreement.

options.text: Agree with the client to proceed on a time-and-materials variation for this item alone, with entitlement expressly reserved, and refer the interpretation to the contract's escalation route.
options.rationale: It unblocks the critical path without either side conceding, because the reservation keeps the entitlement question live. The escalation route exists precisely for a genuine ambiguity that the two project managers have failed to close.

questions.explanation: A genuine ambiguity between two defensible readings will not be resolved by either project manager repeating their interpretation, and after four weeks the evidence is that it has not been. The move is to decouple the two problems: keep the work moving on a basis that preserves both parties' positions, and send the interpretation to whatever forum the contract provides for it. Answers that trade delivery for negotiating position turn a commercial disagreement into a delivery failure that harms both sides.
questions.mindset: When a disagreement starts costing delivery, separate settling the entitlement from unblocking the work.

questions.stem: Three disagreements have surfaced on your programme in the same week. Each has a different underlying cause and each needs a different first move from you. Match each disagreement to the action that addresses its actual source. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: Two teams each believe the other is responsible for maintaining a shared test data set. Both are certain, both are pleasant about it, and the data set has not been refreshed for a month.
A business analyst and a developer disagree about whether a reported behaviour is a defect or the requirement working as written. Both are reading the same specification.
Two senior engineers who have worked together for years are now disagreeing on almost everything, including matters they previously settled quickly.

options.text: Establish and record who owns the item
options.rationale: Nobody disputes what should happen, only whose job it is. That is an ownership gap rather than a conflict, and it closes the moment someone with standing writes the answer down.

options.text: Clarify the requirement with the person who set it
options.rationale: The disagreement is downstream of an ambiguous specification, so neither party can resolve it from the document they are both reading. The requester is the only source of the intent.

options.text: Explore what changed in the working relationship
options.rationale: A pair with a long history of settling things quickly who now disagree about everything are signalling that the issue is not the issues. The pattern, not any single dispute, is what needs the conversation.

options.text: Have the wider team vote on the outcome
options.rationale: Not used. A vote produces a decision without touching the cause and leaves a losing side in each case. It also invites people with no stake into disagreements that are not theirs.

options.text: Divide the disputed work between both parties
options.rationale: Not used. Splitting the work suits a genuine resource contention. None of these three is about capacity, and in the first case dividing an ownership gap in half guarantees it stays open.

questions.explanation: Disagreements that look alike on the surface have different origins, and the first move follows the origin. An ownership gap needs a decision recorded, an ambiguity needs the author of the requirement, and a relationship that has degraded needs a conversation about the relationship rather than about the latest thing it produced. The two unused options are both ways of disposing of a disagreement without diagnosing it, which is why they can be applied to anything and reliably fix nothing.
questions.mindset: Treat the source of a disagreement, not the volume of it.

questions.stem: A developer who joined your team three months ago is visibly struggling. Their work needs rework more often than anyone else's, and in the last two retrospectives other team members have made pointed remarks about carrying the load. The developer has begun staying quiet in standups. Their manager sits in another department and has not been told. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Raise the performance concern with the developer's functional manager, who has not yet been told, so it can be handled through the line.
options.rationale: This is the escalate-before-asking error. That the line manager has not been told is not a reason to tell them first: routing a concern to someone's manager before speaking to them is a serious step on evidence you have not yet tested, and it will be experienced as a report rather than as support.

options.text: Pair the developer with a senior team member so the quality issues are caught before review and stop falling on the rest of the team.
options.rationale: This is the treat-the-symptom error. Pairing may well be part of the answer and it would relieve the team, but applied before the cause is known it may solve the wrong problem while confirming to the team that the person needs minding.

options.text: Bring it to the retrospective so the team can agree together how to support the developer.
options.rationale: This is the transparency-misapplied error. Retrospectives are the right forum for team process and the wrong one for an individual's performance, and the team has already shown it will discuss this pointedly.

options.text: Speak to the developer privately to understand what is making the work difficult and what support would help.
options.rationale: Rework has many causes, from unclear requirements to a missing skill to something outside work entirely, and the remedies differ completely. The one person who knows which it is has not yet been asked.

questions.explanation: An individual performance concern is worked privately with the individual first, because the causes are various and only they can narrow them. Doing so also settles whether this is a performance matter at all: unclear acceptance criteria and an unfamiliar codebase produce the same rework signal as a capability gap. Interventions chosen before that conversation risk fixing something that is not broken while publicly confirming a judgement you have not yet earned.
questions.mindset: Find out why someone is struggling before deciding what to do about it.

questions.stem: You inherit a well-established project team from a project manager who decided everything personally. The team is capable and delivers, but every technical choice, however small, arrives in your inbox for approval, and the team waits. Your predecessor's decision log runs to four hundred entries. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Tell the team at the next meeting that they are empowered to make their own technical decisions from now on, and confirm it in writing so that nobody waits for approval.
options.rationale: This is the announcement error. A team conditioned over months to seek approval will keep asking, because a general permission, written down or not, does not tell anyone whether their particular decision is covered by it.

options.text: Continue approving decisions until the handover is complete, so the team's delivery record is not disturbed, and then begin handing decisions back.
options.rationale: This is the do-not-disturb error. Every week of continuing the pattern makes it more entrenched, the handover gives no natural point at which it ends, and the cost is already being paid in the waiting time between a decision being ready and being approved.

options.text: Agree with the team which categories of decision they will now make themselves, which still come to you, and review the boundary after a month.
options.rationale: A stated boundary is something a team can act on immediately, because it answers the question they actually have, which is whether this decision is one of theirs. Reviewing it converts a fixed line into a moving one as confidence builds.

options.text: Work through the decision log first and delegate ownership of each recurring decision type to a named team member, then publish the list to the team.
options.rationale: This is the over-engineering error. Four hundred entries is a lot of analysis to do first, to produce something the team could tell you in one conversation, and publishing a list of named owners substitutes a new dependency on individuals for the old one on you.

questions.explanation: Autonomy transfers when people know precisely which decisions are theirs, which is why a general statement of empowerment changes so little. Naming the categories removes the ambiguity that keeps a cautious team asking, and setting a review date makes the boundary explicitly temporary so it can widen as trust is demonstrated in both directions. The design of that boundary is also work the team is well placed to do with you, since they know which decisions they have been waiting on.
questions.mindset: Empowerment is granted in specifics, not announced in general.

questions.stem: A department head has attended every governance meeting for your systems replacement and has never objected to anything. Your delivery lead mentions in passing that the same person has twice told their own team that the new system will not last and they should not invest effort in learning it. Go-live is ten weeks away and that department's users are the largest group. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Meet the department head privately to understand their reservations about the system and what would change their view.
options.rationale: Someone who says nothing in governance and something quite different to their own team usually has a concern they do not think the forum will hear. Finding out what it is, privately, is the only route to either resolving it or discovering it is well founded.

options.text: Raise the reported comments at the next governance meeting so the department head can respond to them in front of their peers.
options.rationale: This is the public-confrontation error. It puts the person in a position where the only safe move is denial, and it treats a second-hand report as established fact in a forum that will remember it either way.

options.text: Increase training and communication for that department's users so they are prepared regardless of their manager's view.
options.rationale: This is the go-around error. Users take their cue from their own manager, so more training delivered against an unaddressed message from above tends to raise the cost without changing the adoption.

options.text: Record the department head as a resistant stakeholder in the engagement plan and increase the frequency of updates to them.
options.rationale: This is the classify-and-broadcast error. Labelling the position in a document and sending more of the same information neither discovers the reason nor changes it, and more updates to a sceptic mostly generates more scepticism.

questions.explanation: Engagement is assessed on what stakeholders do rather than on what they say in the meetings you run, and a gap between the two is the most useful signal available. It usually means the concern is one the person judges the forum will not take seriously. That has to be surfaced privately, both because a public version invites denial and because the concern may turn out to be right, in which case ten weeks is enough time to act on it and very little time to discover it.
questions.mindset: Silence in the room is not agreement; read the behaviour outside it.

questions.stem: Your programme spans offices in three time zones. The team nearest you is well informed and shapes most decisions. The other two receive written summaries, contribute little, and have twice built to assumptions that had been superseded in a meeting they were not part of. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Move decision-making into a written asynchronous process where proposals are posted, discussed for a fixed window, and then settled.
options.rationale: Writing decisions down before they are made gives distant teams a way to shape them rather than receive them. The fixed window is what stops the nearest team simply settling matters in the corridor first.

options.text: Rotate the times of key decision meetings so the inconvenience of the schedule falls on each location in turn.
options.rationale: An unchanging meeting time silently decides whose participation is optional. Rotating it distributes the cost and, more importantly, signals that the other locations are expected to be present rather than briefed.

options.text: Appoint a liaison in each remote office to relay decisions to their team promptly after each meeting, with a note of what changed.
options.rationale: This is the faster-broadcast error. The problem is not the speed or clarity with which decisions arrive but the fact that remote teams have no part in making them, and a relay, however well annotated, makes the one-way flow more efficient.

options.text: Have the remote teams work to a longer, more detailed specification so late decisions affect them less.
options.rationale: This is the insulate-them error. It reduces the frequency of the collisions and locks the remote teams further out of the decisions, which will show up as the least adaptable parts of the product.

options.text: Ask the co-located team to document their reasoning more fully in the written summaries, including the alternatives they considered and rejected.
options.rationale: This is the better-minutes error. Richer records of decisions already taken, alternatives included, still arrive after the point at which anyone could have influenced them, which is where the two superseded assumptions came from.

questions.explanation: Distributed teams lose influence through the ordinary physics of being distant, not through anyone's intent, and the correction has to be structural. Making decisions in writing over a defined window converts a conversation the nearest team happens to be in into a process everyone can enter, and rotating the burden of awkward hours makes the expectation of participation real. Improving how decisions are communicated afterwards addresses the symptom and preserves the asymmetry.
questions.mindset: Proximity buys influence by default, and the default has to be corrected deliberately.

questions.stem: Your product owner accepts work at each review and then, two or three sprints later, asks for the same feature to be reworked because a business stakeholder has objected. This has happened four times. The product owner is responsive and well intentioned but appears to be agreeing on behalf of people who have not seen the work. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Establish who genuinely holds the acceptance decision for each area, and get those people into the review or into a short session on the increment.
options.rationale: The reworks are all caused by acceptance being given by someone without the authority to give it. Locating the real decision-maker and putting the working software in front of them is what removes the cause.

options.text: Ask the product owner to obtain written sign-off from the business stakeholders before accepting work at review, so their view is captured.
options.rationale: This is the paperwork error. Sign-off from people who have not seen the working software produces the same uninformed acceptance with a signature attached, and it slows the review without improving the decision; a signature records a view without informing it.

options.text: Extend the definition of done to include business stakeholder validation, so no item is complete until the stakeholder concerned confirms it.
options.rationale: This is the process-patch error. It restates the requirement without solving the access problem, and the team will be left with a growing tail of items that are complete in every respect except a confirmation nobody can obtain.

options.text: Build a two-sprint buffer into the release plan to absorb the rework, since late feedback from the business is normal in this environment.
options.rationale: This is the normalise-the-waste error. It budgets for rework that has an identifiable and fixable cause, and it makes the pattern permanent by making it affordable; feedback that arrives late for a known reason is a cause to remove, not a condition of the environment.

questions.explanation: Repeated rework after acceptance is a symptom of an authority gap rather than of changeable stakeholders. Someone is being asked to accept on behalf of people whose view they cannot actually represent, and no amount of process around that acceptance will make it stick. The fix is to identify where the decision genuinely sits for each area and arrange direct exposure to the increment, which is also the cheapest way to find out whether the product owner needs support or needs authority.
questions.mindset: Find out whether the decision-maker can actually decide before asking them to.

questions.stem: Your sponsor has served notice to vacate the company's leased data centre at the end of March, the date set by the lease break clause, and has asked you to migrate all 140 applications by then. Your analysis, which the sponsor has seen, shows migration finishing about seven weeks later. The sponsor's position is that the notice is served and the team will find a way. Two of your leads have privately said they will not sign up to March. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Re-plan the migration to March, moving the most critical applications first, and manage any shortfall through contingency and overtime as it appears.
options.rationale: This is the plan-to-please error. Moving critical systems first is sensible but does not change that it commits the team to a date the analysis does not support; the gap surfaces late, when the remaining options are far worse and far fewer than the ones available now.

options.text: Write to the sponsor recording your professional view, with the supporting evidence, that March is not achievable, and ask for the schedule risk to be accepted formally.
options.rationale: This is the cover-yourself error. Attaching the evidence makes a better record and still offers no route forward, and a sponsor who reads it as position-taking will be less willing to work the problem with you than before.

options.text: Take the sponsor a small number of concrete options for hitting the earlier date, each with its cost in scope, money or quality, and ask which is acceptable.
options.rationale: It accepts that the date matters and makes the price of it explicit and specific. A sponsor facing a fixed exit date needs a route to it, such as fewer applications moved by March, interim hosting or extra migration crews, or a costed case for an alternative, and options supply both.

options.text: Ask the two leads to re-estimate their workstreams on the assumption that March is fixed, so that the team owns the plan to achieve it.
options.rationale: This is the pressure-the-estimate error. Framing it as ownership does not change that re-estimating to a predetermined answer produces a plan nobody believes, and it asks the two people who have been candid with you to stop being so.

questions.explanation: A date the analysis does not support is a live problem whether it was set by an announcement or by a contract, and neither absorbing it nor formally objecting to it is a response. What moves it is converting the question from whether the date is achievable, on which you and the sponsor disagree, to what it would cost to achieve, on which you can both look at the same figures. That gives the sponsor a decision they can actually make, and it keeps the trade-off where it belongs rather than inside the team's overtime.
questions.mindset: When a date cannot move, its cost can still be seen, so put that cost in front of the person who owns the date.

questions.stem: Your programme reports into a board whose members have begun raising expectation gaps of quite different kinds, and you have noticed that applying the same instrument to all of them has not been working. Complete each sentence with the response that fits the situation described. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: Two directors agree on what the project will deliver but hold very different views on when partial capability becomes useful to the business. The project manager should first
A regulator, a sponsor and an operations director each want a different thing from the same release, and the release cannot satisfy all three. The project manager should first

options.text: agree a staged release plan showing what is usable at each point
options.rationale: The disagreement is about when value arrives rather than about what is being built, so the instrument is a plan that makes the intermediate states explicit and lets both directors see their own threshold on it.

options.text: put the competing demands and their consequences in front of the people who can rank them
options.rationale: Three irreconcilable demands on one release is a prioritisation decision, and it belongs to whoever has standing across all three. The project manager's job is to make the trade-off legible, not to choose.

options.text: reissue the charter with the objectives restated
options.rationale: Not used. Restating objectives helps when people have lost sight of the goal. In both sentences the goal is understood and the disagreement is about sequencing or priority, which a charter does not settle.

options.text: run a structured survey of all affected stakeholders
options.rationale: Not used. A survey is for discovering expectations you do not yet know about. Both situations describe expectations that are already clearly stated and already known to conflict.

questions.explanation: Misaligned expectations divide into those about timing and those about priority, and they take different instruments. A difference about when something becomes useful is closed by making the intermediate states visible, because most such disagreements dissolve once people can see what exists at each point. A genuine conflict of demands cannot be closed by information at all and has to be escalated to whoever can rank them. The two unused options are both discovery tools, applied to situations where the expectations are already on the table.
questions.mindset: Match the instrument to the kind of gap you are closing.

questions.stem: Six sprints into a customer portal, usage data from the beta shows that the feature the customer described as essential is barely touched, while a small utility the team added as a convenience is used daily by most accounts. The customer's programme director is still asking for enhancements to the unused feature. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Continue enhancing the requested feature, since the customer defines what is valuable and the beta population may not be representative.
options.rationale: This is the customer-is-always-right error. It treats a stated preference as immune to evidence, and the whole point of running a beta is to find out where the stated preference and the observed behaviour part company.

options.text: Present the usage data on both features to the programme director, ask what they make of it, and agree together what it means for the next few sprints.
options.rationale: The data is genuinely ambiguous and the customer holds context the team does not, such as a rollout still to come. Taking the evidence to them as a question preserves their ownership while making the pattern impossible to ignore.

options.text: Reprioritise the backlog toward the utility that is actually being used and explain the change at the next review.
options.rationale: This is the act-then-inform error. It substitutes the team's reading of the data for the customer's, and presenting it as settled at review makes it far harder for the director to bring context that would change the conclusion.

options.text: Extend the beta to a wider population before drawing any conclusion from the usage pattern.
options.rationale: This is the more-data error. It is a reasonable instinct and it delays a conversation that should happen now, since the director is currently commissioning enhancements to a feature the evidence already questions.

questions.explanation: Customer expectations are tracked against what customers do as well as what they say, and a divergence between the two is information rather than a verdict. It may mean the feature is wrong, or that it is unusable, or that the people it was built for have not been onboarded yet, and the customer usually knows which. Taking the evidence to them as an open question is what makes a change of direction their decision rather than the team's, which is also what makes it stick.
questions.mindset: Bring evidence to the customer rather than deciding for them what it means.

questions.stem: Your customer's operations director escalates to your managing director, saying the delivered reporting module is unusable because it cannot export to their regulator's format. That format was never in the requirements, and nobody on the customer side raised it. Your managing director wants to know, before the meeting tomorrow, whether this is a defect or a change. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Establish how the customer came to expect the export, what the operational consequence of not having it is, and prepare both the contractual position and the options and rough costs for closing the gap.
options.rationale: The meeting needs two things that are separable: where the expectation came from, which determines fault, and what it would take to fix, which determines the outcome. Arriving with only the first leaves your managing director with no move.

options.text: Check the requirements, change log and meeting minutes to confirm the export was not specified anywhere, so it can be classed as a change, and prepare a priced variation for the meeting.
options.rationale: This is the contract-first error. A thorough check of the record answers the narrow question correctly, and the project manager still walks into the meeting having established only that the customer is wrong, which does nothing about a director who cannot use the module.

options.text: Recommend that your managing director offers to build the export at no charge, given the escalation is already at that level and an early concession would settle it before it hardens.
options.rationale: This is the buy-the-peace error. Recommending it rather than offering it directly changes who concedes, not what is conceded: a commercial position given away before anyone has established the size of the work, which teaches the customer that escalation is the effective route for anything not written down.

options.text: Ask the operations director to confirm in writing that the export format was not raised at any point during requirements, before responding to the escalation, so that the record is clear.
options.rationale: This is the build-the-file error. It asks a director who is already unhappy to sign a document admitting fault, which will not be provided, and it converts an operational complaint into a dispute before anyone has looked at closing the gap.

questions.explanation: An unstated expectation that has surfaced as an escalation raises two questions that are best kept apart. Whether it was owed is a contractual matter and is usually answerable from the record. What happens now is a commercial and relationship matter, and it is answered with options and costs. Preparing only the first leaves the decision-maker with nothing to decide, and conceding before the second is understood gives away a position that may not have needed giving. Finding out how the assumption arose is also what stops the next one.
questions.mindset: Establish what the customer assumed before deciding who is at fault.

questions.stem: Your project's customer is an internal department that will run the system after handover. Their operations manager has been cooperative but has told you twice that the team is at capacity and cannot absorb new work. Handover is in three months and includes new monitoring duties nobody has been recruited for. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Quantify the ongoing effort the new duties will require and take it to the sponsor as a resourcing decision that has to be made before handover.
options.rationale: The operations manager has stated a constraint they cannot resolve at their level. Sizing the demand turns a general warning into a specific decision for the person who can fund or defer it.

options.text: Work with the operations manager to design the monitoring so it fits what their team can realistically carry, and record what is being deferred.
