options.rationale: Some of the load is a design choice rather than a fixed consequence, and the receiving team knows where the expensive parts fall. Recording the deferral keeps the residual gap visible rather than absorbed in silence.

options.text: Deliver comprehensive runbooks, alert playbooks and hands-on training before handover, so the operations team can take on the new monitoring duties as efficiently as possible.
options.rationale: This is the documentation-solves-capacity error. Good runbooks and training reduce the effort per task and do not create the hours, and the manager's objection was about hours rather than about knowing how.

options.text: Proceed to handover on schedule and log the operations capacity concern as a post-implementation risk for the receiving department.
options.rationale: This is the throw-it-over-the-wall error. It transfers a known and quantifiable problem to a team that has said in advance it cannot take it, and relabels it as theirs on the day it becomes theirs.

options.text: Ask the operations manager to escalate the capacity constraint through their own management line, and offer the project's effort figures to support the case they make.
options.rationale: This is the not-my-problem error. The gap is created by your project, so even with your figures attached, making the receiving manager argue for the resources to absorb it puts the case in the hands of the person with least standing to make it.

questions.explanation: An internal customer is still a customer, and a handover only succeeds if the receiving side can operate what it receives. Two things are needed: an accurate size for the ongoing demand so it can be funded or deliberately deferred, and a design conversation with the people who will live with it, since the load is partly a function of choices still open. Training and documentation address competence rather than capacity, and handing over regardless converts a solvable problem into someone else's failure.
questions.mindset: A handover the receiving team cannot absorb is not a handover.

questions.stem: You are ten weeks from handing a new secondary school to a county council, which will run it for forty years. The council's asset information manager wrote the contract's information requirements, which ask for the building models 'in native format'. Your designers' native format belongs to a proprietary authoring tool. The council's facilities team holds no licence for it and will run maintenance from its own asset system, which imports only open exchange formats structured to the council's asset classification. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Deliver the models in native format as the contract specifies, and note in the handover report that the facilities team will need a licence to open and use them.
options.rationale: This is the comply-to-the-letter error. It meets the contract and knowingly hands over forty years of building knowledge in a form the people who need it cannot open, recording the problem instead of resolving it while there is still time.

options.text: Raise the mismatch with the asset information manager now, setting out the formats available and what each would lose, so the council decides what it needs to receive.
options.rationale: The asset information manager owns the requirement and the classification the asset system depends on, so only that manager can say what usable looks like. Raising it ten weeks out leaves time to agree the change formally and deliver to it.

options.text: Have the designers export the models to an open exchange format alongside the native files, at the project's cost, so the facilities team can import them on the first day.
options.rationale: This is the fix-it-yourself error. It changes a contract deliverable without its owner, and an export in an unspecified format will not carry the council's asset classification, so the project pays to deliver a guess at what the asset system needs.

options.text: Buy the facilities team two licences for the authoring tool from project contingency, so the native models can be opened and maintained after handover.
options.rationale: This is the buy-the-receiver-a-tool error. It commits the council to a recurring cost and a tool its team does not use, which is an operating decision the project cannot take for it, and the data still never reaches the asset system that runs maintenance.

questions.explanation: Project knowledge has transferred only when it arrives in a form the receiver can actually use. When the agreed requirement would deliver something unusable, the person who owns that requirement decides how it changes, and the project manager's job is to surface the mismatch early, with the options and their consequences, while there is time to act on the answer. Delivering to the letter, fixing it unilaterally and buying the receiver a tool each settle a question that belongs to the people who will live with the result.
questions.mindset: When a handover requirement would deliver something unusable, take it to whoever owns the requirement rather than to the letter or to a fix of your own.

questions.stem: Your programme is moving into its final phase and several people who have been on it since the start are rolling off within the next two months. Three distinct kinds of knowledge are at risk, and each is best moved by a different mechanism. Match each to the mechanism that suits it. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: The reasoning behind twelve architectural decisions, several of which now look odd without the constraints that drove them.
The step-by-step procedure for the monthly reconciliation run, which one analyst performs and nobody has watched.
A feel for which of the client's stakeholders need warning before a change lands, held by the departing business lead.

options.text: A written record of each decision with its context
options.rationale: Decisions and the constraints that shaped them are explicit, stable and needed by people who will not be in the room. That is exactly what a written record preserves well, and its value grows as the context fades.

options.text: Have a successor perform it under observation
options.rationale: A procedure nobody has watched almost certainly contains steps the performer no longer notices. Having someone else do it while the expert watches exposes those, which reading a description would not.

options.text: Structured introductions and joint meetings during the transition
options.rationale: Relationship knowledge lives in the relationships, so it transfers by the successor being present with the departing lead and being handed the contacts personally rather than in a list.

options.text: Publish it to the team knowledge base for later reference
options.rationale: Not used. Publishing is a storage decision rather than a transfer method, and it assumes someone will later know to look. None of the three is at risk because the material is hard to find.

options.text: Record a walkthrough presentation for future joiners
options.rationale: Not used. A recording is one-way and cannot be asked a question, which makes it weakest for exactly the tacit material in the second and third cases, where the value is in what the observer notices.

questions.explanation: Knowledge transfer methods are chosen by the form of the knowledge rather than by convenience. Explicit reasoning survives in writing and benefits from it. Procedural knowledge held by one practised person is best surfaced by reversing the roles, because the steps that have become automatic are the ones that will be dropped. Relational knowledge only moves through being introduced. The two unused options both make material available without moving it to anyone, which suits reference rather than succession.
questions.mindset: The form of the knowledge decides the method for moving it.

questions.stem: Your agile team of eight has quietly specialised. Two members handle anything involving the payments service and always pick up those stories. Velocity is good and the pair are happy with the arrangement. Last month both were unavailable in the same week and a payments defect sat untouched for four days. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Make it a team decision: put the four-day outage and the concentration of payments knowledge in front of the team, and let them choose how to spread it.
options.rationale: The team owns how it assigns work, and it now has concrete evidence of the cost. Presenting the problem rather than the remedy is what produces a solution the two specialists will cooperate with rather than resist.

options.text: Introduce a rule, starting with payments, that no story may be picked up by the person who worked on the previous story in the same area of the code.
options.rationale: This is the rule-instead-of-reason error. Starting with payments targets the right area, but the rule attacks the symptom mechanically, overrides the team's own way of assigning work, slows delivery wherever it is applied, and invites the team to find ways around it.

options.text: Ask the two payments specialists to write up the service and then run a knowledge-sharing session, so the rest of the team can pick up payments defects.
options.rationale: This is the one-off-transfer error. A write-up and a session give the others familiarity rather than capability, and the next payments defect will still go to the pair because they remain the fastest route.

options.text: Accept the specialisation, since velocity is high, and mitigate the exposure by agreeing a leave rota so the two payments specialists are not away in the same week.
options.rationale: This is the manage-the-calendar error. A leave rota preserves throughput and leaves the concentration intact, and it makes the project's resilience depend on a rota that will not survive illness or a resignation.

questions.explanation: Specialisation raises short-term throughput and accumulates a dependency that stays invisible until it is tested. The recent outage makes that cost concrete, which is what allows it to be weighed against the velocity the arrangement buys. Since the team controls how work is picked up, a durable change comes from the team seeing the evidence and choosing the response, whether that is pairing, rotation or something else. Rules imposed on top of self-organisation get routed around, and single knowledge-sharing events rarely shift who is fastest.
questions.mindset: Comfortable specialisation is a dependency that has not been priced yet.

questions.stem: Your project team currently has 6 people who all need to coordinate directly with one another. The sponsor wants to add 4 more to accelerate delivery. Work out the number of potential communication channels within the team now, then the number after the four join, and finally the increase.

blanks.label: Channels among 6 people
blanks.rationale: With n people the number of pairs is n(n-1)/2, so 6 x 5 / 2 = 15. Each pair is one potential line of direct communication.

blanks.label: Channels among 10 people
blanks.rationale: 10 x 9 / 2 = 45. The headcount rose by two thirds and the pairs among them tripled, because each new person forms a pair with everyone already there.

blanks.label: Increase in channels
blanks.rationale: 45 - 15 = 30. Four additional people introduce thirty new pairs, which is the coordination load the team absorbs before any of them delivers anything.

questions.explanation: The number of pairs in a group grows with the square of its size, so coordination cost rises far faster than headcount does. The practical consequence is that adding people to a late project frequently slows it, and that large teams need deliberate structure, such as sub-teams with defined interfaces, to keep the number of channels anyone must actually maintain roughly constant. The figure counts potential pairs rather than conversations that occur, but it is the right order of magnitude for the coordination burden being created.
questions.mindset: Adding people adds coordination faster than it adds capacity.

questions.stem: Your hybrid programme is replacing the expense-claims system for a manufacturer with plants in five countries. Cutover is fixed for twelve working days from today, and staff need at least ten working days' notice to submit outstanding claims on the old system. The 30-page user guide is ready in English; professional translation into the other four languages takes eight working days, while a one-page notice can be translated in one. About 60 per cent of staff do not read English comfortably. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Send the English guide to every plant today with a covering note that translated versions will follow, so the notice period starts as early as possible.
options.rationale: This is the earliest-is-best error. It starts the clock today for the 40 per cent who read English comfortably and for nobody else; the rest receive a document they cannot use and learn the deadline second-hand from colleagues.

options.text: Hold the announcement until all five translated guides are ready, so that every plant receives the same complete information on the same day.
options.rationale: This is the completeness-over-timing error. Equal treatment is a fair aim, but waiting eight days leaves four days' notice against the ten that staff need, so every plant is treated equally badly.

options.text: Send the English guide to the five plant managers today and ask each of them to brief their own staff in the local language this week.
options.rationale: This is the human-relay error. Five managers interpreting a 30-page guide on the spot will produce five different versions of the deadline and the procedure, and the project loses control of what staff are actually told.

options.text: Issue a one-page notice of the deadline and what staff must do, in all five languages tomorrow, and send each translated guide as it is completed.
options.rationale: The deadline and the action are what everyone must have in time, and that part is short enough to translate in a day. Giving up the full guide for the first week costs little, because the guide is needed at cutover rather than at notice.

questions.explanation: When a message cannot be both complete and timely for every audience, split it: the part people must act on by a deadline goes to everyone at once in a form they can read, and the detail follows when it is ready. Choosing between speed for some and completeness for all is a false choice whenever the time-critical content is small. The test is whether each audience can act correctly, by the date that matters, on what it has actually received.
questions.mindset: Get the actionable core to everyone at once, and let the detail catch up.

questions.stem: Your fortnightly written status report runs to five pages and takes half a day to produce. Analytics on the shared drive show two of the eleven recipients open it. Three of the non-openers have separately asked you in the past month for information the report contained. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Ask the recipients what decisions they need to make and what information would help them make those, then rebuild the report around the answers.
options.rationale: A report nobody opens is failing to match what its audience needs, and the audience is the only source of that. Anchoring on their decisions is what prevents the redesign becoming a shorter version of the same content.

options.text: Replace the single report with the smaller set of formats the recipients actually use, even where that means different content for different groups.
options.rationale: Eleven recipients with different roles rarely share one information need, and one document serving all of them serves most of them badly. Tailoring by group is what makes each version short enough to be read.

options.text: Continue the report unchanged and follow it with a short summary email highlighting the three most important points, with a link to the full report for detail.
options.rationale: This is the add-a-layer error. It increases the effort and the volume, and the summary competes with the report for the same unopened attention rather than replacing it; the link sends readers back to the five pages they were not opening.

options.text: Raise the low readership with the sponsor and ask for recipients to be reminded that reading the report is expected, since it records decisions they rely on.
options.rationale: This is the blame-the-audience error. It treats non-readership as a discipline problem when three recipients have demonstrated they want the information and simply not in this form, and a reminder from the sponsor changes who is at fault rather than what is sent.

options.text: Move the report to a shared dashboard that updates automatically, so recipients can look up the current position whenever they need it and production time falls.
options.rationale: This is the change-the-channel error. A dashboard may well help and would save the half day, but choosing the medium before establishing what people need to know is how the current five pages came about.

questions.explanation: A report is only communication if it is received, and open rates alongside repeated ad hoc requests are unusually clear evidence that it is not. Redesign starts with the decisions each audience has to make, because content follows from that and format follows from content. One artefact addressed to everyone is the usual cause of this failure, and splitting it by audience is generally cheaper than it looks, since each version is far shorter than the composite it replaces.
questions.mindset: Communication is measured at the receiving end.

questions.stem: You are planning a hospital records migration. The regulatory reporting rules are fixed and published, the migration sequence is fully determined by the data, and neither will change. The clinician-facing interface is new, no comparable product exists in the trust, and early user sessions have already produced three contradictory views of the workflow. The programme board wants a single delivery approach chosen and justified. What should the project manager propose?

options.text: A predictive approach throughout, since regulatory reporting and migration sequencing dominate the effort and the interface can be specified once the workflow is agreed.
options.rationale: This is the dominant-component error. It sizes the decision by effort rather than by uncertainty, and it commits the one genuinely unknown part of the work to a specification written before anyone knows what the workflow is.

options.text: An iterative approach throughout, since the interface uncertainty is the main delivery risk and a single approach keeps governance simple.
options.rationale: This is the uniformity-for-convenience error. Iterating on a migration sequence that is fully determined by the data adds ceremony and re-planning to work that has no variability to discover.

options.text: Predictive planning for the reporting and migration components, iterative delivery for the interface, with defined integration points between them and a single integrated schedule.
options.rationale: The two halves of the work differ in the one property that should drive the choice, which is how much is knowable up front. The integration points and the single schedule are what stop the tailoring becoming two disconnected projects.

options.text: Predictive planning throughout, with a series of prototypes run ahead of the interface specification to reduce the workflow uncertainty first.
options.rationale: This is the prototype-then-freeze error. It gets useful early feedback and then locks the interface at the point where real usage has still not happened, which is where contradictory workflow views usually resolve.

questions.explanation: Delivery approach is a property of the work rather than of the project, and a project containing both settled and unsettled work is normally best served by tailoring within it. The test is whether the requirement can be known in advance: fixed regulation and data-determined sequencing can, a novel interface with contradictory user views cannot. What makes a mixed approach hold together is deliberate design of the seams, so that the iterative side has defined points at which it must be stable enough for the planned side to build against.
questions.mindset: Choose the approach the work needs, and choose it component by component.

questions.stem: You have taken over a programme whose planning has been done workstream by workstream, and two separate problems with the resulting plan have surfaced in your first fortnight. Complete each sentence with the response that fits the situation described. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: Three workstream leads have each produced a credible plan, but the totals for shared specialist staff exceed what the organisation has. The project manager should first

The approved plan is eight months old, four assumptions behind it have since proved wrong, and the team is now working to a shared understanding that the plan no longer describes. The project manager should first

options.text: reconcile the workstream plans against the shared constraint before any is baselined
options.rationale: Plans that are individually sound and collectively impossible have not yet been integrated. Baselining any of them first commits the organisation to a total it cannot staff and makes the reconciliation a change.

options.text: seek a re-baseline that reflects what is now known
options.rationale: A plan the team has already stopped using is not controlling anything, and variance against it is meaningless. Re-baselining restores a document that measurements can be taken against.

options.text: decompose the plans to a finer level of detail
options.rationale: Not used. More detail helps when estimates are too coarse to act on. Neither sentence describes an accuracy problem, and finer decomposition of an unaffordable total simply produces a more precise impossibility.

options.text: add schedule buffer to absorb the variation
options.rationale: Not used. Buffer protects against variability around a plan that is otherwise sound. It cannot create staff who do not exist, and it cannot make an eight-month-old set of wrong assumptions right.

questions.explanation: Integration is what turns a set of plans into a plan, and its two common failures are visible here. Workstream plans that are each achievable can be jointly impossible against a shared constraint, which has to be resolved before anything is baselined rather than discovered during execution. Separately, a baseline that no longer matches the working understanding has stopped functioning as a control, and the honest response is to re-establish it rather than to keep reporting against a document everyone has quietly abandoned.
questions.mindset: A plan that is not integrated will be overtaken by whichever part moves first.

questions.stem: Reviewing the last two months, you find your team has delivered eleven small pieces of functionality that appear nowhere in the scope baseline. Each was a reasonable request from a user, each took a day or less, and the developers considered them too small to be worth raising. Together they account for roughly three weeks of effort. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Assess the eleven items, take the aggregate effort and the schedule effect to the change authority, and have their status decided formally.
options.rationale: Three weeks of unauthorised work is a material change regardless of how it accumulated, and the change authority is where its status gets settled. Presenting it in aggregate is what makes the scale visible.

options.text: Agree with the team an explicit threshold below which work may be absorbed, above which it must be raised, and how absorbed items are recorded.
options.rationale: The developers were not being careless; they had no threshold to apply. A stated rule with a recording requirement removes the judgement call that produced eleven independent and individually defensible decisions.

options.text: Remove the eleven items from the delivery, since nobody authorised them and keeping them would set a precedent that informal requests are accepted by default.
options.rationale: This is the undo-it error. It discards completed work that users have and probably now depend on, and spends more effort creating an outcome nobody wants in order to block a precedent that a clear rule would block more cheaply.

options.text: Reduce the developers' direct access to users, so that future requests are routed through the business analyst and logged before anyone starts work on them.
options.rationale: This is the cut-the-contact error. Logging requests is sensible, but direct contact between developers and users is valuable and hard to rebuild, and the failure was the absence of a threshold rather than the conversations happening.

options.text: Update the scope baseline to include the eleven items, so that the documentation matches what has been delivered and future variance reports start from an accurate position.
options.rationale: This is the tidy-the-record error. Amending a baseline to match what happened removes the variance without anyone deciding whether the work should have been done, which is the one decision that still needs making; an accurate record of an undecided change is not control.

questions.explanation: Uncontrolled scope usually arrives as a series of individually trivial additions, each too small to raise, which is exactly why the control has to be a stated threshold rather than a judgement about significance. Two things are needed once it has happened: the accumulated change goes to whoever has authority over the baseline, sized honestly, and the rule that failed gets replaced with one people can apply. Quietly amending the baseline to fit the outcome removes the evidence without addressing either.
questions.mindset: Small unrecorded additions are invisible individually and decisive in aggregate.

questions.stem: Your team's backlog contains around forty items that have never been refined, several written over a year ago by people who have left. In planning, the team spends most of its time trying to work out what old items meant, and twice has built something the product owner did not intend. What should the project manager suggest?

options.text: Introduce regular refinement sessions that prepare only the items likely to be worked on soon, and discard or archive items nobody can now explain.
options.rationale: Refining just ahead of need is what keeps detail from decaying before it is used, and deleting unexplainable items removes the cause of the confusion rather than documenting it.

options.text: Ask the product owner to rewrite all forty items with the team's help, so that each one has clear acceptance criteria before the next planning session.
options.rationale: This is the refine-everything error. Most of those items will never be built, so detailing all forty, even with the team helping, spends significant product owner and team time on specifications for work that will be discarded.

options.text: Have the team estimate all forty items in one session, so that the unclear ones show up through wide estimates and can be refined before they reach planning.
options.rationale: This is the measure-the-problem error. The team already knows which items are unclear, since it loses planning time to them, and estimating a year-old item nobody understands produces a number without meaning before any refinement happens.

options.text: Extend the planning session by a few hours, so there is time to clarify the old items with the product owner as they come up for selection.
options.rationale: This is the more-time error. It budgets for the confusion rather than removing it, and clarification attempted in planning, even with the product owner present, is done under time pressure with the whole team waiting.

questions.explanation: Backlog items carry context that decays, so detail added long before the work is done is often worthless by the time it is needed and misleading in the meantime. Refinement is therefore done continuously and only a short way ahead of delivery, which keeps the detailed portion small and current. Items that can no longer be explained by anyone have lost the thing that made them valuable and cost more to reconstruct than to raise again if they still matter.
questions.mindset: An unrefined backlog is a liability that grows quietly.

questions.stem: Your team could release a working version of the booking feature now, covering the two journeys that account for most bookings, or hold it for a further two months to include four rarer journeys and a redesigned confirmation screen. The business sponsor prefers to release everything at once so the launch communications are simpler. What should the project manager put to the sponsor?

options.text: That the team will release now, since delivering value early is the point of working iteratively and the sponsor's concern is presentational.
options.rationale: This is the method-over-owner error. Release timing is a business decision the sponsor owns, and dismissing a launch concern as presentational ignores real costs in a market where a partial launch can be read as a weak one.

options.text: A compromise in which the two main journeys go live to a limited pilot group now and the full launch proceeds in two months as planned.
options.rationale: This is the split-the-difference error. It may well be the right answer and offering it first forecloses the analysis, since a pilot has its own costs and the sponsor has not yet seen what a full early release is worth.

options.text: A recommendation to release now with the confirmation screen redesign deferred, since it is cosmetic and the rare journeys can be handled manually.
options.rationale: This is the assume-the-workaround error. It commits an operations team that has not been consulted to handling rare journeys by hand, and it judges a confirmation screen cosmetic without evidence about its effect on completion.

options.text: The evidence on what releasing now would earn and learn, against what a single launch is worth, so the sponsor can weigh the two.
options.rationale: The sponsor's preference is legitimate and has a cost that has not been quantified. Putting the earnings foregone and the feedback deferred alongside the communications benefit turns a stylistic preference into a decision.

questions.explanation: Whether to release increments or hold for a single launch is a business decision, so the project's contribution is to make the trade-off visible rather than to settle it. The costs of waiting are usually concrete and quantifiable, being revenue not earned and feedback not received, while the benefits of a single launch are real but rarely stated in comparable terms. Putting both in the same units is what allows the person who owns the decision to actually make it.
questions.mindset: Value delayed for tidiness is still value delayed.

questions.stem: A warehouse automation project will cost £480,000 to deliver and is forecast to reduce operating costs by £160,000 in each full year after go-live. The finance director asks you for the simple payback period, and for the net benefit at the end of year four counting from go-live. Ignore discounting and assume the savings begin immediately at go-live.

blanks.label: Simple payback period, in years
blanks.rationale: Payback is the investment divided by the annual return: 480,000 ÷ 160,000 = 3 years. It is the point at which cumulative savings have covered the delivery cost.

blanks.label: Net benefit at the end of year four (£)
blanks.rationale: Four years of savings is 4 x 160,000 = 640,000, less the 480,000 spent, leaves 160,000. The first three years repay the investment and only the fourth contributes net benefit.

questions.explanation: Simple payback answers how long the organisation waits to get its money back, which is why it is often the first question asked and rarely the only one that matters. Its weakness is visible in the second figure: three of the four years produce no net benefit at all, so a project with a long payback is highly exposed to anything that shortens the asset's useful life or delays go-live. A three-month slip here costs a quarter of the entire year-four net benefit, which is the kind of figure worth having to hand when scope is under discussion.
questions.mindset: Know what the project has to return, and by when, before defending its scope.

questions.stem: Your project is four weeks behind at the end of month five of twelve. The sponsor offers to fund three additional developers, available in a fortnight. Your existing team of six is productive, the codebase has a steep learning curve, and your two most senior developers would be the ones inducting the newcomers. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Accept all three and start their induction the day they arrive, since the schedule gap is significant and the earlier they start the sooner they become productive.
options.rationale: This is the more-hands error. Starting the induction promptly does not change who pays for it: three newcomers inducted by your two strongest developers removes the project's most productive capacity at the point it is already behind, and the recovery may never arrive.

options.text: Model the induction cost in senior time against the schedule recovery each option would deliver, and take a smaller number if that is what the analysis supports.
options.rationale: The right number depends on how quickly the codebase can be learned and how much senior time that consumes, and both are estimable. Modelling it is what distinguishes a resourcing decision from a hopeful one.

options.text: Decline the offer and recover the four weeks by extending working hours for the existing team over the next two months, keeping the senior developers on critical work.
options.rationale: This is the overtime error. Protecting the seniors' time is the right instinct, but sustained extra hours reduce productivity and raise defect rates, so it usually buys a few weeks now at the cost of more than that later, on a project with seven months still to run.

options.text: Accept the three developers but assign them to a separate, loosely coupled workstream so they do not need to learn the main codebase or draw on senior time.
options.rationale: This is the parallel-work error. It protects the senior developers by creating work that was not on the critical path, so the project gains output without gaining recovery on the thing that is late.

questions.explanation: Additional people impose an immediate cost on the team that already exists, and the cost falls hardest on its most capable members. Whether the trade is worth making depends on the size of the induction burden, how much time remains for the investment to repay, and whether the newcomers can reach the work that is actually late. Those are estimable quantities, so the decision is a calculation rather than a matter of accepting or declining what is offered.
questions.mindset: Added capacity is paid for out of existing capacity first.

questions.stem: A test automation task is estimated at 96 person-hours. The only qualified engineer works a 40-hour week but is available to your project 50 per cent of the time, and your organisation plans on the basis that 80 per cent of available time is productive once meetings and administration are taken out. Work out the productive hours this engineer contributes per week, then the calendar duration of the task.

blanks.label: Productive hours per week on this project
blanks.rationale: 40 hours x 50 per cent availability = 20 hours assigned, and 20 x 80 per cent productive = 16 hours of usable effort per week.

blanks.label: Calendar duration of the task, in weeks
blanks.rationale: 96 person-hours ÷ 16 productive hours per week = 6 weeks. The estimate of 96 hours would suggest under three weeks if availability were ignored, which is where most of this kind of overrun comes from.

questions.explanation: Effort estimates describe how much work there is; durations describe how long it will take, and the gap between them is availability. Both reductions apply here and they compound rather than add, which is why a task estimated at under three full-time weeks occupies six on the calendar. Building schedules directly from effort estimates is one of the most common causes of plans that were never achievable, and the correction is arithmetic rather than judgement.
questions.mindset: Effort is not duration until availability has been applied to it.

questions.stem: Your product team's most experienced developer is assigned to it at 50 per cent and to an on-call support rota for the rest of her week, a split the head of engineering set in January. Support calls arrive without warning, and in each of the last five sprints she has been pulled away mid-story. The team has quietly adapted by giving her only non-critical stories, and its commitments have stabilised. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Plan her into each sprint at 50 per cent capacity as designed, and treat the interruptions as normal variability the team absorbs through its planning buffer.
options.rationale: This is the plan-the-paper-number error. A buffer absorbs ordinary variation, not a five-sprint pattern, and the team has already stopped trusting the allocation, so planning to it produces commitments known in advance to be optimistic.

options.text: Accept the team's approach of giving her only non-critical stories, since it has stabilised the sprint commitment and the team chose it for itself.
options.rationale: This is the work-around-it error. Respecting the team's choice is right in most things, but this one restores predictability by wasting the project's most experienced developer on work that does not need her, which is an expensive way to stop being interrupted.

options.text: Take the pattern and its evidence to whoever owns both commitments, and ask for the split to be resolved into predictable blocks or a single assignment.
options.rationale: Only the person who owns both demands can change the arrangement, and five sprints of evidence is what makes the request concrete rather than a complaint about being interrupted.

options.text: Ask her to break her stories into increments of a day or less, so that an interruption leaves little work part-finished and someone else can pick it up.
options.rationale: This is the smaller-slices error. Reducing the damage of each interruption is genuinely useful and does nothing about their frequency, and it puts the responsibility on the person with the least control over the arrangement.

questions.explanation: Split assignments fail when one of the demands is unpredictable, because the interruptible side absorbs all of the variability. The team's local adaptation removes the disruption at the price of the capability it was assigned, which is a worse outcome than either commitment intended. The problem is owned above both, and a documented pattern across several sprints is what turns an appeal for help into a decision someone can actually make about how the person is deployed.
questions.mindset: Fractional assignment on paper is often zero reliability in practice.

questions.stem: You are letting a package for the fit-out of a research laboratory. The building's structural condition is unknown until existing cladding is removed, which cannot happen before contract award. Bidders have priced generous allowances for the unknown, and the lowest fixed-price bid is 40 per cent above your estimate. Your finance director wants the fixed price for budget certainty. What should the project manager recommend?

options.text: Accept the lowest fixed price, since budget certainty is what the finance director needs and the 40 per cent premium is the price of transferring the structural risk.
options.rationale: This is the certainty-at-any-price error. The 40 per cent is not priced against the structural risk but against the supplier's ignorance of it, so the organisation pays for an unknown that will probably not fully occur.

options.text: Recommend a fixed price for the scope that is fully defined and a reimbursable arrangement with a cap for the structural remediation, with the split agreed before award.
options.rationale: The uncertainty is confined to one part of the work, so only that part needs to carry the risk-sharing mechanism. The cap is what preserves most of the finance director's budget certainty without paying the full ignorance premium.

options.text: Delay the tender until the cladding can be removed and the structural condition established, then re-tender the whole package on a fully defined scope.
options.rationale: This is the remove-the-uncertainty error. Surveying first and re-tendering the whole package is the ideal sequence, but the stem rules it out, since removal cannot happen before award, so recommending it does not answer the question the project faces.

options.text: Award the lowest fixed-price bid but negotiate a shared-savings clause before signing, returning half of any unused allowance to the client.
options.rationale: This is the claw-it-back error. It relies on the supplier disclosing what its allowance actually was and how much of it was used, which a fixed-price contractor has no obligation or incentive to do, so the saving is unlikely to be recoverable in practice.

questions.explanation: Contract type follows the distribution of uncertainty across the scope rather than a general preference for certainty. Where a supplier cannot size a risk, a fixed price does not transfer it cheaply; it charges for the worst case and keeps the difference. The efficient structure isolates the uncertain element and shares it, typically with a ceiling so that the client's exposure remains bounded, and leaves the defined majority of the work on the firm price where it belongs.
questions.mindset: You pay a premium to transfer a risk the supplier cannot size either.

questions.stem: Three suppliers on your infrastructure programme have caused concern within the same month, and your commercial manager has asked how you intend to handle each. The underlying problem is different in every case and so is the appropriate response. Match each situation to the action that fits it. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: A supplier is meeting every contractual milestone, but the deliverables consistently arrive at the minimum standard the specification allows, and your users are unhappy.
Filed accounts show a supplier's cash position has deteriorated sharply. Delivery has been fine, but they hold the only copy of a configuration you would need to continue without them.
A supplier has missed two milestones. Their delivery manager attributes both to your team's late provision of test data, and the records confirm the data was late.

options.text: Address it as a specification gap and price the change
options.rationale: A supplier delivering exactly what was specified is performing, so there is no performance remedy to invoke. The gap is between the specification and the expectation, and closing it is a change with a price.

options.text: Secure access to the critical asset and plan for continuity
options.rationale: Financial distress threatens continuity rather than current delivery, and the exposure is the single point of dependency. Securing access is the action that remains available while the supplier is still trading.

options.text: Correct your own contribution and reset the schedule jointly
options.rationale: The records establish that the client caused the delay, so pursuing the supplier would fail and damage a relationship that is not the problem. The obligation is to fix your side and re-agree dates from where things actually are.

options.text: Begin termination for default
options.rationale: Not used. Termination requires a default, and none of the three is in breach: one is compliant, one is delivering, and one has a defence the records support.

options.text: Withhold payment until performance improves
options.rationale: Not used. Withholding is a remedy for non-performance and would be unjustified in all three. Against the supplier in financial difficulty it would also accelerate exactly the failure you are trying to protect against.

questions.explanation: Supplier problems that all present as dissatisfaction have quite different causes, and the response follows the cause rather than the frustration. A supplier meeting a weak specification is a definition problem and costs money to fix. Financial distress is a continuity problem and is addressed by securing what you would need if they failed. A missed milestone the client caused is a client problem. Standard contractual remedies are unavailable in all three, and applying them regardless converts a manageable situation into a dispute.
questions.mindset: Match the response to whether the problem is performance, definition, or solvency.

questions.stem: Your organisation has contracted a development partner on a fixed scope, fixed price basis, but your own delivery runs in two-week iterations with evolving requirements. Eight weeks in, the partner has raised nine change requests, each individually justified, and your product owner is spending most of her time on change paperwork rather than on the product. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree with the partner's delivery lead that changes will be batched into a single monthly submission, to reduce the administrative burden on the product owner and on both commercial teams.
options.rationale: This is the manage-the-symptom error. Batching slows the feedback the iterations exist to produce, and agreeing it with the partner only shares the burden: the underlying incompatibility keeps generating the same volume of change.

options.text: Open a commercial conversation about restructuring the engagement, for example to capacity-based or incremental work packages, and quantify what the change overhead has cost so far.
options.rationale: The change volume is a predictable consequence of the contract form rather than a failure by either party, and only a commercial change addresses it. The cost figures are what make the case to people who will otherwise see a working contract.

options.text: Fix the requirements for the next three months so the partner has a stable scope to deliver against, then review the backlog together at the end of that period.
options.rationale: This is the abandon-the-method error. It solves the contractual friction by suspending the adaptability the iterative approach was chosen for, without anyone deciding that was a good trade, and the friction returns as soon as the backlog is reopened.

options.text: Escalate to procurement that the partner is raising excessive change requests, and ask them to challenge each one more robustly before it reaches the product owner's desk.
options.rationale: This is the blame-the-supplier error. The stem says each request is justified, so screening and challenging them harder produces disputes the partner will win while leaving the cause untouched.

questions.explanation: A fixed-scope contract wrapped around an iterative delivery converts every learning into a contractual event, which is exactly what the iterations are designed to generate. The friction is structural, so process improvements at the edges only change how the burden is distributed. The response is commercial: restructure toward a form that pays for capacity or for successive increments, and support the case with what the current arrangement has already cost in overhead and in product owner time diverted from the product.
questions.mindset: A contract that fights the delivery method will win, one change request at a time.

questions.stem: Your project holds a contingency reserve of £250,000 for identified risks, within a total budget that also includes a separate £100,000 management reserve. By month seven, three identified risks have occurred, drawing £40,000, £75,000 and £30,000 from contingency. Work out the contingency remaining, then the percentage of the original contingency reserve that has been consumed.

blanks.label: Contingency remaining (£)
blanks.rationale: The three drawdowns total 40,000 + 75,000 + 30,000 = 145,000, and 250,000 - 145,000 leaves 105,000. The management reserve is untouched because it is not available for identified risks.

blanks.label: Percentage of contingency consumed
blanks.rationale: 145,000 ÷ 250,000 = 58 per cent. The figure only becomes meaningful once compared with how much of the identified risk exposure remains ahead of the project.

questions.explanation: Contingency covers risks that were identified and quantified, while management reserve covers what was not foreseen, and the two are controlled by different people for that reason. The consumption percentage is a leading indicator only when read against remaining exposure rather than against elapsed schedule: 58 per cent consumed at month seven of twelve looks proportionate, but if the largest remaining risks all sit in the final quarter then the reserve is already in trouble and there is still time to act on it.
questions.mindset: Track reserve consumption against elapsed risk, not against elapsed time.

questions.stem: Your cost forecast shows the project finishing 12 per cent over budget. The overspend is driven by a supplier claim that is disputed and might be settled anywhere between nothing and the full amount. Your sponsor has an investment committee meeting in a week and has asked you for a single number. What should the project manager provide?

options.text: The 12 per cent figure as the single forecast, since it is the current best estimate and the sponsor asked for one number, then a mention of the claim in the commentary.
options.rationale: This is the comply-literally error. Reporting the upper bound as the forecast overstates the likely outcome, a line of commentary beneath the headline does not change the figure the committee acts on, and if the claim settles low the committee learns to discount your future figures.

options.text: The forecast excluding the disputed claim, with the claim reported separately as a contingent liability once the committee has accepted the base figure, so that the headline reflects settled costs only.
options.rationale: This is the exclude-the-awkward-item error. It produces a headline number that is very likely to be wrong in one direction, and disclosing the claim only after the committee has accepted the base figure makes it even less likely that anyone connects the two.

options.text: A most likely figure with the range and the specific event that determines where in it the outcome falls, together with the decision the committee could take if the claim settles high.
options.rationale: It answers the question asked while making the uncertainty and its single cause explicit. Naming the decision that would follow a high settlement is what makes the range actionable rather than merely honest.

options.text: An expected value for the claim, based on your legal team's assessment of the probability of each outcome, added to the base forecast before it goes to the committee as the single figure requested.
options.rationale: This is the false-precision error. An expected value is a useful planning input and a poor description of a binary settlement, since the project will not experience the weighted average of two outcomes, and presenting it as the single figure hides that either end is possible.

questions.explanation: A request for a single number is usually a request for something the committee can act on, not a demand that uncertainty be suppressed. Where a forecast turns on one identifiable and binary event, the honest and useful report gives the likely position, the bounds, the event that decides between them, and the action that each end would call for. That preserves the decision-maker's ability to prepare for the downside, which a point estimate removes whichever value is chosen.
questions.mindset: A single number that hides a real range transfers the uncertainty to whoever acts on it.

questions.stem: Your customer-identity verification team of seven is funded 60 per cent by the retail banking division and 40 per cent by the business banking division, under an agreement the two division heads signed at the start of the year. The product owner ranks the backlog by value, and over the last two quarters retail work has taken about 85 per cent of the team's sprint capacity. Business banking's finance lead has noticed and asks why her division is still paying 40 per cent. What should the delivery lead do?

options.text: Work with the product owner to reserve 40 per cent of each sprint for business banking items from the next sprint onwards, so that capacity follows the funding share in the agreement.
options.rationale: This is the match-the-money error. It lets the funding split override the value ranking without anyone who owns the agreement deciding that it should. Whether the team serves the split or the ranking is a commercial choice for the two divisions, not for the delivery lead and product owner.

options.text: Ask finance to recharge the last two quarters at 85/15, then use each quarter's actual capacity split as the charging basis from now on, so that each division pays for what it receives.
options.rationale: This is the unilateral-recharge error. It rewrites a signed agreement retrospectively on the delivery lead's initiative, and moving to pay-per-use changes how the divisions will compete for priority, a consequence the division heads should choose rather than discover.

options.text: Explain to the finance lead that the team is funded as a whole and ranks work by value rather than by funding share, so the split does not need to change while that ranking stands.
options.rationale: This is the defend-the-process error. Ranking by value is sound, but it answers a question about prioritisation, not about whether the funding agreement still reflects what each division receives. Dismissing the query leaves a funder's concern unresolved and the people who own the agreement uninformed.

options.text: Show both division heads the sprint capacity each division has received each quarter against the agreed 60/40 split, and ask them to decide together whether the split or the ranking should change.
options.rationale: The mismatch is real and the delivery lead did not create it: the product owner ranked by value and the divisions agreed the split. Putting the evidence in front of the two people who signed the agreement lets them choose which one gives way, a decision only they can take.

questions.explanation: When a shared team's funding split and its actual use of capacity drift apart, the gap is a commercial question that belongs to whoever agreed the split. The delivery role is to measure the drift and put it in front of those owners with the options: change the split to match the work, or change the priorities to match the money. Quietly correcting either side, or defending the status quo to one funder, takes a decision that was never delegated.
questions.mindset: When the money and the work have drifted apart, show the people who agreed the split and let them choose which one moves.

questions.stem: Acceptance testing has found the same category of defect eleven times: incorrect handling of dates that fall in the final week of a financial period. Each has been fixed on discovery within a day. Your test manager reports the fix rate as evidence the process is working, and wants to proceed to the next test cycle. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Accept the test manager's assessment, since defects found in testing and fixed quickly is the intended outcome, then review the defect log at the end of the next cycle.
options.rationale: This is the process-is-working error. It measures the detection and repair loop, which is functioning, and ignores that the same fault is being manufactured repeatedly upstream of it. Reviewing the log after the next cycle defers the question while the fault keeps being built.

options.text: Add specific regression tests for period-end date handling before the next cycle starts, so that any further instances are caught automatically and fixed on discovery.
options.rationale: This is the catch-it-faster error. Putting the tests in place before the cycle starts makes detection quicker still, and better detection reduces the escape rate while leaving the injection rate untouched, so the team keeps building the same fault and paying to find it.

options.text: Extend the test cycle by two weeks to allow deeper coverage of date handling across all financial periods, and agree the extension with the sponsor first.
options.rationale: This is the more-testing error. Agreeing the two-week extension with the sponsor makes the schedule cost legitimate without making it well spent: it looks harder for a symptom whose cause has not been established, and will find more of the same defects without reducing how many are created.

options.text: Halt progression to the next cycle and require the team to establish why this defect class keeps being introduced before further fixes are made.
options.rationale: Eleven instances of one defect class is a systemic cause, not eleven coincidences, and every additional fix without that understanding is treating an output. Stopping is what forces the diagnosis that individual fixes have been substituting for.

questions.explanation: A recurring defect class is evidence about the process that produced it, and quality is improved by acting on that rather than by improving the rate at which instances are caught and repaired. The repetition itself is the finding: something in the requirement, the design or the team's shared understanding of period boundaries is generating the fault reliably. Until that is identified, additional testing and faster fixes both increase cost per defect avoided while leaving the injection rate exactly where it was.
questions.mindset: A fast fix rate on a repeating defect measures the wrong thing well.

questions.stem: Your project applies the five quality steps shown in the diagram to every deliverable it produces. Your sponsor has asked where additional investment would reduce the total cost of quality most, and you want to show which single step changes what gets built rather than examining what has already been built. Select the step that prevents defects from being created, rather than detecting defects that already exist.

graphic.title: Quality steps for a deliverable, five steps left to right
graphic.caption: Select a step. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between steps, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Agree standards
regions.rationale: Setting out what good looks like, and the conventions the work must follow, before anyone builds is the only step here that changes what gets created. Everything after it examines work that already exists.

regions.label: Build deliverable
regions.rationale: Building is where defects are introduced rather than where they are prevented or found. What determines how many appear is the quality of the standards and understanding brought into this step.

regions.label: Peer review
regions.rationale: Peer review finds defects early and cheaply, which makes it valuable, but it is still an inspection of finished work. It reduces what escapes rather than what is created.

regions.label: Independent test
regions.rationale: Independent testing is detection at a greater distance from the author, which catches assumptions a peer might share. The defect has already been built and paid for by this point.

regions.label: Release approval
regions.rationale: Release approval is a decision about whether the accumulated evidence is sufficient to proceed. It consumes the results of the earlier steps and produces no new information about quality.

questions.explanation: Quality activity divides into what changes the work being produced and what examines work already produced, and only the first is prevention. Agreeing standards and conventions in advance is the cheapest intervention available because it reduces the number of defects created, whereas review, test and approval all operate on a deliverable that already contains whatever it contains. The general rule is that the cost of correcting a defect rises the further along this sequence it is found, which is why effort spent at the first step repays disproportionately.
questions.mindset: Prevention is cheaper than detection, and it happens before anyone builds anything.

questions.stem: Your team is building the allergen-labelling module of a food manufacturer's production system. A major retailer buying from the manufacturer has made supplier certification a condition of its next contract, and its audit in eight weeks will look for documented verification of every labelling requirement. The team works test-first with pairing and continuous integration, and runs about 1,400 automated tests on every merge, but nothing links any test to the requirement it verifies. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Meet the retailer's audit lead well before the audit, show a sample of the team's automated test output, and agree what form of evidence will satisfy the documented-verification clause.
options.rationale: An evidence clause is satisfied by what the auditor accepts as evidence, and finding that out eight weeks early rather than on the day lets the team adapt output it already produces instead of guessing at a format. Showing real output anchors the conversation in what exists.

options.text: Add to the definition of done that each story's tests are tagged with the requirement they verify, so the build produces the traceability record as part of the work itself.
options.rationale: The verification is already happening; what is missing is the link to the requirement. Making the link part of done means the record is produced continuously by the work, so it stays current after the audit rather than being assembled for it.

options.text: Assign a technical author for the eight weeks to write a verification record for every requirement delivered so far, reconstructed from the code, the tests and the commit history.
options.rationale: This is the paper-it-afterwards error. It produces a one-off document that describes verification rather than evidencing it, goes stale with the next merge, and leaves the team generating no record for anything built after the audit.

options.text: Move the allergen module into a separate phase-gated stream with a formal test phase and signed test reports, so it can be audited while the rest of the product stays in sprints.
options.rationale: This is the change-the-method error. It assumes documented evidence requires a predictive lifecycle, and it gives up the test-first practice that is doing the verification in order to produce paperwork about a weaker version of it.

options.text: Write to the retailer explaining that test-first development verifies every requirement by design, and ask for the documentation clause to be waived for this supplier given the team's record.
options.rationale: This is the argue-away-the-requirement error. The retailer is entitled to evidence rather than assurances, and allergen labelling is exactly where a buyer will decline to take a supplier's word that verification happened.

questions.explanation: When a customer or regulator imposes a requirement for quality evidence, the constraint is legitimate and the work is to meet it in a way that fits how the team actually verifies. Establish early, with whoever will judge the evidence, what will satisfy them, and make the evidence a by-product of the practices that do the verifying so it is continuous and current. Reconstructing records afterwards, changing lifecycle to suit a document format, or arguing the requirement away each trade a sustainable answer for a convenient one.
questions.mindset: Accept a legitimate evidence requirement and meet it by making existing good practice leave a record.

questions.stem: Your programme must recover six weeks. Two options are on the table. Overlapping design and construction on the critical path recovers the full six weeks at no direct cost but risks rework if the design changes. Adding a second installation crew recovers four weeks and costs £320,000. The design is 90 per cent complete and the remaining items are all minor finishes. What should the project manager recommend?

options.text: The second crew, since a known cost of £320,000 is easier to budget and defend than an open-ended rework risk sitting on the critical path.
options.rationale: This is the avoid-all-risk error. A known cost is easier to defend, but here it buys £320,000 of certainty and still leaves two weeks unrecovered, when the rework risk being avoided is small because the outstanding design items are minor finishes.

options.text: Both options together, so the six weeks are recovered with margin against either one of them failing to deliver its full saving on a path this critical.
options.rationale: This is the belt-and-braces error. It spends £320,000 to buy margin beyond the requirement on a risk that is already small, and running two compression techniques at once on the same path makes it harder to tell which one is working.

options.text: Neither, and instead take a six-week extension to the programme, documenting the reasons and the options considered for the sponsor's record.
options.rationale: This is the give-up-too-early error. Documenting the options does not put them to the sponsor as a choice; two viable recovery options exist and one carries little risk in these circumstances, so recommending a slip forfeits the cheaper recovery before the sponsor has weighed it.

options.text: Overlapping design and construction, since the design is nearly complete and the remaining items are unlikely to affect what is being built first.
options.rationale: Fast-tracking's risk is proportionate to how much the design might still change, and 90 per cent complete with only minor finishes outstanding makes that risk small. It also recovers the full six weeks rather than four.

questions.explanation: Compressing a schedule by overlapping activities costs no money and buys risk, while adding resource costs money and buys less time; which is preferable depends on facts specific to the situation rather than on a general ranking. The decisive fact here is design maturity, because the rework exposure created by overlapping is a direct function of how much the design might still change. At 90 per cent complete with only minor finishes remaining, the cheap option is also the low-risk one, which is not usually the case and is why the maturity has to be checked rather than assumed.
questions.mindset: Fast-tracking is cheap in cash and expensive in rework risk, so price the risk before choosing.

questions.stem: Your lead engineer estimates a commissioning activity at 12 days if everything goes well, 30 days in the worst realistic case, and 18 days as the most likely outcome. Your organisation uses a weighted three-point method that gives the most likely estimate four times the weight of each of the other two. Work out the expected duration, then the standard deviation of the estimate.

blanks.label: Expected duration, in days
blanks.rationale: The weighted average is (12 + 4 x 18 + 30) ÷ 6 = 114 ÷ 6 = 19 days. It sits above the most likely value because the pessimistic tail is further from it than the optimistic one.

blanks.label: Standard deviation, in days
blanks.rationale: The spread is (30 - 12) ÷ 6 = 3 days. It depends only on the distance between the extremes, so two activities with the same expected duration can carry very different uncertainty.

questions.explanation: A weighted three-point estimate pulls the expected value toward the most likely case while still respecting an asymmetric tail, which is why the answer here exceeds the engineer's most likely figure. The standard deviation is the more useful of the two outputs and the one most often discarded: it says how much confidence the single number deserves. An activity estimated at 19 days with a spread of 3 is a very different scheduling proposition from one estimated at 19 days with a spread of 9, and only the range makes that visible.
questions.mindset: A three-point estimate carries information about spread that a single figure discards.

questions.stem: Your programme board has complained that it cannot tell from your reports when it is being asked to do something, and two workstreams this week illustrate the problem in opposite ways. Complete each sentence with the reporting response that fits the situation. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: A workstream has been reported amber for eleven consecutive weeks with the same commentary each time, and no decision has ever been requested. The project manager should
A workstream reported green last week is now certain to miss its milestone because a dependency outside the project failed. The project manager should

options.text: convert the status into a specific decision or escalation the board can act on
options.rationale: A status that never changes and never asks for anything has stopped conveying information. Amber is only useful if it names what would move it, so the report must carry a request rather than a colour.

options.text: report the change immediately rather than waiting for the reporting cycle
options.rationale: A certain miss is not news that improves with age, and a board that learns of it on schedule rather than on discovery loses the days in which it might have responded.

options.text: hold the status until the next scheduled report so the position is confirmed
options.rationale: Not used. Waiting to confirm suits a developing situation that might resolve itself. Neither sentence describes uncertainty: one is a stalled report, the other an established fact.

options.text: aggregate the workstream into the programme-level status
options.rationale: Not used. Rolling a problem into a larger aggregate is how bad news gets diluted, and in both cases it would remove precisely the detail the board needs to act on.

questions.explanation: Reporting exists to enable decisions, and both failures here are failures of that purpose rather than of accuracy. A status repeated unchanged for months is technically correct and functionally silent, because nobody has been asked for anything; the fix is to state what would change it and who can supply that. A confirmed miss is reported when it is known rather than when the calendar allows, since the value of the information decays quickly and the recipients' options narrow with it.
questions.mindset: A status report is a decision instrument, not a record of effort.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the sequence your project follows each month to produce its performance report. A new sponsor has asked which part of the process produces the number she should be managing against, having observed that most of the report describes things that have already happened. Select the step at which measured history is first converted into a statement about the project's future.

graphic.title: Monthly performance reporting, five steps left to right
graphic.caption: Select a step. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between steps, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Collect actuals
regions.rationale: Collecting actual cost and progress gathers the raw record of what has happened. It says nothing about whether that is good, bad or indicative of anything ahead.

regions.label: Compare to baseline
regions.rationale: Comparison produces variances, which are still statements about the past expressed against the plan. A negative variance describes what has already occurred.

regions.label: Analyse causes
regions.rationale: Cause analysis explains why the variances arose. It is essential input to a credible forecast and remains an account of history rather than a projection of it.

regions.label: Forecast outturn
regions.rationale: Forecasting applies a judgement about which past performance will continue, and produces an expected final cost and date. This is the first step that makes a claim about what has not happened yet.

regions.label: Report and act
regions.rationale: Reporting communicates the forecast and triggers decisions. It distributes the view of the future produced at the previous step rather than forming it.

questions.explanation: The value of performance reporting comes from the forecast, because that is the only output a decision-maker can act on: variances describe a past that cannot be changed. The forecast also carries the assumption that matters most, which is the judgement about how much of the observed performance will persist, and reports that present a forecast without stating that assumption invite readers to treat a projection as a measurement. Cause analysis is what makes the assumption defensible, which is why it sits immediately before rather than after.
questions.mindset: Measurement describes the past; only forecasting commits you to a view of the future.

questions.stem: Your organisation closes out delivered projects using the sequence shown in the diagram. Several recent projects have stalled in closure for months, and in each case the delivery team believed the work was finished while the customer had never said so. Select the step that establishes whether the customer agrees the project delivered what was agreed.

graphic.title: Project closure, five steps left to right
graphic.caption: Select a step. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between steps, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Complete work
regions.rationale: Completing the outstanding work and clearing open items is what makes acceptance possible. It reflects the delivery team's own view that the work is finished, which is not the same as the customer's.

regions.label: Confirm acceptance
regions.rationale: This is where the customer formally agrees the deliverables meet what was agreed. Every subsequent step assumes that agreement exists, which is why closure stalls badly when it is skipped.

regions.label: Settle contracts
regions.rationale: Contract settlement closes out supplier obligations, final payments and retentions. It is a commercial step that follows acceptance rather than establishing it.

regions.label: Transfer to operations
regions.rationale: Transfer moves ownership, documentation and support responsibility to whoever will run the product. It presumes the deliverable has already been accepted as complete.

regions.label: Capture lessons
regions.rationale: Capturing lessons records what the organisation should carry forward. It is about the project's conduct rather than about whether its deliverables were agreed to be complete.

questions.explanation: Formal acceptance is the pivot of closure because it converts the delivery team's judgement that the work is done into the customer's agreement that it is, and everything downstream depends on that having happened. Contracts settled, responsibility transferred and lessons recorded all assume a scope that is agreed to be complete; performing them against an unconfirmed acceptance is what produces the projects that are finished for months and cannot be closed. The step is also the last point at which a disagreement about scope can be resolved cheaply.
questions.mindset: Closure confirms delivery against the agreement before anything is released or archived.

questions.stem: Your platform build is nine months into eighteen. The client that accounted for roughly seventy per cent of the forecast benefit has been acquired and will move onto its new parent's systems, which removes the primary use case. Two secondary use cases remain valuable and would need about three more months. Your sponsor is reluctant to be associated with a cancelled programme and proposes continuing to the original scope. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Prepare the case for redirecting to the two remaining use cases, showing the spend avoided, the value still available and how the change can be presented as a response to the market.
options.rationale: It addresses both the economics and the sponsor's actual concern, which is how this will be perceived. A redirection framed as a deliberate response to a customer's acquisition is a materially different story from a cancellation.

options.text: Continue to the original scope, since the sponsor owns the decision and the reputational consequences of cancellation are a legitimate business consideration, and record your concerns in the risk register.
options.rationale: This is the defer-entirely error. Reputational cost is legitimate and the sponsor has not been shown the alternative. Logging a concern in the register records the problem without putting a choice to him, so nine months of remaining spend stays committed to an obsolete use case by default.

options.text: Escalate to the steering committee that the business case is no longer valid, attaching the revised benefit analysis, and ask them to overrule the sponsor's proposal to continue to the original scope.
options.rationale: This is the go-over-their-head error. The analysis may be sound and escalation may become necessary, but going there first, before offering the sponsor a workable alternative, turns a solvable problem into a confrontation you will need the sponsor's cooperation to survive.

options.text: Continue delivery while commissioning an independent review of the business case, so that the decision rests on external analysis rather than on opinion.
options.rationale: This is the outsource-the-judgement error. It spends weeks and money establishing something the stem already treats as known, delivery to the obsolete scope continues throughout the review, and an independent verdict does nothing for the sponsor's real concern about how the change will be read.

questions.explanation: When circumstances destroy the rationale for work, continuing it converts a sunk cost into an ongoing one, and the project manager's obligation is to surface that clearly. What makes the difference in practice is recognising that the resistance is usually about how the change will be read rather than about the analysis. Presenting a redirection that preserves the value still available, quantifies the spend avoided and gives the sponsor a defensible account of the decision addresses both, and it is far more likely to succeed than an argument that only proves the original case is dead.
questions.mindset: Closing work that has stopped being worth doing is a success, and it has to be argued as one.

questions.stem: Your project's design phase is complete and the build phase begins next month. The organisation requires a phase closure before the next phase is authorised, but your team regards this as a formality and wants to start build immediately to protect the schedule. Which two actions matter most at this phase boundary?

options.text: Confirm the design deliverables are accepted by those who will build against them, and record any that are conditionally accepted.
options.rationale: The build phase consumes the design, so acceptance by its users is what makes the handover real. Recording conditional acceptances keeps known gaps visible instead of letting them surface as build defects.
