options.text: Re-test the assumptions and estimates the build phase depends on, since the design has changed what is known since they were made.
options.rationale: A phase boundary is the natural point to check whether the plan for the next phase still holds, because the completed phase has produced most of the information that would change it.

options.text: Archive the design phase documentation to the organisational repository before build work begins, so the phase closure record is complete for audit.
options.rationale: This is the administration-first error. Archiving matters and a complete record is worth having, but it can happen in parallel with build starting, since nothing about the next phase depends on the records having been filed.

options.text: Release the design team members from the project as the phase closes, so their time stops being charged to it and the build budget is protected.
options.rationale: This is the close-the-costs error. Protecting the build budget by releasing designers at the moment the build starts removes the people best placed to answer the questions that construction will immediately raise.

options.text: Hold a lessons learned session covering the design phase before the team's recollection fades, and agree which of the lessons the build phase should adopt.
options.rationale: This is the right-activity-wrong-priority error. The session is worth holding and is genuinely time-sensitive, and agreeing what build adopts is useful, but it does not gate the build and can run alongside it.

questions.explanation: A phase boundary earns its cost by doing two things that cannot be done later: confirming that what the phase produced is accepted by those who must use it, and re-testing the assumptions the next phase is planned on, using knowledge that only now exists. Both directly affect whether the build proceeds on a sound footing. Archiving, resource release and retrospection are all legitimate closure activities and none of them gates the next phase, which is why treating the gate as a document set invites teams to skip it.
questions.mindset: A phase gate is where assumptions get re-tested, not where paperwork gets filed.

questions.stem: Reviewing your risk register after fourteen months, you find that eleven of the nineteen open risks have carried the same probability and impact scores since they were first entered. Two of them relate to a supplier that has since been acquired, and one relates to a technology the project stopped using in month six. The register is reviewed monthly and attendance is good. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Re-assess each open risk against current conditions, closing those that no longer apply and re-scoring those whose circumstances have changed.
options.rationale: Scores set fourteen months ago describe a project that no longer exists, and a register containing a risk to an abandoned technology is actively misleading about where attention should go.

options.text: Define for each significant risk the observable conditions that would change its score, so reviews test something specific rather than revisiting a judgement.
options.rationale: Unchanging scores usually mean the review has no way to tell whether anything has moved. Naming the indicators in advance converts an opinion poll into a check against evidence.

options.text: Increase the frequency of risk reviews from monthly to fortnightly so changes in circumstance, such as the supplier acquisition, are picked up sooner.
options.rationale: This is the do-it-more-often error. The monthly review is already failing to detect a supplier acquisition and an abandoned technology, so running the same unproductive session twice as often doubles the cost of missing them without changing how scores are tested.

options.text: Archive the risks whose scores have not changed, on the basis that stable scores indicate they are not active concerns, and focus reviews on the rest.
options.rationale: This is the confuse-stale-with-stable error. An unchanged score is evidence about the review process, not about the risk, and some of the eleven may be growing threats nobody has looked at; narrowing the review to the rest removes them from view entirely.

options.text: Assign each risk to a named owner and require a written update from them ahead of each review, signed off before the meeting.
options.rationale: This is the more-paperwork error. Ownership is worth having and, without defined indicators to report against, signed-off written updates from owners will reproduce the same unchanged judgements in a longer format with an extra approval step.

questions.explanation: Risk registers decay because reassessment asks people to re-form a judgement they have already formed, and the path of least resistance is to carry the previous answer forward. Two things arrest that: a genuine re-baselining against current circumstances, which will usually close a meaningful proportion of the register, and defining in advance the observable conditions that would move each score. The second is what makes subsequent reviews an evidence check rather than a repeated opinion, which is why frequency and paperwork on their own change nothing.
questions.mindset: A register that never changes is being read, not reassessed.

questions.stem: Your team changed how it handles deployment eight months ago and has since reduced release failures from about one in four to almost none. Three other teams in the organisation still deploy the old way and continue to have failures. Nobody outside your team knows what you changed. Your delivery manager asks how to spread it. What should the project manager suggest?

options.text: Offer to help one interested team adopt the practice in their own context, and use what that takes to inform how it spreads further.
options.rationale: Working through one real adoption surfaces the assumptions that made the practice work here, which no write-up captures. It also produces a second team that can vouch for it, which is far more persuasive than your own account.

options.text: Write up the practice in detail, including the steps, the tooling changes and the checks your team added, and publish it to the engineering wiki so the other teams can adopt it.
options.rationale: This is the publish-and-hope error. However thorough, a written practice requires the other teams to find it, believe it and work out how it applies to them, and it records the steps without the context that made them work, which is why most such write-ups are read once and never adopted.

options.text: Present the before-and-after failure figures at the engineering forum so the other teams can see the benefit and decide.
options.rationale: This is the evidence-is-enough error. The numbers establish that the change is worth making and not how to make it, and teams that are convinced but unsupported usually stall at the first contextual difference.

options.text: Ask the delivery manager to make the practice a standard that all four teams are required to follow, with your team's eight months of results as the case for it.
options.rationale: This is the mandate-it error. Good results justify the practice but do not transfer it: imposing a practice developed in one context on three others invites compliance without understanding, and any team where it genuinely does not fit has no route to say so.

questions.explanation: Improvement becomes organisational only when it survives being moved, and the hardest part of moving it is the context that the originating team never had to make explicit. Helping one other team adopt it in their circumstances is what exposes that context, tests whether the practice generalises, and produces an independent advocate. Publication, presentation and mandate all transmit the conclusion without the conditions that made it true, which is why they so often produce a practice that is nominally adopted and quietly abandoned.
questions.mindset: An improvement that stays inside one team is a fraction of the value it could be.

questions.stem: Your new case management system goes live for a frontline team in five weeks. In the same quarter that team is also absorbing a restructure, a new performance framework and a relocation to a different building. Their manager tells you they will cooperate but that people are exhausted and nothing new is landing. The system's benefits depend entirely on people changing how they work. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Take the saturation to whoever owns the portfolio of changes affecting this team, with the adoption risk quantified, and ask for the sequence to be decided across all four.
options.rationale: No single change owner can solve a load created by four of them, and the only person who can sequence them sits above all four. Quantifying the adoption risk is what turns a plea about morale into a portfolio decision.

options.text: Proceed as planned with additional training and floor-walking support, since the go-live date is committed and extra help at the point of use eases the pressure on the team.
options.rationale: This is the more-support error. Extra help, even at the point of use, addresses capability, while the manager has described a capacity problem, and adding sessions and floor-walkers to an exhausted team's weeks competes with the other changes rather than easing them.

options.text: Delay the go-live by a quarter so the team has time to absorb the restructure, the performance framework and the relocation first, and tell their manager the new date in writing.
options.rationale: This is the unilateral-delay error. It may be the right outcome and it is not yours to choose alone, since the other three changes may be more deferrable or the delay may carry costs you cannot see from here; confirming a new date to the manager in writing settles it before anyone who owns the whole load has looked.

options.text: Go live with a reduced initial scope covering only the functions that replace existing tasks, deferring anything that requires new behaviour until the other three changes have settled.
options.rationale: This is the clever-workaround error. It is a genuinely useful option to have in the discussion, but choosing it now settles a portfolio question inside your own project, quietly defers most of the benefit case and assumes the other changes will settle on a timetable nobody has agreed.

questions.explanation: Change saturation is a property of the people receiving change rather than of any one initiative, so it cannot be managed from inside a single project however well that project is run. Recognising it as a portfolio-level constraint and escalating with the adoption risk expressed in benefit terms is what allows a decision to be taken across the whole load. Deferral and scope reduction may both emerge from that conversation, and taken unilaterally they are one project optimising against a constraint everyone else is also consuming.
questions.mindset: Capacity to absorb change is a real constraint, and it is shared across everything hitting the same people.

questions.stem: A third-party service your product calls for address validation announces it will retire the version you use in nine months, with a replacement available now that has a different data model. Your product is mid-release and the migration is estimated at three to four sprints. Your product owner wants to finish the current release first. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Begin the migration immediately, pausing the current release after this sprint, since an external retirement date is not negotiable and any delay reduces the margin available.
options.rationale: This is the react-to-the-deadline error. It halts a release in progress for a deadline nine months away, and starting before the work is understood is how a four-sprint estimate becomes an eight-sprint one.

options.text: Establish what the migration actually requires with a short investigation, then plan it into the roadmap with margin before the retirement date.
options.rationale: Nine months is enough time for this to be a planning matter rather than an emergency, and the three-to-four sprint figure is an estimate made without investigation. Sizing it properly is what makes the scheduling decision real.

options.text: Finish the current release as the product owner prefers, add the migration to the backlog, then reassess it when the release is complete.
options.rationale: This is the defer-without-sizing error. Putting the migration on the backlog records it without sizing it, and accepting the preference over an unexamined estimate means that if the migration turns out to be substantially larger than four sprints the remaining margin may already be gone.

options.text: Ask the supplier, through your account manager, whether the retirement date can be extended for your organisation given the size and age of your integration.
options.rationale: This is the negotiate-the-immovable error. It is worth asking and cannot be planned on, since a published retirement schedule reflects the supplier's own costs and an informal assurance from an account manager is a weak basis for deferring work.

questions.explanation: External changes with a fixed date and a known scope are a planning problem, and the risk is that they are treated as either an emergency or a distant concern. Both errors come from acting on an unexamined estimate. A short investigation converts a range into something specific enough to schedule, which usually reveals both that there is more time than the alarmed view assumes and less slack than the relaxed one does. The margin then belongs in the plan rather than in the final weeks before the date.
questions.mindset: A dated external deadline converts into a delivery decision that gets more expensive to defer.

questions.stem: A second team joins your product six months in. The original team can recite the product vision word for word, but it was written when the product served one customer segment, and the new team's work serves a different one. In planning, the two teams keep making opposite calls on the same trade-offs, each citing the vision in support. Both are reading it honestly. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Have the original team walk the new team through the vision and the decisions it has guided, so both interpret it the same way.
options.rationale: This is the induction error. It treats a stale statement as a comprehension problem, and the new team would be taught to read a vision, and a record of past decisions, that were never written with their segment in view.

options.text: Give each team a vision for its own segment, drafted by the team that serves it, so each has a statement that fits its work.
options.rationale: This is the local-optimisation error. Two visions, however well written, remove the friction by removing the shared goal, and the trade-offs between segments then get settled by whichever team moves first.

options.text: Rewrite the vision with both teams so it covers both segments and states how a conflict between them is resolved.
options.rationale: The statement is out of date rather than misunderstood, and the missing part is the priority rule. Writing that rule in is what lets two teams make the same call without asking.

options.text: Ask the product owner to arbitrate each trade-off between the segments as it comes up in planning, and share each ruling with both teams.
options.rationale: This is the arbitration error. It resolves instances at the cost of making one person a bottleneck, and sharing rulings case by case teaches the teams to escalate rather than to reason from a shared position.

questions.explanation: A vision earns its keep by settling arguments that nobody has anticipated, which means it has to say what is prioritised when two good things conflict. When the population a product serves widens, a statement that was complete becomes silent on the new question, and teams reading it in good faith will diverge. The repair is to widen the statement and to make the trade-off rule explicit within it, jointly, so the people who must apply it have argued it through once rather than every sprint.
questions.mindset: A shared purpose has to be re-earned whenever the scope of who it serves changes.

questions.stem: You take over a fourteen-month-old programme from a departing project manager. The charter states an objective of reducing customer call volume. In your first week, the sponsor describes the programme as a data migration off an unsupported platform, and the operations director describes it as a route to closing a service centre. The plan you inherited was built against the charter. Which two actions matter most now?

options.text: Establish with the sponsor what the programme is now for, and record the answer where the charter can be seen to have moved.
options.rationale: Three descriptions of one programme means the authoritative objective is unknown, and only the sponsor can settle it. Recording the movement is what stops the next handover repeating this week.

options.text: Test whether the inherited plan still delivers the objective that is actually in force, and identify where it does not.
options.rationale: A plan is a route to an objective, so once the objective is in doubt the plan's fitness is too. Checking it is what converts an alignment problem into a specific list of things to change.

options.text: Deliver to the charter as written, since it is the only objective that carries a signature, and note the two other views in the risk register.
options.rationale: This is the document-authority error. A signature records that an objective was agreed at a point in time, and fourteen months of drift is exactly the circumstance in which that record stops being current; logging the other views as risks does not settle which one is in force.

options.text: Survey the wider stakeholder group to find out how many other versions of the objective are in circulation.
options.rationale: This is the more-data error. You already have enough evidence that alignment has failed, and a survey buys detail on a conclusion you have reached while the programme continues to spend.

options.text: Raise a change request to update the charter to the sponsor's description of the programme, so that the baseline matches what the funder now expects.
options.rationale: This is the premature-formality error. The sponsor's description is one of three and has not been tested against the others, so a change request now would baseline whichever version you heard most recently.

questions.explanation: Objectives drift quietly over long programmes, and a handover is the moment the drift becomes visible because someone is finally reading the charter and listening to stakeholders in the same week. The two things that have to happen are re-establishing what the work is for with the person who can decide it, and re-testing the plan against that answer. Everything else, including the paperwork that eventually records the change, depends on those two and produces misleading precision if done first.
questions.mindset: An inherited plan is evidence of an objective that was agreed once, not proof of the one in force now.

questions.stem: Your organisation announces a strategy shift away from the market your project was built to enter. Your project is eight months from delivery, funded through the year, and your sponsor tells you privately to keep going quietly because cancellation would look like an admission that the original decision was wrong. The team has begun to hear the announcement second-hand and morale is dropping. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Work out what the project would be worth under the new strategy, and take that assessment to the sponsor as the basis for a decision on whether and how it continues.
options.rationale: It converts a conversation about embarrassment into one about value, which is the only ground on which the sponsor can defend either outcome. It also leaves the decision with the sponsor rather than going around them.

options.text: Continue as instructed, since the funding is committed and the sponsor has made a decision that is theirs to make, and record the instruction and its reason in the decision log.
options.rationale: This is the deference error. The sponsor has given a reason concerned with how a decision will look rather than with value, and continuing on that basis spends eight months of the organisation's capacity to protect a reputation; logging the instruction protects you without changing the basis of the decision.

options.text: Escalate above the sponsor to the strategy owner, since the sponsor's reasoning is not in the organisation's interest, and ask for a formal review of whether the project should continue.
options.rationale: This is the premature-escalation error. Going over a sponsor who has not yet been given the analysis destroys the relationship you need, and you have not established that they would refuse a value-based case if you put one to them.

options.text: Brief the team honestly about the strategy shift so they stop hearing it second-hand, acknowledge the uncertainty it creates, then continue delivery to plan.
options.rationale: This is the transparency-instead-of-action error. The team deserves the briefing and the acknowledgement, and neither settles anything, because what they are reacting to is the possibility that the work no longer matters.

questions.explanation: When strategy moves under a project, the question is not whether the sponsor is entitled to decide but whether they are deciding on the right basis. A project manager's contribution is the assessment that makes a defensible decision possible: what the work is worth now, what parts of it retain value under the new direction, and what it costs to stop. Presenting that to the sponsor respects their authority while removing the reason they were avoiding the question, and it is also the only version of the conversation that gives the team a truthful answer.
questions.mindset: A project whose purpose has been overtaken does not become worthwhile again by being left unexamined.

questions.stem: A senior analyst allocated to your project half-time keeps missing your deadlines. Her functional manager tells you she is fully committed to operational work and that your project is a lower priority. She tells you privately that she is being asked for full-time output by both of you and has stopped saying so because neither response helped. You have raised it twice with the functional manager and the position has not moved. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor with the record of missed deadlines, and ask for the project's priority over the operational work to be confirmed.
options.rationale: This is the win-the-argument error. The record strengthens your case, but it seeks a ruling in your favour on a question of relative priority that neither you nor the functional manager owns, and it leaves the analyst holding the same double commitment if the ruling is partial.

options.text: Rebaseline your schedule around the capacity the analyst is actually delivering, and agree the revised dates with the sponsor so the project stops reporting missed deadlines.
options.rationale: This is the absorb-it error. It removes the visible symptom by moving your dates, which conceals an over-allocation that will keep producing missed deadlines elsewhere and leaves the analyst still working to two impossible commitments.

options.text: Ask the analyst to put your deliverables first, and to tell the functional manager herself if operational work then slips.
options.rationale: This is the delegate-the-conflict error. It asks the person with the least authority in the situation to arbitrate between two managers and to carry the bad news, which is precisely why she stopped raising it.

options.text: Set out the analyst's total committed workload against her available hours, and take that to the functional manager as a joint allocation problem to solve.
options.rationale: The conflict is a resourcing decision that was never made explicitly, and the arithmetic is what makes it visible to both of you. Framing it as shared makes the functional manager a party to the solution rather than an opponent.

questions.explanation: Conflicts of this shape are usually not disagreements at all, but a resourcing decision that nobody has been asked to make. Both managers are behaving reasonably given what each can see, and the person in the middle absorbs the gap until she goes quiet. The move is to make the total commitment visible in hours against availability, which converts a contest of assertions into a problem with a finite answer, and to take it to the person who can decide allocation rather than to whoever is most likely to side with you.
questions.mindset: Trace a disagreement to the decision that created it, rather than to the person who is caught in it.

questions.stem: Your lead developer has told you privately that your habit of calling a whole-team session for every disagreement is starting to cost more than it saves. You agree to look at each new case on its own terms. Complete each sentence with the response that fits the situation described. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: Two developers disagree about a library choice, both have benchmarked it, and the decision is reversible within a sprint. The project manager should
A tester has twice made remarks about a colleague's competence in front of the team, and the colleague has stopped speaking in reviews. The project manager should
Two team members disagree about who should have caught a defect that reached production, and the argument keeps restarting in stand-up. The project manager should

options.text: let the team resolve it and hold to whichever choice they reach
options.rationale: A reversible technical decision between two informed people is exactly the class of disagreement a team should settle itself. Intervening here would teach them to bring reversible choices to you.

options.text: address the behaviour directly and privately with the person responsible
options.rationale: This is conduct rather than disagreement, and its effect on the colleague is already visible. Handling it privately deals with the behaviour without making the affected person the subject of a team discussion.

options.text: move the discussion out of stand-up and into a review of how the defect escaped
options.rationale: The argument recurs because it is being fought over blame in a forum with no time to resolve it. Relocating it to a review of the escape path replaces the question of who with the question of how.

options.text: put the question to a team vote to settle it quickly
options.rationale: Not used. A vote produces a decision without producing agreement, and none of these three situations is short of a decision. Two need a different conversation and one needs no intervention at all.

options.text: escalate it to the functional managers of those involved
options.rationale: Not used. Escalation is for disagreements that exceed the team's authority to settle. All three of these sit inside the team, and routing them outward would signal that ordinary friction is beyond it.

questions.explanation: Diagnosis comes before response. A reversible disagreement between two informed people is healthy and needs no manager; conduct that has silenced someone is not a disagreement at all and needs addressing directly; and a recurring blame argument is a symptom of an unexamined failure, which is answered by looking at the failure rather than the people. Applying a single favoured style to all three, whether that style is collaboration, escalation or a vote, is what turns manageable friction into either a suppressed grievance or a bottleneck.
questions.mindset: The right response to conflict is set by what the disagreement is about, not by how uncomfortable it feels.

questions.stem: Two workstream leads on your distributed programme have been in unresolved disagreement for months about interface ownership. In meetings they are unfailingly polite and defer to each other. Between meetings, each briefs their own team that the other is the obstacle, decisions get relitigated by email, and the interface has been redesigned three times. Your last attempt to raise it in a joint call produced agreement that evaporated within a fortnight. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Decide the interface ownership yourself, record the decision in the programme's design authority log, and instruct both leads to work to it from now on.
options.rationale: This is the impose-a-decision error. Recording it ends the redesign loop and leaves the underlying relationship intact, so the next shared question produces the same pattern with the added grievance of a ruling neither owns.

options.text: Meet each lead separately to understand what each is actually protecting, then bring them together to work on that rather than on the interface.
options.rationale: Agreements that evaporate are a sign the stated subject is not the real one. Separate conversations are where the underlying concern can be said out loud, and naming it is what makes a joint session address something that will stay resolved.

options.text: Restructure so that both sides of the interface sit under a single lead, removing the shared boundary and with it the need for the two leads to agree on it.
options.rationale: This is the reorganise-around-it error. It resolves this boundary by eliminating it, at the cost of a structural change made to avoid a conversation, and it tells the programme that unresolved conflict is answered with organisation design.

options.text: Set a joint objective for the interface, make both leads accountable for it in their performance reviews, and review it with them monthly.
options.rationale: This is the incentive-fix error. Shared objectives and monthly reviews help people who want to cooperate and are struggling to; they give people in an unresolved dispute a stronger reason to appear cooperative, which is already the problem.

questions.explanation: Surface courtesy with sustained avoidance is a recognisable pattern: the disagreement is real, the stated subject is a proxy, and joint sessions produce agreements that nobody meant. Because the real concern cannot be said in front of the other party, it has to be surfaced separately first. That is slower than deciding for them and it is the only route that leaves two people able to work the next shared problem without a facilitator. Structural and incentive remedies applied before the diagnosis simply move where the conflict expresses itself.
questions.mindset: Politeness in the room is not evidence that the disagreement has been worked through.

questions.stem: Your team is building a track-inspection app for a rail operator. With six working days left in the sprint, the developers find that the mapping SDK they planned around sends location data to servers outside the UK, which the company's security standard prohibits. They argue the data is track coordinates rather than personal data, and ask you, as delivery lead, to approve an exception so the sprint goal survives. Exceptions are granted by the information security officer, who normally replies within five working days. What should you do?

options.text: Help the developers put their case to the information security officer, and agree with the product owner what the sprint can still deliver while it is decided.
options.rationale: The decision belongs to the security officer, and the developers hold the technical argument, so the useful work is getting that argument in front of the owner quickly. Reshaping the sprint with the product owner keeps the team productive whatever the answer is.

options.text: Approve a time-limited exception yourself, since the data is not personal, and send your reasoning to the information security officer for review afterwards.
options.rationale: This is the borrowed-authority error. The developers' argument may well be right, but the standard names who grants exceptions, and approving one yourself with a review afterwards commits the organisation to a data flow before its owner has looked at it.

options.text: Tell the developers the standard applies as written and ask them to switch to a compliant mapping SDK, even if that means renegotiating the sprint goal with the product owner.
options.rationale: This is the cautious version of the same authority error. Whether non-personal coordinates fall under the standard is the security officer's judgement, and ruling the case out yourself teaches the team that a reasoned objection to a rule goes nowhere.

options.text: Let the developers keep building against the SDK behind a disabled feature flag, and submit the exception request to the information security officer yourself so that no sprint time is lost.
options.rationale: This is the assume-the-outcome error. It spends the sprint on a design that may be refused, test traffic would still send location data abroad in the meantime, and submitting the request yourself takes the case away from the developers who can actually argue it.

questions.explanation: When a team asks its leader to remove an obstacle, the first question is who owns the decision that would remove it. Where that is someone else, the leader's job is to get the team's case in front of the owner in a form that can be decided quickly, and to reshape the team's commitments around the wait. Deciding in the owner's place, in either direction, feels like unblocking the team but spends authority the leader never held, and it leaves the team either exposed or convinced that raising a reasoned objection is pointless.
questions.mindset: Clear the path to the person who can decide, rather than deciding in their place.

questions.stem: On a £9 million refurbishment of a county archive building, you promoted Priya, an electrician on the project for a year, to supervise the six-person electrical crew she had worked in. Three weeks on, two of her former colleagues check each of her instructions with you before acting on it, and one questioned her rewiring sequence in front of the whole crew. Priya has not complained, but she has started bringing routine crew decisions to you. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Confirm to the whole crew, with Priya present, which decisions are now hers, and send the two electricians back to her whenever they come to you.
options.rationale: Authority granted in private is easy to test, and the two electricians are testing it by going round her. Stating in front of the crew what she decides, and then refusing to be the alternative route, closes the gap, and only the person who made the appointment can do that.

options.text: Give the crew's instructions yourself alongside Priya for the next few weeks, so the two electricians can see that you are backing her decisions.
options.rationale: This is the borrowed-authority error. Instructions given in your presence carry your weight rather than hers, and the crew learns that the real decision-maker is still you, so the testing resumes the day you step back.

options.text: Meet Priya privately to agree how she will handle the next challenge to an instruction, and which matters she should still bring to you.
options.rationale: She is already handing decisions back, which suggests uncertainty about her footing rather than a lack of skill. A plan for the next challenge and a clear line on what still comes to you give her something to act on, and keeping it private avoids undermining her in front of the crew.

options.text: Move the two electricians to another crew on the project, so that Priya can establish herself without former peers who knew her as an equal.
options.rationale: This is the remove-the-test error. It treats a predictable stage of stepping up from peer to supervisor as a problem with two individuals, costs the crew two experienced electricians, and leaves Priya never having established authority over anyone who knew her before.

options.text: Ask Priya to report any refusal to follow her instructions to you formally, so that it can be dealt with through the disciplinary procedure.
options.rationale: This is the premature-discipline error. Checking an instruction with the project manager is not refusal, and moving to a formal procedure makes her authority rest on sanctions you enforce rather than on her own standing with the crew.

questions.explanation: A person promoted from inside a team draws authority from two sources: a visible grant from whoever appointed them, and their own confidence in using it. The appointing manager supplies the first by stating the new decision rights in front of the team and declining to act as a route around them, and supports the second privately. Stepping in alongside the new leader, removing the people who are testing them, or turning the testing into a disciplinary matter all leave the new leader's standing dependent on somebody else.
questions.mindset: Authority you have conferred has to be seen to be conferred, and then left with the person who holds it.

questions.stem: A supplier team of twelve works alongside your eight employees on the same product. You have been asked to empower the combined team to make its own delivery decisions. The supplier's contract pays on deliverables accepted against a fixed specification, and its team lead refers every decision back to the account manager, who assesses whether it affects the contract. Your employees experience this as the supplier blocking them. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the supplier's team lead to make decisions within the team, since that is how the combined team is meant to work, and offer to back him if the account manager objects.
options.rationale: This is the ask-for-behaviour-you-have-not-enabled error. The team lead is not permitted to commit against a fixed specification, and your backing does not change that: the request still asks him to take a personal risk the contract has placed on his employer.

options.text: Raise the referrals as a performance concern with the supplier's account manager, citing the decisions that have waited and the delay each one has caused the combined team.
options.rationale: This is the blame-the-symptom error. The supplier is doing what its contract requires, and evidence of delay does not turn compliant behaviour into poor performance; a performance conversation will make the account manager more cautious rather than less.

options.text: Open a renegotiation of the contract onto a basis that pays for capacity rather than accepted deliverables, so the supplier team is free to decide alongside your employees.
options.rationale: This is the reach-for-the-largest-lever error. It may well be the right long-term answer, but it is slow, expensive and disproportionate as a first move, when the immediate need is to know what can already be decided locally.

options.text: Establish with the account manager what decisions the supplier team can take without contractual reference, and make that boundary explicit to everyone.
options.rationale: The blockage is a permission problem rather than an attitude one, and the fix is to find and publish where the real boundary sits. A known boundary lets the team decide freely inside it instead of testing it case by case.

questions.explanation: Empowerment is bounded by authority, and where part of a team works under a commercial agreement the authority is written down. Asking people to act beyond it produces either refusal or personal exposure, and reading either as reluctance misdiagnoses a structural constraint as a cultural one. The first move is to map the real boundary with whoever controls it and to publish it, because a team that knows where the edge is can work confidently up to it. Changing the boundary through the contract is a separate and much larger decision, taken on commercial grounds rather than as a fix for daily friction.
questions.mindset: Empowerment stops at the boundary of what a person is actually permitted to decide.

questions.stem: Four weeks from go-live on a payroll replacement, a union representative contacts you to say the change alters how overtime is calculated and that she expects to be consulted before it is implemented. She was not on your stakeholder register and no consultation has taken place. Your sponsor's view is that the calculation is a system detail rather than a change to terms. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Begin consultation with the representative immediately, since she has asked for it and four weeks is little enough time to complete it before go-live.
options.rationale: This is the appease-the-loudest-voice error. Opening a consultation before knowing whether one is owed concedes the point, sets a precedent for the rest of the rollout, and may commit the organisation to a process it does not control, whatever the time pressure.

options.text: Support the sponsor's position that this is a system detail, and inform the representative in writing before go-live.
options.rationale: This is the align-with-authority error. The sponsor's view is a judgement made without analysis, and putting it in writing only fixes it more firmly; if the change does affect terms then defending that position costs both the go-live date and the relationship.

options.text: Establish what the change actually does to overtime calculation, and whether that engages a consultation obligation, before responding on substance.
options.rationale: Both the representative and the sponsor have asserted a conclusion and neither has been tested. The factual answer determines whether this is a courtesy, a negotiation or a legal requirement, and those need very different responses.

options.text: Add the representative to the stakeholder register first, then include her in the existing communication plan so that she receives updates through to go-live.
options.rationale: This is the administrative-response error. Registering her is necessary and answers nothing, since her claim is about a consultation right rather than about not receiving updates; routine updates on a change she says needed consultation can read as confirmation that none will happen.

questions.explanation: When a late stakeholder arrives with a claim, two questions are in play and only one is urgent: what the change actually does, and what obligation that creates. Both parties have already skipped to an answer, which makes an unexamined choice between them a gamble on either the schedule or the relationship. Establishing the facts is quick, and it converts a contest of positions into a question with a determinable answer. The register update and the wider lesson about how this stakeholder went unidentified both matter, and neither is the thing that decides what happens in the next four weeks.
questions.mindset: A stakeholder found late is evidence about your identification process, not just about this project.

questions.stem: You are revising the engagement approach for a delivery whose three most significant stakeholders are behaving in very different ways, and the same treatment will plainly not work for all of them. Each needs a response matched to what they can do to the project and to how they currently regard it. Match each stakeholder situation to the engagement response that fits it best. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: A regulator who cannot influence day-to-day delivery, whose sign-off is required before launch, and who has no view of the project yet.
A department head whose staff must adopt the system, who is publicly supportive and privately telling her managers to wait and see.
An IT security lead who has raised the same objection at three consecutive design reviews and been overruled each time without explanation.

options.text: Establish the sign-off criteria early and report against them on a fixed rhythm
options.rationale: The exposure here is a late refusal on grounds nobody surfaced. Agreeing the criteria in advance and reporting against them converts a gate into a running check with time to respond.

options.text: Address the private position directly, in private, and find out what is behind it
options.rationale: A gap between public support and private hesitation means the real objection has not been said. It cannot be answered until it is heard, and it will not be said in a forum where she has already backed the project.

options.text: Give a reasoned response to the objection and record why the decision went the other way
options.rationale: Being overruled is survivable; being overruled without explanation three times teaches someone that raising concerns is pointless. The reasoning is what keeps a knowledgeable objector engaged.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to instruct them to support the project
options.rationale: Not used. Instructed support produces compliance and leaves the underlying position untouched, which in two of these cases is precisely the information you need.

options.text: Keep them on the distribution list and monitor for changes in position
options.rationale: Not used. Passive monitoring suits stakeholders with little interest and little influence. All three of these have already shown both, and waiting for their position to change loses the time to act on it.

questions.explanation: Tailoring engagement means reading two things: what the stakeholder can do to the project, and the distance between their stated and actual position. A required approver with no view yet needs the criteria established while there is still time to meet them. Public support with private reservation is a signal that the real objection is unspoken, and it surfaces only in private. A repeatedly overruled expert needs the reasoning, not the outcome, because what disengages people is being unable to see how their input was weighed.
questions.mindset: Engagement is tailored to what a stakeholder can do to the project and how they currently regard it.

questions.stem: Your agile team is building a duty-calculation engine for a freight forwarder. Developers message the firm's three customs specialists directly whenever a tariff rule is unclear, about fifteen times a day across the team. One specialist tells you she has missed two declaration deadlines this month and has started leaving the messages unanswered; since then, developers have guessed at two rules and both needed rework. The team needs the specialists' knowledge for at least four more sprints. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the sponsor to have the specialists' manager make the team's questions a priority, since the engine will reduce their declarations workload once it is live.
options.rationale: This is the override-the-constraint error. Missed declaration deadlines are a real cost to the business now, and a future benefit does not pay for it; an instruction from above moves the deadlines problem rather than solving it and turns the specialists' goodwill into reluctant compliance.

options.text: Agree a fixed block of specialist time each sprint with the specialists and their manager, and have the product owner decide which questions use it.
options.rationale: Both needs are legitimate and they compete for the same scarce hours. A bounded, scheduled allowance gives the specialists a predictable cost their manager can plan the queue around, and having the product owner ration it means specialist time goes on the questions that matter most rather than the ones that arise first.

options.text: Have the business analyst gather every open tariff question first, then book the specialists for a single week of workshops so that the rules are documented before development continues.
options.rationale: This is the capture-it-all-upfront error. A week of workshops takes more from the specialists in one block than the messages did, and on an iterative build unclear rules surface sprint by sprint, so the team will be back with questions the workshops could not anticipate.

options.text: Propose that one specialist joins the team full-time for the next four sprints, so that the other two can work the declarations queue without being interrupted.
options.rationale: This is the concentrate-the-cost error. It removes a third of the unit's capacity while it is already missing deadlines, which deepens the problem rather than bounding it, and it routes the whole team's access to customs knowledge through one person.

questions.explanation: Engagement has a cost, and for stakeholders who supply knowledge rather than decisions that cost lands on their own operation. When it becomes a reason to withdraw, the response is to make the cost explicit and bounded: agree a level of access the stakeholder can sustain, and make the team prioritise within it rather than consume whatever it can reach. Overriding the constraint, front-loading the demand or concentrating it on fewer people all leave the underlying trade unnegotiated, and a stakeholder whose cost is ignored eventually stops engaging altogether.
questions.mindset: A stakeholder's time is a budget to be agreed with them, not a resource the project can draw on at will.

questions.stem: Your operations director believes the new warehouse system arrives in March, because that is what she was told at a steering meeting she attended in January. Your current plan shows May, and the change was reported in three subsequent status reports she receives. She has scheduled her seasonal staffing around March and has now discovered the difference. She is angry, and she is not wrong to have expected March. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Show her the three status reports recording the move to May, and confirm that the correct date has been published since February.
options.rationale: This is the paper-trail defence. Walking her through the reports establishes that you are not at fault, does nothing about a staffing plan built on the wrong date, and teaches her that your reports are where bad news is buried.

options.text: Investigate with the team whether May can be pulled back towards March through overtime or descoping, given the seasonal staffing commitment she has already made around it.
options.rationale: This is the rescue-the-expectation error. It treats her plan as a constraint on yours and may commit the project to overtime or reduced scope for a date that was never real, before anyone has established what the staffing consequence actually is or whether it can be absorbed more cheaply.

options.text: Raise the miscommunication at the next steering group, so the record shows the date change was reported properly and the process can be reviewed.
options.rationale: This is the protect-the-record error. Reviewing the process sounds constructive and still escalates a two-person problem into a governance item about who was at fault, which neither fixes her staffing nor makes the next date change more likely to land with her.

options.text: Acknowledge that the change did not reach her, work through the staffing consequence with her, and agree how date changes will be confirmed to her in future.
options.rationale: The immediate harm is to her staffing plan, so that is what needs working through. Agreeing the confirmation route afterwards addresses the mechanism that failed rather than assigning responsibility for it.

questions.explanation: Expectations are held by people rather than by documents, and a change that was published but not absorbed has not been communicated. Arguing the point wins an argument that is not worth winning and confirms that reports can be ignored, since the important news apparently arrived by other means. The work is to deal with the consequence the person is actually facing and then to fix the channel, agreeing explicitly how commitments made in a meeting will be confirmed when they change. Pulling the date back to meet an expectation that was never valid inverts the problem.
questions.mindset: An expectation that was set verbally is not corrected by a document the person did not read.

questions.stem: Your team has averaged forty points a sprint over six sprints, with a range of thirty-one to forty-nine. The remaining backlog is estimated at three hundred and twenty points. A stakeholder has divided one by the other, told the board the product will be complete in eight sprints, and asked you to confirm it. The backlog has also grown in four of the last six sprints. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Confirm eight sprints, since it is derived from the team's own measured velocity, and report progress against it each sprint.
options.rationale: This is the arithmetic-is-neutral error. Tracking drift afterwards does not repair the starting point: the calculation is correct and rests on two assumptions the data contradicts, a stable velocity and a fixed backlog, and confirming it transfers a false precision to the board.

options.text: Give a range built from the observed velocity spread and the rate at which the backlog has been growing, and say what would narrow it.
options.rationale: The honest answer is a range, because both inputs vary and one of them is trending. Saying what would narrow the range turns the forecast into something the board can act on rather than merely receive.

options.text: Decline to forecast, explaining that velocity is a team planning measure rather than a delivery commitment, and point the board to the burnup.
options.rationale: This is the purist refusal. It is technically defensible, and pointing the board at a burnup still leaves a board that needs a date to use the stakeholder's number instead, which is worse than a well-qualified range from you.

options.text: Ask the team to re-estimate the remaining backlog before answering, so the forecast rests on current understanding of the work.
options.rationale: This is the improve-the-input error. Re-estimating sharpens one number while leaving the growth trend and the velocity spread unaddressed, and holding the answer until it is done delays something the board is expecting now while the stakeholder's eight sprints stand.

questions.explanation: Forecasting from empirical data is sound, and the failure is in presenting a single figure drawn from variable inputs. Two properties of the data are being discarded here: the spread in observed velocity, which sets how wide any honest answer must be, and the growth in the backlog, which means the denominator is moving. A range that reflects both, with a statement of what would tighten it, gives a board something it can plan against and tells it where the risk sits. Refusing to forecast at all cedes the question to whoever is willing to do the division.
questions.mindset: A forecast that hides its own uncertainty is a commitment made on someone else's behalf.

questions.stem: Your firm is supplying four switchgear panels to a data-centre operator under a fixed-price contract that requires a factory acceptance certificate for each panel. After the first certificate is issued, the operator's electrical manager asks for the raw test logs behind it, saying her director will not sign off on the strength of a one-page certificate. Your company's delivery procedure lets project managers release test records to clients at their discretion. The logs are long and use internal abbreviations. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Prepare a summary of the key test results for her director instead, since raw logs are easily misread without an engineer on hand to explain the abbreviations.
options.rationale: This is the curate-the-evidence error. It replaces what the customer asked for with the supplier's own selection, and a director who will not accept a one-page certificate is unlikely to be reassured by a summary written by the same supplier.

options.text: Refer the request to your commercial director before releasing anything, since giving out test data beyond the contract could set a precedent for this and future contracts.
options.rationale: This is the escalate-what-is-delegated error. The procedure already gives the project manager this discretion, so referring it upward adds delay and makes a routine request for evidence look like a commercial concession.

options.text: Invite the electrical manager and her director to witness the factory tests on the remaining three panels, so that they see the results first hand rather than reading logs.
options.rationale: This is the substitute-a-better-idea error. Witness testing may be worth offering as well, but it leaves the first panel's evidence withheld and asks people who requested a document to travel to a factory instead.

options.text: Send her the full logs for the first panel with a short key to the abbreviations, and offer the same records for the other three panels as each is tested.
options.rationale: The procedure puts this decision with the project manager, and the request is reasonable and cheap to meet. A key to the abbreviations deals with the real risk of misreading without withholding anything, and offering the rest anticipates the same need for the remaining panels.

questions.explanation: When a customer asks for the evidence behind an assurance, the expectation being expressed is confidence rather than paperwork, and the quickest way to meet it is with the evidence itself. Where the decision to release information is already delegated to the project manager, taking it is part of the job: routing it upward or substituting a filtered version both read as reluctance and weaken the trust the request was trying to build. Context such as a key to unfamiliar notation helps the customer use what they asked for without changing what they receive.
questions.mindset: Use the authority you already hold to give customers the evidence they ask for, rather than escalating or filtering it.

questions.stem: Your team develops a timetabling system for a further-education college, and the first release went live five weeks ago. The college's registry manager reports three to six bugs a week and expects each to be fixed within the current sprint. The team has pulled every one in and has missed its sprint goal twice. Most reports are cosmetic, but one last week stopped staff publishing timetables for a morning. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Agree with the registry manager and the product owner a severity scale with a response for each level, so that blocking faults are fixed at once and cosmetic ones are prioritised in the backlog.
options.rationale: Response time should follow impact, and only the customer can say what impact each kind of fault has on the college. An agreed scale turns an expectation that everything is urgent into one that can be met and checked, with the product owner still ordering the rest.

options.text: Reserve a share of each sprint's capacity for urgent defects, sized from the last few sprints' reports, so the team can absorb them without giving up the sprint goal.
options.rationale: A live system generates interrupt work at a fairly steady rate, so planning for it is more honest than assuming it will not arrive. A sized buffer lets the team honour the agreed response for blocking faults and still make commitments it can keep.

options.text: Keep fixing every reported bug within the sprint, since the registry manager's confidence in the live system matters more at this stage than meeting the sprint goal.
options.rationale: This is the confidence-at-any-cost error. It treats a cosmetic glitch and a blocking fault alike, and two missed sprint goals show the cost is already landing on the planned work the college is also waiting for.

options.text: Ask the registry manager to log every bug in the backlog and have the product owner prioritise them at the next sprint planning, so that the sprint goal is protected.
options.rationale: This is the protect-the-sprint error. It restores predictability by making the customer wait up to a full sprint for a fault like last week's, which replaces one unworkable expectation with another.

options.text: Lengthen the sprints from two weeks to three, so that there is room for the bug fixes alongside the planned work without the sprint goal slipping again.
options.rationale: This is the stretch-the-container error. It makes room for the current volume without distinguishing urgent faults from cosmetic ones, and it delays feedback on every planned item by an extra week.

questions.explanation: Once a product is live, the customer's expectation of how quickly faults are fixed becomes part of what they are buying, and leaving it unstated lets every report become urgent. The durable answer has two halves: an agreed classification that ties response to impact, so the customer knows what to expect for each kind of fault, and planned capacity for the urgent ones, so that honouring the expectation does not quietly consume the team's other commitments. Fixing everything at once and queuing everything for the next planning session are both single-speed answers to a problem that needs two speeds.
questions.mindset: Agree how fast different faults will be fixed, then plan the capacity to keep that promise.

questions.stem: Your company is completing a new stage-machinery control system for a regional theatre under a fixed-scope contract. The theatre's technicians have finished their hands-on training, and what remains is the maintenance documentation, for which the budget allows fifteen days of engineering time. The system has forty subsystems: thirty-four are standard manufacturer units supplied with their own manuals, and six were designed for this venue, including the safety interlocks on the flying system. How should the project manager direct the fifteen days?

options.text: Divide the fifteen days evenly across all forty subsystems, so the maintenance manual gives the theatre one consistent level of detail from start to finish.
options.rationale: This is the even-coverage error. Consistency looks thorough, but most of the effort rewrites material the manufacturers already supply, and the six bespoke subsystems receive a fraction of a day each.

options.text: Spend nearly all fifteen days documenting the six bespoke subsystems in depth, and point the manual to the manufacturers' own material for the other thirty-four.
options.rationale: The six bespoke subsystems hold knowledge that exists nowhere outside the build team, and they include a safety function. Accepting thin coverage of what is documented elsewhere is the price of depth where the gap is real.

options.text: Prioritise the subsystems the technicians will service most often, since routine maintenance is where a manual is used most, then cover the rest if time allows.
options.rationale: This is the frequency-of-use error. Routine servicing falls mostly on standard units whose manuals already exist, while the rarely touched bespoke interlocks are exactly where nobody will remember the procedure when it is needed.

options.text: Raise a change request for more documentation time before starting, so that all forty subsystems can be written up in depth rather than rationing the effort.
options.rationale: This is the buy-out-the-trade-off error. It delays the work on the assumption that the constraint will move, and if it is approved the extra days still go mostly on rewriting manuals the manufacturers have already written.

questions.explanation: Documentation effort is finite, so it goes where the knowledge exists nowhere else and where a reader getting it wrong costs most. Standard components arrive with their makers' manuals; bespoke elements, and above all bespoke safety functions, are known only to the people who built them and are serviced rarely enough that nobody will remember how. Accepting thinner coverage of what is already written down is the price of depth where the gap is real, whereas spreading effort evenly or by frequency of use spends it on what is already covered.
questions.mindset: Spend scarce documentation effort on what nobody else has written down.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the route a lesson takes from the project that learns it to the project that needs it. Your organisation runs retrospectives diligently and maintains a well-populated lessons repository, yet teams keep repeating the same mistakes and say they have never seen a relevant lesson. Select the step at which this organisation's chain is breaking.

graphic.title: Lesson transfer chain, five steps left to right
graphic.caption: Select a step. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between steps, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Experience the problem
regions.rationale: The projects are plainly encountering problems, since they are repeating them. Nothing in the situation suggests a shortage of raw experience to learn from.

regions.label: Discuss in retrospective
regions.rationale: Retrospectives are described as running diligently, so the reflection step is working. A team that has discussed a problem has done everything this step asks of it.

regions.label: Record in repository
regions.rationale: The repository is well populated, which means capture is happening. A full repository is evidence that this step is not the constraint.

regions.label: Retrieved when relevant
regions.rationale: Teams report never having seen a relevant lesson despite a full repository, which places the break precisely here. Retrieval fails when nothing pushes a lesson at the moment a project is making the decision it applies to.

regions.label: Applied to the decision
regions.rationale: Application cannot fail for a lesson that never reached the team. This step is downstream of the break and would only become the constraint once retrieval works.

questions.explanation: Most organisations that complain about not learning have working capture and broken retrieval, because capture is a visible activity someone owns and retrieval is nobody's job. A repository is a passive store, and a team planning a new piece of work has no reliable way of knowing which of several hundred entries bears on the decision in front of them. What closes the gap is pushing lessons at the points where relevant decisions get made, through planning checklists, review agendas or the people who move between projects, rather than adding to a store that is already fuller than anyone reads.
questions.mindset: Knowledge that has been captured but cannot be found has not been transferred.

questions.stem: You are building a flood defence wall along a market town's high street. The town council's chair has written to your sponsor complaining that the council is 'not being kept informed'. The council has received every fortnightly bulletin and attended all four public briefings. Most of her letter is about the construction haul road, whose route was chosen and contracted without asking the council. The footpath diversion and the riverside reinstatement design are still open. The sponsor asks you to add a monthly letter to the council. What should you do?

options.text: Add the monthly letter as the sponsor asks, and use the first one to set out the reasoning behind the haul road route so the council understands the choice.
options.rationale: This is the more-information error. It treats a grievance about having no say as a shortage of updates, and explaining a decision after the fact to people who wanted to be asked tends to confirm the grievance rather than settle it.

options.text: Reply to the chair with a dated list of every bulletin and briefing the council has received, so that the complaint can be answered and closed on the record.
options.rationale: This is the prove-we-sent-it error. The list is accurate and wins the argument about information, which is not the argument the council is having, and a formal rebuttal turns a complaint about voice into a dispute.

options.text: Tell the sponsor that more updates will not answer a complaint about not being consulted, and propose involving the council in the footpath and riverside decisions still open.
options.rationale: The council already has every update, so the complaint is about involvement, and the sponsor's fix answers a different problem. Offering a genuine say where decisions remain open addresses the real grievance without reopening work already contracted.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to reopen the haul road route for consultation with the council, so that its main grievance is addressed directly before work goes further.
options.rationale: This is the relitigate-the-closed-decision error. It meets the grievance head-on, but reopening a contracted route that is already being built spends real time and money and invites a consultation whose outcome can change very little.

questions.explanation: Complaints about communication are often complaints about involvement. 'Not kept informed' from a stakeholder who demonstrably received every update usually means they expected a say and did not get one, and no increase in volume, frequency or explanation will answer that. The response is to name the real gap to whoever is proposing the wrong fix and to offer genuine involvement where decisions are still open, rather than proving the updates were sent or relitigating decisions already closed.
questions.mindset: Before adding communication to answer a complaint, check whether the complaint is about information at all.

questions.stem: A refinery turnaround employs 640 contractor staff, and a revised permit-to-work rule takes effect on Monday. The site safety manager wants to know who has not yet received it. So far 470 people have attended a shift-start briefing on the change, 310 have confirmed receipt in the site app, and 220 of those did both. Work out how many people have received the rule through at least one channel, how many have not received it, and the percentage of staff reached.

blanks.label: People reached through at least one channel
blanks.rationale: The 220 who did both are counted in each channel's figure, so they are subtracted once: 470 + 310 − 220 = 560. Adding the channel totals alone gives 780, more than the whole workforce.

blanks.label: People not yet reached
blanks.rationale: 640 − 560 = 80. These are the people the plan now has to target specifically, for example at the gate or through their supervisors, before Monday.

blanks.label: Percentage of staff reached, to one decimal place
blanks.rationale: 560 ÷ 640 = 0.875, so 87.5 per cent. For a safety rule the figure that matters is the 12.5 per cent remaining, not the high proportion already reached.

questions.explanation: Reach is a count of distinct people, and channels overlap, so channel figures cannot simply be added: the overlap has to be subtracted once or coverage is overstated. For a message that people must act on, the useful output is the number not yet reached, because that is what the next communication has to be aimed at. Reporting deliveries or channel totals instead of distinct recipients is how a plan appears complete while a group never hears the message.
questions.mindset: Count the people a message has reached, not the number of times it was delivered.

questions.stem: Your agile team of seven used to sit together. Since an office move to bookable hot desks, the five developers sit on the third floor and the two testers work in the device lab on the first. Over three sprints the time from a tester finding a defect to a developer starting on it has risen from half a day to three days, because testers now log defects in the tracker instead of walking over. Facilities will not reserve desks for teams. What should you do?

options.text: Escalate the defect data to the sponsor and ask her to secure an exception to the hot-desking policy, so that the team can sit together again.
options.rationale: This is the fight-the-constraint error. Facilities have already said no, an exception for one team sets a precedent the sponsor may not want to set, and defects keep waiting for however long the argument takes.

options.text: Work out with the team how to restore quick contact, such as an open voice channel in core hours and a developer working in the lab on a daily rota.
options.rationale: What the move removed is the cheap, immediate conversation, and the team can rebuild that itself within the constraint it has been given. Its own channels and working patterns can change this sprint, whereas the desk policy is someone else's decision and has already been made.

options.text: Ask the testers to write fuller defect reports, with steps, screenshots and logs, so developers can pick each defect up from the tracker without needing to talk.
options.rationale: This is the document-instead-of-talk error. Better reports help, but they make the slow channel more thorough rather than restoring the fast one, and most defects need a two-minute conversation more than a longer write-up.

options.text: Add a short triage meeting at four each afternoon, where testers and developers go through that day's defects together and agree who takes each one.
options.rationale: This is the batch-the-conversation error. A daily slot is a real improvement on three days, but it still builds in up to a day of waiting for every defect and adds a ceremony to recover something that used to cost nothing.

questions.explanation: Co-location matters because it makes the quick, unplanned conversation cheap, and when the room is lost that conversation has to be designed back in deliberately. A team controls its own channels and working patterns, so the fastest remedy is continuous low-friction contact and people spending time where the work is. Writing more, meeting on a fixed schedule or contesting a settled policy all leave the gap open for longer than it needs to be.
questions.mindset: When proximity is lost, rebuild the quick conversation rather than replacing it with paperwork or meetings.

questions.stem: You are integrating the plan for a city council programme with two workstreams. A contractor will replace 1,100 on-street parking meters, and its costs depend on ground conditions at each site. An in-house agile team of six, funded at a fixed £70,000 a month, is building the permit and payment app, which must be live when the first new meters are switched on in month five. The app's main uncertainty is how many of the council's fourteen permit types it can support by then. Risk analysis supports £280,000 of contingency, and the finance director proposes splitting it in proportion to each workstream's budget. What should you propose?

options.text: Hold the contingency against the meter replacement's cost risks, and plan the app's uncertainty as a scope reserve, agreeing with the product owner which permit types give way first if the team runs short.
options.rationale: The two workstreams carry different kinds of uncertainty. The meter work's is cost, which money covers; the app's cost and date are fixed by its funding, so its uncertainty shows up as scope, and an agreed order in which permit types give way is the reserve that actually protects it.

options.text: Split the contingency in proportion to each workstream's budget as the finance director proposes, so that each lead holds a reserve sized to their spend and the board can see the allocation is even-handed.
options.rationale: This is the proportional-split error. Reserve should follow where the risk sits, not where the spend sits, and the app's share could only buy more months of a team whose cost and go-live date are already fixed, while the meters' ground-condition risk is left under-covered.

options.text: Hold the full £280,000 as one programme pool that either workstream can draw on, so the app team can add developers if the permit types take longer than expected and nothing sits idle.
options.rationale: This is the money-for-scope error. A pool is sensible for the meter risks, but letting the app draw on it to add developers converts a question about which permit types ship into a cost overrun, and people joining weeks before a fixed go-live rarely add capacity in time.

options.text: Allocate most of the contingency to the app, since software estimates are usually the least reliable in a programme, and use it to fund a second agile team for the final two months to protect all fourteen permit types.
options.rationale: This is the reputation-not-evidence error. It sizes reserve by a belief about software in general rather than by this programme's risk analysis, and a second team arriving two months before a fixed go-live spends much of that time being onboarded while the meter risks go uncovered.

questions.explanation: In a hybrid plan, reserves should take the form that fits each component's uncertainty. Where cost and duration are genuinely uncertain, as in physical work exposed to site conditions, contingency is held as money and time. Where a team is funded at fixed capacity to a fixed date, its uncertainty appears as how much scope it completes, and the reserve is an agreed order in which lower-value scope gives way. Allocating money by budget share or by a sector's reputation puts reserve where it cannot be used and leaves the real cost risk short.
questions.mindset: Hold each reserve in the form its uncertainty takes: money for uncertain cost, ordered scope for work whose capacity and date are fixed.

questions.stem: You are six weeks from the sponsor's baseline approval meeting for a £7.8 million ice rink at a council leisure centre, due to open for a national junior championship next October. While integrating the procurement and schedule components, you find the refrigeration plant has a 32-week manufacturing lead time, so it must be ordered within three weeks for the opening date to hold. The supplier will reserve a production slot for a non-refundable deposit of £48,000; your delegated commitment limit is £20,000. Which two actions should you take?

options.text: Ask the sponsor now for a limited early commitment to pay the deposit and reserve the slot, separate from the decision on the full baseline.
options.rationale: The deposit is a bounded commitment that keeps the opening date alive, and the sponsor can authorise it without approving a plan that is still being integrated. Separating the urgent decision from the larger one is what lets it be made in time.

options.text: Check the rest of the procurement plan for other items whose lead times also start before the approval meeting, so they can go to the sponsor in the same request.
options.rationale: An item found this late rarely travels alone: the same gap between lead times and the approval date may affect other specialist equipment. Checking now lets one request cover them all, instead of finding the next one after its slot has gone.

options.text: Pay the deposit now under your own authority and report it at the approval meeting, since the plant is certainly needed and three weeks will not wait for governance.
options.rationale: This is the urgency-as-authority error. A genuine deadline does not enlarge a delegated limit, and committing £48,000 against a £20,000 limit makes the project manager's judgement the subject of the approval meeting instead of the plan.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to bring the baseline approval meeting forward by three weeks, presenting the plan as it stands so that the order is placed under an approved baseline.
