options.rationale: This is the whole-plan-for-one-decision error. Pulling the meeting forward approves an integration that is only half done in order to unlock a single order, when a limited commitment achieves the same result without baselining figures nobody has reconciled.

options.text: Hold the order until the baseline is approved, and record the late-opening risk in the register with the lead time so that the sponsor can weigh it at the meeting.
options.rationale: This is the record-it-and-wait error. By the meeting the three-week window has closed, so the register would describe a missed date rather than a risk, and the sponsor is left approving a plan whose opening date has already gone.

questions.explanation: When a lead time is longer than the time left before a planned approval, the approval sequence itself has become part of the critical path. The response is to separate the small commitment that preserves the option from the larger decision about the whole plan, take it now to someone with authority to make it, and check whether the same gap affects anything else. Waiting for the full baseline turns a choice into a report of a missed date, acting beyond a delegated limit swaps one problem for another, and rushing the whole baseline to unlock one order commits far more than the situation needs.
questions.mindset: When a deadline falls before the meeting that would normally decide it, take the smallest decision that keeps the option open to someone who can make it now.

questions.stem: Your portfolio office has asked you to recommend a delivery approach for three pieces of work about to be funded. They differ in how well their requirements are understood and in what an error would cost, and your recommendation has to be defensible on those two grounds rather than on anyone's preference. Match each piece of work to the delivery approach that suits its characteristics. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: A regulator has published a rule change with a fixed compliance date, a precise specification, and a substantial fine for non-compliance.
A team is building a customer-facing feature nobody has attempted before, where the main uncertainty is whether customers will use it at all.
A hardware product must be manufactured to a settled design, while its control software is still being explored with early users.

options.text: Plan the sequence in full and control against a baseline
options.rationale: A precise specification with a fixed date and a penalty for missing it is the case where planning pays: there is nothing to discover, and the risk is in execution and timing rather than in requirements.

options.text: Deliver in short increments and let evidence from each shape the next
options.rationale: When the dominant uncertainty is whether anyone wants the thing, the cheapest information comes from putting a small version in front of real customers. Planning it in full would elaborate an assumption rather than testing it.

options.text: Plan the component with settled requirements and iterate the one still being explored
options.rationale: The two halves differ on the factor that decides approach, and manufacturing to a settled design has a long lead time and a high cost of change while the software does not.

options.text: Run a pilot in one location and roll out once it succeeds
options.rationale: Not used. Piloting manages deployment risk for a solution already built. None of these three is asking how to release something finished; all three are asking how to develop it.

options.text: Defer the work until the requirements become clearer
options.rationale: Not used. Deferral suits work with no deadline and no way to learn, and in these cases the deadline is fixed, the uncertainty is only resolvable by building, or the work is already under way.

questions.explanation: Two questions decide approach: how much is genuinely known about what is wanted, and what it costs to be wrong. A precise external specification with a penalty date has low requirement uncertainty and a high cost of error, which favours planning the whole sequence. Uncertainty about demand can only be resolved by exposure to real users, which favours short increments. Work that contains both kinds needs both, applied to the components they suit, which is what separates deliberate tailoring from indecision about method.
questions.mindset: What is known about the requirements and what an error costs decide the approach between them.

questions.stem: On a £6.8 million accessibility upgrade at four railway stations, lift refurbishment has come in £290,000 over estimate. At last week's project board you argued against funding it by removing the £310,000 passenger-information screens package, pointing to the passenger-satisfaction target in the business case. The board heard you out and approved the removal. The screens supplier has finished design, and manufacture is due to start in three weeks. What should the project manager do now?

options.text: Keep the screens' design work ticking over at a low level, so that if the lift costs come in under estimate the package can restart without losing the supplier's team.
options.rationale: This is the keep-a-hedge error. It spends money on scope the board has removed, from a budget it has just redirected to the lifts, and quietly keeps open a decision the board has already closed.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to bring the decision back to next month's board with a fuller passenger-benefit analysis, before any of the baseline documents are amended.
options.rationale: This is the relitigate error. The board weighed the passenger-satisfaction case before deciding, so returning with the same case in more detail reopens a settled decision and leaves the baseline wrong for a month while manufacture approaches.

options.text: Amend the scope baseline now, but hold the supplier's stop instruction until the lift contractor's price is firm, since cancellation charges only begin once manufacture starts.
options.rationale: This is the half-implement error. It looks prudent, but it leaves the baseline and the supplier's instructions contradicting each other, and it replaces the board's decision with the project manager's own wait-and-see while the supplier keeps preparing to manufacture.

options.text: Amend the scope statement, WBS and WBS dictionary to remove the screens, instruct the supplier in writing to stop that package, and tell the station managers what has changed and why.
options.rationale: The decision was taken by the body with authority over the baseline after hearing the argument against it. Making it real in the documents, the supplier's instructions and the expectations of the people affected, all at once, is what stops the project running on two versions of its scope.

questions.explanation: When the body with authority over the scope baseline has heard the arguments and decided, the project manager's job is to make that decision real everywhere at once: in the baseline documents, in the instructions to suppliers and in the expectations of the people affected. Partial implementation, quiet hedges and repeat appeals with the same case all leave the project running on two versions of its scope. Disagreement belongs before the decision, or afterwards only when genuinely new information appears.
questions.mindset: Argue your case before the decision, then carry out the decision you lost as thoroughly as one you won.

questions.stem: A backlog item reading as a complete claims submission journey has been carried over three sprints running. Each time the team starts it, finds a dependency or an unanswered question, and stops. Estimates have grown from eight points to twenty-one. The product owner wants it finished next sprint and has asked you to have the team commit to it. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Have the team commit to it as the product owner has asked, protect the sprint by removing other work, and agree a daily check on its blockers with her so that they are cleared quickly.
options.rationale: This is the commit-harder error. Nothing about the item has changed, and the three carry-overs were not caused by insufficient focus or slow unblocking, so this most likely produces a fourth with less delivered around it.

options.text: Park the item outside the backlog until its dependencies and open questions are resolved, and have the product owner chase the answers with the teams and people who own them.
options.rationale: This is the wait-for-clarity error. Chasing answers is useful, but some of the questions can only be answered by building part of it, and parking it defers the learning while the item continues to be re-estimated upward.

options.text: Work with the product owner and team to split it into pieces that each deliver something and can finish inside a sprint, starting next sprint with the part that resolves the most uncertainty.
options.rationale: Three failed attempts and a growing estimate are evidence that the item is too large and too unclear to complete as a unit. Splitting by uncertainty first means the next sprint produces both working software and answers.

options.text: Ask the team to re-estimate the item with all of its known dependencies included, so the product owner can see how much it has grown before she decides whether to commit.
options.rationale: This is the measure-the-symptom error. The growth from eight to twenty-one points is already visible, and a fourth number describes the problem more precisely without changing the size or uncertainty of the unit being committed to.

questions.explanation: Repeated carry-over is diagnostic: it means the unit of work is larger than the unit of delivery, and no amount of commitment closes that gap. Splitting is the standard response, and the ordering matters more than the split itself, because taking the slice that resolves the most uncertainty first converts open questions into answers while still shipping something. Deferring the whole item until it is clear is the opposite bet, and it fails whenever the clarity is only obtainable by building, which the repeated dependency discoveries suggest is the case here.
questions.mindset: An item that will not finish is usually telling you it is more than one item.

questions.stem: Usage data six months after launch shows that four of the eleven features your team built are used by fewer than two per cent of customers. Those four consumed about a third of the development effort. Your product owner is uncomfortable and points out that each was requested by a named stakeholder who still defends it. The backlog for the next quarter contains three more items of the same kind. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree with the product owner to remove the three similar items from next quarter's backlog, since features of this kind have demonstrably not been used.
options.rationale: This is the overcorrection error. Four cases do not establish that all stakeholder-requested features fail, and removing items without an agreed basis for judging them makes the next prioritisation a contest of authority, with the requesting stakeholders left out of it.

options.text: Present the usage data to the stakeholders who requested the four features, so that they understand the outcome before next quarter's planning begins.
options.rationale: This is the confront-with-data error. It is likely to be heard as an accusation, and there is no decision available to the stakeholders about work that has already been built and paid for; timing it before planning does not turn it into a method for judging the next three.

options.text: Use the four as evidence to agree how value will be predicted and checked for the next three, rather than reopening the decisions already made.
options.rationale: The four are sunk and their real worth is as evidence about the prioritisation method. Turning them into an agreed test for the pending items changes future decisions without putting stakeholders on the defensive about past ones.

options.text: Propose removing the four unused features first, to reduce the maintenance burden they create.
options.rationale: This is the tidy-the-product error. Removal has its own cost and risk, benefits the small group who do use them not at all, and addresses the least important consequence of a prioritisation problem while the three pending items go ahead unexamined.

questions.explanation: Usage data is the first honest feedback most teams get about their prioritisation, and its value lies forward rather than backward. Relitigating delivered features costs relationships and recovers nothing, whereas using the same evidence to agree in advance how the next candidates will be judged, and how their value will be checked after release, changes the decisions that are still open. Framing it as improving the method rather than auditing the requesters is what makes it possible for the stakeholders concerned to participate in it.
questions.mindset: The value of a feature is what its use demonstrates, not what its requester asserted.

questions.stem: A national museum's hybrid programme is refurbishing six galleries to a fixed plan while an agile team builds the visitor app. After ten sprints, the released features, timed-entry booking and paid audio tours, already deliver about 85 per cent of the app benefit in the business case. The product owner values the 26 remaining backlog items at about £30,000 a year in total. The team costs £45,000 a sprint and estimates six more sprints. The sponsor says the funding for those sprints is approved and should be used. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Set the product owner's £30,000-a-year estimate against the £270,000 the six sprints would cost, and put stopping, trimming or continuing to the sponsor with those figures.
options.rationale: An approved budget is permission to spend, not a reason to. Putting the remaining value beside the remaining cost, with the options laid out, gives the sponsor what is needed to retake a funding decision that is the sponsor's to make.

options.text: Agree with the product owner how the released features will be supported and fixed once the team stands down, so that the value already delivered keeps being realised.
options.rationale: Stopping a product team is only a sound option if what it has already released keeps earning. Settling who supports the booking and audio-tour features is what makes an early stop safe to recommend rather than a threat to the 85 per cent already realised.

options.text: Continue the six sprints as approved, since the funding is ring-fenced for the app and budget handed back now is unlikely to be granted again if needs emerge later.
options.rationale: This is the use-it-or-lose-it error. Spending £270,000 to gain about £30,000 a year because the money is available treats the budget as the objective, and the fear of losing future funding is a reason to argue for it later, not to spend it poorly now.

options.text: Ask the product owner to re-value the 26 items more rigorously, with input from the gallery curators, before any decision, so that a choice to stop rests on firmer numbers.
options.rationale: This is the refine-before-deciding error. The remaining items would need to be worth several times the product owner's estimate to cover their cost, so a more rigorous figure is unlikely to change the answer, while the team keeps costing £45,000 a sprint in the meantime.

options.text: Reduce the team to two developers who work through the remaining items in priority order for the rest of the gallery programme, at a fraction of the current cost.
options.rationale: This is the cheaper-but-still-unjustified error. A smaller team spends less per sprint yet still assumes the remaining backlog has to be built, and choosing it inside the project settles a funding question that belongs to the sponsor.

questions.explanation: An increment is worth building only while its value covers its cost, and in most backlogs value falls item by item while the cost per sprint stays flat. When the remaining backlog no longer pays for the team, the response is to show the funder the marginal comparison and let them retake the decision, rather than treating approved funding as an instruction to spend it. Stopping early is only a real option once the value already delivered has someone to sustain it, so the hand-off to support belongs in the case rather than after it.
questions.mindset: Approved funding is a limit on spending, not a target for it.

questions.stem: Two proposals compete for the same funding. Yours requires an investment of £1,800,000 and is forecast to return net benefits of £450,000 a year, starting in the first full year after delivery and continuing for six years. The finance committee assesses proposals on how long the investment takes to repay itself and on total return against cost. Work out both figures for your proposal.

blanks.label: Payback period, in years
blanks.rationale: £1,800,000 ÷ £450,000 a year = 4 years. Payback measures exposure, which is how long the organisation's money is at risk before it is recovered, and it ignores everything that happens afterwards.

blanks.label: Ratio of total benefits to cost over the six years
blanks.rationale: Six years at £450,000 gives £2,700,000 against £1,800,000, a ratio of 1.5. This measures the return over the whole life and, unlike payback, is indifferent to whether the money comes back early or late.

questions.explanation: The two measures answer different questions and can rank the same pair of proposals in opposite orders. Payback rewards getting the money back quickly and is silent about everything beyond that point, which makes it a measure of risk exposure rather than of value. A benefit-to-cost ratio counts the whole life and is indifferent to timing, so it favours long-lived returns that a payback test would reject. Knowing which test a committee applies is what determines how a case should be argued, and quoting the figure that flatters a proposal without the other is how business cases lose credibility.
questions.mindset: How quickly an investment repays and how much it returns are different questions, and a proposal can win on one and lose on the other.

questions.stem: Your resource plan assumes two database specialists from a shared pool for the whole of the build phase. Six weeks before build starts, the pool manager tells you that both are being committed to a regulatory project for the same period and that you may have one of them half-time. Your schedule was built on two full-time. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Work out what the reduced allocation does to the schedule and to what can be delivered, then take the costed options to the sponsor for a decision.
options.rationale: Until the effect is quantified there is nothing concrete to negotiate with or decide between. Establishing the consequence first is what turns a resourcing complaint into a choice the sponsor can make.

options.text: Meet the pool manager first and negotiate for at least one full-time specialist, since the regulatory project is unlikely to need both of them continuously.
options.rationale: This is the negotiate-first error. It bargains before knowing what you need or what the shortfall costs, and it argues about the other project's requirements from a position of no information.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor immediately so that the competing demand is resolved at a level above both projects before the build phase starts.
options.rationale: This is the escalate-empty-handed error. The sponsor will ask what the impact is, and an escalation that arrives without it either stalls or invites a decision made on the relative volume of the two projects.

options.text: Recruit two contract database specialists to cover the shortfall, using the contingency held for resource risk, and confirm their start dates before build begins.
options.rationale: This is the buy-your-way-out error. It may be the right answer, but it commits contingency to two hires before the size of the problem is known, and contract specialists on an unfamiliar database rarely deliver at the assumed rate from their start date.

questions.explanation: Resource shortfalls become tractable once they are expressed as an effect on dates and deliverables, because that is the form in which other people can decide about them. Negotiation, escalation and procurement are all plausible responses and each of them is stronger when it carries the number, and considerably weaker without it. Quantifying first also frequently changes which response is chosen: a shortfall that costs three weeks on a non-critical path is a different problem from one that moves a committed date, and the two deserve different amounts of anyone's political capital.
questions.mindset: A resource shortfall is a schedule and scope question before it is a negotiation.

questions.stem: You are refurbishing the departure lounge of an operating regional airport. A new national security rule requires every delivery vehicle entering airside to be searched at the single staffed checkpoint, and the airport's security manager has confirmed it can take at most six of your vehicles a day, with no extra search staff funded this year. Your plan for the eight-week fit-out phase, starting in a month, assumes about fifteen small deliveries a day of partitions, ceiling tiles and fixtures. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the security manager for a second search lane or longer checkpoint hours during the fit-out, so that the planned fifteen deliveries a day can continue as scheduled.
options.rationale: This is the relitigate-the-constraint error. The security manager has already said no extra capacity will be funded, and a month spent waiting on a request outside that manager's gift is a month not spent adapting the supply plan.

options.text: Extend the fit-out phase in the baseline in proportion to the delivery capacity lost, and raise a change request to the client for the additional weeks and prolongation cost.
options.rationale: This is the face-value-delay error. It assumes the number of vehicles is fixed by the work, when consolidated loads can carry the same material in fewer of them, and it asks the client to pay prolongation costs for a delay that redesigning the supply may largely avoid.

options.text: Redesign fit-out supply around six searched vehicles a day, consolidating loads at an off-site holding yard and kitting materials by zone, then re-run the schedule.
options.rationale: The limit is set by a regulator and confirmed by the person who controls the checkpoint, so the useful work is inside it. Fifteen small loads a day is a habit rather than a requirement, and consolidation and kitting usually recover most of the throughput before any delay needs to be claimed.

options.text: Pass the six-vehicle limit to each trade subcontractor and ask them to agree among themselves how the daily slots are shared, then adjust and resubmit their own delivery plans.
options.rationale: This is the fragment-the-bottleneck error. Six slots shared among independent trades become a daily contest with nobody balancing them against the critical path, and a shared constraint needs a single owner allocating it, not a set of separately resubmitted trade plans.

questions.explanation: When a constraint on a physical resource is imposed by someone with the authority to impose it, the productive question is how the work can be reshaped to fit, not how to remove the constraint or what delay it implies at face value. Delivery capacity is usually more elastic than it looks: consolidating loads, holding stock off site and preparing materials by work area can move far more through the same number of slots. A shared bottleneck also needs one owner allocating it, because divided among parties it becomes a contest. Only once the flow has been redesigned is the remaining schedule effect worth quantifying and reporting.
questions.mindset: When a constraint is settled, spend the effort redesigning the work around it rather than relitigating it.

questions.stem: You are buying the integration of your product with an unfamiliar third-party system. Neither you nor any bidder can specify the work precisely, because the interface is undocumented and its behaviour has to be established. Your procurement policy prefers fixed price. Two bidders have quoted fixed prices roughly three times your internal estimate, and a third has offered to work on a time and materials basis. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Accept the lower of the two fixed prices, since the policy prefers fixed price and the cost is then certain, and hold the supplier to its scope through change control.
options.rationale: This is the certainty-at-any-price error. It buys a known cost at roughly three times the estimate, and holding a supplier through change control to a scope nobody could specify invites exactly the scope arguments a defensively priced bid was built to win.

options.text: Award on time and materials to the third bidder, since the work genuinely cannot be specified in advance, with weekly reporting of effort against your estimate.
options.rationale: This is the open-ended-commitment error. It correctly identifies that the scope is unknown, but weekly reporting only shows the cost rising: the buyer carries all of the cost risk with no ceiling and little incentive on the supplier to converge.

options.text: Seek an exception to the procurement policy so the work can be awarded on a cost-reimbursable basis with an incentive fee measured against your internal estimate.
options.rationale: This is the right-instrument-wrong-moment error. An incentive arrangement needs a credible target, and an internal estimate made without knowing how the interface behaves cannot serve as the fee's target until somebody has established what it requires.

options.text: Propose a small, separately-priced investigation phase to establish what the interface requires, then contract the build once it can be specified.
options.rationale: The premium in the fixed quotes is the price of an unknown that nobody can size, and the cheapest way to remove it is to buy the knowledge first. It also leaves the eventual build contractible on the policy's preferred basis.

questions.explanation: Contract type is a decision about who carries which risk and at what price. Where the scope genuinely cannot be specified, a fixed price does not remove the uncertainty but converts it into a premium plus a strong supplier incentive to dispute scope, while pure time and materials leaves the buyer exposed without limit. Splitting the procurement so that a small piece of work buys the information first is what makes the larger commitment specifiable, and it is usually far cheaper than the premium being quoted for the unknown.
questions.mindset: The contract type that transfers risk also prices it, and unknowable risk prices badly.

questions.stem: Your incentive contract sets a target cost of £800,000, a target fee of £100,000, a target price of £900,000 and a ceiling price of £1,040,000. Cost underruns and overruns against target are shared 70 per cent to the buyer and 30 per cent to the supplier. The supplier completes the work for an actual cost of £760,000. Work out the final price paid, and the cost at which the supplier stops being protected by the sharing arrangement.

blanks.label: Final price paid, in pounds
blanks.rationale: The £40,000 underrun is shared, so the supplier's 30 per cent adds £12,000 to the fee, giving £112,000. Final price is the £760,000 actual cost plus that fee, or £872,000. The buyer keeps £28,000 of the saving.

blanks.label: Cost at which the supplier begins to absorb every further pound, in pounds
blanks.rationale: The ceiling is £140,000 above target price, and the buyer absorbs 70 pence of each pound of overrun, so the ceiling is reached £140,000 ÷ 0.70 = £200,000 above target cost. Beyond £1,000,000 of cost the supplier funds the whole of any further overrun.

questions.explanation: Sharing arrangements are symmetrical until the ceiling: an underrun rewards the supplier at their share and an overrun costs them at the same rate, which is what aligns both parties on cost control. The point worth knowing is where that alignment stops, because past it the supplier is spending its own money on every additional pound while the buyer's cost is fixed. Suppliers approaching it behave very differently, pressing hard on scope interpretation and change, so a buyer who has calculated it knows in advance where the commercial relationship will come under strain.
questions.mindset: An incentive contract stops sharing risk at the ceiling, and the supplier bears everything above it.

questions.stem: At the end of month seven your project reports planned value of £600,000, earned value of £660,000 and actual cost of £750,000. Your sponsor reads the report, sees that more work has been completed than was scheduled, and concludes the project is performing well. He asks you to confirm this before he repeats it to the board. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Explain that the project is ahead of schedule and over cost, and that the overspend is proportionally larger than the schedule gain, then establish why before the board is told anything.
options.rationale: Both readings are true and they point in opposite directions, so reporting either alone misleads. The cost variance is the larger of the two and its cause determines whether it continues, which is what the board actually needs.

options.text: Confirm the sponsor's reading, since completing more work than planned is the primary measure of progress, and add a note to the board pack that cost performance will be reviewed next month.
options.rationale: This is the single-index error. Earned value exceeding planned value says only that work is ahead of schedule and is silent on what that work cost, which here was substantially more than it earned; a note deferring the cost review still lets the board hear a favourable verdict.

options.text: Report that the project is over cost and that the schedule position is not material while the overspend continues, and present the £90,000 cost variance to the board as the headline finding.
options.rationale: This is the opposite single-index error. Being ahead of schedule is real information, and it may even be part of the explanation for the overspend if work was accelerated deliberately, so leading with the £90,000 cost variance alone gives the board half the picture.

options.text: Recalculate the planned value, earned value and actual cost with the cost controller before responding to the sponsor, since a project ahead of schedule would not normally be over cost by this margin.
options.rationale: This is the distrust-the-data error. The combination is common rather than anomalous, arising whenever work is pulled forward at premium cost, and a full recalculation before responding to the sponsor means the board hears the sponsor's version first.

questions.explanation: Cost and schedule performance are independent readings and the temptation is always to summarise them into one verdict. The pair here describes a recognisable situation: work is being completed faster than planned and each unit of it is costing more than budgeted, which is what deliberate acceleration, unplanned overtime or an underestimated scope all look like from the outside. Which of those it is determines whether the pattern persists, and that diagnosis is the useful thing to take to a board, rather than a favourable index chosen from a pair.
questions.mindset: Being ahead of schedule and being over cost are separate findings, and one does not offset the other.

questions.stem: Your project has a budget at completion of £2,400,000. At the reporting date, earned value is £1,080,000 and actual cost is £1,350,000. Your sponsor wants two forecasts of the final cost: one on the basis that the overspend so far was caused by a one-off event that will not recur, and one on the basis that the project keeps performing exactly as it has. Work out both.

blanks.label: Forecast assuming the overspend does not recur, in pounds
blanks.rationale: Remaining work is valued at £2,400,000 - £1,080,000 = £1,320,000, and if it runs at budgeted rates the total is £1,350,000 already spent plus £1,320,000, or £2,670,000. This assumes the past overspend is sunk and non-recurring.

blanks.label: Forecast assuming performance continues, in pounds
blanks.rationale: Cost performance is £1,080,000 ÷ £1,350,000 = 0.8, so the whole budget inflates by that factor: £2,400,000 ÷ 0.8 = £3,000,000. This assumes whatever produced the overrun is systemic and will apply to the remaining work too.

questions.explanation: The two forecasts differ by £330,000 on the same data, and the whole of that difference is the assumption about why the overspend happened. That is why a forecast presented without its assumption is close to useless: the recipient cannot tell whether they are being shown a best case or an expected one. The discipline is to identify the cause first, decide on that evidence whether it is one-off or systemic, and then present the figure with the reasoning attached, quoting both where the cause is genuinely still in doubt.
questions.mindset: A forecast is an assumption about the future made explicit, and the assumption matters more than the arithmetic.

questions.stem: A port is replacing its gate-entry system. Barrier and camera installation is planned predictively and carries £180,000 of contingency sized from its risk register. The software is built by an agile team on a £900,000 budget, and the programme manager proposes no contingency for it, arguing that the backlog can flex to fit the money. About £780,000 of that backlog is the customs authority's mandatory data interface and an integration with the shipping lines' booking platform, whose interface specification has not yet been published. What should the project manager recommend?

options.text: Accept the proposal, and agree with the product owner that any overrun on the mandatory items will be funded by dropping lower-priority features from the rest of the backlog.
options.rationale: This is the flex-will-cover-it error. Flexing scope absorbs uncertainty only where scope can actually flex, and here about £120,000 of optional work stands behind £780,000 of mandatory work that includes an unpublished specification. Dropping features cannot release more money than they were budgeted at.

options.text: Apply the programme's standard 10 per cent contingency to the software budget, so that both streams carry reserves calculated on a consistent basis before the baseline is set.
options.rationale: This is the flat-percentage error. A uniform uplift ignores where the risk actually sits, giving optional features cover they do not need and leaving the unpublished interface with whatever share happens to fall to it, so the reserve cannot be defended against any named risk.

options.text: Separate the software backlog into the items that must ship and those that can genuinely flex, and propose a contingency sized against the identified risks on the must-ship items.
options.rationale: The programme manager's premise holds only for scope that can move. Distinguishing the two parts of the backlog shows where flexing still works and where it cannot, and sizing a risk-based reserve for the mandatory part puts money behind the exposure the backlog cannot absorb.

options.text: Ask the programme manager to make the installation stream's £180,000 available to the software team as well, then draw on it first if the interface specification arrives late or changes.
options.rationale: This is the borrow-the-other-reserve error. That contingency was sized for installation risks, so sharing it leaves those risks underfunded and hides the software exposure inside a figure that was never calculated for it.

questions.explanation: Scope flexibility is the main way an agile stream absorbs cost uncertainty, but it only works for the part of the scope that is genuinely optional. Where a backlog contains fixed regulatory or third-party commitments, those items behave like predictive work and need a reserve sized against their identified risks, while the flexible remainder can continue to act as the buffer. The analysis that separates the two comes before any decision about whether, and how much, contingency to hold.
questions.mindset: Find out how much of the scope can really flex before relying on flexing to absorb the risk.

questions.stem: You are three weeks from a committed release date and two weeks behind. Your test manager reports that the regression suite will not complete in the time available. Your delivery director proposes running only the tests covering areas the team changed this release, which would fit. The system is an internal scheduling tool with a well-understood architecture and no regulatory exposure. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Refuse the reduction and record why in the quality log, since releasing without full regression testing exposes the organisation to defects the suite exists to catch.
options.rationale: This is the quality-absolutism error. Full regression is a means rather than an end, and for a well-understood internal tool with no regulatory exposure the proposal may be a sound trade. Recording the reasons makes the veto traceable and does not make it the project manager's to exercise alone.

options.text: Accept the director's proposal, since he is senior, the exposure is low and the release date is committed, and run the remaining tests after release.
options.rationale: This is the defer-to-seniority error. The judgement may be right, and running the remaining tests after release is sensible follow-up, but the decision has been made without anyone stating what is left untested in the meantime, so nobody is deciding with the information in front of them.

options.text: Establish what the reduced coverage would leave untested and what failure in those areas would cost, and put that to the person who owns the release decision.
options.rationale: The proposal may be entirely reasonable here, and it cannot be judged until the exposure it creates is described. Presenting it as a risk decision puts it with whoever carries the consequence rather than settling it in the test plan.

options.text: Propose moving the release date by a week so the full suite can run, since verification is not the place to absorb a schedule slip, and present the slip to the sponsor.
options.rationale: This is the protect-the-process error. Taking the date to the sponsor puts it with someone who can decide, but the option has already treated the test plan as fixed and the committed date as movable, without weighing what the reduced coverage would actually risk, which may be very little.

questions.explanation: Compressing verification under schedule pressure is neither automatically wrong nor a decision for the project manager to make alone. What the role contributes is the translation: what specifically would go untested, what failure there would cost, and how likely it is given what changed. That turns a contest between a test manager and a delivery director into a decision the release owner can take on the record. The context here matters and does not decide it either, since low regulatory exposure lowers the stakes without removing the need for someone accountable to accept them.
questions.mindset: Reducing verification is a risk decision, and it belongs to whoever owns the consequence.

questions.stem: Your team builds the rider app for a city bike-share operator. A separate platform team, with its own product owner, owns the pricing service the app calls for every journey. Three of the platform team's last five weekly releases renamed or removed a response field without notice, and each time riders saw fares shown as zero for up to a day until your developers patched the app. Both teams report to the same engineering manager. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Take the three incidents and their effect on riders to the platform team's product owner, and ask for changes to the pricing response to be agreed with consuming teams before release.
options.rationale: The defects originate in a service your team does not own, so a change in how it is released has to be decided by whoever prioritises that team's work. Bringing the incidents and the rider impact puts a quality problem in her backlog rather than a complaint from a neighbouring team.

options.text: Propose contract tests: your team writes down the response fields the app depends on, and the platform team runs those checks in its own pipeline so a breaking change fails their build.
options.rationale: A contract test puts the check where the defect is created, so a breaking change is caught before it is released rather than discovered by riders. It makes the dependency explicit without either team inspecting the other's work.

options.text: Have your developers build a validation layer in the app that detects an unexpected pricing response and falls back to the last fares it received, so riders are shielded from the next change.
options.rationale: This is the absorb-it-downstream error. Defensive handling is reasonable resilience, but it leaves the platform team releasing breaking changes unaware, can show riders stale fares, and makes your team the permanent catch for defects created elsewhere.

options.text: Ask the engineering manager to require the platform team to freeze the pricing response format until your app's next major release, so your team has a stable interface to build against.
options.rationale: This is the freeze-the-producer error. It goes over the platform product owner's head to stop change that other consumers may need, and it postpones rather than solves the problem of changes arriving unannounced.

options.text: Request read access to the platform team's repository so one of your developers can review every pull request touching the pricing service and flag breaking changes before they merge.
options.rationale: This is the inspect-their-work error. It makes your team an unofficial reviewer of code it does not own, relies on one person spotting every breaking change by eye, and leaves the platform team's own release process unchanged.

questions.explanation: When defects keep arriving from a component another team owns, the lasting fix sits with that team, and the route to it is through whoever sets their priorities, carried by evidence of the impact. Checks that sit where the defect is introduced, such as tests the producer runs against what its consumers depend on, prevent the problem instead of detecting it downstream. Absorbing the failures, freezing the producer or inspecting its work all leave the process that creates the defects unchanged.
questions.mindset: Take a quality problem to the team that creates it, and give them a way to catch it themselves.

questions.stem: Your critical path runs through design, then build, then commissioning, and you must recover four weeks. Design is complete. Build is resource-driven and your supplier will add a second shift at a cost of £180,000. Commissioning is a sequence of safety tests with mandated waiting periods between them. Your sponsor asks you to overlap build and commissioning instead, since that costs nothing. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Accept the sponsor's proposal, since overlapping activities is a standard way to compress a schedule, it avoids an unbudgeted £180,000, and testing can start on completed sections of the build.
options.rationale: This is the free-option error. Overlapping transfers the cost from the budget to the risk register by testing an incomplete build, and here it collides with mandated waiting periods that no amount of overlap will shorten.

options.text: Set out that overlapping build and commissioning creates rework exposure and cannot shorten the mandated waiting periods, and put the second shift forward with its cost and its own risks.
options.rationale: The sponsor's option is free only in cash terms and buys time by accepting the risk of testing an incomplete build. Presenting both with what each actually costs is what lets the sponsor choose between money and risk knowingly.

options.text: Add the second shift now without further discussion, since it is the only option that shortens the path without introducing rework risk and the supplier's offer may not stay open.
options.rationale: This is the unilateral-spend error. £180,000 is the sponsor's money and the choice between cost and risk is his to make, even where your technical judgement favours the paid option and the offer is time-limited.

options.text: Propose reducing the commissioning test sequence so the waiting periods can be shortened, and ask the safety lead which of the mandated intervals have margin built into them.
options.rationale: This is the compress-the-uncompressible error. The waiting periods are mandated by the safety regime, so looking for margin in them turns a compliance requirement into a scheduling variable it was never meant to be.

questions.explanation: The two ways of shortening a path are paying for more capacity and accepting risk by overlapping work that would otherwise be sequential, and neither is universally preferable. What makes the choice tractable is knowing which lever the work responds to: resource-driven activities shorten when capacity is added, and activities governed by elapsed time or external constraint do not shorten at all. Presenting both options with their real costs, one in money and one in rework exposure, leaves the decision with the person whose budget and risk appetite are at stake.
questions.mindset: Compression buys time with either money or risk, and which one is available depends on the work.

questions.stem: A 12-month ferry terminal upgrade has just reached the end of month 6. Cumulative planned value was £1,200,000 at the end of month 4 and £1,500,000 at the end of month 5, and earned value today is £1,350,000. Your PMO reports schedule performance in time: earned schedule is the point on the planned-value curve at which today's earned value was due, interpolated linearly within a month. Work out the earned schedule, the time-based schedule performance index, and the forecast total duration if this rate of progress continues.

blanks.label: Earned schedule, in months
blanks.rationale: Earned value of £1,350,000 sits between the month-4 figure of £1,200,000 and the month-5 figure of £1,500,000. It is (1,350,000 − 1,200,000) ÷ (1,500,000 − 1,200,000) = 0.5 of the way through month 5, so the earned schedule is 4.5 months.

blanks.label: Time-based schedule performance index, to two decimal places
blanks.rationale: The index is earned schedule divided by actual time: 4.5 ÷ 6 = 0.75. Six months of calendar have produced four and a half months of planned progress, so the project is a month and a half behind.

blanks.label: Forecast total duration, in months
blanks.rationale: If progress continues at 0.75 months of plan per month elapsed, the 12-month plan takes 12 ÷ 0.75 = 16 months, a forecast finish four months after the planned one.

questions.explanation: Earned value tells you how much planned work has been done, and earned schedule converts that into the date by which the plan expected it, so the gap between that date and today is a slippage measured in time. Dividing the planned duration by the time-based index gives a duration forecast that rests on the assumption that the rate so far continues, and that assumption should be stated with the number. Because earned value aggregates all work, including work with float, the forecast should be read alongside the critical path rather than in place of it: it shows the trend, and the network shows whether the finish date is actually being driven.
questions.mindset: Answer a schedule question in units of time, because a sponsor deciding about a date needs months, not money.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the five sequential stages of your delivery with their planned durations. You have been asked to shorten the overall duration and have been offered additional skilled people, at cost, for whichever stage would benefit. Ordering covers a supplier lead time you do not control, and commissioning is a fixed sequence of tests with mandated intervals. Select the stage where adding people would actually shorten the chain.

graphic.title: Five delivery stages in sequence with planned durations
graphic.caption: Select a stage. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between stages, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Design 10d
regions.rationale: Design is complete or nearly so by the time compression is being considered, and adding people to design work in progress typically slows it through coordination rather than speeding it.

regions.label: Order parts 15d
regions.rationale: This duration is a supplier lead time, so it is elapsed time rather than effort. No number of your own people shortens someone else's manufacturing queue.

regions.label: Assemble 20d
regions.rationale: Assembly is effort-driven work that can be divided among more hands, and at twenty days it is the longest stage. This is the only stage where additional capacity converts directly into elapsed time saved.

regions.label: Commission 8d
regions.rationale: Commissioning is a fixed test sequence with mandated intervals between tests. The waiting periods are set by the safety regime and do not respond to staffing.

regions.label: Handover 3d
regions.rationale: At three days handover is too short to yield a meaningful saving even if it were divisible, so effort spent compressing it would be disproportionate to the return.

questions.explanation: Before choosing where to compress, each activity has to be classified by what governs its duration. Effort-driven work shrinks when capacity is added, within the limits of how far it can be divided. Work governed by an external queue or by a mandated elapsed interval does not respond to staffing at all, and money spent there buys nothing. The reliable method is to identify the effort-driven activities on the critical path, rank them by duration, and compress the largest, which is also why the longest bar on a chart is not automatically the right target.
questions.mindset: Adding capacity only shortens work whose duration is set by effort.

questions.stem: Your hybrid programme is replacing a regional energy supplier's billing platform, with a predictive data-migration workstream and three agile teams building the customer portal. The board approved go-live for March at £4.1 million. Two approved change requests were each followed by a rebaseline, and the current baseline shows go-live in October at £5.3 million. Every monthly report since has rated the programme green against that baseline. A newly appointed non-executive director asks how a programme seven months late can be green. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep reporting against the current baseline, and add the originally approved March date and cost, the cumulative movement since approval, and the change that authorised each step.
options.rationale: The current baseline is the right reference for controlling the remaining work and the original approval is the right reference for judging the programme. Showing both, with the authorised steps between them, lets the board see a drift that no single month's report revealed.

options.text: Explain to the non-executive that both rebaselines went through change control with board approval, so green against the current baseline is the accurate status.
options.rationale: This is the formally-correct error. Each step was authorised, yet the reports have shown green while the commitment moved seven months and £1.2 million, and a board whose membership changes cannot see that from a current-baseline view alone.

options.text: Report the programme as red against the original March baseline from now on, since that is the commitment the board first approved and the business case was built on.
options.rationale: This is the discard-the-baseline error. The rebaselines were approved, so measuring against March reports authorised changes as failure and leaves the board with no variance it can use to control the work still ahead.

options.text: Commission a review of why the programme has needed two rebaselines, and hold any change to the report's format until its findings show whether estimating is at fault.
options.rationale: This is the diagnose-before-reporting error. Asking why the plan keeps moving is a fair question, but the non-executive is asking what the report shows, and nothing needs diagnosing before the history can be added to it.

questions.explanation: Rebaselining resets variance to zero, which is right for control because the team needs a plan it can genuinely be measured against, and wrong for accountability because each reset erases the movement that came before it. A status built only on the current baseline can be green every month while the commitment drifts by months, so a report should carry the original approved figures and the cumulative change alongside current variance. Which reference a figure is measured against is part of the figure.
questions.mindset: A baseline that moves with the plan measures control, not commitment, so show where it started.

questions.stem: Your team maintains a wall of charts showing velocity, burndown, defect counts and cycle time, updated automatically. Nobody looks at them. In stand-up, blockers are raised verbally and forgotten, and the same dependency has been mentioned for six days without anyone tracking it. Your sponsor believes the team is well instrumented because the charts exist. Which two actions matter most?

options.text: Find out which decisions the team and its stakeholders actually take, and display only what those decisions need.
options.rationale: Four automated charts that nobody reads are noise with a maintenance cost. Starting from decisions is what determines the small number of things worth showing and gives each of them a reader.

options.text: Make blockers visible and owned, with the age of each one shown, so a six-day dependency is impossible to overlook.
options.rationale: The concrete failure described is a blocker surviving six days unowned, and age is the property that makes drift obvious. Visibility with an owner is what turns a mention into something that gets chased.

options.text: Move the charts to a digital dashboard the team and stakeholders can open remotely, with a link sent out before each sprint review.
options.rationale: This is the change-the-medium error. Charts nobody reads on a wall are charts nobody reads on a screen, and sending a link does not give them a reader; the accessibility of the display was never the constraint.

options.text: Review the charts as a standing item in each stand-up so the team engages with them and acts on what they show.
options.rationale: This is the mandate-attention error. It compels daily engagement with metrics that have not earned it, lengthening a meeting whose existing content, including the six-day dependency, is already not being acted on.

options.text: Add a cumulative flow diagram to the wall so the team can see where work, including the stalled dependency, is accumulating between stages.
options.rationale: This is the one-more-chart error. The diagram is genuinely informative, and adding a fifth unread display to four others addresses the symptom by increasing it; an unowned dependency does not get chased because it appears in a chart.

questions.explanation: Displays earn their place by changing behaviour, and a wall of automatically generated charts is easy to build and easy to stop seeing. The two useful moves are subtractive and specific: work out what decisions are actually taken and show only what informs them, and give the one thing that is visibly failing, in this case blockers, a form that makes neglect obvious through ownership and elapsed time. Adding charts, relocating them, or requiring people to look at them all treat inattention as the problem rather than as the symptom of displays with no reader.
questions.mindset: Information is only radiating if it changes what somebody does.

questions.stem: Your customer has been using the delivered system in production for six weeks and is satisfied with it. Nineteen low-severity defects remain open, all agreed as cosmetic, and your contract requires formal acceptance before final payment and closure. The customer's project sponsor keeps deferring the acceptance meeting, saying he will sign once the list is empty. Your team has been redeployed. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Propose accepting against the agreed criteria with the nineteen defects listed, owned and scheduled under a separate arrangement, so closure and the remaining work are separated.
options.rationale: Acceptance turns on the agreed criteria, which six weeks of satisfied production use suggest are met. Separating the residual list with owners and dates gives the sponsor what he is actually protecting without holding closure open indefinitely.

options.text: Recall enough of the team to clear the nineteen defects within a fortnight, since the customer's position is clear and the contract requires acceptance before final payment and closure.
options.rationale: This is the meet-the-stated-demand error. A fortnight's recall buys a signature with unbudgeted effort taken from other work, and it concedes that cosmetic defects are an acceptance criterion, which will shape every future engagement.

options.text: Escalate to the customer's executive sponsor, since production use for six weeks constitutes acceptance in practice, and ask for the certificate to be signed on that basis.
options.rationale: This is the assert-constructive-acceptance error. It may be contractually arguable, and asking a senior figure to sign on that basis goes over the head of the person you need, before offering him any way to say yes.

options.text: Invoice for final payment on the basis that the system is in productive use and acceptance is being unreasonably withheld, citing the contract's acceptance clause.
options.rationale: This is the escalate-commercially error. Citing the clause converts a solvable scheduling standoff into a dispute, and does so while the customer is satisfied with the product, which is the strongest position you will have.

questions.explanation: Deferred acceptance is usually about exposure rather than about the defects: a sponsor who signs fears losing the leverage that gets the remaining items done. The productive move addresses that fear directly by separating the two questions, confirming delivery against the criteria that were agreed while giving the residual list its own owners, dates and route. That is also why an empty defect list is the wrong standard to concede, since it makes acceptance conditional on an ideal nobody agreed to, and every future project inherits the precedent.
questions.mindset: Acceptance records that the agreed thing was delivered, not that nothing further could be improved.

questions.stem: Your programme closes next month. The delivery is complete and accepted, the team is being released, and your closure review has surfaced three obligations that will outlive the programme by anywhere between one and three years. Each needs different treatment while the people who understand it are still here. Complete each sentence with the response that fits the situation. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: A risk the programme identified will not materialise until the second year of operation, well after the team disbands. The project manager should
Two of eleven benefits in the business case cannot be measured until twelve months of operating data exist. The project manager should
A supplier contract has been fulfilled but a warranty obligation runs for a further three years. The project manager should

options.text: transfer it to the operational owner with the analysis and the planned response attached
options.rationale: A risk that outlives the project needs an owner who will still exist when it lands. Passing the analysis with it is what stops the receiving team re-discovering the problem from scratch.

options.text: hand the measurement plan to whoever owns the benefit, with the dates it falls due
options.rationale: Benefits that mature after closure are the ones most often never checked. Naming the owner and the date is what converts a claim in a business case into something somebody is expected to report.

options.text: record the ongoing obligation and confirm who administers it after the project closes
options.rationale: A live warranty is a commercial asset that becomes worthless if nobody knows it exists when a fault appears. Confirming the administrator is what keeps it enforceable.

options.text: keep the programme formally open until the item is discharged
options.rationale: Not used. Holding a programme open for years to hold obligations that operational functions own well is expensive and blocks the release of the people and budget the closure exists to free.

options.text: close it out and note that it fell outside the project's period
options.rationale: Not used. Writing an obligation off because it matures late is how warranties go unclaimed and benefits go unmeasured, and it leaves the organisation carrying a risk nobody has been told about.

questions.explanation: Almost every project ends with commitments that outlive it, and closure is the one moment when they can be given owners while the people who understand them are still present. Each of these three needs the same treatment in a different form: a named recipient outside the project, the supporting analysis or measurement plan, and a date. The two failure modes are opposite and equally common, keeping the project open to hold things that operational owners should hold, and closing cleanly by declaring anything maturing later to be somebody else's problem without telling anybody whose.
questions.mindset: Closure is the point at which everything unfinished acquires an owner outside the project.

questions.stem: Your governance framework requires steering group approval for any change over £50,000 or affecting the delivery date. A proposed change costs £38,000 and moves an internal milestone by three weeks without touching the committed end date. Your sponsor says it falls below the threshold and can be approved by you. Two workstreams plan around that milestone and your delivery director has previously been unhappy with decisions taken this way. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Approve it within your authority as the sponsor suggests, but report it to the steering group with the milestone effect and the two workstreams affected.
options.rationale: The framework's letter is satisfied and its purpose is visibility of decisions that affect others. Reporting a decision you were entitled to take costs nothing and removes the surprise the delivery director has objected to before.

options.text: Take it to the steering group for approval, since two workstreams are affected and the delivery director has objected to decisions of this kind.
options.rationale: This is the escalate-to-be-safe error. Referring decisions you hold authority over transfers your judgement to a board that meets monthly, and a governance body that receives everything soon scrutinises nothing.

options.text: Approve it as the sponsor suggests and inform the two affected workstreams directly, since they are the parties with a practical interest.
options.rationale: This is the tell-the-affected-only error. It handles the immediate coordination and leaves the governance record showing nothing, so the pattern the delivery director objects to continues out of sight.

options.text: Ask the steering group to clarify whether internal milestone changes fall within the threshold before deciding.
options.rationale: This is the seek-a-ruling error. The framework is clear on its face, and asking for interpretation of an unambiguous threshold delays a modest decision while signalling that you will not exercise the authority you hold.

questions.explanation: Governance thresholds define where a decision must go, and they are silent about what should be visible. Treating them as the whole of the obligation produces two opposite failures: escalating routine matters until the board cannot see the significant ones, and taking authorised decisions in a way that surprises people who planned around the thing you changed. Deciding within your authority and reporting the decision with its effects resolves both, and it is also how a project manager builds the standing to be trusted with a higher threshold later.
questions.mindset: Thresholds set the minimum that must be escalated, not the maximum that may be.

questions.stem: Three compliance matters have arisen on your project in the same month, and your compliance officer is on extended leave. An external audit is scheduled for the spring, so anything still unresolved will be examined then. The three have little in common beyond their timing and each calls for a different response. Match each to the action that fits it. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: A supplier has been operating a required security control correctly for a year but has kept no record that it was operating.
A team has been following a documented control that, on reading the underlying regulation, does not actually satisfy it.
A new obligation takes effect in eight months and nobody has yet established whether it applies to your product at all.

options.text: Start recording now and disclose the period for which no evidence exists
options.rationale: The control is working, so the deficiency is purely evidential and cannot be repaired backwards. Disclosing the gap is treated far more leniently than presenting reconstructed records as contemporaneous ones.

options.text: Stop relying on the control, correct it, and assess what the shortfall exposed
options.rationale: A control that does not meet the regulation provides no protection however diligently it is followed, so correction is urgent and the exposure created while it was trusted has to be established.

options.text: Carry out an applicability assessment and plan from its result
options.rationale: Nothing can be decided until it is known whether the obligation reaches your product. Eight months is ample for an assessment and easily consumed if the question is left open.

options.text: Transfer the exposure through insurance or a contractual indemnity
options.rationale: Not used. Financial instruments can cover the cost of a compliance failure and cannot discharge the obligation itself, since a regulator holds the accountable party regardless of who pays.

options.text: Wait for the regulator or auditor to raise it before acting
options.rationale: Not used. A known gap that was left for someone else to find is treated as a governance failure rather than an oversight, which is materially worse than the original deficiency.

questions.explanation: Compliance problems divide by where the failure sits. A gap in evidence, with the control itself sound, is repaired going forward and disclosed backward, because reconstructing records is the one response that converts a lapse into a misrepresentation. A gap in the control means the protection was never there, so correction is immediate and the exposure has to be assessed. A gap in knowing what applies is answered by assessment, and the common thread is that none of the three improves by being deferred until an outsider raises it.
questions.mindset: What a compliance situation needs depends on whether the gap is in the requirement, the control or the proof.

questions.stem: Your programme has a plan-driven hardware workstream under formal change control and a software team working from a backlog the product owner reorders freely. A stakeholder complains that software scope changes weekly without any change request, while a comparable hardware change took five weeks to approve. He wants one process applied to both. Which two points should the project manager establish?

options.text: That reordering within an agreed scope, cost and time envelope is not the same event as changing that envelope, and only the second needs a change request.
options.rationale: The stakeholder is comparing two different things. Naming the distinction is what shows that the software team is operating a control, with the envelope as the baseline rather than the item list.

options.text: That software changes crossing the agreed envelope, or affecting the hardware interface, go through the same control as any other baseline change.
options.rationale: The concern is legitimate wherever the boundary is unguarded. Confirming that envelope breaches and interface effects are controlled is what makes the distinction principled rather than an exemption.

options.text: That the hardware workstream's five-week approval cycle should be reviewed first, since a long cycle is itself a risk to delivery and explains much of the stakeholder's frustration.
options.rationale: This is the change-the-subject error. The cycle time may well deserve review, and leading with it answers a question about consistency with a complaint about a different process.

options.text: That applying formal change control to the backlog, with each reordering logged and approved by the board, would give the stakeholder the consistency he is asking for.
options.rationale: This is the consistency-for-its-own-sake error. Logging and approving every reordering would impose a five-week cycle on decisions taken weekly, removing the responsiveness the approach exists to provide and buying no additional protection.

options.text: That the product owner is accountable for backlog decisions and answers for them at each sprint review, so scrutiny of individual reordering by others is unnecessary.
options.rationale: This is the accountability-as-answer error. Naming an accountable person and a review forum explains who decides and does not address the stakeholder's actual worry, which is that some of those decisions may cross a boundary unnoticed.

questions.explanation: Uniform change control across differently-governed work looks consistent and controls the wrong things. What a control protects is a commitment, so the question is always which commitment is at stake: reordering inside an agreed envelope of scope, cost and time changes nothing anyone else relied on, while altering the envelope or the interface between workstreams does. Establishing both halves matters, because the distinction only holds if the boundary is genuinely guarded, and a stakeholder raising this concern is usually right that somebody should be watching it.
questions.mindset: Change control protects commitments, and different commitments justify different controls.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the levels your organisation uses for clearing blockers. Your team cannot test because the shared environment is booked for the next three weeks by another programme, and the booking is administered centrally under a schedule your delivery lead has no authority to alter. Select the level at which this blocker should first be raised.

graphic.title: Four escalation levels for clearing blockers, left to right
graphic.caption: Select a level. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between levels, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Within team
regions.rationale: The team has no access to the booking schedule, so there is nothing it can do beyond confirming the blocker is real. Time spent here is time the environment stays unavailable.

regions.label: Delivery lead
regions.rationale: The scenario states the delivery lead has no authority over the central schedule. Raising it here is the reflex of following the ladder one rung at a time, and it adds a hop without adding a decision.

regions.label: Programme level
regions.rationale: The conflict is between two programmes over a shared resource, and programme level is the lowest point at which both are visible and the booking can be renegotiated. This is where the authority to clear it first exists.

regions.label: Executive sponsor
regions.rationale: The sponsor can certainly clear it and should not need to. Going here first spends senior attention on a scheduling conflict and bypasses the level that owns the resource.

questions.explanation: Escalation is often taught as a ladder to be climbed in order, which wastes days on rungs that hold no authority over the problem. The more useful rule is to identify what the blocker requires, ask who holds that power, and go there directly while informing the levels in between. Here the constraint is a resource shared between two programmes, so the answer is the lowest level from which both are visible. Stopping short leaves the team blocked politely, and going straight to the sponsor clears this instance while teaching the organisation that ordinary contention needs executive attention.
questions.mindset: Raise a blocker at the lowest level that can actually clear it, and no lower.

questions.stem: Over a year, your team at a pensions administrator cut its average lead time from idea to production from eleven days to five, and the delivery director set a target of four. Last month the chief information security officer, following a breach at a peer firm, introduced a mandatory security sign-off for every production change, which has added about three days. The team is dispirited, and two developers want to push back on the new step. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the chief information security officer to exempt the team from the sign-off before the gains are lost, citing its clean security record and a year of lead-time improvement.
options.rationale: This is the treat-the-control-as-the-obstacle error. The sign-off is a risk decision taken by the person who owns that risk after a real incident, and a team's past record is not what it assesses. Seeking an exemption spends credibility on undoing a legitimate constraint rather than working within it.

options.text: Keep the four-day target in place so that the team keeps working to recover the lost ground, then review whether it is still realistic at the end of the quarter.
options.rationale: This is the hold-the-line error. With about three days now spent in a step the team does not control, four days would mean cutting the team's own remaining five days to one, and a target nobody can realistically meet teaches the team that improvement effort no longer shows up in the measure.

options.text: Re-baseline lead time with the sign-off included, agree a revised target with the delivery director for the coming quarter, and aim the next improvement at the team's own input to the new step.
options.rationale: The control is legitimate and is staying, so the honest move is to accept it into the baseline and reset the target to match. The team's input to the sign-off, such as how complete its security evidence is and how early it arrives, is within its control and is where the lost days are most likely to be won back.

options.text: Report the security wait separately and exclude it from the headline lead time, so that the trend stays comparable with the year of improvement already achieved.
options.rationale: This is the protect-the-trend error. It keeps the chart tidy by taking the largest new wait in the flow out of the team's own measure, which is exactly the part where the next improvement is most available.

questions.explanation: Improvement targets are set against a baseline, and when a legitimate change outside the team's control moves that baseline, the target has to move with it or it stops measuring the team's effort. Accepting the constraint does not mean accepting its full cost: most imposed steps have an input side the team owns, and that is where the next improvement belongs. Lobbying for exemption, holding an unreachable target or editing the measure all avoid the new reality rather than improving within it.
questions.mindset: When a legitimate constraint moves the baseline, reset the measure and keep improving what is still yours to improve.

questions.stem: A government-funded programme exists to shorten the time claimants wait for a decision on their benefit. Reporting to the sponsoring department is built entirely around applications processed per week, which has risen 30 percent. Median waiting time has not moved. Your suppliers are paid against the processing figure and your own team now describes success in those terms. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Restate the programme's purpose to the team and to the suppliers at the next monthly review, so everyone is clear that waiting time, not throughput, is the objective.
options.rationale: This is the exhortation-against-incentives error. Suppliers are paid on processing volume and the department asks about processing volume, so a restatement, however clearly it contrasts the two, competes with the two things that actually direct behaviour and loses to both.

options.text: Add median waiting time to the existing weekly report to the sponsoring department, so both measures are visible alongside each other from now on.
options.rationale: This is the add-a-column error. Visibility to the department helps a little, and while payment and attention remain attached to the processing figure the second number is decoration that nobody is accountable for moving.

options.text: Put the divergence between the processing figure and median waiting time to the sponsoring department, and get the reported measures changed to ones that track the outcome.
options.rationale: The measure has quietly replaced the purpose for everyone involved, including the team, so changing what is reported is what re-anchors them. The evidence that the two numbers have parted company is what makes the case unarguable.

options.text: Investigate where applications are queuing after processing, find out why the extra throughput has not cut waiting time, and address the bottleneck that explains it.
options.rationale: This is the operational-diagnosis-first error. Tracing the queue is worth doing, and it accepts the current measurement regime while working inside it, so the programme keeps being steered and paid on a number that does not track its purpose.

questions.explanation: When a proxy measure is what gets reported and paid for, it stops standing in for the objective and becomes the objective, and the drift is invisible precisely because the proxy is improving. Re-anchoring means changing what is measured and rewarded, not reminding people what the real goal is, because the reminder has no leverage against a payment mechanism. Diagnosing the operational bottleneck matters later, once the programme is being judged on something that would reveal whether the diagnosis worked.
questions.mindset: What you measure becomes what the work is for, whatever the charter says.

questions.stem: You are launching the third attempt in five years to replace a claims platform. The two previous attempts were cancelled after substantial spend, and several of your team worked on both.
