At the kickoff, people were polite and disengaged, and one architect said afterwards that she would start caring once she saw something reach production. The sponsor wants you to build enthusiasm for the vision. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Say plainly what went wrong on the previous two attempts and what is specifically different this time, including what is not different.
options.rationale: The team already knows the history, so not naming it signals either ignorance or evasion. Being explicit about what has not changed is what makes the claims about what has changed believable.

options.text: Get something small into production early, and let the fact of it do the work that argument cannot.
options.rationale: The architect stated the condition on which she would engage, and it is a reasonable one. A delivered increment is the only evidence that distinguishes this attempt from two that consumed money and produced nothing.

options.text: Run a vision workshop where the team articulates what success would look like, to build shared ownership.
options.rationale: This is the ceremony-against-scepticism error. The team is not short of a shared picture of the goal; it doubts the goal will be reached, and a workshop asks people to invest emotionally in exactly the thing that has disappointed them twice.

options.text: Avoid dwelling on the previous attempts, since revisiting failures will reinforce the team's pessimism, and focus team communications on the new platform's benefits.
options.rationale: This is the fresh-start error. The history is present whether or not it is mentioned, and replacing it with talk of benefits removes the only route to establishing that this attempt has learned anything from the last two.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to communicate her personal commitment to the programme at an all-hands session, including the funding she has secured for it.
options.rationale: This is the borrowed-conviction error. Sponsors presumably declared commitment to, and secured funding for, the two cancelled attempts as well, so a statement of commitment is the category of evidence the team has already learned to discount.

questions.explanation: A team that has watched the same work fail twice is not lacking a vision; it is withholding investment until it sees a reason to expect a different outcome. That is answered by honesty about the history, including what has not changed, and by early delivered evidence that this attempt behaves differently. Workshops, silence about the past and senior declarations of commitment all ask for belief in advance, which is the one thing prior experience has taught this team not to give.
questions.mindset: Scepticism earned by experience is answered with evidence, not with enthusiasm.

questions.stem: A developer tells you that a business analyst on the team is impossible to work with, changes her mind constantly, and is making his sprint miserable. Speaking to the analyst, you find she is being given different priorities each week by two product managers, neither of whom knows the other is briefing her. She has been absorbing the contradiction and passing on whichever version is most recent. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Bring the developer and the analyst together to work through how they will handle changing requirements, and agree a simple protocol for flagging changes between them.
options.rationale: This is the treat-the-symptom-as-the-conflict error. A joint session would have them negotiate a protocol for something neither controls, and it implicitly confirms the developer's view that the difficulty is between the two of them.

options.text: Ask the analyst to hold any change in priority until the start of the next sprint, so that the developer has a stable target and the churn stops reaching his work.
options.rationale: This is the buffer-the-contradiction error. Freezing changes until the next sprint makes the churn less visible to the developer and leaves the analyst absorbing two conflicting briefs, which is the position that generated the behaviour in the first place.

options.text: Get the two product managers to agree a single set of priorities and a single route to the analyst, and tell both team members what was actually happening.
options.rationale: The instability originates outside the team and neither person can fix it from where they sit. Explaining the cause to both is what repairs the relationship, since the developer currently believes the analyst is the problem.

options.text: Escalate to the two product managers that their conflicting direction is damaging team relationships and the sprint, and ask them to sort it out between themselves.
options.rationale: This is the escalate-without-facilitating error. It is aimed at the right people but hands them a complaint rather than a decision to make, and two managers who have not yet noticed each other are unlikely to reconcile priorities unprompted.

questions.explanation: Apparent interpersonal conflict is often the visible end of a structural contradiction, and the diagnosis is worth making before any intervention aimed at the relationship. Here the fix is upstream, with the two managers issuing incompatible direction, and it is incomplete unless both team members learn what was really happening, because otherwise one of them keeps a false explanation of the other's behaviour. Joint sessions, buffering and bare escalation each work on the symptom or hand the problem on without shaping it into something anyone can act on.
questions.mindset: Before treating a clash between two people, check whether the organisation is putting them there.

questions.stem: Your integration vendor and your internal infrastructure team each insist the other is responsible for a firewall configuration that has blocked testing for two weeks. The statement of work is genuinely ambiguous on the point. The vendor has stopped work pending clarification and is claiming standby costs. Your infrastructure manager says agreeing would set a precedent for every future gap. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Obtain a legal reading of the statement of work, then direct the responsible party once the ambiguity has been resolved.
options.rationale: This is the resolve-the-document-first error. Waiting for a legal reading before directing anyone keeps the schedule burning while it is obtained, the reading takes longer than the work does, and an ambiguity that genuinely exists may not resolve cleanly in anyone's favour.

options.text: Reject the standby claim, since the vendor chose to stop work rather than continue and raise the issue commercially.
options.rationale: This is the win-the-claim error. It takes a defensible commercial position, hardens a relationship you depend on for the rest of the integration, and does nothing about the firewall, which is still blocking testing afterwards.

options.text: Get the configuration done now under a documented reservation of rights, and settle the responsibility question and standby claim separately.
options.rationale: Two weeks of blocked testing costs more than the configuration does, and the reservation preserves both parties' positions so acting quickly is not read as conceding. It splits an operational problem from a commercial one that has a different timescale.

options.text: Have your infrastructure team do the work now and absorb it, treating the ambiguity as your organisation's own drafting failure.
options.rationale: This is the concede-to-unblock error. Absorbing the work clears the blockage and answers the manager's precedent concern in the worst way, by establishing that every drafting gap resolves against you at the vendor's convenience.

questions.explanation: When a dispute over responsibility is stopping delivery, the sequence is to restore progress on terms that prejudice nobody, then resolve the responsibility question on its own timescale. A reservation of rights is what makes that separation possible, which is why it beats both fighting the claim now and paying it now. Waiting for the contract to be interpreted treats the ambiguity as the emergency when the stopped testing is the emergency, and conceding quietly buys today's progress by making every subsequent gap more expensive.
questions.mindset: Separate clearing the blockage from settling who pays for it, and do the first one first.

questions.stem: Two people on your team have visibly disengaged over the last quarter and their reasons are different. A senior tester says nobody outside the team has any idea what she does and her work only becomes visible when something breaks. A developer says he has built variations of the same integration for eleven months and could do the next one in his sleep. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: For the tester whose work is invisible outside the team, the response is mostly to
For the developer who has done the same work for eleven months, the response is mostly to

options.text: route her work and its effect in front of the people it protects
options.rationale: What is missing is any connection between the work and someone who benefits from it, which is what makes effort feel worth making. Showing the effect to the people it protects supplies that directly rather than by praise.

options.text: move him onto work that requires something he has not done
options.rationale: Eleven months of variations on one problem removes the learning that keeps skilled work interesting. New territory restores it, and it also reduces the concentration of that integration knowledge in one person.

options.text: recognise both of them publicly at the next team session
options.rationale: Not used. Recognition is pleasant and short-lived, and it addresses neither cause: the tester's problem is that her work has no visible consequence, and the developer's is that it has no remaining challenge.

options.text: increase the frequency of one-to-one meetings with each of them
options.rationale: Not used. More conversation is how you would discover these causes and is not itself the remedy. Having already found out what each needs, adding meetings substitutes attention for the change that would help.

questions.explanation: Disengagement has causes that differ between people, and the useful move is to identify which ingredient has gone missing rather than to apply a general motivational remedy. Work that nobody sees the effect of needs its consequences made visible; work that no longer demands anything new needs a change in what is being asked. The two unused options are the defaults, and both are applied to the person rather than to the condition that produced the problem.
questions.mindset: Find out what has gone missing for this person before reaching for the standard remedy.

questions.stem: A developer tells you privately that she found a defect in her own work after it had passed review, fixed it quietly, and said nothing, because the team's quality dashboard is reviewed by the head of engineering each month and she did not want to be the reason the numbers moved. She asks you not to mention it. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Respect the confidence, and separately raise with the head of engineering that reviewing the dashboard by team is discouraging people from surfacing defects.
options.rationale: Keeping the confidence is what makes the next disclosure possible, and the reporting arrangement is a legitimate thing to raise without attributing it to anyone. It addresses the cause rather than this one instance.

options.text: Thank her for telling you, and encourage her to raise the next one openly at standup so the team can learn from it, offering to stand beside her when she does.
options.rationale: This is the exhortation error. It asks one person to bear a cost the system imposes on everybody, and your support does not change the dashboard, so the encouragement competes with an incentive that will still be there next month.

options.text: Explain that concealing a known defect is not acceptable and that it must be recorded in the defect log, while reassuring her that a defect she fixed herself will not be held against her.
options.rationale: This is the enforce-the-rule error. The rule is right, but applying it here punishes the only person who told you the truth, and the reassurance is not yours to give while the dashboard is reviewed as it is. The likely result is that the next quiet fix becomes a silent one nobody hears about at all.

options.text: Raise it anonymously in the retrospective as a hypothetical, so the team can discuss the behaviour.
options.rationale: This is the thin-anonymity error. On a team small enough for one person's defect to move the dashboard, a hypothetical of this specificity identifies her, and it breaks the confidence while appearing to keep it.

questions.explanation: When someone hides a problem to protect a metric, the metric and the way it is reviewed are the thing to change, because behaviour follows the incentive rather than the instruction. Preserving the confidence matters as much as the fix: the information arrived only because trust existed, and spending it here means the next warning does not come. Encouragement, enforcement and disguised disclosure all leave the incentive in place and put the cost of the system's flaw on the individual who reported it.
questions.mindset: If reporting a problem costs more than hiding one, the measurement system is the defect.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the sequence your organisation follows when working with stakeholders on a new project. A regulator who was never listed has just objected publicly to an approach your team settled three months ago, and the objection is substantive. Select the step the project manager should return to first.

graphic.title: Stakeholder engagement, five steps left to right
graphic.caption: Select a step. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between steps, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Identify stakeholders
regions.rationale: A stakeholder with standing to object was never on the list, so every step after this one operated on an incomplete population. Returning here is what surfaces whoever else was missed by the same blind spot.

regions.label: Analyse influence
regions.rationale: Analysis assigns influence and interest to people already identified. It cannot rate someone who is absent from the register, so re-running it changes nothing about this regulator.

regions.label: Plan engagement
regions.rationale: Planning tailors the approach for each stakeholder. Going straight here produces a plan for the one regulator you now know about and leaves the identification gap that produced the surprise intact.

regions.label: Engage and communicate
regions.rationale: Engaging is the natural reflex, and contacting the regulator immediately is worth doing. As the step to return to it treats this objection as the whole problem rather than as evidence about the register.

regions.label: Monitor engagement
regions.rationale: Monitoring tracks whether existing relationships are moving in the right direction. It watches the people on the list and is therefore blind in exactly the way that allowed this to happen.

questions.explanation: When a stakeholder nobody identified appears with a substantive objection, the failure is in identification and every downstream step inherited it. Returning to the first step is what finds the others missed by the same reasoning, which is the difference between fixing one surprise and fixing the process that produced it. Contacting the objector urgently is still correct, but it is a parallel action rather than the step the process restarts from.
questions.mindset: An unexpected objection is usually a gap in who you looked for, not in how you talked to them.

questions.stem: On a hybrid finance transformation, a regional director with no formal role on the programme has twice persuaded the steering group to reverse decisions after they were taken, both times by raising concerns privately beforehand. She holds no budget and is not on the stakeholder register as a decision-maker. Delivery has lost five weeks. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the steering group to confirm that decisions taken in session are final, and that any reversal needs a formal change request.
options.rationale: This is the tighten-the-rules error. It aims a governance instrument at a symptom, and a board that finds a private concern persuasive will keep finding it persuasive; the decision then reverses through a change request instead, with the extra paperwork adding cost rather than preventing the reversal.

options.text: Raise with the sponsor that the director is undermining the programme by lobbying outside the governance process, and ask for it to stop.
options.rationale: This is the frame-influence-as-misconduct error. Nothing described is improper, and asking for it to stop recruits the sponsor to suppress a stakeholder rather than to engage her; losing that argument leaves the relationship worse and the influence intact.

options.text: Add her to the stakeholder register as a key stakeholder and include her in the standard programme reporting distribution from now on.
options.rationale: This is the register-as-remedy error. Recording her and copying her into reports from now on acknowledges she exists without changing when she gets to speak, and the reversals happen because her input arrives after the decision, not because she is uninformed.

options.text: Reassess her influence, engage her before decisions reach the steering group, and reflect the revised picture in the engagement plan.
options.rationale: Twice reversing a board decision is a demonstration of influence regardless of what the register says. Bringing her in before the decision is the only version of this that converts a late objection into an early one.

questions.explanation: Influence is demonstrated by what people can make happen, not by the roles assigned to them, and a register that disagrees with observed behaviour is out of date rather than authoritative. The response is to re-analyse, then to move the engagement earlier so the concerns land while a decision is still being formed. Governance tightening, escalation and mere inclusion in reporting all leave the timing untouched, and timing is the mechanism producing the five weeks.
questions.mindset: Map influence as it actually flows, then engage it early rather than resenting it late.

questions.stem: The same director asks when your systems replacement will be finished at three different points, and you want each answer to be honest about how much is actually known at that moment rather than firmer than the evidence supports. Match each moment to the form of answer that fits it. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: At initiation, before any decomposition or estimating has been done.
After planning is complete and the schedule has been baselined.
Two weeks out from a milestone, with the remaining work under way and visible.

options.text: A wide range, described as an order of magnitude that will narrow
options.rationale: Before the work has been broken down there is nothing to support a narrow figure, and a wide range stated as such is both honest and useful for early decisions. Saying it will narrow is what stops it being quoted later as a commitment.

options.text: A committed date with the tolerance that surrounds it
options.rationale: A baseline is the point at which a date can properly be committed to, and the tolerance is part of the commitment rather than a caveat on it. Quoting the date without it invites the tolerance to be discovered as a slip.

options.text: A confirmation, or an early warning if the evidence no longer supports it
options.rationale: Close in, the remaining work is visible enough to say whether the date holds. The obligation at this point is symmetrical: confirm it, or warn while there is still time for anyone to react.

options.text: The date recorded in the approved business case
options.rationale: Not used. The business case date reflects what was hoped for at funding, and repeating it at any of the three moments substitutes an aspiration for whatever the project has since learned.

options.text: A refusal to give any date until certainty is available
options.rationale: Not used. Certainty never arrives, and declining to answer pushes the questioner to construct her own estimate from worse information than you hold.

questions.explanation: The honest answer to a question about dates changes as the project learns, and the skill is matching the precision of the answer to the evidence behind it while labelling which kind of answer it is. Early, that is a wide range; at baseline, a commitment with its tolerance; close in, a confirmation or a warning. Quoting the business case date ignores everything learned since funding, and refusing to answer leaves the stakeholder worse informed than the project can make her.
questions.mindset: Give an answer whose precision matches what you actually know, and say which it is.

questions.stem: Your programme has been called Single Customer View since it was funded. It builds a data layer that lets existing systems query consistent customer records. Three separate business teams have now asked when they will get the new screen, and one has deferred hiring on the assumption it arrives in June. Nothing in any document promises a screen. What should the project manager do?

options.text: State explicitly, to the teams and in the programme's own materials, what will and will not be delivered, and press for the name to be changed if it keeps generating the same expectation.
options.rationale: Three independent teams reaching the same wrong conclusion points at the label rather than at any one conversation. Correcting the expectation and removing its source are both needed, since a correction alone will be re-created by the name.

options.text: Meet each of the three teams individually to correct the expectation, starting with the team that deferred hiring, since they are the ones currently holding a mistaken picture of what will be delivered.
options.rationale: This is the correct-the-instances error. Starting with the team that deferred hiring is sensible triage, and it still repairs three misunderstandings while leaving the mechanism producing them in place, so the fourth team forms the same expectation next quarter.

options.text: Point out to the three teams, with the scope statement and deliverables list to hand, that no project document commits to a user interface, so the expectation did not come from the programme.
options.rationale: This is the documents-are-the-message error. What the programme is called is communication whether or not it appears in a deliverable list, and being technically blameless, however well documented, does not help the team that has deferred hiring.

options.text: Assess whether a simple customer screen could be added to the scope through change control, since three business teams evidently want one and one has already planned its hiring around it.
options.rationale: This is the scope-chases-the-misunderstanding error. Routing it through change control makes it orderly, not right: there may be a genuine case for a user interface and it should be raised on its merits, not adopted because a naming accident led three teams to expect it.

questions.explanation: Expectations are formed by everything a stakeholder encounters, and a programme's name is usually the part they encounter most often. Where the same misunderstanding arises independently in several places, the correction has to reach both the people holding it and whatever keeps producing it. Correcting instance by instance leaves the source running, disclaiming responsibility because no document said so mistakes the record for the message, and adding scope lets a naming problem drive what gets built.
questions.mindset: If the name makes a promise, the name is part of what you have communicated.

questions.stem: A warehouse automation project will finish on time and on budget. The operations director who sponsored it has moved on, and her successor tells you he expects the system to cut order-picking cost by a third, a figure that appears in no project document. The business case promised eighteen percent. He has repeated the third publicly, including to his own board. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Meet him with the business case, establish where the higher figure came from, and agree what he will now tell his board.
options.rationale: Finding the origin matters because it may rest on an assumption worth testing rather than a simple error. Agreeing the correction with him lets him retract it on his own terms, which is what makes the correction survive.

options.text: Write to him confirming that the approved business case commits to eighteen percent, and file the correspondence.
options.rationale: This is the paper-trail-as-protection error. It establishes that you were right, does nothing about a board now expecting a third, and converts a relationship you need at handover into a defensive exchange of letters.

options.text: Investigate whether a third is achievable with additional configuration work, and propose it as a change.
options.rationale: This is the chase-the-expectation error. It treats a number someone invented as a requirement to be met, and commits the project to new scope on the strength of a misunderstanding nobody has yet examined.

options.text: Raise it with the project board as a benefits realisation risk, since the shortfall will fall to operations after handover.
options.rationale: This is the log-it-and-hand-it-on error. Recording the exposure is accurate and routes a correctable misunderstanding into a register instead of into the one conversation that would fix it while it is still cheap.

questions.explanation: An expectation that exceeds what was ever promised is closed by going to its holder directly, establishing where it came from, and agreeing how it gets corrected downstream. The correction has to be something the stakeholder can carry, since he is the one who stated the figure publicly and he is the one who has to withdraw it. Written assertions of the contract position, new scope to chase the number, and risk entries all avoid that conversation, and each leaves a board holding a commitment the project was never going to meet.
questions.mindset: Correct a wrong number before it is built into someone else's commitments, not after.

questions.stem: Three sprints into an implementation, your new customer is increasingly unhappy. Reviewing the sales cycle, you find a pre-sales consultant demonstrated a bulk reconciliation workflow using a prototype that was never built into the product, and the customer's operations manager based her migration plan on it. The consultant has since left. Nothing in the signed scope mentions it. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Establish exactly what was shown and claimed, then go through it with the customer, saying plainly what exists, what does not, and what it would take.
options.rationale: The customer is not mistaken about what she saw, so the conversation has to start from what was actually demonstrated rather than from the signed scope. Setting out the options honestly is what lets her replan the migration on real information.

options.text: Get the pre-sales material and demonstration environment corrected, so the next customer does not arrive with the same expectation.
options.rationale: A prototype presented as product will keep producing this outcome for every deal it appears in. Fixing the source is the part that protects future projects rather than just this one.

options.text: Explain to the operations manager that the signed scope is the contractual position, that the demonstration does not vary it, and that additions will go through change control.
options.rationale: This is the retreat-to-the-contract error. It is probably a sound legal position, and pointing to change control does not soften it: it answers a customer who was misled with a technicality, which reliably converts a recoverable relationship into a dispute.

options.text: Add the reconciliation workflow to the top of the backlog and deliver it over the next two sprints, since the customer was led to expect it and her migration plan depends on it.
options.rationale: This is the absorb-it-quietly error. It may end up being the agreed outcome, and committing to it unilaterally gives away scope with no decision by anyone accountable and no assessment of what it displaces from the next two sprints.

options.text: Report the departed consultant's conduct to the sales director as the cause of the problem, with the demonstration material and the customer's migration plan as evidence.
options.rationale: This is the attribute-and-stop error. Documenting who did it feels like progress and produces nothing for the customer, whose migration plan is still built on a workflow that does not exist.

questions.explanation: Customer expectations frequently originate before the delivery team is involved, and where they do, the record of what was actually shown matters more than the signed scope. The two moves that help are an honest reconciliation with the customer about what exists and what it would take, and correction of the material that created the expectation so it stops recurring. Retreating to the contract, silently absorbing the work, and attributing blame each address the organisation's position rather than the customer's problem.
questions.mindset: The customer's expectations were set before you met them; find out by whom and with what.

questions.stem: Three months into a twelve-month customer portal build, your client's marketing head asks for a change to the visual design that would take four days. The requirements were signed off and the design is baselined. She is the customer's main point of contact and says the current design will embarrass them at launch. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Assess the impact of the change and put it through the agreed change process, telling her what you are doing and when she will have an answer.
options.rationale: A baselined design is changed through the process that protects it, and four days is small enough that the assessment is quick. Telling her the route and the timing is what keeps a legitimate concern from being experienced as a refusal.

options.text: Absorb the four days within contingency, since the change is small, then record it in the change log after the design work is done so the baseline stays accurate.
options.rationale: This is the small-enough-to-skip error. Contingency exists for uncertainty rather than for scope, and logging the change after it is made records a bypass rather than a decision. A customer who learns that small changes skip the process will bring the next one the same way.

options.text: Explain that the design was signed off, that changes now would require a formal variation the client may not want to fund, and ask her to confirm in writing whether to proceed.
options.rationale: This is the sign-off-as-shield error. It is accurate and leads with the obstacle, so a customer raising a real launch risk hears the process being used to avoid a conversation rather than to structure one, and the impact is still unassessed when she is asked to decide.

options.text: Ask her to raise it with the client's project sponsor first, so that it comes through the correct channel on their side, with funding agreed, before you assess it.
options.rationale: This is the redirect-the-requester error. She is the designated point of contact, so sending her elsewhere first, even to settle funding, adds delay, signals that her concern is a procedural inconvenience, and holds the impact assessment back for no reason.

questions.explanation: A change request from a customer is both a relationship event and a control event, and handling only one of them creates the failure. Assessing impact and routing it through the agreed process is what protects the baseline; explaining the route and the timescale is what keeps the customer engaged while that happens. Absorbing the work quietly trades a durable process for a moment of goodwill, and leading with the sign-off preserves the process at the cost of the concern that prompted the request.
questions.mindset: Take the concern seriously and the process properly; neither substitutes for the other.

questions.stem: A hybrid platform serves two internal customers. Claims processing needs the release in March to meet a regulatory commitment. Underwriting needs a feature in the same release that will not be ready until May, and says shipping without it will force manual workarounds for six months. Both are sponsors, both are funding the platform, and each has told you their need is non-negotiable. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Set out the options and their consequences for both customers, and take the trade-off to the governance body that is accountable for both, with a recommendation.
options.rationale: Two sponsors with equal standing and incompatible needs is a decision above both of them, and it belongs where the competing interests are already reconciled. The recommendation is what stops escalation being an abdication.

options.text: Confirm the March release, since a regulatory commitment outranks an internal workaround, and explain your reasoning to underwriting's sponsor before the decision is announced to both teams.
options.rationale: This is the rank-it-yourself error. The reasoning may well be right, and explaining it does not supply the authority: taking the decision alone commits one sponsor to six months of manual work on your judgement, without the standing to make that commitment stick.

options.text: Split the release so claims gets its scope in March and underwriting's feature follows in May, and ask the team to plan the extra regression testing that a second release will need.
options.rationale: This is the technical-answer-first error. Splitting may be the right solution, and it is being chosen and planned before anyone has established the cost, the feasibility or whether underwriting's six-month workaround is actually avoided by a May follow-on.

options.text: Bring the two sponsors together in a facilitated session, set out each one's constraints, and help them reach an agreement between themselves.
options.rationale: This is the facilitate-past-your-remit error. It is worth attempting, and both have declared their position non-negotiable, so a session between the two of them without a decision-maker present tends to formalise the deadlock rather than break it, however clearly the constraints are set out.

questions.explanation: When two legitimate customers have needs that cannot both be met, the project manager's job is to make the trade-off legible rather than to resolve it privately. That means setting out the options and their consequences honestly for both, and taking the choice to the body accountable for the whole, with a recommendation attached so the escalation carries analysis rather than merely the problem. Deciding on your own authority, jumping to a delivery mechanism, or facilitating between two parties who have both refused to move all leave the decision unmade by anyone entitled to make it.
questions.mindset: When two customers are both right, do not decide for them; make the trade-off visible to whoever owns both.

questions.stem: You are starting an integration that your organisation attempted and abandoned four years ago. The closure report is two pages and says only that the work was stopped on cost grounds. Some technical artifacts survive in an archive, and four people who worked on it are still employed here. You want to understand both why it was stopped and what it ran into technically. Complete each sentence with the source that fits. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: To understand why the attempt was really stopped, the more reliable source is mostly to
To understand the technical constraints the attempt ran into, the more reliable source is mostly to

options.text: talk to the four people who worked on it
options.rationale: Reasons for cancellation are the part least likely to survive in writing, because closure reports are written to be read by the people who took the decision. The participants hold the account that was never recorded.

options.text: work through the surviving technical artifacts
options.rationale: Design notes, interface definitions and defect records preserve technical detail with a precision that memory does not, four years on. They are also checkable against the current state of the systems.

options.text: rely on the closure report as the authoritative account
options.rationale: Not used. Two pages citing cost is a summary written for a governance audience, and it is the source that most tempts a reader into thinking the question has been answered.

options.text: commission a fresh feasibility study and set the history aside
options.rationale: Not used. A new study would rediscover at full cost what four colleagues and an archive already contain, and it would carry the same risk of hitting whatever stopped the work last time.

questions.explanation: Knowledge transfer runs into a project as well as out of one, and the two kinds of question a predecessor raises are best answered from different sources. Why something was abandoned survives in people, because the real reasons are rarely the ones committed to a closure report; what it ran into technically survives in artifacts, with a precision memory cannot match. Treating the closure summary as authoritative or starting again from scratch both discard the cheapest information available before the project has spent anything.
questions.mindset: Artifacts carry what was built; people carry why it was abandoned.

questions.stem: Your agile team of seven has worked together for two years and everything it knows lives in conversation. Two new developers joined six weeks ago and are still asking basic questions daily; the existing team is patient but losing hours to it. The team's position is that documentation always goes stale and that pairing is the answer. Both new developers say pairing helps but that they cannot look anything up between sessions. What should the project manager suggest?

options.text: Ask the existing team to produce onboarding documentation covering the areas the new developers keep asking about, time-boxed to one story per sprint.
options.rationale: This is the ask-the-experts error. Time-boxing contains the cost, but people who have held knowledge for two years can no longer tell which parts are unobvious, so they document what is easy to describe rather than what blocks a newcomer.

options.text: Increase the amount of pairing until the new developers are productive, since the team is right that documentation goes stale.
options.rationale: This is the accept-the-team's-framing error. Pairing is working and the newcomers have named its specific limit, which is that nothing is available between sessions, and more of it does not address that.

options.text: Assign each new developer a named mentor from the existing team, so questions go to one person at set times rather than interrupting everyone through the day.
options.rationale: This is the route-the-interruptions error. Scheduled questions to a named mentor concentrate the cost on two people instead of seven and leave the same questions being answered verbally, so the third new joiner starts from nothing again.

options.text: Have the two new developers write down what they had to ask about, as they learn it, and have the team review it rather than author it.
options.rationale: The newcomers are the only people who can still see what is not obvious, and writing as they learn costs them nothing extra. It also keeps the team's objection intact, since they are reviewing rather than maintaining a document nobody needed.

questions.explanation: Documentation written by the people who already know the system tends to record what is easy to explain rather than what is actually missing, because expertise hides the gaps. The person currently learning can see them, which makes newcomers the right authors and the existing team the right reviewers. More pairing and assigned mentors both improve the transfer happening in conversation without leaving anything behind, so each new arrival pays the same cost over again.
questions.mindset: The person learning is the best person to write down what was missing.

questions.stem: Your PMO has scheduled the knowledge capture session for your two-year platform programme in its final month, which is the organisation's standard practice. Looking at the team, the people who made the architectural and vendor decisions in the first eight months left the programme over a year ago, and two have left the company. The remaining team can describe what was built but not why most of it was chosen. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Trace and contact the departed decision-makers, including the two who have left the company, to reconstruct the reasoning before the session.
options.rationale: This is the recover-the-unrecoverable error. It is worth a limited attempt for the most consequential decisions and recollection a year or more later, from people with no remaining stake, is thin material to build a record on.

options.text: Run the session as scheduled and record clearly that the rationale for the early decisions could not be captured.
options.rationale: This is the document-the-gap error. Noting the loss is honest and it treats the timing as fixed, so the same loss is recorded again by the next programme that follows the standard practice.

options.text: Reconstruct the decision rationale from the architecture documents and board papers of the period.
options.rationale: This is the infer-the-reasoning error. Those records show what was decided and the case made for it externally, which is frequently not the reasoning that actually drove the choice, and a plausible reconstruction is worse than an acknowledged gap.

options.text: Capture what the current team still holds now, and propose to the PMO that capture happens at phase boundaries rather than at closure.
options.rationale: Acting immediately salvages what has not yet been lost from this programme, and the process change is what stops the next one arriving in the same position. Both are needed, since either alone leaves half the problem.

questions.explanation: Knowledge decays with the movement of people rather than with the calendar, so capture timed to closure systematically loses whatever belonged to the early phases of a long project. The response operates on two horizons: take what is still recoverable now, and change the point at which capture happens so the loss is not rebuilt into the next programme. Chasing departed staff, recording the gap and inferring reasoning from formal documents all accept the timing that caused the problem.
questions.mindset: Capture knowledge while the people who hold it are still in the room.

questions.stem: Your programme's business case assumes around forty roles will be removed once the new system is live. No announcement has been made and the consultation process has not started. Rumours are circulating, and in a one-to-one a delivery team member asks you directly whether the project will cost people their jobs. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Tell him honestly that role changes are part of the case, that nothing is decided about individuals, that it is not yours to announce, and who will communicate it and when.
options.rationale: It answers what he actually asked without disclosing what belongs to a formal process, and it gives him the one thing that reduces the anxiety, which is knowing when he will hear properly.

options.text: Press the sponsor and HR to bring the communication forward or give you an agreed line, on the evidence that rumours are already circulating.
options.rationale: The information gap is being filled by rumour, which is worse for the organisation and for the people in it. Reporting that upward with evidence is what lets the people who own the announcement decide with the facts.

options.text: Tell him you do not know, since no decisions about specific roles have been taken, and suggest he puts the question to the directors at the next all-staff briefing.
options.rationale: This is the technically-true-and-misleading error. It is defensible word by word and creates a false impression that you have no knowledge, and pointing him to a briefing does not undo that; when the announcement comes he will know you did.

options.text: Tell him in confidence what the business case assumes, asking him to keep it to himself, so that he hears it straight from you rather than through the rumours.
options.rationale: This is the private-disclosure error. Wanting him to hear it straight is a decent instinct, but it puts an unfair burden on him, cannot be contained on a team that is already speculating, and pre-empts a consultation process that exists to protect the people affected.

options.text: Refer him to HR without further comment, since employment matters are outside the project's remit and anything you say could pre-empt the formal consultation.
options.rationale: This is the deflect-to-the-function error. Protecting the consultation is a real concern, but the question was asked of you by someone who works for you, and a referral with nothing attached reads as confirmation delivered evasively.

questions.explanation: There is a real difference between information a project manager may not disclose and information a project manager may misrepresent, and the second is never available. The workable answer states the shape of the situation, is explicit about what is not yours to announce, and says when the person will hear properly, while separately pushing the people who own the communication to close a gap that rumour is already filling. Feigned ignorance, private leaks and bare referrals each protect the project manager rather than the person asking.
questions.mindset: You can decline to disclose what is not yours to announce; you cannot mislead about it.

questions.stem: You submit your monthly programme report to the programme director, who consolidates it for the board. A board member mentions in passing a risk rating you did not recognise, and checking the circulated pack you find your assessment of a supplier's viability has been softened from red to amber and the supporting paragraph removed. This has happened at least twice. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Send your original assessment directly to the board member who raised it, so the board has the accurate position, then confirm the record with the board secretary.
options.rationale: This is the correct-the-record-first error. The board would get the right rating and the minutes would match it, but you would have gone around your own line without asking a single question, which forecloses every version of this that ends well.

options.text: Accept the amendment for now, since the programme director is accountable for the consolidated report and may be moderating across workstreams.
options.rationale: This is the defer-to-accountability error. Moderation is a legitimate reason and it is an assumption you have not tested; accepting it 'for now' leaves the next board pack to be altered in the same way, and if the assessment is being suppressed rather than moderated, acquiescence makes you part of it.

options.text: Go to the programme director with the two versions, establish why the change was made, and agree how your risk assessment will be represented in future.
options.rationale: He may have a reason you do not have, such as a moderation process or information about the supplier you lack. Establishing that first is both fair and the only way to reach a durable arrangement rather than a single corrected report.

options.text: Include the full supplier assessment as an appendix to your next report before it goes to the programme director, so the detail reaches the board whichever rating is used.
options.rationale: This is the route-around-quietly error. It attempts to defeat the alteration without naming it, leaves the underlying practice unexamined, can be removed as easily as the paragraph was, and is easily read as manoeuvring when it is noticed.

questions.explanation: Where reporting is consolidated, alterations may be legitimate moderation or may be suppression, and the two are indistinguishable from the outside. The first step is therefore to establish the reason with the person who made the change and to agree how the assessment will be carried in future. Going straight to the board, accepting the change on an untested assumption, and smuggling the detail into an appendix all skip the conversation that determines which situation this actually is, and only the first of them is likely to be noticed as a breach of trust.
questions.mindset: Raise an alteration with the person who made it before you raise it with anyone else.

questions.stem: You are planning a five-year defence infrastructure programme. Years one and two are well understood; years three to five depend on a technology selection that will not be made until the end of year two. Your investment board will not approve funding without a fully detailed schedule for all five years, and your planner says he can produce one. What should the project manager propose?

options.text: Detailed planning for the near term and progressively coarser planning beyond it, with named points at which the later years are elaborated, and explain to the investment board why detail past year two would be invented.
options.rationale: Detail is only meaningful where the information supports it, and a schedule for year four built before the technology choice is a guess formatted as a plan. Naming the elaboration points is what gives the board the control it is actually asking for.

options.text: Produce the full five-year schedule as requested, flagging the later years clearly as based on assumptions that will be revised, and record those assumptions in the log for review at each board meeting.
options.rationale: This is the comply-with-a-caveat error. The caveat and the assumption log are read once and the dates are quoted for five years, so the programme is held to numbers everyone agreed were speculative at the moment they were produced.

options.text: Ask the board to approve funding for the first two years only, and return with a detailed schedule for years three to five once the technology selection is made, so every approved figure rests on real information.
options.rationale: This is the shrink-the-ask error. It solves the planning problem by removing the programme's funding certainty, which is likely to be refused and would leave years three to five competing for money again from a weaker position, however well founded the later figures are.

options.text: Build the five-year schedule using the technology option the planner considers most likely, and agree with the board that years three to five will be re-planned if a different option is selected.
options.rationale: This is the pick-an-assumption error. It produces a plan that looks defensible, with a re-plan clause that seems to cover the risk, and quietly commits the programme to one option two years early, making the eventual selection harder to take on its merits.

questions.explanation: Planning horizon is set by how far the available information reaches, and elaborating beyond it manufactures precision that later gets treated as commitment. The proposal that meets both needs is detailed near-term planning, coarser planning further out, and defined points at which the later work is elaborated, presented to the board as a control rather than as a gap. Producing the full schedule with caveats, reducing the funding request, and planning against a presumed technology choice all resolve the board's discomfort by inventing certainty the programme does not have.
questions.mindset: Plan in detail as far as you can see, and say plainly where the visibility ends.

questions.stem: Your infrastructure workstream must book a data centre migration window with an external provider six months ahead, and the booking is expensive to change. The window is only useful if the software team's replacement service is ready. The software team works in three-week increments and says it cannot commit to scope six months out. Both positions are reasonable and the two leads are now escalating to you. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Have the software team commit to the minimum scope required for the migration before the booking is made, and treat everything beyond that minimum as optional work that later increments can pick up once the window is secured.
options.rationale: This is the force-the-commitment error. Shrinking the scope does not change the fact that it extracts a promise six months out from a team that has said it cannot forecast that far, and a commitment given under pressure is not information the booking can safely rest on.

options.text: Book a later window that gives the software team more room to finish, accepting the delay to the migration, and confirm the new date with the provider before the current slot is lost.
options.rationale: This is the buy-slack-with-schedule error. It relieves the tension by spending programme time, and nothing about the underlying question changes: the later booking will need the same commitment at the same notice, however promptly it is confirmed.

options.text: Establish precisely what the infrastructure workstream needs committed, which is a date and a go or no-go decision point, and agree with the software team when that decision can be made reliably.
options.rationale: The infrastructure team needs a booking and a decision deadline, not a scope guarantee, and the software team can usually commit to the second even when it cannot commit to the first. Separating the two dissolves a disagreement that only exists because the ask was overstated.

options.text: Book two windows to preserve optionality, then release whichever is not needed once the software team's progress shows which one the migration can realistically use.
options.rationale: This is the pay-for-both-options error. It buys genuine flexibility at a cost the scenario says is high, and waits on progress evidence before anyone has established whether an agreed decision point would have made the second booking unnecessary.

questions.explanation: Where a predictive workstream depends on an iterative one, the disagreement is usually about the form of the commitment rather than its substance. The integrating move is to establish what the dependent party genuinely requires, which is typically a date and a reliable decision point, and to agree when that decision can be made on real evidence. Forcing a long-range scope commitment, moving the window, and buying two of them all treat the stated positions as fixed rather than examining what each side actually needs.
questions.mindset: Ask what the other side actually needs committed; it is rarely the whole scope.

questions.stem: You inherit a work breakdown structure for an eighteen-month plant upgrade. Its lowest level contains fourteen work packages, several lasting five to six months, with descriptions such as "mechanical installation". Progress is reported as a percentage that the workstream leads estimate by judgement, and two packages have reported 80 percent complete for seven weeks. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Decompose the large packages further, to a level where completion of each piece is something that can be observed rather than estimated.
options.rationale: A package lasting five months has no verifiable state between started and finished, which is exactly what produces a percentage stuck at 80. Smaller pieces convert an opinion about progress into a countable fact.

options.text: Define for each package what evidence constitutes completion, and assign a single owner to each.
options.rationale: Decomposition without a completion criterion produces more packages reported by judgement. Naming the evidence and the owner is what makes each one answerable, and it is where a vague description like mechanical installation gets pinned down.

options.text: Require workstream leads to support their percentage estimates with a written justification each month, reviewed by the project controls lead before reporting.
options.rationale: This is the improve-the-estimate error. It adds effort and review to producing a number that cannot be verified at this level of decomposition, so a better-argued and better-checked 80 percent is still an assertion.

options.text: Decompose every package to a uniform duration of no more than two weeks, so the structure is consistent throughout.
options.rationale: This is the rule-instead-of-judgement error. Decomposition depth follows what has to be controlled and measured, and applying a fixed duration everywhere creates administrative overhead on parts of the work that never needed it.

options.text: Replace percentage complete with a milestone report drawn from the existing fourteen packages, with each milestone signed off by its workstream lead.
options.rationale: This is the change-the-display error. Fourteen milestones across eighteen months, however formally signed off, give the same visibility problem in a different format, since the underlying pieces are still too large to show movement.

questions.explanation: The purpose of decomposition is to reach a level at which work can be assigned, estimated and verified, and a package stuck at 80 percent for weeks is the standard symptom of stopping too soon. Two things fix it together: smaller pieces whose completion can be observed, and an explicit completion criterion with an owner for each. Demanding better-justified estimates, imposing a uniform size rule, or switching the reporting format all leave the underlying units too coarse for anyone to see what is actually happening.
questions.mindset: Decompose until progress can be observed rather than asserted.

questions.stem: During sprint planning, your team says it cannot size a story called "improve reporting performance" because it does not know what improvement is needed or which reports matter. The product owner says the details will become clear during the sprint and asks the team to take it anyway, since the sprint has capacity. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Have the team take the story with a two-day timebox, stop when it is spent, and report what they learned to the product owner at the sprint review.
options.rationale: This is the timebox-the-unknown error. A timebox limits how long is spent and not what is delivered, so the sprint ends with effort consumed, no defined outcome met, and the story still unsized, however well the learning is reported to the product owner.

options.text: Take the story as a spike to investigate what improvement is needed and which reports are slowest, then split the delivery work out afterwards.
options.rationale: A spike is the right instrument when the uncertainty is technical. Which reports are slowest can be measured, but which reports matter and what target counts as success is the product owner's to supply rather than something the team discovers by investigation.

options.text: Keep the story out of the sprint and have the product owner define which reports and what target, refining it for a later sprint.
options.rationale: A story the team cannot size is not ready, and pulling it in converts spare capacity into an open-ended commitment. The specific missing pieces are named, so refinement has something concrete to close.

options.text: Accept the story with a placeholder estimate based on similar past work, and revise it with the product owner once the details emerge.
options.rationale: This is the estimate-anyway error. It produces a number with nothing behind it, and the number then enters the forecast and the velocity record as though it meant something, whatever revision follows later.

questions.explanation: Scope has to be defined well enough to be sized before it can be committed to, and the useful move when it is not is to name precisely what is missing so refinement can close it. Spare capacity is a reason to pull forward ready work, never a reason to commit to unready work. Timeboxing, spikes and placeholder estimates each have proper uses, and all three are being applied here to a gap in what the customer wants rather than to a gap in what the team knows how to build.
questions.mindset: Work that cannot be sized cannot be committed to; find out what would make it sizeable.

questions.stem: Your team completes and demonstrates working increments every two weeks and has done so for eight months. Nothing reaches customers between quarterly release windows administered by a central change function, so on average a completed feature waits about six weeks before anyone outside the organisation can use it. The team reports 100 percent sprint completion and the sponsor considers delivery healthy. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Measure and report the time from a feature being completed to being usable by customers, alongside sprint completion.
options.rationale: Sprint completion measures a handoff inside the team and says nothing about value realised, which is why the sponsor sees health where six weeks of finished work is sitting idle. The second measure is what makes the delay visible enough to act on.

options.text: Work with the change function on what would allow more frequent releases, treating the release constraint as the programme's main impediment to value.
options.rationale: The constraint is outside the team and is the binding one, so no improvement in team throughput will change customer outcomes until it moves. Approaching it as a joint problem is what makes a central function willing to examine its own cadence.

options.text: Extend the team's sprints to six weeks so that the cadence aligns with the release process and each sprint review shows work customers are about to receive.
options.rationale: This is the align-to-the-constraint error. It removes the visible mismatch by slowing the team down, which lengthens feedback loops and accepts the quarterly window as permanent rather than questioning it; reviews held nearer a release do not bring the release any closer.

options.text: Batch completed features and release the largest possible set at each window, so each release carries more value.
options.rationale: This is the optimise-the-batch error. Larger releases carry more value per event and more risk per event, and they lengthen the average wait rather than shortening it.

options.text: Report sprint completion to the sponsor as the delivery measure, since it is what the team controls, and record the release delay as an external dependency in the risk log.
options.rationale: This is the report-what-you-control error. It keeps the reporting comfortable and continues to tell the sponsor that a system with a six-week queue in it is performing perfectly; the delay is a certainty rather than a risk, and a risk-log entry is not where a sponsor reads delivery health.

questions.explanation: Work that is finished but not usable has produced no value, so a team can be fully effective inside its own boundary while the system it sits in delivers slowly. Making the delay visible and attacking the release constraint are the two moves that matter, because the constraint is what actually determines when value is realised. Aligning the team's cadence to the window, batching larger releases and reporting only sprint completion each accommodate the constraint and leave the customer waiting exactly as long.
questions.mindset: Value is realised at the point of use, so measure the distance to it.

questions.stem: Your product owner prioritises the backlog strictly by customer value and has deferred a mandatory accessibility conformance workstream for four consecutive quarters, each time in favour of revenue features. The legal deadline is now eleven months away and the work is estimated at four months. He argues that accessibility delivers no measurable customer value and should keep giving way. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Reframe the conformance work as a fixed constraint with a deadline and a consequence, schedule it, and have value prioritisation operate on what remains.
options.rationale: Work whose absence carries a legal consequence is not competing on value and will always lose if it is made to. Treating it as a constraint that bounds the backlog puts it beyond the comparison that has deferred it four times.

options.text: Quantify the cost of non-compliance, including potential fines and remediation, and add it to the scoring model so the conformance work ranks appropriately against revenue features.
options.rationale: This is the price-the-obligation error. However fully the cost of non-compliance is counted, it makes the item score well and keeps it inside a ranking where a large enough revenue opportunity can still displace it, which is precisely what must not be possible.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor that the product owner has deferred mandatory work for four quarters and is creating legal exposure, and ask the sponsor to direct that it be scheduled.
options.rationale: This is the escalate-the-person error. Eleven months is enough time to resolve this directly, and escalating first turns a solvable disagreement about method into a challenge to the product owner's judgement, with the sponsor asked to settle what a conversation still could.

options.text: Agree with the product owner that a fixed share of each quarter's capacity goes to the conformance work until it is complete.
options.rationale: This is the allocate-a-slice error. It is a reasonable delivery mechanism once the work is committed to, and adopted on its own it leaves the quarterly negotiation open and the deadline unowned.

questions.explanation: Prioritising by value assumes the candidates are genuinely optional, and mandatory work breaks that assumption because its absence produces a consequence no amount of customer value offsets. The correct treatment is to lift it out of the ranking, fix it against its deadline, and prioritise by value within whatever capacity remains. Pricing the obligation into the model keeps it contestable, escalating skips a conversation that can still be had, and a capacity share is a delivery mechanism rather than the decision the situation needs.
questions.mindset: Mandatory work is a constraint on the backlog, not a competitor within it.

questions.stem: You run two agile teams. One has lost a developer to another programme and its throughput has dropped by roughly the expected amount. The other has kept all its people but its throughput has halved since it was asked to support a legacy system alongside its project work. Both team leads have asked for help and you have one conversation with the resource manager to spend. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: For the team that lost a developer and dropped proportionally, the response is mostly to
For the team that kept its people and halved, the response is mostly to

options.text: seek a replacement, and re-forecast honestly until one arrives
options.rationale: A proportional drop after losing a person is straightforward capacity loss with no hidden cause to find. Replacing is the direct remedy, and re-forecasting in the meantime is what keeps commitments truthful while it takes effect.

options.text: get the interrupting demand routed elsewhere or bounded, and protect the team's focus
options.rationale: A halving with no headcount change points at the interruption rather than at capacity, since support work fragments attention far beyond the hours it consumes. Bounding or removing the demand recovers more than any addition would.

options.text: authorise overtime until throughput recovers
options.rationale: Not used. Overtime buys hours at declining quality and does not address either cause: it cannot replace an absent person durably, and it adds hours to a team whose problem is that its attention is already split.

options.text: reduce the scope of the current increment and continue
options.rationale: Not used. Reducing scope is an honest response to lower capacity and it is an adjustment to the plan rather than to the constraint. Both teams would keep the underlying condition and simply commit to less of it indefinitely.

questions.explanation: A throughput drop is diagnosed by whether it is proportional to the change in people. A proportional fall after losing someone is a capacity problem answered by replacement and honest forecasting; a disproportionate fall with the team intact points to fragmented attention, where the remedy is to remove or bound the interrupting demand. The two unused options treat the symptom in both cases, adding hours or lowering commitments without touching whichever constraint is actually operating.
questions.mindset: Diagnose whether the constraint is how many people you have or what you are asking them to do.

questions.stem: Your team develops firmware for a handheld scanner and works in two-week iterations. The next three iterations need twelve pre-production units for testing. Your hardware colleague mentions that these take nine weeks to arrive and nobody has raised a purchase request. The team's planning has been entirely about which stories to take, and the product owner assumed the units would simply be available. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Raise the order immediately and pay the supplier to expedite all twelve units, since the nine-week lead time is the whole problem and every week recovered brings testing forward.
options.rationale: This is the fix-the-instance error. Expediting all twelve units may recover some time, and it leaves three iterations planned around units that will not arrive and the planning gap that produced the situation untouched.

options.text: Raise the order now, replan the affected iterations around what can be done without the units, and bring long-lead items into the team's planning as a standing input.
options.rationale: The order and the replan are both urgent, and neither is sufficient alone. Adding long-lead items to planning is what stops the same discovery recurring, since nothing in the team's current routine would have surfaced it.

options.text: Reorder the backlog so that hardware-dependent stories are scheduled after the units are expected to arrive, and bring forward stories that can be tested on emulators.
options.rationale: This is the sequence-around-it error. It is the right instinct for this quarter, and without the order being raised and the lead time entering planning, the units still do not arrive and the next hardware dependency surfaces exactly the same way.

options.text: Raise it with the product owner as a high-impact risk in the register, since procurement of physical items sits outside the team's control and belongs with whoever funds it.
options.rationale: This is the register-the-known error. It is not a risk; the lead time is certain and the order has not been placed, so recording it as something that might happen and passing it on delays the purchase that is already late.

questions.explanation: Iterative delivery compresses the cycle for decisions the team controls and does nothing to procurement, manufacturing or anything else with a fixed lead time, so those items have to enter planning on their own horizon. The complete response places the order, replans the iterations that are now unsupportable, and changes the planning routine so long-lead items are visible in advance. Expediting, resequencing and logging a risk each handle part of this occurrence and leave the team to rediscover the same gap at the next hardware dependency.
questions.mindset: Iterative planning shortens decisions, not procurement lead times.

questions.stem: Three supplier problems have landed on your programme this quarter and your commercial director wants to know where the procurement process should have caught each one, so the next round of packages is set up differently. Match each problem to the stage at which it should have been prevented. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: The supplier is delivering competently, but a quarter of the work it is being paid for duplicates a capability your organisation already owned, and nobody checked before the package was scoped.
The supplier was the cheapest compliant bid and has repeatedly proved unable to staff the work at the skill level required.
The supplier and your team disagree monthly about whether particular activities are included, and both readings of the wording are tenable.

options.text: Requirements definition, before anything was put to market
options.rationale: The supplier is doing what it was engaged to do, so the failure sits upstream: nobody established what the organisation actually needed before approaching the market. No evaluation method or drafting could remove work that should not have been requested.

options.text: Evaluation criteria and their weighting
options.rationale: Awarding to the cheapest compliant bid is what the criteria instructed, so the criteria are where capability should have been weighted and tested. The supplier is performing exactly as the selection method selected for.

options.text: Drafting of the statement of work
options.rationale: Two tenable readings of the same wording is a drafting defect rather than a dispute about intent. It is settled at the point the scope of the work is written, and every month afterwards it costs both parties time.

options.text: Contract administration during delivery
options.rationale: Not used. Administration manages performance against what was agreed and is where all three of these surfaced. Surfacing a problem is not the same as being the stage that could have prevented it.

options.text: Procurement closure and final settlement
options.rationale: Not used. Closure discharges the contract and settles claims, which is the last point at which any of these can be dealt with and far too late for any of them to have been avoided.

questions.explanation: Supplier problems are usually visible during delivery and caused much earlier, so the diagnostic question is which upstream stage owned the decision that produced them. A supplier competently delivering work the organisation did not need points to requirements; a supplier that performs exactly as the selection method rewarded points to evaluation criteria; a genuine ambiguity in wording points to the statement of work. Administration and closure are where these become apparent and where the remedy costs the most, which is why treating either as the answer guarantees the next package repeats the pattern.
questions.mindset: Ask which stage should have caught a supplier problem, not only how to resolve it now.

questions.stem: You are deciding whether to build or buy a document rendering component. Buying it costs a licence fee of 50,000 plus 30 for each document processed. Building it costs 200,000 of development plus 10 for each document processed, and the running costs of the two options are otherwise the same. Work out the volume at which the two options cost the same, then the saving from the cheaper option at a forecast volume of 6,000 documents.

blanks.label: Volume at which the two options cost the same, in documents
blanks.rationale: Building costs 150,000 more up front and saves 20 on each document, so the crossover is 150,000 divided by 20, which is 7,500 documents. Below that volume buying is cheaper, above it building is.

blanks.label: Saving from the cheaper option at 6,000 documents
blanks.rationale: Buying costs 50,000 plus 180,000, which is 230,000. Building costs 200,000 plus 60,000, which is 260,000. Buying is cheaper by 30,000, because 6,000 falls short of the 7,500 crossover.

questions.explanation: A make-or-buy comparison is a fixed cost against a variable one, and the crossover volume tells you which side of the decision you are on rather than what to do. The forecast volume is what determines the answer, which is why the second figure matters more than the first: at 6,000 documents the option with the higher unit cost still wins because the volume never repays the development. The usual error is to compute the crossover, observe that building is cheaper beyond it, and decide without checking where the expected volume actually falls.
questions.mindset: A make-or-buy decision turns on the volume you actually expect, not on the crossover point.

questions.stem: A rail systems project has a budget at completion of 5,000,000. At the reporting date the earned value is 2,000,000 and the actual cost is 2,400,000. Your sponsor has told the board the project will still finish within its approved budget. Work out the cost performance index achieved so far, then the efficiency the remaining work would have to achieve for the sponsor's statement to hold.

blanks.label: Cost performance index achieved so far, to two decimal places
blanks.rationale: Earned value divided by actual cost gives 2,000,000 over 2,400,000, which is 0.83. The project has been converting each unit spent into 83 units of value.

blanks.label: Efficiency required on the remaining work, to two decimal places
blanks.rationale: The work left is 5,000,000 minus 2,000,000, and the money left is 5,000,000 minus 2,400,000, so the required index is 3,000,000 over 2,600,000, which is 1.15. Every remaining unit spent must now return 115 units of value.

questions.explanation: The index achieved and the index required are most informative side by side, because the distance between them is a direct statement of how plausible a recovery claim is. A project running at 0.83 that must now run at 1.15 is being asked to improve its cost efficiency by nearly 40 percent, with no stated reason why the conditions that produced 0.83 would change. Presenting the two figures together converts an argument about optimism into an arithmetic question the sponsor and the board can answer for themselves.
questions.mindset: Compare the efficiency you have achieved with the efficiency the plan now requires, and let the gap speak.

questions.stem: Your project's cost baseline totals 4,200,000 across three years and the forecast remains within it. Your finance business partner points out that the organisation releases funds in annual tranches, and your spend profile requires 2,100,000 in year two against a tranche of 1,600,000. The overall budget is not in question; the money simply is not available when the plan needs it. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Proceed with the planned work and manage the shortfall through supplier payment terms, agreeing with the main suppliers to defer 500,000 of year-two invoices into year three.
