options.rationale: This is the push-the-payments error. It moves when the cost is paid rather than when the funding is needed, usually at a price the suppliers will build into their terms, and it conceals the constraint from the people who could resolve it properly.

options.text: Reconcile the year-by-year spend profile against the annual funding tranches, and either re-phase the work to fit or make a specific case for re-phasing the funding.
options.rationale: The mismatch is between two profiles rather than two totals, so the resolution is to move one of them and to know which is cheaper to move. Presenting a specific alternative is what turns a funding problem into a decision someone can take.

options.text: Draw the 500,000 difference from the contingency reserve in year two, since the reserve exists to absorb variances, and replenish it later from the year-three tranche.
options.rationale: This is the wrong-reserve error. Contingency covers identified risks within the cost baseline and is itself funded from the same tranches, so drawing on it creates no cash the year's allocation does not contain, and replenishing it assumes year-three headroom nobody has confirmed.

options.text: Report the year-two funding gap to the sponsor as an issue in the next highlight report, and ask them to secure additional budget to cover the 500,000 shortfall.
options.rationale: This is the ask-for-more error. No additional budget is needed, since the total is unchanged, and framing the gap as extra money invites a challenge to the whole cost baseline instead of a conversation about phasing.

questions.explanation: A cost baseline and a funding profile are separate things, and a project can be entirely within budget while requiring money in periods when none is available. Reconciling the two means comparing the profiles and deciding which to move, then presenting that as a specific choice rather than as a shortfall. Manipulating payment terms hides the constraint, contingency is drawn from the same constrained tranche, and requesting additional budget misdescribes a timing problem as a cost overrun.
questions.mindset: Being within budget overall is no help if the cash is not there when the work is.

questions.stem: You have taken over quality on a components line feeding your project's assembly. Three separate quality situations are on your desk this week, and your predecessor's habit was to respond to all of them by increasing inspection. You want each response to fit the evidence in front of it. Match each situation to the response that fits it best. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: Measurements sit comfortably inside the control limits, but the last seven consecutive readings are all above the mean.
Ninety detected defects fall into eleven categories, and two of those categories account for sixty-three of them.
A batch passes every dimensional and material check on the specification, and the customer reports the components are unusable on their line.

options.text: Investigate for an assignable cause, despite nothing being out of limits
options.rationale: A long run on one side of the mean is not random variation, so the process has shifted even though no individual reading has breached a limit. Waiting for a breach means investigating later with the same cause and more scrap.

options.text: Concentrate corrective effort on the two categories carrying most of the defects
options.rationale: A small number of categories accounting for most of the defects is the case where effort spread evenly across eleven categories wastes most of itself. Ranking by frequency is what makes the effort proportionate.

options.text: Check the specification itself against how the customer actually uses the part
options.rationale: Every check passing while the part is unusable means the specification does not capture what the customer needs. Conformance has been confirmed; fitness for use has never been tested.

options.text: Tighten the specification limits so problems are caught sooner
options.rationale: Not used. Specification limits express what the customer will accept and are not a detection setting. Narrowing them changes what counts as a defect without changing the process producing them.

options.text: Increase the inspection sampling rate
options.rationale: Not used, and it is the predecessor's reflex. More inspection finds more of what is already being produced, which adds appraisal cost to all three situations and removes the cause in none of them.

questions.explanation: Quality data indicates which response is warranted, and the three signals here are distinct. A sustained run on one side of the mean indicates a process shift worth investigating before any limit is breached; a concentration of defects in a few categories directs effort to where most of the problem is; and conformance to every check while the customer cannot use the part indicates the specification, rather than the process, is what is wrong. The two unused options change what is measured or how often, and neither alters what the process is producing.
questions.mindset: Read what the data is telling you before deciding how much more of it to collect.

questions.stem: On your team an item is done when the code is merged and reviewed. Testing happens in a dedicated hardening iteration before each quarterly release, run by a separate test team. The last two hardening iterations each found defects in work completed up to three months earlier, and both overran, delaying the release. Developers say they can barely remember the code by then. What should the project manager suggest?

options.text: Move testing inside the definition of done so each item is tested as it is built, and use the hardening iteration only for what genuinely cannot be tested per item.
options.rationale: A three-month gap between building and testing is what makes each defect expensive, because context has to be rebuilt before anything can be fixed. Testing per item closes the gap, and reserving hardening for genuinely cross-cutting checks keeps what the separate iteration is actually good for.

options.text: Increase the length of the hardening iteration so it can absorb the defect volume without delaying the release, sized from the last two overruns.
options.rationale: This is the size-the-container error. Sizing it from past overruns makes the estimate realistic and plans for the same defect volume to recur rather than for finding defects sooner, and a longer hardening period lengthens the average gap between writing code and testing it.

options.text: Have the test team begin testing completed items during the development iterations rather than waiting for hardening, and pass each finding straight back to its developer.
options.rationale: Earlier testing and routing findings to the author both genuinely help, and this still leaves quality outside the definition of done, so an item is counted complete before anyone has tested it and findings arrive as rework on work the developer has already moved on from.

options.text: Introduce a defect budget for each hardening iteration, above which the release is held, and publish the running count at each sprint review.
options.rationale: This is the threshold-as-control error. It creates a consequence for a defect count, and publishing the count adds visibility, without changing anything that produces the count, so the likely result is a delayed release and pressure to reclassify defects.

questions.explanation: The cost of a defect rises with the distance between causing it and finding it, and a definition of done that excludes testing guarantees that distance is as long as the release cycle. Bringing the test inside done shortens the loop for every item, while the separate iteration keeps its legitimate use for checks that can only be made against the whole. Lengthening hardening, starting it earlier, and imposing a defect threshold all operate on what happens after the gap rather than closing it.
questions.mindset: Defects get cheaper the closer the test sits to the work that caused them.

questions.stem: Your critical path runs through two activities that can be shortened by adding shifts. Activity A can be shortened by up to 3 days at a cost of 4,000 per day. Activity B can be shortened by up to 4 days at a cost of 2,500 per day. Both remain on the critical path throughout, and no other path becomes critical. Work out the least cost of recovering 5 days, then the additional cost of recovering a sixth.

blanks.label: Least cost of recovering 5 days
blanks.rationale: Take all 4 days available on B at 2,500 each, which is 10,000, then 1 day on A at 4,000. The total is 14,000, and taking any day from A before B is exhausted would cost more.

blanks.label: Additional cost of recovering a sixth day
blanks.rationale: B is fully compressed after the fifth day, so the sixth can only come from A at 4,000. The marginal cost has risen from 2,500 to 4,000 because the cheap option has been used up.

questions.explanation: Crashing is bought a day at a time from the cheapest source still available on the critical path, which is why the total is not the number of days multiplied by an average rate. The marginal cost rises as cheaper options are exhausted, and that rising curve is the useful thing to show a sponsor asking for one more week. The other check this problem sets aside is whether compressing far enough makes another path critical, at which point further days stop buying any reduction in the project's duration at all.
questions.mindset: Crash the cheapest day first, and expect each further day to cost more than the last.

questions.stem: Reviewing your team's estimates, you find each developer adds private safety to their own items so that they are almost never late individually. Items still finish close to their padded estimates rather than early, and the release date has slipped twice. Your team lead proposes estimating each item at the duration it would take if things go normally, and holding a single visible buffer at the release level. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep the current approach, since estimates that individuals can reliably meet are the basis of a trustworthy forecast, and ask the team to finish early wherever it can.
options.rationale: This is the reliability-of-the-part error. Each estimate is met and the release date is not, which is the signature of protection being absorbed at every step; asking for early finishes does not release padding that work expands to fill.

options.text: Adopt the proposal and remove the buffer entirely, so the team works to the duration the work actually requires and the release date is brought forward.
options.rationale: This is the strip-the-slack error. Variation is real, and an aggregate estimate with no protection at all commits the release to the average outcome, which it will miss about half the time however much earlier it looks.

options.text: Support the proposal, and make the buffer's consumption visible so the team can see how much protection remains as the release approaches.
options.rationale: Safety distributed across every estimate is consumed invisibly and never returned, which is why padded items still finish late. Aggregating it makes the protection a shared resource, and tracking consumption is what converts it from a cushion into a control.

options.text: Ask each developer to justify the safety they have added to their items, so the padding can be reduced where it is not warranted and kept where it is.
options.rationale: This is the audit-the-estimates error. It treats a rational individual response to being held to dates as something to be argued down item by item, and it teaches the team to conceal the padding rather than to stop needing it.

questions.explanation: Safety added to every individual estimate is consumed by whichever item it sits on and never becomes available to the item that actually needs it, so a plan can meet every step and still miss the end date. Pooling the contingency at the level that matters, and making its consumption visible, lets protection flow to wherever the variation turns up. Defending the current approach mistakes local reliability for schedule reliability, removing the buffer altogether ignores that the variation is real, and auditing individual padding attacks the symptom while giving people a reason to hide it.
questions.mindset: Contingency held in one visible place is spent deliberately; hidden in every estimate it is spent silently.

questions.stem: Your programme reports on the first working day of each month. Your board meets on the third Tuesday, and its members say the pack is accurate but always describes a position three weeks old by the time they discuss it. Twice this year the board has taken a decision that the intervening weeks had already made irrelevant. Nobody disputes the quality of the reporting. Which two changes should the project manager make?

options.text: Move the reporting cut-off so the pack reflects the position as close as practical to the meeting that uses it.
options.rationale: The defect is entirely in timing rather than content, and aligning the cut-off to the meeting removes most of the staleness at no cost to accuracy. It is the change that addresses what the board actually complained about.

options.text: Establish an exception route so anything material arising between cut-off and meeting reaches the board before it decides.
options.rationale: No cut-off can be instantaneous, so a gap always remains and it is the gap that produced the two irrelevant decisions. A defined exception route covers it without rebuilding the pack.

options.text: Report fortnightly rather than monthly, so the information the board receives is no more than two weeks old at any point.
options.rationale: This is the increase-the-frequency error. It doubles the production effort without aligning any cut-off to the meeting, so the board can still decide on a position up to two weeks old and the gap that produced the irrelevant decisions remains.

options.text: Ask the board to move its meeting closer to the reporting cut-off.
options.rationale: This is the move-the-audience error. It asks the least flexible party to accommodate the most flexible one, and the reporting cycle exists to serve the board rather than the other way round.

options.text: Add a verbal update at the start of each board meeting covering anything that has changed since the pack was issued.
options.rationale: This is the patch-it-in-the-room error. It puts material information in front of the board with no time to consider it and no record, which is the worst moment to introduce something that might change a decision.

questions.explanation: Status reporting is instrumentation for decisions, so its cadence and cut-off are set by when those decisions are taken rather than by the calendar. Aligning the cut-off to the meeting removes the bulk of the staleness, and an exception route covers the residue that no cut-off can eliminate. Reporting more often costs effort without fixing the alignment, moving the board is the wrong party to ask, and a verbal update at the table delivers new information at the point where it can least be absorbed.
questions.mindset: Report to the rhythm of the decisions, not to the rhythm of the calendar.

questions.stem: Your team maintains a task board in the team room and a project management tool that the PMO reads. The board is accurate and used every day. The tool is updated by one developer on Friday afternoons, often from memory, and the PMO's reports are drawn from it. Last week a PMO report showed a completed feature as not started. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Establish one source of truth, and make updating it a by-product of the work the team already does rather than a separate Friday task.
options.rationale: Two records diverge because keeping them aligned is somebody's extra job, and manual reconciliation always loses to the record people actually use. Making the update fall out of the work is what makes accuracy the default.

options.text: Ask the developer to update the tool at the end of each day rather than on Fridays, so that the gap between the two records narrows to a day at most.
options.rationale: This is the increase-the-diligence error. It multiplies a manual reconciliation by five, which raises the cost without removing the duplication that causes the drift, and the tool is still updated from memory by one person.

options.text: Ask the PMO to draw its reports from the physical board instead, by photographing it each Friday, since the board is the record the team keeps accurate.
options.rationale: This is the shift-the-burden error. The duplication does not go away; it moves to the PMO, which now transcribes photographs of a room it is not in, and the data is still unavailable as soon as anyone needs it elsewhere.

options.text: Correct the erroneous report, and have the team lead check the tool against the board before each PMO report is issued.
options.rationale: This is the inspect-the-output error. Verification catches errors after they are made, adds a step to every reporting cycle, and leaves the duplicate records generating new discrepancies each week.

questions.explanation: Where the same information is maintained in two places, one of them will be wrong, and the one people use to do their work is the one that stays right. The fix is to make a single record authoritative and to arrange things so keeping it current is part of doing the work rather than an additional task. More frequent manual updates, asking the consumer to read the team's own artifact, and adding verification all accept the duplication and pay for it in effort, delay or errors.
questions.mindset: Two records of the same truth means one of them is wrong; decide which one is the record.

questions.stem: Your eighteen-month programme completes next month. Twenty-six people return to their functional departments or to other projects, most within a fortnight. Two contracts remain unsettled and the final claim from one supplier depends on records only your commercial analyst understands. Your sponsor has asked you to release everyone as soon as the deliverables are accepted. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Sequence the releases so people whose knowledge the outstanding closure obligations depend on, including the commercial analyst, are retained until those obligations are discharged.
options.rationale: Two unsettled contracts and a claim that rests on one person's understanding are live obligations, and releasing that person turns a settlement into a dispute nobody can evidence. Sequencing costs a few weeks of one role rather than the value of the claim.

options.text: Give each person's line manager specific, evidenced feedback on their contribution while it is fresh, and tell each person what you have said.
options.rationale: Performance information that reaches a line manager while it can still influence someone's next role is one of the few things closure can give the team. Telling them what was said is what makes it accountable rather than a report behind their backs.

options.text: Release everyone as the sponsor has asked, and retain access to the commercial analyst through her new manager if the supplier claim requires it.
options.rationale: This is the borrow-them-back error. It depends on the goodwill of a manager with their own priorities, and the analyst's attention will belong to new work exactly when the claim needs sustained effort.

options.text: Ask the team to document what they know before they leave, including the records behind the supplier claim, so that no individual's departure blocks closure.
options.rationale: This is the documentation-in-a-fortnight error. Broad documentation produced under time pressure captures the general and misses the specific, and the supplier claim needs someone who can answer questions about those records rather than a file.

options.text: Hold a closure event recognising the programme's achievement before the team disperses, inviting the sponsor and the line managers who are receiving people back.
options.rationale: Worth doing and it is not one of the two things that matter here. Even with line managers in the room, a general celebration gives them no specific, evidenced information about any individual, and it does nothing for the unsettled contracts.

questions.explanation: Releasing a team is a sequencing decision rather than a single event, because closure obligations outlive the delivery and some of them depend on named individuals. The two actions that matter are retaining the people those obligations require until they are discharged, and passing specific performance information to line managers while it can still affect what happens to each person next. Borrowing people back, hurried documentation and a closure event each substitute a lower-cost gesture for one of those two, and the supplier claim is the thing that pays for it.
questions.mindset: Release people in the order the remaining obligations allow, and send their contribution with them.

questions.stem: Your customer formally accepted the delivered platform seven weeks ago. Since then your team has completed nineteen small changes requested by the customer's users, each taking a day or two, none through any process. The team is still fully allocated, closure has not progressed, and the support contract that should now be handling these requests started five weeks ago and has received nothing. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Complete the current requests, then announce to the customer's users a date after which all further requests go to the support contract, and brief the support provider so it is ready for them.
options.rationale: This is the one-more-batch error. Nineteen requests in seven weeks means more will arrive before any announced date, and each one completed after acceptance teaches the customer that the boundary moves when they ask. A briefed support provider is ready for work that is still not being sent to it.

options.text: Assess the nineteen changes against the accepted scope to establish which were defects and which were new requests, and agree with the customer which of them should have gone to support.
options.rationale: This is the reconcile-the-past error. The analysis is worth having for the commercial record and it consumes time while the flow of new requests continues to reach the team, so the situation is unchanged when it finishes.

options.text: Stop taking requests directly, route them to the support contract that is now live, and agree with the customer's sponsor how anything genuinely outstanding from delivery is distinguished and handled.
options.rationale: The support arrangement exists and is being paid for while the project absorbs its work, so redirecting the flow is the substantive move. Agreeing the distinction with the customer is what stops the redirection being experienced as a refusal.

options.text: Raise the situation with the sponsor as scope creep after acceptance, and ask for the team to be released and for the customer to be told that requests must now go to support.
options.rationale: This is the escalate-for-permission error. Redirecting requests to a live support contract, and telling the customer so, is within the project manager's authority, and asking to be released describes the outcome you want rather than the arrangement that produces it.

questions.explanation: Formal acceptance is only a boundary if something observable changes when it is crossed, and here nothing did, so the project has been operating as an unfunded support function for seven weeks. The move is to redirect the flow to the arrangement that now owns it and to agree explicitly with the customer how residual delivery obligations are distinguished from new requests. Finishing the current batch, reconciling what has already happened, and escalating for permission all leave requests arriving at the team while they are carried out.
questions.mindset: Acceptance is a boundary, and it only exists if something changes when you cross it.

questions.stem: Your project has met every acceptance criterion and the test evidence is complete and agreed with the customer's technical team. Your sponsor is refusing to sign the acceptance certificate. In conversation it emerges that his real objection is that the operating model chosen two years ago, before you were appointed and outside this project's scope, has left his division with running costs he considers unreasonable. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Escalate to the project board that the sponsor is withholding acceptance on grounds unrelated to the delivered scope, attaching the test evidence and asking the board to confirm the criteria are met.
options.rationale: This is the escalate-over-the-sponsor error. It may be where this ends, and going there with the evidence before attempting to resolve it directly spends the relationship, and it presents his concern as illegitimate when it is merely misdirected.

options.text: Investigate the running costs and propose changes to the operating model that would reduce them, so that his objection is answered and the acceptance certificate can then be signed.
options.rationale: This is the solve-the-other-problem error. It takes on work outside the project's scope and mandate at the point of closure, and by making the signature wait on the fix it accepts the premise that acceptance depends on satisfying an unrelated grievance.

options.text: Close the project on the technical team's confirmation that the criteria are met, record the sponsor's refusal to sign, and attach the evidence against each criterion to the closure report.
options.rationale: This is the proceed-without-the-signature error. The sponsor's acceptance is what closure requires, and however complete the attached evidence, recording a refusal produces a closed project with an unresolved objection in the permanent record.

options.text: Set out the acceptance criteria and the evidence against each, ask him to accept on that basis, and offer to document the operating model concern separately and route it to whoever owns it.
options.rationale: Acceptance is a judgement against agreed criteria, so restating what the certificate does and does not attest to is what separates the two issues. Offering a real route for the running cost concern is what makes the separation acceptable rather than dismissive.

questions.explanation: When acceptance is withheld for reasons outside the acceptance criteria, the task is to separate the two rather than to satisfy the wrong one. That means restating precisely what the certificate attests to, evidencing it, and giving the unrelated concern a genuine route to whoever owns it, since a concern with nowhere to go will keep attaching itself to whatever document needs signing. Escalating first, taking on out-of-scope work, and closing without the signature each treat the objection as an obstacle rather than as information about where the sponsor's real problem sits.
questions.mindset: Separate what a person is entitled to withhold from what they are actually unhappy about.

questions.stem: Your programme's steering group has not met for four months, as members keep withdrawing. In that period three decisions have been taken by the chair over email, and one was reversed six weeks later when a member who had not been copied objected. The terms of reference require quarterly meetings and a quorum of four. Delivery has absorbed about three weeks of rework. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Put the position to the sponsor: reinstate the forum with a quorum that can actually be assembled, or formally amend the governance to something workable, and re-take the three decisions properly under whichever results.
options.rationale: The choice is between making the defined governance work and changing it to something that will, and the sponsor is the person who can authorise either. Re-taking the three decisions is what stops the current ambiguity being inherited by everything built on them.

options.text: Continue with email decisions through the chair, since they have proved faster than convening the steering group and the chair has the authority to take them, and copy every member on each one so that nobody is missed again.
options.rationale: This is the it-works-in-practice error. Copying everyone patches the omission that caused the reversal, but a chair deciding by email with no quorum is still not the body the terms of reference name, so every decision taken this way remains open to challenge by a member who disagrees.

options.text: Record the three email decisions formally in the decision log, with the date, rationale and people consulted for each, so there is a proper record of what was agreed and on whose authority.
options.rationale: This is the record-it-and-move-on error. Documenting a decision does not confer the authority it lacked, and a clean log makes an unsound decision harder to spot rather than sounder, while the forum that should be taking decisions still has not met.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor that steering group members are not fulfilling their governance responsibilities, and ask her to write to each member requiring attendance at a quorate meeting this month.
options.rationale: This is the complain-about-attendance error. Four months of withdrawals suggests the forum as designed does not fit what members can commit to, and pressing them to attend treats the symptom rather than the design, leaving the three email decisions as unsound as before.

questions.explanation: Governance that is not operating as defined leaves decisions with no traceable authority, and the failure shows up later as rework when someone with standing objects. There are only two sound resolutions, reinstating the forum or formally changing it to something that can actually run, and both belong to the sponsor. Continuing informally, tidying the record, and pressing members to attend all preserve a gap between how the programme is governed on paper and how it is governed in fact.
questions.mindset: Either the governance operates as written or it gets changed; running it informally gives you neither.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the chain your organisation relies on to demonstrate compliance. Your monthly access review is genuinely performed every month by a named manager, and everyone involved confirms it. The auditor has raised a finding because nothing exists that would let an independent reviewer confirm it happened. Select the link in the chain that has failed.

graphic.title: Compliance assurance chain, five links left to right
graphic.caption: Select a link. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between links, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Obligation identified
regions.rationale: The obligation was identified, which is why a monthly access review exists at all. Nothing in the finding suggests the requirement itself was missed or misread.

regions.label: Control designed
regions.rationale: A named manager performing a monthly review is a designed control that addresses the obligation. The design is sound; the finding is not about what the control is meant to do.

regions.label: Evidence produced
regions.rationale: The control operates and produces nothing an independent party can inspect, which is precisely the gap the auditor has identified. Evidence is the link that converts an activity into something demonstrable.

regions.label: Assurance performed
regions.rationale: Assurance tests whether the control operated by examining the evidence. It cannot function here, but it is failing because it has nothing to examine rather than because the assurance activity is defective.

regions.label: Position reported
regions.rationale: Reporting communicates the compliance position upward. It is the last link and it faithfully reports whatever assurance concluded, so a defect here would be one of communication rather than of proof.

questions.explanation: A control that operates but leaves no trace is indistinguishable, to anyone who was not present, from one that never operated at all. Evidence is the link that makes the difference, which is why confirmation from the people involved does not answer the finding: their word is testimony rather than an inspectable record. The practical consequence is that a control should be designed together with the artifact it produces, since retrofitting evidence after an audit is announced is either impossible or improper.
questions.mindset: Compliance is a claim you have to be able to prove to someone who was not there.

questions.stem: A failure in a live payroll interface will stop three thousand staff being paid on Friday unless a configuration change is made today. The change board next meets on Monday. Your organisation's change process has an emergency route, but your predecessor never used it and nobody on the team knows how it works. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Make the change now given the consequences, and submit a change request to the board on Monday for retrospective approval.
options.rationale: This is the act-now-paper-later error. It reaches a defensible outcome by an indefensible route, and where an emergency procedure exists, choosing not to use it is a control breach rather than a pragmatic shortcut.

options.text: Use the emergency route, obtaining whatever authority it specifies, and make the change today.
options.rationale: The process already anticipates exactly this situation, so the urgency is a reason to use the designed path rather than to leave it. Unfamiliarity is a gap to close in the next hour, not grounds to bypass a control.

options.text: Convene an out-of-cycle change board meeting today with whichever members are available.
options.rationale: This is the improvise-the-forum error. A quorum assembled by availability may not be the authority the process recognises, and it recreates by hand a mechanism the organisation has already defined.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor and ask her to authorise the change directly, given that three thousand staff are affected.
options.rationale: This is the seniority-as-authority error. A sponsor's authority over the project is not the same as authority over a change control process, and it substitutes a person's rank for the route the process specifies.

questions.explanation: Change control is designed to hold under pressure, which is why emergency provisions exist, and the correct response to genuine urgency is to use them rather than to treat the situation as outside the process. Not knowing how the emergency route works is a gap to close immediately, since the alternatives all involve constructing an approval that the organisation's records will not recognise. Acting first, assembling an ad hoc board or borrowing a sponsor's authority each produce a change that was made without the control that governs it.
questions.mindset: Emergency routes exist so that urgency does not become a reason to have no process at all.

questions.stem: Your team's impediment board carries seven items. Two are stopping work today. The other five read as "the vendor may not deliver the API on schedule", "our cloud costs could rise next year" and similar. The daily standup works through all seven, and the team has begun treating the whole board as background noise. Your delivery lead says removing items would discourage people from raising things. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Move the five may-happen items to the risk register, where each gets an owner and a review cadence, and keep the impediment board to the two items that are blocking work now.
options.rationale: The five are risks, and they need owners and periodic review rather than daily recitation. Separating them restores the impediment board to something short enough to act on, which is what makes raising an item worthwhile.

options.text: Keep all seven visible on the board, since the five future concerns genuinely affect the team and removing them would suppress reporting, as the delivery lead warns.
options.rationale: This is the visibility-at-any-cost error, taking the delivery lead's concern at face value. The team has already stopped attending to the board, so the five items are not visible in any useful sense, and the two real blockers are being lost among them.

options.text: Escalate all seven to the programme level, so items outside the team's control are owned by someone who can act and the standup can return to the team's own work.
options.rationale: This is the escalate-in-bulk error. Freeing the standup this way sends two live blockers and five speculative concerns upward with equal weight, which trains the recipient to treat the whole list as low priority.

options.text: Move the discussion of the five longer-term items to the retrospective, so the standup stays focused and the concerns still get a hearing.
options.rationale: This is the relocate-the-meeting error. It shortens the standup and gives the five risks an occasional hearing with no owner and no analysis, in a forum aimed at how the team works rather than at managing exposure.

questions.explanation: Impediments and risks are handled by different mechanisms because they are different things: one is stopping work now and needs clearing, the other might stop work later and needs an owner, an assessment and a review point. Mixing them produces a list too long to act on, at which point it stops functioning entirely, which is the state this board has reached. Preserving everything for visibility, escalating the lot, or moving the conversation to another meeting all keep the categories merged and leave the five concerns unmanaged either way.
questions.mindset: An impediment stops work now; anything that might stop work later belongs somewhere else.

questions.stem: Three quantified threats sit on your risk register ahead of a response planning workshop, and your team's habit is to propose additional controls for every one of them. You want each response chosen on the characteristics of the risk instead. Match each threat to the response strategy that fits it best. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: A remote chance of catastrophic third-party liability, which a specialist insurer will cover for a premium the project can comfortably afford.
A significant threat that exists only because of a proprietary integration method the team selected; a standard method carries no equivalent exposure and costs slightly more.
A threat with low probability and an impact of about 8,000, where every identified response costs more than 15,000.

options.text: Move the financial consequence to a third party
options.rationale: A low-probability, high-impact liability that a specialist will price affordably is the textbook case for transfer, because the project cannot absorb the impact and the insurer can. The risk still occurs; only the financial consequence moves.

options.text: Change the approach so the risk cannot arise
options.rationale: The exposure is created entirely by a choice the team made, and an alternative removes it rather than reducing it. Avoidance is available here precisely because the cause is internal and the switching cost is small.

options.text: Take no action beyond a defined trigger for review
options.rationale: Where every response costs roughly twice the exposure, acting destroys value. Acceptance is a deliberate decision rather than inattention, which is what the review trigger records.

options.text: Add controls to reduce the probability
options.rationale: Not used, and it is the team's default. Mitigation suits a risk whose probability is genuinely reducible at proportionate cost; here it is unnecessary for the insurable one, inferior to removing the cause for the second, and uneconomic for the third.

options.text: Refer it to programme level as outside the project's authority
options.rationale: Not used. Escalation is for risks whose response lies beyond the project manager's authority or whose impact falls outside the project. All three of these can be responded to with decisions available within the project.

questions.explanation: Risk response strategy follows the characteristics of the individual risk: whether the impact can be borne, whether the cause is something the project chose, and whether any response costs less than the exposure it removes. Transfer suits an unbearable impact somebody else will price; avoidance is available when the project created the cause; acceptance is correct when action costs more than the risk. Defaulting to additional controls is the common habit and it spends money on risks that should have been transferred, designed out, or knowingly carried.
questions.mindset: Choose the response from the shape of the risk, not from the strategy you always reach for.

questions.stem: Your team proposes automating a manual regression suite. Building the automation is estimated at 30 person-days. The manual suite currently occupies 2 testers for 1.5 days at every release, and the team releases fortnightly, which is 26 releases a year. Assume the automation removes the manual effort entirely and needs no maintenance. Work out the annual saving in person-days, then the payback period in months.

blanks.label: Annual saving, in person-days
blanks.rationale: Each release consumes 2 testers for 1.5 days, which is 3 person-days, and there are 26 releases, so 3 multiplied by 26 gives 78 person-days a year.

blanks.label: Payback period, in months
blanks.rationale: The build costs 30 person-days against a saving of 78 a year, so it repays in 30 divided by 78 of a year, which is about 0.38 years or roughly 4.6 months.

questions.explanation: Improvement work competes with delivery for the same capacity, and the argument for it is far stronger expressed as a payback period than as an appeal to good practice. The assumptions are what the number rests on, which is why they are worth stating explicitly: automation that needs maintenance, or that replaces only part of the manual effort, lengthens the payback and may reverse the decision. A team that can put a figure like this in front of a product owner is asking for an investment rather than for permission.
questions.mindset: An improvement proposal becomes a decision the moment somebody puts numbers against it.

questions.stem: A new dispatch system goes live across eleven depots next month. Frontline controllers will use it from day one for work they currently do from memory and paper. At the pilot depot, allocating each job took about a quarter longer for five weeks before becoming quicker than before, and the drivers waiting on those allocations, who had not been told to expect any delay, began phoning the depot to complain. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: For the controllers using the system for the first time on live work, the response is mostly to
For the drivers who will wait longer for their jobs during the transition, the response is mostly to

options.text: put experienced support alongside them at the moment they are doing the work
options.rationale: The difficulty appears in live conditions with real pressure, which is where classroom learning does not reach. Support at the point of use is what converts training into competence and shortens the dip.

options.text: tell them in advance how long the slower period should last and how to raise a job that cannot wait
options.rationale: A deterioration nobody has explained reads as the change failing, and the pilot depot's drivers filled that silence with complaints. Telling them beforehand what to expect, for how long, and what to do when a job is urgent turns a grievance into a known, temporary cost.

options.text: explain the benefits the new system will bring once it is embedded
options.rationale: Not used. The benefits are not in dispute and explaining them does nothing about the five weeks in between, which is the part both groups actually have to get through.

options.text: set a firm cutover date after which the old process is unavailable
options.rationale: Not used. A hard cutover is often necessary and it is a decision about timing rather than support. Applied as the answer to either group it removes the alternative without helping anyone through the transition.

questions.explanation: Performance usually falls before it improves when people change how they work, and the people affected during that window need different things according to how the dip reaches them. Those doing the work need help at the moment they are doing it, because that is where the difficulty actually occurs; those on the receiving end of slower output need to know in advance what is coming, for how long and what to do when something cannot wait, because an unexplained deterioration is read as the change failing. The two unused options address the case for the change and its timing, neither of which is what makes the transition survivable.
questions.mindset: Plan for the dip, and tell the people it lands on before it reaches them.

questions.stem: Six weeks after rolling a new client management system out to fourteen branches, usage varies enormously. In the five branches whose managers use it themselves, most staff have adopted it. In the other nine, usage is close to zero and staff say their manager has told them to carry on as before. The branch managers were briefed once, have no objective relating to the system, and are measured entirely on sales. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Deliver additional training to staff in the nine branches, since usage there is lowest, and ask each of those branches to nominate a member of staff as a local system champion.
options.rationale: This is the train-the-visible-gap error. Staff in those branches have been told by their manager not to use the system, so ability is not the constraint, and neither more training nor a staff-level champion will outweigh an instruction from the person they report to.

options.text: Work with the nine managers to establish what the system costs them day to day and what it would take for them to back it, and get their objectives changed so adoption is something they are accountable for.
options.rationale: The five-and-nine split tracks manager behaviour exactly, which identifies where the intervention has to land. Understanding their position and changing what they are measured on together address both why they are indifferent and why indifference is currently rational.

options.text: Escalate to the regional director and ask for use of the system to be made mandatory across all fourteen branches, with usage reported to her monthly so the nine managers are held to it.
options.rationale: This is the mandate-over-the-manager error. Monthly usage reporting may produce logins without use, and it bypasses nine managers whose cooperation the system needs daily, leaving them with a requirement imposed and monitored rather than a reason to support it.

options.text: Publish a branch-by-branch adoption league table so the nine underperforming branches are visible to their peers, alongside short case studies from the five branches where the system is working well.
options.rationale: This is the shame-into-compliance error. Case studies alongside a league table still create pressure to move a usage figure rather than to use the system, and they make public an underperformance whose cause nobody has yet asked the managers about.

questions.explanation: Where adoption splits cleanly along the line of who manages each group, the middle layer is the mechanism and therefore the place to intervene. That means finding out what the change costs those managers and aligning what they are accountable for with what the organisation wants, so that supporting it stops being an act of goodwill. Training the frontline addresses an ability problem that does not exist, and mandates and league tables both apply pressure to people who have not been given a reason, which reliably produces the appearance of adoption rather than the substance.
questions.mindset: Frontline adoption follows the line manager, so the line manager is who the change has to convince.

questions.stem: Your project imports specialist equipment under a two-year contract priced in the supplier's currency. Since signature that currency has strengthened about 12 percent against yours, and roughly 60 percent of the contract value is still to be paid. Your budget was set at the signature rate. Your commercial lead suggests simply drawing the difference from contingency and carrying on. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Quantify the exposure on the remaining payments at current and plausible future rates, and take it to the function that owns currency risk for the organisation.
options.rationale: Hedging and currency policy sit above the project, so the exposure has to reach the people who can act on it. Quantifying it across a range of rates is what lets them decide rather than merely be informed.

options.text: Review the contract for currency, price adjustment or share-of-movement clauses before assuming the full movement falls to your organisation.
options.rationale: Two-year supply contracts frequently allocate currency movement explicitly, so the actual exposure may be smaller than the headline. Establishing the contractual position first prevents both overstating the problem and conceding an allocation the contract does not require.

options.text: Draw the difference from contingency reserve as the commercial lead suggests, record the drawdown in the monthly cost report, and continue with the payment schedule unchanged.
options.rationale: This is the absorb-it-quietly error. Contingency was sized for identified project risks rather than for a market movement, and a line in the project cost report still conceals an organisational exposure from the only people equipped to manage it.

options.text: Open renegotiation with the supplier's account director, asking them to share the movement equally since neither party caused it.
options.rationale: This is the negotiate-before-reading error. The supplier has no obligation to reopen an agreed price, however even-handed the proposal, and approaching them before establishing what the contract already says gives away the strongest position you might hold.

options.text: Re-tender the remaining equipment to suppliers who will price in your own currency, so that the project carries no further exposure for the rest of the delivery period.
options.rationale: This is the disproportionate-response error. Re-tendering specialist equipment mid-project to remove the currency from the contract carries delivery, compatibility and schedule risk far larger than the movement it would avoid.

questions.explanation: External economic movements produce exposure that the project carries but does not own, and the correct handling is to size it accurately and route it to the function with the mandate and instruments to manage it. Establishing what the contract already allocates comes first, because it determines whether there is an exposure of the size assumed. Absorbing it in contingency hides an organisational risk inside a project reserve, and renegotiating or re-tendering both act on the supplier relationship before anyone has established what the position actually is.
questions.mindset: Exposure the project did not create and cannot control still has to be quantified and routed to whoever owns it.

questions.stem: An industry body has launched a security certification scheme for products in your sector. It carries no legal force. Within four months two of the three largest buyers in your market have written it into their procurement requirements, and your two main competitors have announced they are pursuing it. Your platform would need roughly five months of work to qualify. Your sponsor's view is that the project is not obliged to do anything not required by law. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Add the certification to scope and start the qualification work now, then inform the sponsor of the change, since two of the three largest buyers require it and the product will otherwise be unsellable.
options.rationale: This is the decide-it-yourself error. The conclusion may well be right, and informing the sponsor after starting is not the same as asking: five months of work against a sponsor who has expressed a contrary view is not a decision the project manager can take alone.

options.text: Accept the sponsor's position, record the certification as a market risk with an owner, and agree with the sponsor a date to revisit it once more buyers have adopted the scheme.
options.rationale: This is the defer-to-the-stated-view error. The sponsor's position rests on a distinction between legal and commercial requirements that nobody has yet tested against the market evidence, and scheduling a later review watches a five-month qualification window close.

options.text: Brief the sales and product functions on the buyers' new requirements first, so that they can make the case for certification to the sponsor through their own channels.
options.rationale: This is the outsource-the-argument error. Briefing other functions first routes the question to people with an interest in the answer while the project manager, who holds the cost and schedule evidence, stays out of the conversation that needs it.

options.text: Assess what qualification would cost and what remaining unqualified would cost in accessible market, and put it to the sponsor as a decision about the product's value rather than about compliance.
options.rationale: The scheme is voluntary in law and effectively mandatory commercially, so the framing that fits is value rather than obligation. Costing both sides is what lets the sponsor take the decision that is actually in front of him.

questions.explanation: The external environment includes commercial requirements that carry no legal weight and still determine whether a product can be sold, and treating obligation as the only trigger for action misses them entirely. The response is to convert the situation into a decision the sponsor can take, by costing qualification against the market that remaining unqualified forecloses. Adding the scope unilaterally, accepting an untested framing, and handing the argument to another function each avoid putting the actual trade-off in front of the person who has to make it.
questions.mindset: A requirement does not have to be legally binding to decide whether anyone will buy the thing.

questions.stem: Two insurers have merged and you are running the integration of their claims operations. Each company's project office has issued its own staff briefing about what the integration is for. One describes it as adopting the acquirer's proven platform; the other describes it as selecting the best of both. Neither briefing is wrong about the eventual outcome, but the two teams have started making design decisions from different assumptions. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Withdraw both briefings, then issue a single corrected one from the integration office and ask both project offices to cascade it to their staff.
options.rationale: Correcting the message without settling the question underneath it is the error here. The two offices are not describing the project differently by accident; they are describing different decisions that nobody has actually taken, and a third briefing, however widely cascaded, will be read as a third opinion.

options.text: Establish which of the two readings the executive team has actually decided, then rebuild the shared statement of purpose with both project offices in the room.
options.rationale: The divergence is a symptom of an undecided question, so the sequence is decide, then align, then communicate. Bringing both offices into the rebuild is what stops the losing reading resurfacing as quiet resistance in design decisions.

options.text: Let each team continue under its own briefing, then reconcile the design decisions at the integration checkpoint once both sets of designs can be compared.
options.rationale: Deferring alignment to an integration point is the classic false economy. By the time both designs can be compared, the divergent assumptions are embedded in built work, and the reconciliation costs rework rather than a conversation.

options.text: Escalate to the merger steering group that the two project offices are undermining the integration, and ask it to instruct both to stop issuing separate briefings.
options.rationale: Framing an alignment gap as misconduct converts a solvable problem into a political one. Silencing the two offices also skips the step that would tell you whether the executives have even made the decision the briefings assume.

questions.explanation: Divergent statements of purpose usually mark an open decision rather than a communication defect. Settling the underlying question first, then rebuilding the shared articulation with the people who were publishing the competing versions, addresses the cause and buys their commitment to the result. Reissuing a message over the top of an unresolved decision produces compliance in words and divergence in the work.
questions.mindset: When two accounts of the purpose are circulating, look for the decision nobody has made rather than the message somebody got wrong.

questions.stem: A research consortium funds your programme through four partners. Each partner's grant agreement names a different primary measure of success: publications, a working prototype, trained staff, and a commercialisation route. All four measures are legitimate and all four partners expect their own to be the headline. Your teams are being pulled toward whichever partner spoke most recently. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Work with the four partners to agree a single ordering of the four measures for the programme as a whole, with the reasoning recorded.
options.rationale: Four legitimate aims do not need to be reduced to one, but they do need an order, because every real trade-off will ask which yields. Recording the reasoning is what lets the order survive the partner who was not in the room that day.

options.text: Make the agreed ordering visible in how work is selected, so teams can see which measure a decision is serving.
options.rationale: An ordering that lives only in a signed document does not reach the people making daily choices. Wiring it into how work is picked is what converts an agreement between funders into a decision aid for teams.

options.text: Ask each partner to nominate a representative who attends the programme board, so all four voices are heard equally.
options.rationale: Equal representation without a settled priority reproduces the problem in a meeting room. Four voices with equal standing and no agreed order is exactly the arrangement that has teams chasing whoever spoke last.

options.text: Split the programme into four workstreams, one per partner measure, each with its own backlog and a lead accountable to that partner.
options.rationale: Structuring around the funders rather than the work is a common misstep. It removes the friction by removing the shared programme, and giving each partner its own lead hard-wires the competition, when the four measures were supposed to be served by one body of work.

options.text: Report progress against all four measures each month in a single dashboard, so that no partner feels their interest is being neglected.
options.rationale: Even reporting is a reasonable practice and a poor substitute for prioritisation. A shared dashboard reassures the partners without helping a team decide what to do on a Tuesday when two measures conflict.

questions.explanation: Where several sponsors each hold a valid definition of success, alignment means agreeing which yields to which when they collide, and then making that order visible at the point of daily choice. Governance arrangements that give every funder equal standing, or reporting that treats every measure as equally weighted, leave the trade-off unresolved and push it down to whoever is closest to the work.
questions.mindset: Competing legitimate aims need an agreed order, not equal airtime.

questions.stem: In yesterday's retrospective, two developers disagreed sharply about whether the team should keep pairing on complex work. The exchange got heated, and the discussion moved on without a conclusion. Today one of the two has said almost nothing in standup and has declined an offer to pair. The other appears unaffected. What is the most appropriate response from the project manager?

options.text: Put the pairing question first on the agenda of the next retrospective so the team can settle it properly with both developers present.
options.rationale: This is the wait-for-the-ceremony error. It treats the unresolved topic as the whole problem. The topic can wait a fortnight; a team member who has withdrawn after a public exchange usually cannot, and by the next retrospective the withdrawal has hardened.

options.text: Ask the team to agree how disagreements are handled in retrospectives, so that heated exchanges are dealt with in the moment.
options.rationale: This is the generalise-it-into-policy error. A working agreement is a good preventative measure and does nothing for the rupture that already exists. Introducing it now also invites the team to relitigate yesterday in the abstract while the two people involved are still not talking.

options.text: Speak to each of them separately to understand what happened, then help them resolve it between themselves.
options.rationale: Talking to both privately first surfaces whether this is about pairing at all, and often it is not. Handing the resolution back to the two of them keeps ownership where it belongs while making sure someone has checked that resolution is actually happening.

options.text: Give it a few days, since a single heated exchange between colleagues usually settles on its own.
options.rationale: Waiting is right for friction that is genuinely trivial, and the observable signal here says this one is not: one party has changed their behaviour and stopped participating. Reading withdrawal as cooling off is how a two-day problem becomes a two-month one.

questions.explanation: The signal worth acting on is asymmetry: one person's participation has dropped and the other's has not. That points to something between two individuals rather than an open team question, so the intervention is individual and prompt, and its aim is to put the resolution back in their hands. Deferring to the next ceremony, or generalising the incident into a team policy, both leave the specific rupture untouched.
questions.mindset: Watch what changes in behaviour after a disagreement, not how loud the disagreement was.

questions.stem: Six weeks before a regulatory milestone, a senior engineer submits a formal grievance to human resources about a colleague on your project, alleging persistent undermining in meetings. Both are on the critical path and neither can be replaced in the time available. Human resources has told you the process will take several weeks and has asked you not to investigate the allegations yourself. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep the grievance with human resources, and separately restructure the immediate work so the two do not depend on each other day to day.
options.rationale: It respects the boundary the formal process draws while acting on the part that is genuinely the project manager's: how the work is arranged. Reducing forced interaction protects both people and the milestone without touching the allegations.

options.text: Bring the two together for a facilitated conversation, keeping human resources informed, to resolve the working disagreement before it damages the milestone.
options.rationale: Mediating in parallel with a live formal process is the serious error here, and keeping human resources informed does not make it safe. It can compromise the investigation, may be read as pressuring the complainant to withdraw, and exceeds the project manager's standing once the matter is formally lodged.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor that the grievance places the regulatory milestone at risk, and ask for the human resources process to be expedited.
options.rationale: Asking for a people process to be accelerated for schedule reasons subordinates a fairness process to a date. It also signals to the complainant that raising a concern is treated primarily as a delivery inconvenience, which is the opposite of what the process exists to protect.

options.text: Reassign the engineer who raised the grievance to non-critical work until the process concludes, to reduce friction.
options.rationale: Moving the person who complained is the response that looks neutral and is not. Whatever the intent, it visibly disadvantages the complainant and is the pattern most likely to be read afterwards as retaliation.

questions.explanation: Once a matter is formally lodged, the project manager's remit narrows to what remains legitimately theirs: sequencing, dependencies and who has to work with whom. Reorganising the work to remove forced interaction protects delivery and both individuals. Mediating, expediting or moving the complainant all reach into a process that is deliberately outside the project's control, and the last of these carries a specific risk of being construed as detriment.
questions.mindset: When a formal process owns the dispute, the project manager's job is the working arrangements around it.

questions.stem: Your strongest engineer is technically outstanding and consistently dismissive in design reviews, cutting people off and calling suggestions naive. Over three months you have watched two junior members stop proposing anything. The engineer is unaware of the effect and would be genuinely surprised to hear it. Delivery is currently on track and no one has complained formally. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep notes on the next few design reviews and wait for a concrete incident you can point to, so the feedback is specific and defensible.
options.rationale: Holding out for a single citable incident is how this pattern goes unaddressed for a year. The evidence is already there in the form of a three-month behavioural trend, and gathering more notes before acting sets the bar where it will never be met.

options.text: Give the engineer direct private feedback describing the observed behaviour and the effect you have seen it have on others.
options.rationale: Someone unaware of their impact can only act on information, and the useful form of it is observed behaviour plus observed consequence rather than a character assessment. Doing it privately preserves the standing they will need to change.

options.text: Introduce a rule that every design review ends with each person contributing one idea, so the quieter members are heard without anyone being singled out.
options.rationale: Engineering the turn-taking treats the symptom and leaves the cause in the room; avoiding singling anyone out is exactly what keeps the conversation that is needed from happening. Compelled contributions in front of the person whose reaction people are avoiding tend to produce safe suggestions rather than real ones.

options.text: Ask the two junior members whether they would like you to raise it, and act only if they agree.
options.rationale: Making the intervention conditional on the consent of the people with least power is a subtle abdication. They are likely to decline out of the same caution that stopped them contributing, and the request itself puts the burden back on them.

questions.explanation: Team environment is the project manager's responsibility whether or not anyone has complained, and delivery being on track is not evidence that it is healthy. The lever is direct, private, behaviourally specific feedback to the person who can change, given early enough that the pattern is still describable as behaviour rather than reputation. Procedural workarounds and consent-seeking both leave the cause untouched and shift the cost onto those already bearing it.
questions.mindset: A team that has gone quiet is data about the leader's environment, not about the team's ideas.

questions.stem: Your squad has asked for more autonomy and you agree in principle, but you have decided that how much you hand over should vary with the decision rather than being granted wholesale. Three decisions are in front of the squad this month: choosing a testing library, setting the order of the next quarter's themes, and deciding whether to accept a defect into the release. Complete each sentence with the level of involvement that fits. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: On the choice of testing library, which is reversible and squarely within the team's craft, the leader should
On the order of next quarter's themes, which commits the organisation and depends on information the squad does not hold, the leader should
On accepting a defect into the release, where the squad holds the technical facts and the leader holds the customer commitments, the leader should

options.text: hand the decision over entirely and not ask to be told
options.rationale: A reversible decision inside the team's own discipline is where autonomy costs nothing and buys ownership. Asking to be informed of it anyway is the small habit that tells a team the autonomy is provisional.

options.text: make the decision and explain the reasoning to the squad
options.rationale: A commitment that binds the organisation and rests on information the squad does not have is not theirs to make. Explaining the reasoning is what keeps this from reading as a reversal of the autonomy agreed elsewhere.

options.text: decide it together, with the squad supplying the technical judgement
options.rationale: When the facts sit on one side and the consequences on the other, neither party can decide well alone. Joint decision-making here is not a compromise; it is the only arrangement in which both inputs are present.

options.text: gather the squad's views and then decide alone
options.rationale: Not used. Consulting then deciding suits a decision the leader must own but where the team holds useful context. It is the wrong shape for all three above: too heavy for the first, too light on reasoning for the second, and it discards the shared ownership the third needs.

options.text: leave the decision until the squad has demonstrated more maturity
options.rationale: Not used. Withholding decisions pending proven maturity is the trap that makes maturity unreachable, since the practice that builds judgement is the making of decisions. None of the three is waiting on capability the squad lacks.

questions.explanation: Autonomy is not a single setting applied to a team; it varies with reversibility, with where the relevant information sits, and with who carries the consequence. Reversible decisions inside the team's craft can be handed over completely. Decisions that bind the organisation and rest on information the team does not hold stay with the leader, with the reasoning shared. Where facts and consequences are split across the two, the decision has to be made together. Granting or withholding autonomy wholesale gets at least one of these wrong.
questions.mindset: Delegate by the decision, not by the person.

questions.stem: Your project will widen a road through a residential area. A residents' association has formed, has begun writing to local councillors, and is being quoted in the local press. It has no formal role in your project, no contractual relationship with your organisation, and no place in the stakeholder register you inherited. Your sponsor's view is that the association is not a project stakeholder because it has no standing. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Route all contact with the association through the communications team, so that the project speaks with one voice.
options.rationale: Channelling contact is a sensible detail mistaken here for a strategy. Speaking with one voice settles who speaks without settling what the project understands about the group's interests, which is the thing currently missing.

options.text: Accept the sponsor's assessment and monitor local press coverage and councillors' public statements for any escalation.
options.rationale: Deferring to a sponsor's judgement on who counts as a stakeholder is the error, because the sponsor is applying a test of formal standing that stakeholder identification does not use. Monitoring, however attentive, converts an engageable group into a risk you watch.

options.text: Add the association to the stakeholder register, analyse its interest and influence, and plan engagement on that basis.
options.rationale: Stakeholder status follows from being affected by or able to affect the project, not from holding a formal role. A group already reaching councillors and press has demonstrated influence, and analysis is what turns that observation into a proportionate plan.

options.text: Arrange a public meeting so the association can put its concerns to the project team directly and be heard.
options.rationale: A public meeting may well follow, but holding it before you understand who the group is and what it wants risks a session that hardens positions, and being heard in public is not the same as being understood. The sequence is analyse, then engage in the format the analysis suggests.

questions.explanation: Identification asks who is affected by the work or capable of affecting it, and a group with no contract and no seat at the table can score high on both. Once identified, the interest and influence assessment is what makes engagement proportionate rather than reactive. Treating an unofficial group as outside the register leaves the project without a plan for the party currently shaping its public reception.
questions.mindset: Being affected by the project is what makes someone a stakeholder; formal standing only changes how you engage them.

questions.stem: The operations director is your most significant stakeholder and has sent a junior analyst to every review for the past two months. The analyst attends diligently, takes notes and cannot make decisions. Twice, decisions the analyst relayed have been reversed a week later by the director. Your next two reviews contain choices that will be expensive to unwind. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Ask the director directly what level of decision the analyst is authorised to take, and confirm it in writing to both.
options.rationale: The reversals show that the delegation's limits are undefined rather than that the analyst is failing. Naming the boundary and confirming it to both makes the analyst's relayed decisions stick or explicitly not stick.

options.text: For decisions above that level, arrange a short, scheduled slot with the director rather than relying on the review.
options.rationale: Where a decision exceeds the delegate's authority, engagement is tailored to who actually decides. A brief targeted session respects the director's time constraint, which is almost certainly why a deputy was sent in the first place.

options.text: Continue with the analyst and record each relayed decision in the log, so reversals are visible and attributable.
options.rationale: Building an audit trail of reversals prepares a defence rather than preventing the problem. It also treats the director's changes of mind as misconduct to be evidenced when they are the predictable result of an undefined delegation.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to require the operations director to attend reviews personally until the expensive decisions in the next two reviews have been settled.
options.rationale: Compelled attendance is the wrong instrument for a senior stakeholder who has rationally delegated, even for a limited period. It spends sponsor authority on a symptom and is likely to damage a relationship the project needs after go-live.

options.text: Send the director a written summary after each review, listing decisions taken, and treat silence within three days as agreement.
options.rationale: A deemed-consent rule manufactures agreement from inattention. It gives the project a defensible position and no more certainty than it had, since the decisions being reversed are exactly the ones the director had not really considered.

questions.explanation: A deputy who cannot decide is a signal about delegated authority, not about the deputy. The pair of moves is to establish where that authority stops and to route anything above the line to the person who holds it, in a format that fits their constraints. Logging reversals, compelling attendance, and treating silence as approval all leave the authority question unanswered while adding process.
questions.mindset: Engage the person who decides, at the level they can decide.

questions.stem: Your steering group approved delivering a minimum viable product in June before scaling up. Preparing the June demonstration, you interview the six members and find that three assume the June release will handle live customer transactions, two assume it is an internal pilot, and one assumes it includes the reporting suite. All six believe they approved the same thing and the minutes record unanimous agreement. The demonstration is three weeks away. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Run the demonstration as planned, showing what will be delivered in June, and let the differences surface in the room, where they can be settled together.
options.rationale: Letting a demonstration do the disclosing is the appealing and costly option. Three members discover in public that they approved something other than what they thought, and the surprise, not the scope, becomes the story, however concrete the product on screen.

options.text: Expand the June scope to include live customer transactions, since that is the reading held by the largest group, and brief the other three members on the change before the demonstration.
options.rationale: Deciding an alignment question by counting holders of each view is the error, and briefing the minority once it is decided only tells them they lost. A majority reading is not an approval, and committing to the most demanding interpretation three weeks out trades a conversation for a delivery risk.

options.text: Set out in advance what the June release will and will not include, name the three different readings you found, and have the steering group confirm one before the demonstration.
options.rationale: Surfacing the divergence before the event converts an ambush into a decision. Naming the readings explicitly is what stops each member privately assuming their own version survived, which a bare scope list would allow.

options.text: Ask the chair to reissue the approval minutes with a precise definition of the June release attached, and circulate them to all six members before the demonstration so the record is clear.
options.rationale: A more precise record circulated in advance makes the next disagreement easier to adjudicate and does nothing to change the six expectations already formed.
