Documents that arrive after an assumption has set are rarely read against it, and no member is asked to choose between the readings.

questions.explanation: Where a shared label conceals different expectations, the work is to make the divergence explicit and force a single choice before an event exposes it. Naming each reading back to the group is what makes the reconciliation real, because each holder can see their own version being considered and either confirmed or set aside. Demonstrating first, deciding by weight of numbers, or tightening the record afterwards all leave expectations to collide in public.
questions.mindset: Unanimous approval of an ambiguous phrase is six different approvals.

questions.stem: A depot modernisation programme has three expectation gaps open at once, each with a different cause. The finance director expects savings from a month you have never committed to. The depot managers expect to keep a manual override the design removed after a decision they were not part of. The safety regulator expects a level of evidence your team believes it has already supplied. Match each gap to the move that addresses its cause. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: The finance director's savings date, which came from an early forecast that has since been superseded twice.
The depot managers' manual override, removed by a design decision taken without them.
The regulator's evidence expectation, where both sides believe they are talking about the same submission.

options.text: Walk the stakeholder through how the figure changed, and agree which version now stands
options.rationale: An expectation anchored to a superseded number is corrected by showing the path from the old figure to the current one. Agreeing explicitly which version now stands is what prevents the original from being quoted again at the next board.

options.text: Reopen the decision with the affected group present, and either confirm or change it
options.rationale: A decision made without the people it affects has a process defect, and no amount of explanation repairs it. Reopening with them present is what makes the outcome legitimate, whichever way it then goes.

options.text: Put both parties' understanding side by side and identify precisely where they diverge
options.rationale: When two sides each believe they agree, the gap is definitional and invisible until the two readings are set against each other. Comparing them directly locates the divergence before either party invests in being right.

options.text: Refer the disagreement to the sponsor for a ruling
options.rationale: Not used. Escalation suits a gap where the parties cannot agree and someone with authority must choose. None of the three has reached that point; each still has an unexplored cause that a ruling would simply paper over.

options.text: Reissue the baseline document with the correct position highlighted
options.rationale: Not used. Restating the record helps where the gap is genuine unawareness of a published position. Here one gap is a superseded figure, one is an illegitimate decision, and one is a definitional mismatch, and a reissued document addresses none of them.

questions.explanation: Expectation gaps look alike from the outside and diverge entirely underneath. One caused by a stale figure is closed by tracing the change and agreeing which version stands. One caused by exclusion from a decision is closed by including the excluded, because the objection is to the process rather than the outcome. One caused by two parties using the same words differently is closed by putting both readings side by side. Escalation and reissued documents are general-purpose responses that fit none of these causes specifically.
questions.mindset: Fix the cause of the expectation gap, not the gap itself.

questions.stem: Your team demonstrates every two weeks to a customer representative who has begun comparing each increment unfavourably with a competitor's mature product. Rough edges in early increments are read as evidence the team is not capable, and after four reviews the representative has started forwarding critical notes to her own director. The increments are genuinely early-stage and are progressing as expected. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Polish the user interface of the next increment before the review, so that the comparison with the competitor's product is less unfavourable and the critical notes stop.
options.rationale: Spending capacity on appearance to manage a perception is the trap here. It buys one better review, sets the expectation that every increment will look finished, and takes effort from the functionality that would actually close the gap with the competitor.

options.text: Explain at the next review that comparing an early increment with a mature product is not a fair comparison, then show her the release plan for where the product will be at launch.
options.rationale: It is true, and delivered as a correction it puts the customer in the wrong for the reaction she had; adding the release plan is still a one-way explanation rather than an agreed basis for judging the next increment. She is not making an argument; she is applying the only reference point she has been given.

options.text: Move to demonstrating only at the end of each quarter, when increments are substantial enough to compare well, and send the representative short written progress notes in between.
options.rationale: Reducing feedback frequency to improve the impression is the wrong direction. Written notes do not replace seeing the work, so it protects the reviews at the cost of the early correction they exist to produce, and the quarterly session will carry the same expectation.

options.text: Agree with the representative what each fortnightly review is for, and what an increment at this stage should and should not be judged on, so she has an agreed basis to give her director.
options.rationale: The problem is an unstated standard, and the fix is to agree one explicitly. Naming what the session is for gives both sides a shared basis for judging, and gives the representative something defensible to tell her director.

questions.explanation: A reviewer with no agreed frame of reference will supply their own, and the most available one is usually a finished product. Establishing jointly what each session is for and what the work should be assessed against replaces that borrowed standard with an appropriate one. Cosmetic investment, correcting the customer, and demonstrating less often all respond to the discomfort rather than to the absent shared expectation.
questions.mindset: When a customer judges harshly, check what standard they were given before questioning the judgement.

questions.stem: Two weeks before go-live on a system built for an internal department, the department head mentions in passing that she expects your team to remain available for about a year to make adjustments as her staff learn the system. Nothing in the charter, the business case or the acceptance criteria mentions post-implementation support, and your team is committed to another project a month after go-live. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Explain that post-implementation support is outside the agreed scope, point to the acceptance criteria the department head signed, and suggest she raises a separate request after go-live.
options.rationale: Being contractually right is available and unhelpful. The customer's expectation is real whether or not it was documented, and closing the conversation with the signed record, or deferring it until after go-live, converts a solvable gap into a dispute at handover.

options.text: Agree informally to help where you can, and manage the requests as they arrive after go-live.
options.rationale: An undefined promise made to avoid an awkward conversation is the error. It commits a team that is unavailable, and the reckoning arrives later with a customer who reasonably believes they were assured.

options.text: Raise the gap now with the department head and the sponsor, and agree an explicit support arrangement before go-live.
options.rationale: An unstated assumption discovered before handover is still cheap to settle. Bringing in the sponsor is what makes the outcome binding, since the answer may involve funding or resourcing that the department head alone cannot commit.

options.text: Add a twelve-month support line to the project's closure plan and inform the receiving department in the handover pack.
options.rationale: Documenting a commitment the project cannot staff does not create the capacity to honour it. It also decides unilaterally what the arrangement is, when the point of the discovery is that nobody has agreed anything.

questions.explanation: Customer expectations extend past the acceptance criteria into what happens afterwards, and support arrangements are the most commonly assumed and least commonly documented of them. Surfacing the assumption while there is still time, with the party who can commit resources present, converts it into an agreed arrangement. Refusing on documentary grounds, promising informally, or recording a commitment nobody has resourced each defer the collision to handover.
questions.mindset: An expectation you discover before handover is a negotiation; the same expectation discovered after is a complaint.

questions.stem: Your programme runs five workstreams, each integrating with the same ageing customer master file. Reviewing recent technical decisions, you find that four of the five have independently discovered the same undocumented behaviour in the file's date handling, and each has built its own workaround. Three of the four workarounds differ. None of the workstreams knew the others had hit it. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Have the design authority assess the four workarounds and instruct all workstreams to adopt the strongest, to remove the inconsistency.
options.rationale: This is the rule-on-the-instance error. Standardising the answer, however well assessed, leaves untouched the way the answer failed to travel. The next shared discovery will be found four more times, and next time the programme may not happen to notice.

options.text: Record the date-handling behaviour and the four workarounds in the programme's lessons learned log, for the benefit of future projects.
options.rationale: This is the record-for-later error. A lessons log is a store for the end of the project and this is knowledge four teams need this month. Writing it somewhere nobody currently reads mistakes recording for transferring.

options.text: Establish a way for technical findings to be published across workstreams as they are made, and seed it with this one.
options.rationale: The failure is that knowledge had no route sideways, so the fix has to be a route rather than a ruling. Seeding it with the live example is what gives it immediate value and makes the habit likely to take.

options.text: Ask each workstream lead to raise technical discoveries as a standing item at the fortnightly programme board, so all leads hear them.
options.rationale: This is the route-through-governance error. Funnelling technical findings through a fortnightly board is slow and lossy and puts the transfer at the mercy of an agenda; detailed engineering knowledge rarely survives the summarisation a board session imposes.

questions.explanation: Repeated independent discovery of the same fact means knowledge has no lateral path, and the durable response is to build one rather than to arbitrate this instance. Publishing findings as they are made, and starting with the example that exposed the gap, addresses cause and symptom together. Mandating a single workaround, filing it for future projects, or funnelling it through governance all leave the next shared discovery to be made four more times.
questions.mindset: The same thing learned four times is a routing failure, not four discoveries.

questions.stem: Your two-year programme is scaling up and twelve contractors join over the next six weeks. The existing team of nine holds most of what matters in conversation and habit, and the written material is a wiki last updated eleven months ago. Your delivery manager proposes pausing feature work for a fortnight so the team can bring the wiki up to date before the newcomers arrive. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Pair each newcomer with an existing team member on real work from their first week.
options.rationale: Tacit knowledge transfers by working alongside someone, which is the only mechanism that reaches the habits and judgement calls nobody thinks to write down. It also starts returning value immediately rather than after a documentation phase.

options.text: Have newcomers write and correct the documentation as they learn, rather than having the existing team write it first.
options.rationale: Newcomers are the only people who can still see what is unobvious, and existing members reliably omit exactly what they have stopped noticing. It also converts documentation from a pause into a by-product of onboarding.

options.text: Adopt the delivery manager's proposal, since a fortnight is a small price for a current wiki before twelve people arrive.
options.rationale: A documentation sprint written by people who already know everything produces a record of what they think is important, with the gaps intact. The cost is certain, the coverage is not, and the material starts ageing the day it is finished.

options.text: Record a series of walkthrough videos covering the architecture and key processes for newcomers to watch in their first week.
options.rationale: Recorded material scales the explanation and not the questions, which is where most of the learning is. It suits stable reference content rather than the working knowledge that changes as the programme moves.

options.text: Delay the contractors' start dates by two weeks so the existing team can prepare properly.
options.rationale: Deferring the arrival buys preparation time and pushes the same problem two weeks right, at direct cost. It also assumes readiness can be reached before contact with the newcomers, which is what the stale wiki disproves.

questions.explanation: Where a team's knowledge is largely tacit, transfer happens through joint work rather than through documents produced in advance. Pairing on real tasks moves the judgement that never reaches a page, and having the arriving people write the record captures precisely what the established team can no longer see is missing. Documentation sprints, recorded walkthroughs and delayed starts all assume the knowledge can be packaged before contact, which is the assumption an eleven-month-old wiki already tested.
questions.mindset: Knowledge that lives in habit moves by working together; write it down as you go, and let the newcomers hold the pen.

questions.stem: Your delivery team of fourteen works across two sites, and for eleven of them English is a second language. You communicate mostly in writing because of the time difference. Over the past month you have seen three instances where written instructions were followed to the letter but not as intended, and in each case the person had read the words differently than you meant them. Nobody has said they found the message unclear. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask the team to flag anything they find ambiguous before acting on it, and to ask questions whenever unsure.
options.rationale: It asks people to identify their own misunderstanding, which by definition they cannot: in all three cases the reader was confident they had understood, so an invitation to ask goes unused. It also puts the burden on the person least able to spot the gap.

options.text: Move important instructions to a synchronous call during the overlap window, where people can ask questions.
options.rationale: Speaking rather than writing is part of a good answer and is not sufficient on its own. People confident they have understood will not ask on a call either, a spoken instruction misheard leaves no artefact at all, and the overlap window will not hold everything that matters.

options.text: Arrange language training for the eleven team members, funded by the project, on reading technical instructions.
options.rationale: Locating the deficiency in the recipients is the error, and a months-long intervention does not address this month's instructions. Precise written English is difficult to read exactly as intended even among first-language speakers, however well targeted the training.

options.text: Change how the messages are written and confirmed, so understanding is checked rather than assumed.
options.rationale: The sender controls clarity and the sender can build in the check, whether by having the intent read back, by adding a worked example, or by using a short call for anything consequential. It addresses the mechanism rather than asking readers to be more careful.

questions.explanation: Instructions followed to the letter but not as intended point to a sending practice rather than to careless readers, particularly where nobody reports confusion because nobody experienced any. The effective changes are the sender's: build a confirmation of understanding into the message, illustrate intent concretely, and choose the channel by consequence. Asking recipients to self-identify ambiguity, or treating the situation as a language deficit, both move the obligation to the wrong end of the exchange.
questions.mindset: Responsibility for being understood sits with the sender, and understanding has to be checked rather than assumed.

questions.stem: You inherit the plan for a laboratory information system replacement. It is detailed, internally consistent and complete. Reading it closely, you notice its phase structure, contingency percentages and quality gates are identical to those of a building refurbishment your organisation completed last year, and several activity descriptions still reference site access and weather. The sponsor regards the plan as a strength, since it follows a proven template. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Rewrite the plan from scratch, since a template taken from a different type of work cannot be adapted reliably to this one.
options.rationale: Discarding a complete and coherent plan wholesale is disproportionate and wasteful, and the claim that it cannot be adapted to this project is asserted rather than tested. Parts of it will transfer, and the sponsor's confidence in it is worth something the project will need later.

options.text: Test the plan's assumptions against this project's actual characteristics, and change what does not hold.
options.rationale: A template is a starting position whose fitness has to be checked against the work in front of you. Testing assumptions rather than accepting or rejecting the whole plan is what separates tailoring from either laziness or theatre.

options.text: Remove the references to site access and weather and proceed, since the structure is sound and the sponsor has confidence in it.
options.rationale: Cleaning up the visible traces of the source project is the error most likely to be made here, because it makes the mismatch invisible without addressing it, and the sponsor's confidence rests on the template rather than on its fit. The contingency percentages and gate structure carry the borrowed assumptions, not the wording.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to confirm that the template is approved for use on software projects.
options.rationale: Seeking a procedural blessing substitutes authority for judgement. Approval that the template may be used says nothing about whether its assumptions fit a laboratory system replacement.

questions.explanation: Tailoring is the act of testing each planning assumption against the characteristics of the work at hand: its uncertainty, its dependencies, its regulatory context and its delivery approach. A plan carried over from unlike work can be coherent and still wrong in every parameter that matters. Rejecting it entirely wastes what transfers, and tidying its surface leaves the borrowed contingency and gate assumptions in place while removing the clues that they are borrowed.
questions.mindset: A plan inherited from other work is a hypothesis about this one.

questions.stem: At the planning review for a hybrid programme, three stakeholders each raise a question that planning has not yet answered. The commercial lead asks how you will handle a supplier whose scope cannot be fixed yet. The regulator's liaison asks what happens if the rules consulted on last month are adopted in month nine. The operations director asks which of two capabilities her staff will get first. Match each question to the planning decision that has to be settled before it can be answered. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: The commercial lead's supplier, whose scope cannot yet be fixed.
The regulator's liaison, on rules that may change in month nine.
The operations director, on which capability arrives first.

options.text: How commercial risk is shared while the scope remains open
options.rationale: An unfixable scope is first a question of who carries the uncertainty and on what terms, and every other commercial detail follows from that. Settling it later means the contract form gets chosen by whoever drafts first.

options.text: What the programme will do differently under each plausible outcome, and when it must commit
options.rationale: A pending external decision is planned for by identifying the divergent responses and the last responsible moment to choose between them. Without that, month nine arrives as a surprise rather than as a branch that was anticipated.

options.text: The basis on which capabilities are sequenced when they compete
options.rationale: Answering which capability arrives first requires an agreed rule for ordering rather than a single answer, because the question will be asked again about the next pair. The rule is what makes the answer defensible to the director who is not first.

options.text: How much confidence the current estimates carry and what would improve them
options.rationale: Not used. Estimate confidence is a real planning decision and answers none of the three questions above, each of which turns on an arrangement or a rule rather than on the precision of a number.

options.text: What the programme reports, to whom, and how often
options.rationale: Not used. Reporting arrangements determine how each stakeholder learns the answer once it exists. All three questions are asking for the answer itself, and settling the reporting cadence would leave every one of them open.

questions.explanation: Integrated planning holds together a set of decisions rather than a set of documents, and awkward stakeholder questions are a reliable way of finding which decisions are still open. Open supplier scope is a risk-sharing decision, a pending regulatory outcome is a decision about branches and commitment points, and competing capabilities are a decision about the ordering rule. Estimating confidence and reporting arrangements are genuine planning decisions that happen to answer none of these, which is what makes them attractive substitutes.
questions.mindset: Planning questions from stakeholders usually name a decision the plan has not yet made.

questions.stem: Reviewing your product backlog, you notice the product owner has split each feature by technical layer: a database story, a service story and a user interface story. The team delivers all three reliably within a sprint or two. At the last review the stakeholders could not tell what had been achieved, because no single item produced anything a user could do. What should the project manager suggest?

options.text: Combine the three layer stories for each feature into one larger item so each delivers something usable.
options.rationale: Merging the layers back into one item removes the reporting problem by removing the decomposition, and a single item spanning all three layers of a whole feature will be too large to finish predictably. The aim is to slice differently, not to stop slicing.

options.text: Split items by the smallest piece of user-visible behaviour instead, so each one delivers something demonstrable.
options.rationale: Slicing vertically keeps items small while making each one independently valuable and demonstrable. It is the change that fixes the review and the feedback loop at once, because stakeholders can only react to behaviour they can see.

options.text: Keep the current split, and group the three related stories into an epic that is demonstrated once all its parts are done.
options.rationale: Grouping for reporting preserves the underlying problem, which is that no increment is usable until the whole set is done. Stakeholders do see something eventually, but feedback still arrives only at the end, which is the cost the decomposition was supposed to avoid.

options.text: Demonstrate the technical work at reviews, with a short walkthrough of how each layer contributes to the eventual feature.
options.rationale: Explaining rather than showing asks stakeholders to imagine value from an architecture walkthrough. It also normalises reviews in which nothing works, which is exactly the habit that hides slipping progress.

questions.explanation: Backlog items are sized for predictability and shaped for feedback, and splitting along architectural boundaries satisfies the first while defeating the second. A thin slice through every layer that produces one usable behaviour keeps items small and lets stakeholders evaluate real outcomes each iteration. Recombining, grouping for reporting, or narrating the architecture all leave the project unable to learn anything from its reviews.
questions.mindset: Decompose so that every piece can be judged by someone who does not know how it was built.

questions.stem: A workstream lead has drafted the second level of the work breakdown structure for a depot systems rollout, shown below. You are reviewing it before the scope baseline is set. Select the element that does not belong at this level of a work breakdown structure.

graphic.title: Draft work breakdown structure, five second-level elements
graphic.caption: Select an element. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between elements, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Site survey reports
regions.rationale: A set of survey reports is a tangible output that can be produced, checked and accepted. It decomposes further into one report per depot, which is what a work breakdown structure element should do.

regions.label: Installed hardware
regions.rationale: Installed hardware is an outcome with a definable completion state at each depot. Whether it is present and working can be judged without reference to how long anyone spent on it.

regions.label: Weekly progress meetings
regions.rationale: This names an ongoing activity rather than something the project produces. It has no completion state, cannot be accepted, and would run for the project's whole duration regardless of how much scope was delivered.

regions.label: Migrated depot data
regions.rationale: Migrated data is a result that can be verified against acceptance criteria such as record counts and reconciliation. It has an unambiguous done state.

regions.label: Trained depot staff
regions.rationale: Trained staff is an outcome with a testable completion condition, such as a stated proportion of staff assessed as competent. The training sessions are how it is achieved, not what the element is.

questions.explanation: A work breakdown structure decomposes what the project delivers, so each element needs a completion state that someone can verify. Elements named for outputs and outcomes satisfy that test. An element named for a recurring activity has no such state: it cannot be finished, only stopped, and including it makes the structure's totals meaningless because effort spent on it never converts into delivered scope.
questions.mindset: Every element of a breakdown should be something you could hand over, not something you would do.

questions.stem: Your product owner has five remaining backlog items and has estimated the annual benefit of each: £540,000, £360,000, £180,000, £90,000 and £30,000. The team will build them in that order, and estimates them at 6, 4, 5, 3 and 2 weeks respectively. The sponsor has assumed a single release once all five are complete. Work out the totals below, then state what they imply about the release plan.

blanks.label: Total annual benefit of all five items, in £
blanks.rationale: 540,000 + 360,000 + 180,000 + 90,000 + 30,000 = £1,200,000. This is the figure the sponsor's single release is implicitly waiting for.

blanks.label: Share of that benefit represented by the first two items, as a percentage
blanks.rationale: (540,000 + 360,000) ÷ 1,200,000 = 0.75, so 75 per cent of the total annual benefit sits in the first two items.

blanks.label: Weeks of work to complete those first two items
blanks.rationale: 6 + 4 = 10 weeks, against 20 weeks for all five. Three quarters of the benefit is available at the halfway point of the build.

blanks.label: What the figures imply the release plan should do
blanks.rationale: Three quarters of the annual benefit is ready after ten of the twenty weeks, so holding it back until week twenty forfeits ten weeks of it. Releasing once the high-value items are ready starts the return sooner and does not delay the rest.

questions.explanation: Benefit is rarely spread evenly across a backlog, and where it concentrates in the early items the cost of a single end-loaded release is the delay applied to the majority of the value. Calculating what proportion is available at what point turns an abstract preference for incremental delivery into a specific case: a defined share of annual benefit, forfeited for a defined number of weeks. That figure is what makes the conversation with a sponsor concrete.
questions.mindset: Ask what the benefit is worth per week of waiting, not just what it is worth.

questions.stem: Your schedule assumes six weeks in the company's environmental test chamber starting in week 22. You have just learned that another programme booked the same chamber for those weeks eleven months ago and has a signed facility agreement. Your test engineers are available and there is no external chamber within the budget. Your test lead suggests reducing the test programme to fit the two weeks that remain available. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Establish what the chamber constraint actually allows, then rework the schedule and the options around it before choosing.
options.rationale: A physical resource with a signed prior claim is a constraint to be understood before it is worked around, since its real shape often differs from the headline. Resequencing, partial slots and shared windows only become visible once someone asks.

options.text: Accept the test lead's suggestion and agree which tests to drop first, since two weeks of testing is better than none and the schedule is preserved.
options.rationale: This is the shrink-the-work error. Compressing the test programme to fit a facility booking decides a quality question on availability grounds, and choosing what to drop settles the matter before anyone has established whether the constraint is genuinely immovable.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor at once so that your project's need can be prioritised over the other programme's booking.
options.rationale: This is the contest-of-importance error. Going straight to escalation treats a resource conflict as a question of which programme matters more, burns sponsor capital on the first move and offers no analysis of what a reallocation would cost the other programme.

options.text: Add the chamber unavailability to the risk register with a high impact rating and continue planning to the current schedule.
options.rationale: This is not a risk, it is a known conflict with a signed agreement behind it. Recording a certainty as an uncertainty removes the pressure to act while leaving the schedule built on an assumption already disproved.

questions.explanation: Resource management covers equipment and facilities as much as staff, and a scheduled dependency on a shared facility is only as sound as the booking behind it. When a conflict emerges, the first move is to establish the true shape of the constraint, because remedies such as splitting the window, resequencing tests or sharing the slot only appear once it is understood. Compressing the work, escalating, or reclassifying a certainty as a risk all commit to a response before the problem has been characterised.
questions.mindset: Physical resources are planned like people: know the real constraint before you design around your guess at it.

questions.stem: Your product team of seven has committed to and missed its last five iteration goals. Tracking where time actually went, you find roughly a third of the team's capacity is consumed by production support requests that arrive directly from users and are handled by whoever is asked. The team has never included this work in its forecasts, treating each request as an interruption rather than as work. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Make the support work visible on the board and account for its historical share when the team forecasts capacity.
options.rationale: Work that consumes a third of capacity is not an interruption, it is a workstream, and a forecast that excludes it will fail every time. Making it visible is the precondition for both honest commitments and any argument about reducing it.

options.text: Analyse the support requests for recurring causes and fix the largest, so the underlying demand falls.
options.rationale: Accounting for the load makes the plan honest; reducing it makes the team faster. Support demand generated by a small number of recurring defects is usually the cheapest capacity a team can recover.

options.text: Route all support requests through you, so the team is protected and can focus on the iteration goal.
options.rationale: Shielding the team hides the demand without reducing it, and the requests still need answering by whoever knows the system. It also removes the team's exposure to the failures its own product is causing.

options.text: Reduce the iteration commitment by a third so the team stops missing its goals.
options.rationale: Cutting the commitment fixes the symptom by lowering the number and leaves an unmeasured, uncontrolled workstream running underneath. Next quarter the support share moves and the forecast is wrong again.

options.text: Assign one team member each iteration to handle all support requests, rotating the duty.
options.rationale: A rotation is a reasonable tactic once the demand is understood, and adopting it now fixes the allocation before anyone knows whether a third of a person or three is the right answer. It also leaves the causes of the demand unexamined.

questions.explanation: Capacity that is being consumed but not counted makes every forecast optimistic by a fixed and invisible margin. The pair of moves is to bring the hidden work into the same view as everything else so commitments reflect real availability, and to attack the demand at its source so the share shrinks. Absorbing the requests personally, cutting the commitment, or fixing a rotation all address the visible failure while leaving both the measurement gap and the underlying causes intact.
questions.mindset: Unmeasured work does not stop consuming capacity; it just stops appearing in the plan.

questions.stem: A supplier has offered your migration package on two bases: time and materials at £850 per day, or a firm fixed price of £102,000 for the whole package. Your estimator's best judgement is 100 days, and she is confident the true figure lies between 90 and 115 days. Work out the point at which the two offers cost the same, the cost of the time and materials option at the best estimate, and which basis your estimator's confidence range supports.

blanks.label: Break-even duration, in days
blanks.rationale: 102,000 ÷ 850 = 120 days. Below 120 days the time and materials option costs less; above it, the fixed price does.

blanks.label: Cost of the time and materials option at 100 days, in £
blanks.rationale: 100 × 850 = £85,000, which is £17,000 less than the fixed price. That difference is what the buyer is paying to transfer the duration risk.

blanks.label: Which basis the estimator's range supports
blanks.rationale: The whole confidence range of 90 to 115 days sits below the 120-day break-even, so even the pessimistic end costs less than the fixed price. The buyer would be paying a premium to transfer a risk the analysis shows is unlikely to materialise.

questions.explanation: The choice between a fixed price and a reimbursable basis is a decision about who carries duration risk and what that transfer costs. Finding the duration at which the two are equal turns the comparison into a single number, and the question then becomes whether the plausible range of outcomes falls above or below it. A range entirely on one side makes the answer clear; a range straddling the break-even point is the case where the premium may be worth paying, and where the buyer's tolerance for cost variability decides.
questions.mindset: Compare contract types at the point where they cost the same, then ask where your uncertainty actually sits.

questions.stem: Your systems integrator is four weeks late on a firm fixed-price package. Investigating, you find the delay sits entirely with a specialist subcontractor the integrator engaged, whose own staffing has collapsed. The subcontractor has no contract with your organisation. Your engineering manager has been dealing with the subcontractor directly for a fortnight to try to unblock the work, and your commercial lead has just discovered this. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Stop the direct contact, hold the integrator to its obligation, and require a recovery plan covering its subcontractor.
options.rationale: The integrator is accountable for the whole package including the parts it chose to subcontract, and the recovery plan is the instrument that keeps it there. Ending the direct contact removes the ambiguity your engineering manager has been creating.

options.text: Formalise the direct relationship with the subcontractor in a side agreement, so your team can manage the recovery properly.
options.rationale: Stepping into a relationship outside the main contract is the most damaging option available. A side agreement dilutes the integrator's accountability for its own supply chain and can hand it a defence against the delay it is currently answerable for.

options.text: Issue a formal notice of default to the integrator and begin evaluating replacement suppliers for the specialist work.
options.rationale: Reaching for default and a replacement specialist four weeks in escalates past the remedies that have not yet been tried. It also assumes a replacement is faster than a recovery, which for a specialist package is rarely true.

options.text: Continue the direct engagement informally while your commercial lead documents the integrator's failure for later.
options.rationale: Running an informal workaround while quietly building a case is the worst of both. The direct contact keeps undermining the accountability the documentation is meant to establish, and the record will show it.

questions.explanation: A supplier is answerable for the whole of its scope, including work it has subcontracted, and the buyer's remedies run against that supplier alone. Direct dealings with a subcontractor, however well intended, blur that line and can compromise the buyer's position when the delay is later disputed. The response is to restore the contractual channel and use it: require a plan that covers the failing part of the supply chain, with the accountability for delivering it left exactly where the contract put it.
questions.mindset: Accountability follows the contract; helping around it dissolves the obligation you are relying on.

questions.stem: A hydro-electric turbine refurbishment has a budget at completion of £2,750,000. At month nine the actual cost is £1,180,000, and the control account managers' bottom-up estimate to complete the remaining work is £1,740,000. The cost management plan grades the forecast variance at completion as a percentage of the budget at completion: green up to 2 per cent, managed by the project manager; amber above 2 and up to 6 per cent, needing a sponsor-approved recovery plan; red above 6 per cent, needing a re-baselining request to the investment board. Work out the figures below.

blanks.label: Variance at completion (£, negative for an overrun)
blanks.rationale: The estimate at completion is actual cost plus the estimate to complete: 1,180,000 + 1,740,000 = £2,920,000. Variance at completion is budget minus forecast: 2,750,000 − 2,920,000 = −£170,000, an overrun.

blanks.label: Size of the forecast overrun as a percentage of the budget at completion, to one decimal place
blanks.rationale: 170,000 ÷ 2,750,000 = 6.18 per cent, which rounds to 6.2. Dividing by the estimate at completion instead gives 5.8 per cent, a figure taken on the wrong base that lands in the wrong band.

blanks.label: Grading under the cost management plan (green, amber or red)
blanks.rationale: 6.2 per cent is above the 6 per cent ceiling for amber, so the forecast is red and the plan routes it to the investment board as a re-baselining request. A sponsor-approved recovery plan would be the amber response, applied to a variance beyond the sponsor's threshold.

questions.explanation: Variance at completion compares the budget with the current forecast, so it is only as good as the estimate at completion behind it; actual cost plus a bottom-up estimate to complete is the defensible forecast once the original estimate can no longer be relied on. Thresholds in a cost management plan are read against the base they name, and a percentage taken on the wrong base can move a variance down a band and send it to someone without the authority to act on it. Grading is a routing decision, so both the arithmetic and the base matter.
questions.mindset: Read a threshold against the base it names, because the grading decides who has to act.

questions.stem: Your team has invested heavily in automated unit tests and reports 94 per cent code coverage. The build has been green for six weeks. In the same period, users have reported eleven failures, and every one occurred where two components interact or where real data differed from the test fixtures. Your technical lead proposes pushing coverage to 98 per cent. How should the project manager respond?

options.text: Support the proposal, since higher coverage will reduce the chance of defects reaching users.
options.rationale: It assumes the coverage figure is measuring the risk that is actually materialising. Every reported failure occurred outside the boundary unit tests examine, so more of the same testing has no path to preventing them.

options.text: Redirect the effort toward testing the interactions and data conditions where the failures are actually occurring.
options.rationale: The defect evidence points precisely at integration boundaries and realistic data, so that is where test investment buys prevention. Following the failure pattern rather than the metric is what makes quality effort economic.

options.text: Add a manual regression pass before each release to catch what the automated tests miss.
options.rationale: Manual regression is inspection added at the end rather than prevention built in, and it grows with every release. It may catch some of the eleven and does nothing to stop the twelfth being created.

options.text: Accept the current position, since six weeks of green builds and 94 per cent coverage indicate a healthy quality practice.
options.rationale: Treating green builds as evidence of quality when users are reporting eleven failures is trusting the instrument over the observation. The signal that matters is arriving from production, not from the pipeline.

questions.explanation: Coverage measures how much of the code a particular kind of test executes, not how much of the risk is covered, and a high figure can coexist with systematic blindness to whole classes of defect. When failures cluster at component boundaries and around real data, that is direct evidence of where the gap sits and where prevention should be built. Raising the metric, adding inspection at the end, or reading a green pipeline as health all respond to something other than the defects being reported.
questions.mindset: Test where the failures are, not where the measurement is easiest.

questions.stem: A quality audit of your project finds full compliance: every design review was held, every checklist completed, every sign-off obtained, with records to prove it. In the same period, acceptance testing rejected four of nine deliverables for the same class of requirements defect, all of which passed through the compliant review process untouched. Your quality manager reports the audit as a strong result. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Examine why the review process passed defects it was designed to catch, and change the process accordingly.
options.rationale: A process followed correctly that lets a repeating defect class through has a design fault rather than an adherence fault. Investigating the mechanism is the only route to preventing the fifth rejection.

options.text: Treat the audit result and the rejection rate as one finding when reporting quality, rather than two separate ones.
options.rationale: Reporting compliance and outcomes separately lets a strong audit conceal a failing product. Presenting them together is what stops the organisation drawing false comfort from the record-keeping.

options.text: Add a further review stage before acceptance testing, run by someone outside the design team, so the defects are caught earlier.
options.rationale: Adding inspection on top of a review process that already misses this defect class buys cost without buying detection, and an outside reviewer changes who looks rather than what the process is designed to see. It is the standard reflex and it treats the volume of checking as the variable.

options.text: Ask the quality manager to tighten the audit criteria and sample more review records, so future audits are harder to pass.
options.rationale: A stricter audit that samples more records measures conformance more severely and still measures conformance. The process is being followed; the problem is what following it achieves.

options.text: Accept the audit finding and address the four rejected deliverables through the defect management process, tracking each to closure.
options.rationale: Handling the four rejections as individual defects, however carefully each is tracked to closure, fixes the instances and leaves the generator running. A defect class recurring across four of nine deliverables is a systemic signal being read as four separate events.

questions.explanation: Process compliance shows that the agreed steps were performed; it says nothing about whether those steps are capable of detecting the defects that matter. A repeating defect class surviving a fully compliant review is evidence of a process design gap, and the fix belongs in the process rather than in additional inspection or stricter auditing. Reporting the two measurements together is what keeps the organisation from mistaking an orderly record for a sound deliverable.
questions.mindset: Conformance to the process and quality of the product are two different measurements, and only one of them is the point.

questions.stem: An approved change added twelve days to your commissioning chain, which previously carried eight days of float and was not critical. Your weekly schedule meeting still tracks the original critical path through civil works, which is running to plan and is now reported as green. The programme has slipped nine days at completion and nobody in the meeting can account for it. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Add resources to the civil works path to recover the nine days lost at completion.
options.rationale: Compressing a path that is not driving the finish date spends money and changes nothing. This is the predictable consequence of managing yesterday's critical path: effort goes where attention already was.

options.text: Rerun the schedule model, identify which path now determines the completion date, and manage that path each week.
options.rationale: A change of twelve days against eight days of float will have moved the critical path, and only recalculating reveals where. Managing the path that now sets the finish date is what makes any subsequent recovery effort effective.

options.text: Update the reported status to amber and explain the nine-day slip in the narrative of the weekly report.
options.rationale: Correcting the status colour describes the problem accurately and leaves the meeting managing the wrong chain of work. The reporting error is a symptom of the analysis gap, not the cause.

options.text: Reset the baseline to absorb the twelve days, since the change was formally approved.
options.rationale: Approval of a change authorises a baseline adjustment for its agreed impact, not the disappearance of the variance it caused. Rebaselining before understanding which path now drives completion buries the analysis that has not been done.

questions.explanation: Float is consumed by change, and a path with modest float can become the longest path after a single approved variation. A schedule meeting that continues to track the original chain will report a healthy path while the finish date slips elsewhere, which is exactly the pattern described. The response is to recalculate, establish which sequence now determines completion, and direct management attention and any compression effort there rather than where it has always been.
questions.mindset: The critical path is a result of the current model, not a property of the project.

questions.stem: Your hybrid programme publishes one status pack that every audience receives. Three groups have told you it does not answer their question. The board wants to know whether the programme will land inside its agreed tolerances. The delivery teams want to know whether they can commit to the next iteration. The operations department wants to know when to book its staff onto training. Complete each sentence with the measure that answers the question asked. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: For the board, deciding whether intervention is needed, the report should lead with
For the delivery teams, deciding what to commit to next, the report should lead with
For the operations department, deciding when to schedule staff, the report should lead with

options.text: the forecast outturn against the agreed tolerance, with the variance explained
options.rationale: A governance body acts on whether the project is heading outside the limits it set, so the forecast against tolerance is the figure that triggers or withholds intervention. Anything more granular invites the board into decisions that are not its own.

options.text: the recent range of completed work per iteration, not the average
options.rationale: A team commits against what it has actually been able to finish, and the spread matters more than the mean because commitment is a question about the bad case. A single average conceals exactly the variability the decision turns on.

options.text: the confidence range around the date each capability becomes available
options.rationale: Scheduling people against a single date guarantees either idle staff or an unready system, so a receiving department needs the range and its confidence. That is what lets them book provisionally and firm up as the range narrows.

options.text: cumulative spend against the profile in the cost baseline
options.rationale: Not used. Spend against profile answers a question about financial pacing, which none of the three groups asked. It is the measure most often included by default because it is easy to produce.

options.text: the count of open risks and issues by severity
options.rationale: Not used. A severity count summarises a register rather than informing a decision, and none of the three audiences is deciding anything a count would settle. It is a familiar page in a status pack that rarely changes what anyone does.

questions.explanation: Status reporting fails most often by being uniform: one pack, sent to every audience, built from whatever is easiest to produce. Each audience is making a different decision, and the measure that serves it follows from that decision. Governance needs the forecast against tolerance because its choice is whether to intervene. A delivery team needs the observed spread because its choice is what to commit to. A receiving department needs a date range with its confidence because its choice is when to schedule people. Spend profiles and severity counts fill pages without answering any of these.
questions.mindset: Report the measure that answers the decision the reader has to make.

questions.stem: Your team reports progress at standup as a percentage complete per item. Reviewing the last three iterations, you find items sat at ninety per cent for an average of four days before finishing, and two items reported at ninety per cent were later abandoned. The team finds the percentages easy to give and stakeholders find them reassuring. What should the project manager change?

options.text: Ask the team to be more rigorous in estimating the percentage, basing it on the remaining task list for each item rather than on a feel for progress.
options.rationale: This is the refine-the-estimate error. A more methodical self-assessment of unfinished work is still a self-assessment of unfinished work. The last ten per cent contains the integration and the unknowns, which is why it consistently takes longer than any task list suggests.

options.text: Report progress by items actually finished against the definition of done, rather than by estimated completeness.
options.rationale: A binary measure against an agreed standard cannot be inflated by optimism and cannot report ninety per cent on something later abandoned. It costs the comfort of smooth-looking progress and buys a number that means something.

options.text: Introduce a rule that no item may be reported above eighty per cent until it has passed testing, so the final stretch is not overstated.
options.rationale: This is the cap-the-scale error. It treats the symptom by adjusting the scale: the measure is still an estimate of an unfinished thing, and a team that reported ninety optimistically will report eighty optimistically.

options.text: Keep the percentages for the team's own day-to-day use and report only completed items to stakeholders.
options.rationale: This is the split-by-audience error. Two sets of numbers leaves the team steering by the unreliable one. The percentages are not just poor for reporting; they are what let two abandoned items look nearly finished internally.

questions.explanation: Percentage-complete reporting on individual items is an estimate of the unknown remainder, and it fails in a characteristic direction because the hardest part is usually last. The reliable alternative is a binary judgement against an agreed standard of done, which resists optimism and makes stalled work visible immediately. Refining the estimate, capping the reportable figure, or splitting the measure by audience each preserve the underlying instrument that produced two items reported at ninety per cent and then abandoned.
questions.mindset: Measure what is finished, not how finished something feels.

questions.stem: The construction package on your project is physically complete and the client has occupied the building. The contractor has demobilised, two of its invoices are disputed, and a claim for extended preliminaries submitted four months ago has never been answered. Your commercial lead has left the organisation. Your sponsor asks you to mark the package closed so the project can report completion this month. What two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Verify the delivered work against the contract's requirements and confirm formally what has and has not been accepted.
options.rationale: Closure rests on a documented verification that the contracted scope was delivered, and physical completion with occupation is not the same thing. Recording what remains unaccepted is what preserves the position on the disputed items.

options.text: Resolve or formally record the outstanding claim and disputed invoices before the package is declared closed.
options.rationale: A contract with live financial matters cannot be closed, only abandoned. Settling them or documenting their status and the agreed route to resolution is what makes the closure real rather than administrative.

options.text: Mark the package closed and transfer the outstanding commercial matters to the operations budget for resolution.
options.rationale: Moving unresolved obligations to another budget to clear a reporting milestone is closure in name only. The claim does not become easier to defend once the project that holds the evidence has disbanded.

options.text: Ask the contractor to confirm in writing that it has no further claims, and treat silence as acceptance.
options.rationale: A claim already submitted and unanswered is not extinguished by an unanswered request. Constructing acceptance from silence is a weak position that tends to unravel precisely when it is tested.

options.text: Retain the package as open indefinitely until the claim is resolved, and report the project as incomplete.
options.rationale: Holding an entire project open for one commercial matter is disproportionate and stalls everything else closure delivers. The two are separable: the position on the claim can be documented and progressed without leaving the whole package unfinished.

questions.explanation: Procurement closure requires verification that the contracted scope was delivered and the settlement or formal recording of every outstanding financial matter. Physical completion, occupation and a demobilised contractor are not evidence of either. Declaring closure to meet a reporting date transfers unresolved liability to a party without the records to defend it, while holding the whole package open indefinitely confuses one unsettled claim with the state of the project.
questions.mindset: Closing a contract means settling what is owed and recording what was received, not filing the paperwork.

questions.stem: A six-month pilot of a new scheduling tool in two of your organisation's forty depots ends next week. The pilot met its technical objectives, but usage data shows depot staff used the tool for about half of the shifts it was intended to cover, and the expected reduction in overtime did not appear. The programme plan moves straight from pilot into national rollout. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Proceed to rollout, since the pilot met its technical objectives and adoption usually improves once the tool is used more widely across the depots.
options.rationale: Treating the technical result as the whole answer ignores the evidence the pilot was run to produce. Adoption problems seen in two depots reliably scale to forty rather than dissolving once the tool is in wider use.

options.text: Extend the pilot by three months in the same two depots to see whether usage improves as staff grow used to the tool.
options.rationale: Extending without changing anything tests patience rather than a hypothesis. The pilot has already produced a clear signal, and waiting for familiarity to fix it is a way of deferring the decision the gate exists to force.

options.text: Proceed to rollout while adding a change management workstream to address adoption in the remaining depots, funded from the programme's contingency.
options.rationale: Bolting on a remedy, however it is funded, assumes the cause of the shortfall is known, and nobody has yet established why staff used the tool on half their shifts. The commitment to forty depots is made before the diagnosis.

options.text: Hold the phase gate as a genuine decision point, present the adoption and benefit evidence, and let the decision be taken on it.
options.rationale: A phase boundary exists so a deliberate choice can be made with the evidence the phase produced, and the options include continuing, changing the approach or stopping. Presenting the shortfall alongside the technical success is what makes the choice a real one.

questions.explanation: Phase closure is the point at which a project confirms what the phase actually established and decides deliberately what follows, with continuing, changing course and stopping all genuinely available. A pilot that succeeds technically and fails on adoption and benefit has produced exactly the evidence the gate was designed to weigh. Proceeding on the strength of the technical result, extending without a changed hypothesis, or attaching a remedy to an undiagnosed problem all convert the decision point into a formality.
questions.mindset: A gate you cannot fail is not a gate.

questions.stem: Your project is delivered for an external client and runs under two governance frameworks. Your own organisation requires a design authority approval before build; the client's framework requires its investment committee to approve at the same point, and the two bodies use different criteria and meet in different weeks. Last month a decision approved by one was reopened by the other, costing three weeks. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Follow the client's framework from now on, since the client is funding the work and its committee holds the money, and then report each outcome to your design authority.
options.rationale: This is the follow-the-money error. Reporting outcomes to your design authority is not the same as obtaining its approval, so your own organisation's obligations go unmet, and those exist for reasons that do not disappear because the work is external. It also concedes a decision that has not been negotiated.

options.text: Comply fully with both frameworks, design authority first and investment committee second, and build the additional time into the schedule.
options.rationale: This is the absorb-the-friction error. It treats an unresolved governance overlap as a scheduling cost, and fixing which body approves first does nothing about the specific failure that occurred, which was the later body reopening a decision the earlier one had already approved.

options.text: Map where the two frameworks overlap and conflict, and agree a single reconciled route with both sponsors, naming who decides what and on which criteria.
options.rationale: Two frameworks over one project need reconciling once, deliberately, with the decision rights explicit. Doing it with both sponsors present is what makes the result binding on both bodies rather than a preference the project has adopted.

options.text: Escalate the conflict to your own sponsor for a ruling on which framework takes precedence, then brief the client's project lead on that ruling before the next gate.
options.rationale: This is the one-sided-ruling error. A ruling from your own sponsor cannot bind the client's committee, and briefing the client afterwards informs it of an internal answer to a joint problem rather than agreeing one. The conflict recurs at the next gate with your project formally committed to one side of it.

questions.explanation: Overlapping governance is a design problem to be solved once rather than a friction to be absorbed at every gate. The work is to establish where the two structures genuinely conflict, agree a single route through them, and record which body holds which decision. Choosing one framework unilaterally, satisfying both in full, or obtaining a ruling from only one side each leave the other structure free to reopen decisions it was never party to.
questions.mindset: Where two governance structures meet, the first deliverable is an agreement about who decides what.

questions.stem: Your predictive project is commissioning a solvent recovery unit at a paint factory. On day two of commissioning, an inspector from the health and safety regulator arrives unannounced. The site director is abroad until Friday, so you are the senior person on site, and the inspector has statutory powers to examine records, question staff and give instructions. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: The inspector asks for the 14 pressure-test records for the unit's distillation vessel, one of which shows a retest that has not yet been signed off. You should
The inspector asks a commissioning technician what level the vapour detectors are set to alarm at, and he is unsure and begins to estimate. You should
The inspector instructs you verbally to stop filling the unit with solvent until the bund around it has been leak-tested. You should

options.text: provide what was asked for as it stands and point out the open item yourself
options.rationale: The regulator is entitled to the source records, and an open item you flag yourself reads as a control that is working. The same item found by the inspector after you said nothing reads as concealment, which is a far worse finding than an unsigned retest.

options.text: undertake to supply a verified answer by an agreed time rather than offer an estimate now
options.rationale: An estimate given to an inspector becomes a statement of fact on the record, and a wrong one is a misstatement however innocent. Stopping the guess and committing to a verified answer by a stated time keeps what the regulator is told accurate.

options.text: comply at once and confirm in writing what was instructed and what was done
options.rationale: An inspector's instruction takes effect when it is given, and as the senior person present you hold the authority to act on it. A written note of the instruction and the response protects both sides when the site director and the regulator later compare accounts.

options.text: offer the prepared compliance summary from the project file in place of the source material
options.rationale: Not used. It tempts because a summary looks organised and controlled, but an inspector with statutory powers examines source records and direct answers, and offering a curated version in their place invites the suspicion that the originals are being kept back.

options.text: ask the inspector to take the matter up on Friday, when the site director can answer for the site
options.rationale: Not used. It treats the director's absence as a reason to postpone, but the inspector's powers do not depend on who is on site, and asking to defer anything raised on an unannounced visit signals that the site is not ready to be seen as it is.

questions.explanation: During a regulatory inspection the project's job is to give the regulator an accurate picture of the site as it actually is. Records are produced in their original form with known defects pointed out, questions nobody can answer reliably are answered later with verified facts rather than now with estimates, and instructions are carried out at once and recorded. Curating, postponing or guessing each turns a manageable finding into a question about whether the site can be trusted.
questions.mindset: Treat an inspection as a request for the truth as it stands, not a visit to be managed.

questions.stem: An internal audit of your programme finds three changes that were properly requested, assessed and approved by the change board over the last quarter. In all three cases the requirements specification and the associated test cases were never updated. Your test team has been testing against superseded requirements for two months and did not know. The change board's records are complete and correct. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Update the affected specifications and test cases, and change the approval step so it cannot complete until the artifacts are updated.
options.rationale: It repairs the immediate damage and closes the mechanism that produced it. A change process whose final step is a decision rather than a propagation will keep producing approved changes that never reach the work.

options.text: Re-run the affected tests against the current requirements first, to establish the true state of the product before deciding on any further action.
options.rationale: Retesting is necessary and is not the answer to what should be done, because it addresses only the consequence. Doing this first and alone means the same gap silently reopens with the next approved change.

options.text: Remind the workstream leads in writing that approved changes must be reflected in the specifications and test cases, and ask each to confirm it is done.
options.rationale: A reminder, even with a confirmation request, relies on the same individual diligence that has already failed three times out of three. Where a process depends on people remembering an unenforced step, the failure rate is a property of the design.

options.text: Record the finding as a lesson learned and raise it with the change board at its next quarterly process review.
options.rationale: Deferring to the next quarterly review leaves the test team working against superseded requirements in the meantime. Logging a live defect as a lesson treats a current failure as historical.

questions.explanation: Change control ends where the approved decision has been propagated into every artifact that governs downstream work, not where the board signs. A complete and correct approval record alongside stale specifications is the signature of a process that stops at the decision. The durable response pairs correcting the affected artifacts with making propagation part of the step itself, so the control does not depend on anyone remembering to finish it.
questions.mindset: A change is not controlled until every artifact that depends on it has moved.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the average time a work item spends at each stage of your team's delivery flow, measured over the last two months. Your team has proposed adding a second person to development to speed delivery up. Select the stage where clearing the impediment would most reduce the time from starting an item to releasing it.

graphic.title: Average time per stage across five stages of the delivery flow
graphic.caption: Select a stage. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between stages, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Analysis · 2 days
regions.rationale: Two days is a small share of the total and the stage is inside the team's control. Even eliminating it entirely would change the end-to-end time by a fraction of what the largest stage costs.

regions.label: Build · 3 days
regions.rationale: This is where the team's proposal would add capacity, and it is not where the time is going. Optimising the stage the team can see is the most common misdirection of improvement effort.

regions.label: Security review · 14 days
regions.rationale: Fourteen days is more than half the total elapsed time and dwarfs every other stage. It is also a queue outside the team, which is why it has persisted while the team optimised the stages it owns.

regions.label: Test · 3 days
regions.rationale: Three days is proportionate to the work being done and is not where items are waiting. Attention here would improve a stage that is already performing.

regions.label: Approval · 2 days
regions.rationale: A two-day approval is a modest overhead at the end of the flow. It is worth trimming eventually and cannot account for the delivery times the team is experiencing.

questions.explanation: End-to-end time is dominated by whichever stage items wait longest at, and adding capacity anywhere else leaves the total essentially unchanged. Long queues frequently sit at handoffs to groups outside the team, which is precisely why they escape the team's own improvement efforts and why they persist. Locating the largest wait first, and treating it as the impediment to be escalated and cleared, is what makes the improvement effort proportionate to the delay it removes.
questions.mindset: Improve where the time is going, which is rarely where the effort is going.

questions.stem: A supplier building a subsystem for your plant upgrade tells you a different client has cancelled, freeing its production line. It can deliver your subsystem six weeks earlier than contracted at no additional cost. Your installation contractor is booked to the original dates, your site will not be ready six weeks early, and the subsystem's warranty period begins at delivery. Your sponsor is enthusiastic. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Assess whether the project can actually realise value from the earlier date, including site readiness, installation availability and the warranty start.
options.rationale: An opportunity is only worth what the project can convert it into, and three constraints here suggest the conversion is not automatic. Assessing before accepting is what distinguishes an opportunity from a change someone else has made to your plan.

options.text: Record it as an opportunity with an owner and a planned response, and confirm any agreed change to the delivery date in writing with the supplier.
options.rationale: Opportunities need the same discipline as threats: named ownership, a chosen response and a record. Confirming a varied delivery date in writing keeps the contractual position clear whichever way the assessment goes.

options.text: Accept the earlier delivery immediately, since delivery ahead of schedule at no extra cost carries no downside, and tell the sponsor the milestone has moved forward.
options.rationale: Treating early and free as self-evidently good ignores the costs that arrive with it: storage, insurance, a warranty running while the subsystem sits idle, and an installation contractor unavailable. Telling the sponsor the milestone has moved assumes the benefit rather than assessing it.

options.text: Decline the offer, since the delivery date is contractually agreed and the schedule is baselined, and thank the supplier for the flexibility.
options.rationale: Reading the baseline as a prohibition rather than a control point is the error. A favourable variation is exactly what change control exists to evaluate, and refusing without assessment forfeits an option at no gain, however courteously it is done.

options.text: Record it as a threat in the risk register, since an unexpectedly early delivery may indicate the supplier is cutting quality.
options.rationale: Converting an opportunity into a suspicion on no evidence is a familiar defensive reflex. The supplier has given a specific and checkable reason, and the response to doubt about it is verification rather than reclassification.

questions.explanation: Favourable uncertainty is subject to the same process as adverse uncertainty: assess, choose a response, assign ownership and record it. Whether an early delivery is worth having depends entirely on downstream readiness and on costs that begin at delivery rather than at use. Accepting immediately assumes a benefit that the constraints contradict, declining on baseline grounds forfeits it without analysis, and reclassifying it as a threat substitutes suspicion for the verification that doubt would actually warrant.
questions.mindset: An opportunity is managed, not merely accepted; the question is what the project can convert it into.

questions.stem: Your team's retrospective produces three improvement ideas of quite different reach. One changes how the team runs its own code reviews and affects nobody outside it. One requires the platform group, which owns the shared deployment pipeline, to change how releases are staged. One traces a recurring delay to an organisational policy setting minimum procurement lead times, which affects every team in the division. Match each idea to where it should be taken. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: The change to the team's own code review practice.
The change to the shared deployment pipeline owned by the platform group.
The recurring delay traced to the divisional procurement lead time policy.

options.text: Adopt it in the team now and measure whether it helped
options.rationale: An improvement entirely within a team's own control needs no permission and no forum, only a decision and a way of telling whether it worked. Routing it anywhere else adds delay and teaches the team that improvement requires approval.

options.text: Take it to the group that owns the asset, with the evidence of the cost it is causing
options.rationale: A change to something another group owns is a request that competes with that group's own priorities, so it travels with evidence rather than as an opinion. Going to the owner directly is faster and more likely to succeed than escalating over them.

options.text: Raise it where the policy is set, with the aggregated cost across affected teams
options.rationale: A policy affecting a whole division changes only where policy is made, and a single team's inconvenience is rarely sufficient reason. Aggregating the cost across the teams affected is what converts a local complaint into a case.

options.text: Add it to the retrospective action list and revisit it next fortnight
options.rationale: Not used. Deferring to the next retrospective is the default that quietly absorbs all three. Two of these need to leave the team entirely, and the third needs doing rather than discussing again.

options.text: Record it as a lesson learned for the closure report
options.rationale: Not used. A closure report reaches future projects at best and none of the three teams that need to act now. Writing a live improvement into a historical record is how improvement backlogs become archives.

questions.explanation: Improvement ideas differ in reach, and the reach determines the route. What a team controls it should simply change and then measure. What another group owns becomes a negotiation carried by evidence of cost. What a policy sets requires aggregation across everyone affected to make a case at the level where policy changes. The default responses of deferring to the next retrospective and recording a lesson feel like action and move nothing, which is how the same three problems appear in retrospective after retrospective.
questions.mindset: Take each improvement to the level that can actually decide it.

questions.stem: Your hybrid project is running a 12-week trial of cross-skilled cell teams at two of a food manufacturer's five plants, with the rota and work design adjusted every fortnight from trial feedback. At launch the manufacturing director, who sponsors the project, told staff that the trial results would decide whether the other three plants follow. In week 7 he tells you the board has already approved the investment for all five plants, and asks you to keep the trial message unchanged so that engagement stays high. What should the project manager do?
